stem: An engineer creates an Ingress with two ImplementationSpecific paths, `/impl` and `/impl.*`, and expects requests to `/impl` to be handled by the first rule. What does Cilium actually do?

options.text: It sorts `/impl.*` ahead of `/impl` in the generated Envoy config, so the `/impl` match is never hit.
It sorts `/impl` ahead of `/impl.*` because the shorter string takes precedence within a path type.
It rejects the Ingress because two ImplementationSpecific paths may not overlap.
It treats both paths as Prefix matches, so `/impl` is matched exactly and `/impl.*` is ignored.

explanation: Within each path type, paths are sorted in decreasing order of string length, so the longer `/impl.*` is placed ahead of `/impl`. Because `*` is in use, any request to `/impl` matches the regex `/impl.*` first, meaning the `/impl` match is never reached.

optionRationale.b: Sorting within a path type is in decreasing order of string length, so the longer regex path comes first, not the shorter one.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes no validation that rejects overlapping ImplementationSpecific paths; it only warns about the resulting behaviour.
optionRationale.d: ImplementationSpecific is defined by Cilium as Regex, not Prefix, and the excerpt does not say the second path is ignored.

Only the first entry in the list is used; the remaining entries are ignored until the first node fails.
The policy is rejected because multiple gateways require a separate policy per gateway.

explanation: The excerpt states that with multiple gateways the matched source endpoints still egress through a single gateway rather than all of them, and that endpoints are assigned to a gateway based on its CiliumEndpoint's UID.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says endpoints egress through a single gateway, not all of them, so there is no spreading of traffic across the list.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes a first-entry-only or failover behaviour; assignment is based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt opens by saying it is possible to select multiple gateway nodes in the same policy, so such a policy is not rejected.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
When using multiple gateways the source endpoints matched by the policy will still egress traffic
    through a single gateway, not all of them.

stem: A platform team has an egress gateway policy with several entries in `egressGateways`. They add a new node that matches one of the `nodeSelector` fields. What does the excerpt say will happen to the endpoints matched by the policy?

options.text: The list of gateways will change and the endpoints will be reassigned.
Nothing changes, because endpoint-to-gateway assignment is fixed for the lifetime of the policy.
The policy stops matching endpoints until it is reapplied manually.
All endpoints immediately move to the newly added node.

explanation: The excerpt says that if a node matching one of the `nodeSelector` fields is added or removed, the list of gateways will change and the endpoints will be reassigned.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt only promises stable assignment for an endpoint's lifetime as long as the matched gateway nodes do not change; adding a matching node is such a change.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes reassignment of endpoints, not loss of policy matching.
optionRationale.d: Reassignment is described, but the excerpt does not say all endpoints move to the new node; assignment is based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
If a
    ``nodeSelector`` field is added, removed, or modified, or if a node matching one of the
    ``nodeSelector`` fields is added or removed, the list of gateways will change and the endpoints
    will be reassigned.

stem: Which field is used to configure multiple gateway nodes within a single egress gateway policy?

options.text: `egressGateways`
`egressGateway`
`nodeSelector`
`gatewayNodes`

explanation: The excerpt states that when selecting multiple gateway nodes in the same policy, the gateway nodes can be configured using the `egressGateways` list field.

optionRationale.b: `egressGateway` is the singular field; the excerpt says entries on the `egressGateways` list have the same configuration options as it, but it is not the list field itself.
optionRationale.c: `nodeSelector` is a field inside each list entry, not the field that holds the list of gateways.
optionRationale.d: `gatewayNodes` is not mentioned anywhere in the excerpt.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
In this case, the gateway nodes
can be configured using the ``egressGateways`` list field.

stem: How does the excerpt say endpoints are assigned to a gateway when a policy selects multiple gateway nodes?

options.text: Based on the gateway's CiliumEndpoint's UID.
Based on the order of entries in the `egressGateways` list.
Based on the source endpoint's node name.
Based on a round-robin scheme across the matched gateway nodes.

explanation: The excerpt says the endpoints will be assigned to a gateway based on its CiliumEndpoint's UID.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives the CiliumEndpoint's UID as the basis, not the position of entries in the list.
optionRationale.c: No node-name-based assignment for the source endpoint is described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Round-robin is not mentioned; the excerpt describes assignment based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
The endpoints will be assigned to a gateway based on
    its CiliumEndpoint's UID.

stem: An engineer is comparing a policy with a single `egressGateway` field against one with an `egressGateways` list. Which statement about the configuration options of the list entries is correct according to the excerpt?

options.text: Entries on the `egressGateways` list have the exact same configuration options as the `egressGateway` field, and the same restrictions apply to each item.
Entries on the `egressGateways` list support a reduced set of options compared with the `egressGateway` field.
Entries on the `egressGateways` list support additional options that the `egressGateway` field does not.
The `egressGateways` list has no restrictions, unlike the `egressGateway` field.

explanation: The excerpt says entries on the `egressGateways` list have the exact same configuration options as the `egressGateway` field, and that the same restrictions apply to each item of the list.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the options are exactly the same, not reduced.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the options are exactly the same, not extended.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says the same restrictions as with the `egressGateway` field apply to each item of the list.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
Entries on this list have the exact same
configuration options as the ``egressGateway`` field

stem: An endpoint has been egressing through one of several gateway nodes selected by a policy. The cluster's gateway nodes matched by the `nodeSelector` fields remain unchanged. What does the excerpt say about that endpoint's gateway for the rest of its lifetime?

options.text: It should use the same gateway during its lifetime as long as the matched gateway nodes do not change.
It will be rotated to a different gateway periodically to balance load.
It will be reassigned whenever any other endpoint in the cluster is created.
It will always use the gateway with the lowest CiliumEndpoint UID in the cluster.

explanation: The excerpt says an endpoint should use the same gateway during its lifetime as long as the gateway nodes matched by the `nodeSelector` fields do not change.

optionRationale.b: No periodic rotation is described; stability is tied to the matched gateway nodes not changing.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt ties reassignment to changes in the `nodeSelector` fields or the matched nodes, not to creation of other endpoints.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt refers to assignment based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID but does not describe always choosing the lowest UID in the cluster.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
Hence, an endpoint should use the same gateway during its lifetime
    as long as the gateway nodes matched by the ``nodeSelector`` fields don't change.

stem: You are running Cilium 1.16 in a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available. You enable the Cilium Gateway API with host network mode through Helm, and a colleague asks what happened to the LoadBalancer type Service mode. What is the result?

options.text: Enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode, because the two are mutually exclusive.
Both modes remain active, and Cilium chooses between them per request at runtime.
Host network mode is rejected unless the LoadBalancer type Service mode is disabled first in a separate step.
The LoadBalancer type Service mode stays enabled but is limited to IPv6 listeners only.

explanation: The excerpt states that enabling the Cilium Gateway API host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode, and that the two are mutually exclusive. No separate manual step is required, and there is no per-request selection between the modes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the modes are mutually exclusive, so they cannot both remain active with runtime selection.
optionRationale.c: The disabling happens automatically on enabling host network mode; the excerpt describes no separate prerequisite step.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no such IPv6-only limitation on the LoadBalancer type Service mode; it simply says the mode is disabled.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium Gateway API host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

stem: A platform team wants cross-cluster service discovery that follows a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard and gives them status condition reporting plus a dedicated `clusterset.local` DNS domain. Which Cluster Mesh option should they choose?

options.text: MCS-API, because it is the SIG Multicluster standard with higher-level features such as status condition reporting and the `clusterset.local` domain
Global Services, because they are the only option that provides a dedicated DNS domain
Global Services, because MCS-API cannot report status conditions
Neither; cross-cluster service discovery requires both options to be enabled together

explanation: The excerpt states that MCS-API is a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard based on ServiceExport and ServiceImport, and that it provides higher-level features such as consistent global service properties, status condition reporting and a dedicated `clusterset.local` DNS domain. Global Services are described as Cilium-specific cross-cluster load-balancing driven from Service annotations, so they are not the standard-based option.

optionRationale.b: The dedicated ``clusterset.local`` DNS domain is attributed to MCS-API, not to Global Services.
optionRationale.c: Status condition reporting is listed as an MCS-API feature, so this reverses the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says you can use either option, or both, depending on your needs — not that both are required.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
MCS-API  is a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard
based on the ServiceExport and ServiceImport resources. It provides higher-level
features such as consistent global service properties, status condition reporting,
and a dedicated ``clusterset.local`` DNS domain

stem: An engineer needs cross-cluster load-balancing configured directly from Cilium Service annotations, and wants granular control over how backends are shared between clusters. Which option fits, and why?

options.text: MCS-API, because it exposes Service annotations for backend sharing
Global Services, because they provide Cilium-specific cross-cluster load-balancing directly from Service annotations and allow more granular control
MCS-API, because it is the only option that supports differing Service properties per cluster
Global Services, because they replace the need for any Service annotations

explanation: The excerpt describes Global Services as providing Cilium-specific cross-cluster load-balancing directly from Service annotations, and notes they are useful when you want different Service properties in each cluster or more granular control over how backends are shared.

optionRationale.a: Annotation-driven load-balancing is attributed to Global Services, not MCS-API.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt associates differing Service properties per cluster with Global Services, not MCS-API.
optionRationale.d: Global Services work directly from Service annotations, so they do not remove the need for them.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
Global Services  provide Cilium-specific
cross-cluster load-balancing directly from Service annotations.

stem: A cluster uses MCS-API and the team wants the `clusterset.local` DNS domain to work without manually editing CoreDNS configuration. According to the excerpt, what makes this possible?

options.text: CoreDNS auto-configuration, which Cilium can manage automatically when it is enabled
Global Services annotations, which inject the DNS domain
ServiceExport resources, which configure CoreDNS directly
ServiceImport resources, which replace CoreDNS entirely

explanation: The excerpt says the dedicated `clusterset.local` DNS domain requires CoreDNS configuration that Cilium can manage automatically when CoreDNS auto-configuration is enabled.

optionRationale.b: Global Services are described as annotation-based load-balancing, not as the mechanism for the DNS domain.
optionRationale.c: ServiceExport is named as a resource underlying MCS-API, not as the CoreDNS configuration mechanism.
optionRationale.d: ServiceImport is named as a resource underlying MCS-API; the excerpt does not say it replaces CoreDNS.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
which requires CoreDNS configuration
that Cilium can manage automatically when CoreDNS auto-configuration is enabled.

stem: A team is deciding between the two Cluster Mesh options for cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing. What does the excerpt say about using them?

options.text: Only MCS-API may be used; Global Services must be disabled first
Only Global Services may be used; MCS-API is mutually exclusive with it
You can use either option, or both, depending on your needs and environment
Both must always be enabled, since neither works on its own

explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium supports two options for cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing with Cluster Mesh, and that you can use either option, or both, depending on your needs and environment.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt presents MCS-API as one of two supported options, not the only permitted one.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not make the options mutually exclusive; it allows either or both.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says either or both, not that both are mandatory.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote: You can use either option, or both, depending on your needs and environment.

stem: An engineer reads that MCS-API is built on two Kubernetes resources. Which pair does the excerpt name?

options.text: ServiceExport and ServiceImport
ServiceMonitor and ServiceImport
ServiceExport and GlobalService
ServiceImport and CiliumService

explanation: The excerpt states that MCS-API is a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard based on the ServiceExport and ServiceImport resources.

optionRationale.b: ServiceMonitor is not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: GlobalService is not named as an MCS-API resource; Global Services are a separate option.
optionRationale.d: CiliumService is not mentioned in the excerpt.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
MCS-API  is a Kubernetes SIG Multicluster standard
based on the ServiceExport and ServiceImport resources.

stem: You are defining a security policy for the Star Wars demo and want it to apply to the deathstar pods no matter which node they are scheduled on or when they are started. What does Cilium use to identify the pods the policy applies to?

options.text: The endpoint IP addresses of the pods
The labels assigned to the pods
The Kubernetes namespace of the pods
The node hostname the pods are running on

explanation: Cilium applies policies based on pod labels, so the policy reaches the right pods irrespective of where or when they run in the cluster. Endpoint IP addresses are explicitly described as irrelevant for defining security policies.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention namespaces as the selection mechanism; it describes label-based selection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says policies apply irrespective of where the pod is running, so node hostname is not the mechanism.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote:
endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security
policies. Instead, you can use the labels assigned to the pods to define
security policies.

stem: You apply a policy that restricts deathstar landing requests to ships carrying the label org=empire. You then run a landing request from a tiefighter pod, which has that label. What is the expected result?

options.text: The request hangs and must be killed with Control-C.
The request is rejected with a connection refused error.
The request succeeds and returns 'Ship landed'.
The request succeeds only after the policy is deleted.

explanation: The excerpt shows that after applying the policy, only the tiefighter pods with the org=empire label succeed, and the sample output for the tiefighter request is 'Ship landed'.

optionRationale.a: The hanging behaviour is described for the xwing request, not the labelled tiefighter.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe a connection refused error; the blocked request hangs instead.
optionRationale.d: The tiefighter request succeeds with the policy in place, as shown in the sample session.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: Now if we run the landing requests again, only the *tiefighter* pods with the label ``org=empire`` will succeed.

stem: After applying the L3/L4 policy in the demo, you run the same landing request from an xwing pod. What happens?

options.text: The request returns 'Ship landed' immediately.
The request hangs, and you must press Control-C or wait for it to time out.
The request is allowed because reply packets are always permitted.
The request is allowed because xwing pods are matched by the endpointSelector.

explanation: The excerpt states that the xwing pods will be blocked, and that the request will hang, so you press Control-C to kill the curl request or wait for it to time out.

optionRationale.a: 'Ship landed' is the response for the labelled tiefighter pod, not the blocked xwing.
optionRationale.c: Stateful connection tracking applies to reply packets within an allowed connection, not to a new request from a pod the policy blocks.
optionRationale.d: The policy whitelists traffic from pods with the org=empire label; the xwing request is blocked.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: This request will hang, so press Control-C to kill the curl request, or wait for it to time out.

stem: A policy allows the frontend to reach the backend. What does Cilium's stateful connection tracking do about the backend's reply packets?

options.text: It requires a separate explicit policy rule for every reply packet.
It drops reply packets unless the backend also carries the org=empire label.
It automatically allows all required reply packets within the context of the same TCP/UDP connection.
It allows reply packets only on a different TCP/UDP connection.

explanation: Because Cilium performs stateful connection tracking, once policy allows the frontend to reach the backend, all required reply packets that are part of the backend replying to the frontend within the same TCP/UDP connection are automatically allowed.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says replies are automatically allowed, not that each needs its own rule.
optionRationale.b: The org=empire label is specific to the demo policy, not a condition of connection tracking.
optionRationale.d: The automatic allowance is scoped to the same TCP/UDP connection, not a different one.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote:
Cilium performs stateful *connection tracking*, meaning that if policy allows
the frontend to reach backend, it will automatically allow all required reply
packets that are part of backend replying to frontend within the context of the
same TCP/UDP connection.

stem: Which field do CiliumNetworkPolicies use to match on pod labels in order to identify the sources and destinations to which the policy applies?

options.text: endpointSelector
podSelector
labelFilter
ipSelector

explanation: The excerpt states that CiliumNetworkPolicies match on pod labels using an 'endpointSelector' to identify the sources and destinations to which the policy applies.

optionRationale.b: podSelector is not the field named in the excerpt for CiliumNetworkPolicies.
optionRationale.c: labelFilter is not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: ipSelector is not mentioned, and endpoint IP addresses are described as irrelevant for defining policies.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: CiliumNetworkPolicies match on pod labels using an "endpointSelector" to identify the sources and destinations to which the policy applies.

stem: The demo policy filters only on IP protocol and TCP protocol. What is such a policy commonly called?

options.text: An L7 HTTP policy
An L3/L4 network security policy
A DNS-based policy
A cluster-wide egress policy

explanation: The excerpt explains that a policy filtering only on IP protocol (network layer 3) and TCP protocol (network layer 4) is often referred to as an L3/L4 network security policy.

optionRationale.a: L7 is not mentioned; the policy filters on layers 3 and 4 only.
optionRationale.c: DNS-based filtering is not described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe the policy as cluster-wide or egress-specific.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: This is a simple policy that filters only on IP protocol (network layer 3) and TCP protocol (network layer 4), so it is often referred to as an L3/L4 network security policy.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement on nodes where the native devices differ between machines, though every device name begins with the prefix eth. They want NodePort services reachable through those devices without listing each name individually. Which Helm option value should they use?

options.text: devices=eth+
nodePort.directRoutingDevice=eth+
devices='eth0,eth1,eth2'
nodePort.range="10000\,32767"

explanation: The excerpt states that if the devices do not match across different nodes, the wildcard option can be used, for example devices=eth+, which matches any device starting with the prefix eth. The directRoutingDevice option concerns the single device used for direct routing between Cilium nodes, not the set of devices on which NodePort services are exposed.

optionRationale.b: The wildcard is available for directRoutingDevice too, but that option selects the direct routing device, not the devices through which NodePort services are made accessible.
optionRationale.c: This lists explicit device names, which the excerpt says must be named the same on all Cilium managed nodes — precisely the problem the team has.
optionRationale.d: This sets the NodePort port range to match a non-default kube-apiserver configuration; it has nothing to do with device selection.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
Alternatively
if the devices do not match across different nodes, the wildcard option can be
used, e.g. ``devices=eth+``, which would match any device starting with prefix
``eth``.

stem: An administrator sets nodePort.directRoutingDevice=eth+ on a cluster where several devices match that wildcard. How does Cilium choose the direct routing device?

options.text: It sorts the matching devices in increasing alphanumerical order and picks the first one.
It picks the matching device that carries the Kubernetes ExternalIP, preferring it over InternalIP.
It refuses to start until a single explicit device name is supplied.
It uses all matching devices for direct routing between Cilium nodes.

explanation: The excerpt says that if more than one device matches the wildcard option, Cilium sorts them in increasing alphanumerical order and picks the first one. It also notes that only one device can be used for direct routing between Cilium nodes.

optionRationale.b: The InternalIP/ExternalIP preference applies when no single device was detected or specified and when choosing among devices generally; it is not the rule given for resolving a wildcard match.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly allows the wildcard option for directRoutingDevice, so no explicit single name is required.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that only one device can be used for direct routing between Cilium nodes.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
If more than one devices match the wildcard option, Cilium will sort them
in increasing alphanumerical order and pick the first one.

stem: A cluster's kube-apiserver has been configured to use the NodePort range 10000-32767 instead of the Kubernetes default. What must be done on the Cilium side?

options.text: Pass the same range to Cilium via nodePort.range, for example nodePort.range="10000\,32767".
Nothing; Cilium always assumes the default range of 30000-32767.
Set nodePort.autoProtectPortRanges to false so the new range is accepted.
Set nodePort.bindProtection to false so the new range is accepted.

explanation: The excerpt states that if kube-apiserver was configured to use a non-default NodePort port range, then the same range must be passed to Cilium via the nodePort.range option, giving nodePort.range="10000\,32767" for a range of 10000-32767.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives 30000-32767 only as the default Kubernetes NodePort range; it explicitly requires passing a non-default range to Cilium.
optionRationale.c: autoProtectPortRanges controls whether the NodePort range is appended to the reserved ports, not whether a non-default range is communicated to Cilium.
optionRationale.d: bindProtection controls whether application bind(2) requests to NodePort service ports are prevented, not the port range configuration.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
If ``kube-apiserver`` was configured to use a non-default NodePort port range,
then the same range must be passed to Cilium via the ``nodePort.range``
option, for example, as ``nodePort.range="10000\,32767"`` for a
range of ``10000-32767``.

stem: On a node, the configured NodePort range overlaps with the ephemeral port range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range. What does Cilium do by default, and why?

options.text: It appends the NodePort range to net.ipv4.ip_local_reserved_ports, to prevent a NodePort service from hijacking traffic of a host local application whose source port matches the service port.
It shrinks the ephemeral port range so that the two ranges no longer overlap.
It refuses to start the Cilium agent until the overlap is removed manually.
It disables NodePort services on that node until the overlap is resolved.

explanation: The excerpt says that if the NodePort port range overlaps with the ephemeral port range, Cilium will append the NodePort range to the reserved ports, which is needed to prevent a NodePort service from hijacking traffic of a host local application whose source port matches the service port.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes appending to the reserved ports, not modifying the ephemeral port range itself.
optionRationale.c: No such refusal is described; the excerpt describes an automatic modification of the reserved ports.
optionRationale.d: NodePort services are not disabled; the protection is applied through the reserved ports list.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
If the NodePort port range overlaps with the ephemeral port range
(``net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range``), Cilium will append the NodePort range to
the reserved ports (``net.ipv4.ip_local_reserved_ports``).

stem: An application running in the host network namespace of a Cilium node attempts a bind(2) to a port that is used by a NodePort service. What does the application typically observe by default, and which setting opts out of this behaviour?

options.text: A bind: Operation not permitted error; setting nodePort.bindProtection to false opts out.
A bind: Operation not permitted error; setting nodePort.autoProtectPortRanges to false opts out.
The bind succeeds but traffic is silently redirected to the NodePort service; setting nodePort.range opts out.
A bind: Operation not permitted error; setting nodePort.directRoutingDevice opts out.

explanation: The excerpt states that by default the NodePort implementation prevents application bind(2) requests to NodePort service ports, with the application typically seeing a bind: Operation not permitted error, and that expert users can opt out by switching nodePort.bindProtection to false.

optionRationale.b: autoProtectPortRanges controls the modification of the reserved ports list, not the prevention of bind(2) requests.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the bind being prevented with an error, not succeeding with redirection.
optionRationale.d: directRoutingDevice selects the device used for direct routing; it does not govern bind protection.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
By default, the NodePort implementation prevents application ``bind(2)`` requests
to NodePort service ports. In such case, the application will typically see a
``bind: Operation not permitted`` error.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the default set of IP addresses through which a NodePort, LoadBalancer or externalIPs service is accessible when Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement runs?

options.text: Through the IP addresses of native devices that have the default route on the host or have Kubernetes InternalIP or ExternalIP assigned, with InternalIP preferred over ExternalIP if both exist.
Through the IP addresses of every native device on the host, regardless of routing or Kubernetes IP assignment.
Only through the loopback address, because socket-LB restricts access to 127.0.0.1.
Through the IP addresses of native devices that have Kubernetes ExternalIP assigned, with ExternalIP preferred over InternalIP if both exist.

explanation: The excerpt states that by default such a service will be accessible through the IP addresses of native devices which have the default route on the host or have Kubernetes InternalIP or ExternalIP assigned, and that InternalIP is preferred over ExternalIP if both exist.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt limits the default set to devices with the default route or with Kubernetes InternalIP or ExternalIP assigned.
optionRationale.c: The loopback address is mentioned as one of several addresses available thanks to socket-LB, not as the only one.
optionRationale.d: The preference is the other way round: InternalIP is preferred over ExternalIP if both exist.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
by default, a NodePort or
LoadBalancer service or a service with externalIPs will be accessible through
the IP addresses of native devices which have the default route on the host or
have Kubernetes InternalIP or ExternalIP assigned. InternalIP is preferred over
ExternalIP if both exist.

stem: You have applied a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that denies all traffic by default, and you then curl the /details/1 endpoint through the Cilium Ingress from outside the cluster. What does the excerpt show happening?

options.text: The request is dropped by policy and the client receives an HTTP 403 Forbidden response served by envoy.
The request is dropped by policy and the client receives an HTTP 503 Service Unavailable response served by envoy.
The request is allowed because Cilium Ingress traffic is exempt from default deny policies, and the JSON payload is returned.
The request is dropped by policy and the connection times out with no HTTP response at all.

explanation: With the default-deny CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy applied, the excerpt states that the request to the /details endpoint will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic, and the curl output shows an HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden response with server: envoy. The Hubble flow confirms the http-request was DROPPED and the http-response was FORWARDED with status 403.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows a 403 Forbidden, not a 503 Service Unavailable; no such status appears in the source.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly says the request will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic once the default-deny policy is applied; the JSON payload only appears after ingress traffic to /details is allowed.
optionRationale.d: The curl output shows a complete HTTP response with status 403 and server: envoy, so the connection is not left to time out.

citations.title: Default Deny Ingress Policy
citations.quote: With this policy applied, the request to the ``/details`` endpoint will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic.

stem: You are following the manual verification steps for monitoring generic IP options with Cilium. You want to inject a known Trace ID into packets sent from a client Pod to a server Pod, and you need a tool that can set IP options manually. Which approach does the tutorial take?

options.text: Deploy an nginx server and a netshoot client, then run nping from the client with a manually specified IP Option hex string.
Deploy an nginx server and a netshoot client, then run curl from the client with a custom header carrying the Trace ID.
Deploy two nginx Pods and use kubectl exec to write the Trace ID into the Pod annotations.
Deploy a netshoot server and an nginx client, then run nping from the server towards the client.

explanation: The excerpt states that verification is done by manually injecting a known Trace ID into packets using nping, and the first step deploys an nginx server and a netshoot client containing nping. The traffic is then triggered by executing nping from the client to the server with a manually specified IP Option hex string.

stem: A cluster administrator is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that includes a `toPorts` entry with both an `http` rule list and a `dns` rule list for the same port. What is the outcome?

options.text: The policy is rejected, because mixing different port level rule types in a single port is disallowed.
Both rule sets are applied, with HTTP evaluated before DNS.
The DNS rules are silently ignored and only the HTTP rules take effect.
The policy is accepted but the port is treated as having no layer 7 rules.

explanation: The `L7Rules` structure is a union: exactly one of the protocol-specific fields must be set per port, and mixing different port level rule types is disallowed. Supplying both `http` and `dns` for the same port therefore makes the policy invalid.

optionRationale.b: The union design forbids combining members on one port, so they are not both applied in any order.
optionRationale.c: Silently dropping one member is not what the excerpt describes; mixing is disallowed outright.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that if none are specified no additional port level rules apply, but here two conflicting types are specified, which is a rejection case.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote:
The structure is implemented as a union, i.e. only one member field can be used
per port.

stem: Two `toPorts` rules in a policy have identical `PortProtocol` values and select an overlapping set of endpoints. One carries HTTP layer 7 rules and the other carries DNS layer 7 rules. What happens?

options.text: The layer 7 rules are combined, with HTTP taking precedence over DNS.
The policy is rejected, because the layer 7 rule types differ.
Only the first rule encountered is used and the second is discarded.
Both rules are applied independently to the endpoints without interaction.

explanation: When multiple `toPorts` rules with identical `PortProtocol` select an overlapping list of endpoints, layer 7 rules are combined only if they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

optionRationale.a: Combining happens only for rules of the same type; differing types cause rejection, not precedence.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes combining or rejecting, not first-match discarding.
optionRationale.d: Overlapping selection with identical `PortProtocol` triggers the combine-or-reject rule, so they are not treated independently.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote:
If multiple ``toPorts`` rules with identical ``PortProtocol`` select
an overlapping list of endpoints, then the layer 7 rules are combined together
if they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

stem: A layer 7 HTTP rule list contains three separate rules. An incoming HTTP request matches only the second of them. What is the result?

options.text: The request is denied, because all rules must match.
The request is permitted, because at least one of the rules matches.
The request is permitted only if the first rule also matches.
The request is dropped at the network layer without any application response.

explanation: Each member of `L7Rules` consists of a list of application protocol rules, and a layer 7 request is permitted if at least one of the rules matches.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: matching at least one rule is sufficient.
optionRationale.c: There is no requirement for the first rule to match; any single match suffices.
optionRationale.d: For layer 7 violations the excerpt says an application protocol specific access denied message is crafted where possible, not a silent packet drop.

citations.quote:
A layer 7
request is permitted if at least one of the rules matches.

stem: A policy author writes a `toPorts` entry that specifies a port and protocol but leaves both the `http` and `dns` fields unset. How is traffic to that port treated at layer 7?

options.text: All traffic is denied until a layer 7 rule is added.
No additional port level rules are applied, so all traffic is permitted.
The policy is rejected because a union member must always be set.
Traffic is permitted only for HTTP, as the default protocol.

explanation: The `L7Rules` comment states that if none of the union members are specified, no additional port level rules are applied, and the excerpt adds that if no rules are specified then all traffic is permitted.

optionRationale.a: An empty rule set permits rather than denies; the excerpt says all traffic is permitted.
optionRationale.c: The fields are marked optional and the excerpt explicitly covers the case where none are specified.
optionRationale.d: No default protocol is described; with no rules, all traffic is permitted.

citations.quote: If none are specified, then no additional port level rules are applied.

stem: A policy contains a layer 4 rule for a set of endpoints, and also a similar layer 4 rule for the same endpoints that additionally carries layer 7 rules. What is the effect of the layer 7 portion?

options.text: It is enforced in addition to the plain layer 4 rule.
It has no effect.
It causes the whole policy to be rejected.
It overrides the plain layer 4 rule entirely.

optionRationale.c: Rejection applies to differing layer 7 types on overlapping `toPorts` rules, not to this situation.
optionRationale.d: The layer 7 portion has no effect; it does not replace the plain layer 4 rule.

with layer 7 rules is also specified, then the layer 7 portions of the

stem: An engineer runs Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement with socket-LB enabled. A pod has an established connected UDP socket to a Service backend, and that backend is then deleted. What does the Cilium agent do?

options.text: It forcefully terminates the application socket connected to the deleted backend so the application can be load-balanced to active backends.
It leaves the socket untouched and silently drops all further packets from that socket until the application closes it.
It rewrites the socket's destination to the Service cluster IP and keeps the connection alive indefinitely.
It disables socket-LB for that pod and falls back to iptables masquerading for the remainder of the connection.

explanation: The excerpt states that when socket-LB is enabled, pods can keep sending traffic to a deleted backend, and Cilium handles this by forcefully terminating application sockets connected to deleted backends so applications can be load-balanced to active backends.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says Cilium forcefully terminates such sockets, not that it leaves them and drops packets.
optionRationale.c: No such rewriting of the destination to the cluster IP is described; the described action is termination of the socket.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe disabling socket-LB or falling back to iptables in this situation.

options.text: `cilium config delete hubble-export-file-path`
`kubectl -n kube-system rollout status ds/cilium`
`kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- tail -f /var/run/cilium/hubble/events.log`
`cilium config set hubble-export-file-path stdout`

explanation: The excerpt gives `cilium config delete hubble-export-file-path` and notes that this command will restart the Cilium pods.

optionRationale.b: This command waits for the `cilium` pod to become ready; it does not delete configuration.
optionRationale.c: This command tails the export file to verify stored flow logs.

stem: After installing SPIRE with the default configuration, you inspect the cilium-spire namespace and see two spire-agent pods and one spire-server pod. How does the excerpt say these workloads are deployed?

options.text: The SPIRE server is a StatefulSet and the SPIRE agents are a DaemonSet, so you should see one SPIRE agent per node.
The SPIRE server is a DaemonSet and the SPIRE agents are a StatefulSet, so you should see one SPIRE server per node.
Both the SPIRE server and the SPIRE agents are deployed as Deployments with a single replica each.
The SPIRE server is a StatefulSet and the SPIRE agents are bare pods created directly, one per node.

explanation: The excerpt states that the SPIRE server is deployed as a StatefulSet and the SPIRE agents as a DaemonSet, which is why one agent appears per node.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the two workload types; the server is the StatefulSet and the agents the DaemonSet.
optionRationale.c: No Deployment appears in the excerpt; the resources listed are a DaemonSet and a StatefulSet.
optionRationale.d: The agents are managed by a DaemonSet, as shown by the daemonset.apps/spire-agent entry, not created as bare pods.

citations.title: Verify SPIRE Health
citations.quote: The SPIRE server is deployed as a StatefulSet and the SPIRE agents are deployed as a DaemonSet (you should therefore see one SPIRE agent per node).

stem: A colleague asks why the cluster was configured to use Projected Service Account Tokens for SPIRE agent attestation rather than traditional Service Account Tokens. What reason does the excerpt give?

options.text: PSATs provide additional security guarantees over traditional Service Account Tokens and are the recommended attestation strategy when supported by the cluster.
PSATs are the only attestation method the SPIRE server supports, so no alternative exists.
PSATs remove the need for the SPIRE server to run a healthcheck.
PSATs allow the SPIRE agents to be deployed as a StatefulSet instead of a DaemonSet.

explanation: The excerpt says Projected Service Account Tokens provide additional security guarantees over traditional tokens and that PSAT is the recommended attestation strategy when the Kubernetes cluster supports it.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt presents PSAT as recommended over traditional tokens, not as the only supported method.
optionRationale.c: The healthcheck is a separate verification step and is not linked to the attestation strategy.
optionRationale.d: The agents are a DaemonSet regardless; the excerpt does not tie workload type to the attestation strategy.

Projected Service Account Tokens provide additional security guarantees over traditional Kubernetes
Service Account Tokens and when supported by a Kubernetes cluster, PSAT is the recommended attestation strategy.

stem: In the agent list output, each attested agent is identified by a SPIFFE ID. Which form does that identifier take in the excerpt?

spire-agent-27jd7.cilium-spire.svc.cluster.local

optionRationale.b: The trust domain shown is spiffe.cilium and the path includes agent/k8s_psat, not spire/server.
optionRationale.c: That is a Kubernetes DNS name pattern; the excerpt shows SPIFFE IDs, not DNS names, for the agents.
optionRationale.d: That is the ClusterIP and port of the spire-server service, not an agent identity.

stem: An engineer is planning a Cluster Mesh between three clusters. One cluster runs Cilium 1.18.x, a second runs 1.17.x, and a third runs 1.16.x. What does the excerpt say about this combination?

options.text: It is acceptable, because all three versions are within two minor releases of each other.
It is not acceptable, because 1.18.x can connect to 1.17.x or 1.19.x, but not 1.16.x.
It is acceptable, because only the datapath mode must match across clusters.
It is not acceptable, because all clusters must run exactly the same Cilium version.

explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium versions must differ by no more than one minor release, and gives the example that 1.18.x can connect to 1.17.x or 1.19.x but not 1.16.x. The third cluster at 1.16.x therefore breaks the requirement.

optionRationale.a: The permitted spread is one minor release, not two; the excerpt explicitly excludes 1.16.x for a 1.18.x cluster.
optionRationale.c: Matching datapath mode is a separate requirement; the version rule is stated independently and is still violated.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt allows a difference of one minor release, so identical versions are not required.

citations.title: Cluster Addressing Requirements
citations.quote:
The Cilium versions of all clusters must differ by no more than one minor
  release. For example, Cilium ``1.18.x`` can connect to clusters running
  Cilium ``1.17.x`` or ``1.19.x``, but not ``1.16.x``.

stem: A platform team is preparing two clusters for Cluster Mesh. Cluster A was installed with Cilium defaulting to arch_overlay mode, while cluster B was installed with Cilium defaulting to native_routing mode. What is the consequence according to the excerpt?

options.text: The clusters can be meshed, provided their PodCIDR ranges are unique.
The clusters can be meshed, because the datapath mode is chosen per node rather than per cluster.
The clusters cannot be meshed, because all clusters must be configured with the same datapath mode.
The clusters can be meshed, but only if a VPN tunnel is established between them.

explanation: The excerpt's first requirement is that all clusters must be configured with the same datapath mode, noting that Cilium may default to arch_overlay or native_routing depending on the cloud environment. A mismatch between the two clusters therefore fails this prerequisite.

optionRationale.a: Unique PodCIDR ranges are a separate requirement and do not remedy a datapath mode mismatch.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the datapath mode as a per-cluster configuration, not a per-node choice.
optionRationale.d: Peering or VPN tunnels address node IP connectivity, which is a different requirement from datapath mode.

citations.title: Cluster Addressing Requirements
citations.quote:
All clusters must be configured with the same datapath mode. Cilium install
  may default to arch_overlay or native_routing mode depending on
  the specific cloud environment.

stem: Which statement about Cilium version compatibility across clusters in a Cluster Mesh is supported by the excerpt?

options.text: Cilium 1.18.x can connect to clusters running 1.17.x or 1.19.x, but not 1.16.x.
Cilium 1.18.x can connect to any cluster running 1.16.x or later.
All clusters must run the identical patch release of Cilium.
Cilium 1.18.x can connect only to clusters running 1.18.x.

explanation: The excerpt gives this exact example: versions must differ by no more than one minor release, so 1.18.x connects to 1.17.x or 1.19.x but not 1.16.x.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says 1.16.x cannot connect to a 1.18.x cluster.
optionRationale.c: The rule is expressed in minor releases, and the example uses the 1.18.x form rather than requiring identical patch releases.
optionRationale.d: A one-minor-release difference is permitted, so 1.17.x and 1.19.x are also allowed.

citations.title: Cluster Addressing Requirements
citations.quote:
For example, Cilium ``1.18.x`` can connect to clusters running
  Cilium ``1.17.x`` or ``1.19.x``, but not ``1.16.x``.

stem: An engineer is validating addressing before enabling Cluster Mesh. Which requirement does the excerpt place on PodCIDR ranges?

options.text: They must be identical in every cluster so that pods keep the same addresses.
They must be non-conflicting and unique IP addresses across all clusters and all nodes.
They must be allocated from the node's InternalIP subnet.
They must be routable over the public internet between clusters.

explanation: The excerpt requires that PodCIDR ranges in all clusters and all nodes be non-conflicting and unique IP addresses.

optionRationale.a: Identical ranges would conflict, which is the opposite of the stated requirement.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not tie PodCIDR allocation to the InternalIP subnet; it only requires uniqueness and non-conflict.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt mentions peering or VPN tunnels between node networks, not public internet routability of PodCIDRs.

citations.title: Cluster Addressing Requirements
citations.quote:
PodCIDR ranges in all clusters and all nodes must be non-conflicting and
  unique IP addresses.

stem: Two clusters are to be meshed, and the engineer must ensure nodes can reach each other. According to the excerpt, what must be true of node connectivity?

options.text: Nodes must have IP connectivity between each other using the configured InternalIP for each node.
Nodes must have IP connectivity using the PodCIDR assigned to each node.
Nodes must share a single flat Layer 2 network with no tunnelling.
Nodes must be reachable through a load balancer exposed by each cluster.

explanation: The excerpt states that nodes in all clusters must have IP connectivity between each other using the configured InternalIP for each node, typically met by peering or VPN tunnels.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt specifies the configured InternalIP, not the PodCIDR, as the address used for node connectivity.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the requirement is typically met by peering or VPN tunnels, so a flat Layer 2 network is not required.
optionRationale.d: No load balancer mechanism is mentioned; the excerpt refers to peering or VPN tunnels between node networks.

citations.title: Cluster Addressing Requirements
citations.quote:
Nodes in all clusters must have IP connectivity between each other using the 
  configured InternalIP for each node.

stem: A security reviewer asks what must be permitted for a Cluster Mesh to function between clusters. What does the excerpt say?

options.text: Only ICMP must be allowed between the clusters.
All traffic between the clusters must be permitted without restriction.
The network between clusters must allow the inter-cluster communication, with the exact ports documented in the firewall_requirements section.
Only the Kubernetes API server port must be reachable between clusters.

explanation: The excerpt requires that the network between clusters allow the inter-cluster communication, and points to the firewall_requirements section for the exact ports.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt does not restrict the requirement to ICMP.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt refers to specific ports documented in the firewall_requirements section rather than permitting all traffic.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not single out the Kubernetes API server port; it defers to the firewall_requirements section.

citations.title: Cluster Addressing Requirements
citations.quote:
The network between clusters must allow the inter-cluster communication. The
  exact ports are documented in the firewall_requirements section.

stem: An engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy for endpoints with label env=prod. They want to ensure that only source endpoints that also carry env=prod can reach those endpoints, but they do not want this rule alone to grant any access. Which field should they use to establish this base requirement?

options.text: fromRequires
fromEndpoints
toRequires
toEntities

explanation: The fromRequires field establishes label requirements that serve as a foundation for any fromEndpoints relationship. It does not grant access by itself; additional rules matching fromEndpoints are needed to allow traffic. toRequires is for egress policies, fromEndpoints grants access, and toEntities is a different egress construct.

optionRationale.b: fromEndpoints is used to allow traffic from specific endpoints, not to set base requirements that do not grant access.
optionRationale.c: toRequires is the egress counterpart used with toEndpoints, not for ingress fromEndpoints.
optionRationale.d: toEntities is an egress rule that allows traffic to entities, not a base requirement field.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
For this purpose, the ``fromRequires`` field can be used to establish label
requirements which serve as a foundation for any ``fromEndpoints``
relationship.

stem: A policy uses fromRequires to require that any source endpoint must have label env=prod to reach endpoints with label env=prod. The same policy also includes a fromEndpoints rule that allows traffic from endpoints with label role=frontend. Which source endpoints will be able to reach the env=prod endpoints?

options.text: Only endpoints that have both env=prod and role=frontend.
Any endpoint with role=frontend, regardless of env label.
Any endpoint with env=prod, regardless of role label.
No endpoints, because fromRequires blocks all traffic.

explanation: The fromRequires rule sets a base requirement that the source must have env=prod. The fromEndpoints rule allows traffic from role=frontend. Both conditions must be met, so only endpoints with both labels can connect. The excerpt confirms this: when combined, the endpoint becomes accessible from endpoints that have both labels env=prod and role=frontend.

optionRationale.b: The fromRequires requirement for env=prod remains in effect and is not overridden by the fromEndpoints rule.
optionRationale.c: The fromEndpoints rule only allows role=frontend, so env=prod alone is insufficient.
optionRationale.d: fromRequires does not block all traffic; it only adds a requirement that must be satisfied alongside other rules.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
when combined with the
example policy below, the endpoint with label ``env=prod`` will become
accessible from endpoints that have both labels ``env=prod`` and
``role=frontend``.

stem: An engineer is reviewing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that uses fromRequires to limit ingress to endpoints with label app=db. The policy also contains a fromEndpoints rule that allows traffic from app=web. The engineer worries that the fromEndpoints rule might limit the scope of the fromRequires requirement. What is the effect of combining these rules?

options.text: The fromRequires requirement stays in effect regardless of what the fromEndpoints rule allows.
The fromEndpoints rule overrides the fromRequires requirement for matching sources.
The fromRequires requirement only applies to traffic not matched by fromEndpoints.
The combination is invalid and the policy is rejected.

explanation: The excerpt states that other ingress and egress rules do not limit the scope of fromRequires or toRequires. Pairing them results in valid policy, but the requirements set in fromRequires stay in effect no matter what would otherwise be allowed by the other rules.

optionRationale.b: The fromEndpoints rule does not override fromRequires; the requirement remains.
optionRationale.c: fromRequires applies to all traffic for the endpoint selector, not just traffic not matched by fromEndpoints.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says pairing other rules with fromRequires results in valid policy.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
Pairing other
ingress and egress rules with a ``toRequires`` or ``fromRequires`` will result in valid
policy, but the requirements set in ``toRequires`` and ``fromRequires`` stay in effect
no matter what would otherwise be allowed by the other rules.

stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between fromRequires and fromEndpoints in a CiliumNetworkPolicy?

options.text: fromRequires sets additional constraints that must be met for the selected endpoints to be reachable, but does not grant access by itself; fromEndpoints rules are also needed to allow traffic.
fromRequires grants access to all endpoints that meet its constraints, making fromEndpoints unnecessary.
fromEndpoints sets base requirements, and fromRequires allows specific traffic.
fromRequires and fromEndpoints are mutually exclusive and cannot be used together.

explanation: The excerpt explains that fromRequires is a list of additional constraints which must be met for the selected endpoints to be reachable. These constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves, so to allow traffic there must also be rules which match fromEndpoints.

optionRationale.b: fromRequires does not grant access; it only sets requirements.
optionRationale.c: The roles are reversed: fromRequires sets base requirements, fromEndpoints allows traffic.
optionRationale.d: They are designed to be used together, as the excerpt shows.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
``fromRequires`` is a list of additional constraints which must
be met in order for the selected endpoints to be reachable. These additional
constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves, so to allow traffic
there must also be rules which match ``fromEndpoints``.

stem: An engineer is designing an egress policy for endpoints with label env=prod. They want to ensure that traffic can only go to destination endpoints that also have label env=prod, and they want this requirement to apply to all egress rules for those endpoints. Which field should they use?

options.text: toRequires
fromRequires
toEndpoints
fromEndpoints

explanation: For egress policies, the toRequires field is used with toEndpoints, analogous to fromRequires with fromEndpoints. toRequires establishes base requirements for egress traffic. fromRequires is for ingress, toEndpoints allows egress traffic, and fromEndpoints is for ingress.

optionRationale.b: fromRequires is for ingress policies, not egress.
optionRationale.c: toEndpoints is used to allow egress traffic to specific endpoints, not to set base requirements.
optionRationale.d: fromEndpoints is for ingress policies.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
The same applies for
egress policies, with ``toRequires`` and ``toEndpoints``.

stem: A cluster is running Cilium 1.18. An engineer deploys a CiliumNetworkPolicy that uses the fromRequires field. What is the status of this field in this version?

options.text: It is deprecated as of Cilium 1.17.x and will be removed in Cilium 1.19.
It is fully supported and not deprecated.
It was removed in Cilium 1.17.x.
It is only available in Cilium 1.19 and later.

explanation: The excerpt states that the fromRequires and toRequires fields are deprecated as of Cilium 1.17.x and have been removed as of Cilium 1.19. Therefore, in Cilium 1.18 they are deprecated but still present.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says they are deprecated as of 1.17.x.
optionRationale.c: They are deprecated in 1.17.x, not removed; removal is in 1.19.
optionRationale.d: They are removed in 1.19, not introduced.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
The ``fromRequires`` and ``toRequires`` fields are deprecated as of Cilium
   1.17.x. They have been removed as of Cilium 1.19.

stem: An engineer wants to use HTTPRoute Retry, a feature currently marked as experimental, with Cilium's Gateway API support. Which statement describes what must be done, according to the excerpt?

options.text: The experimental release channel includes everything in the standard channel plus some experimental resources and fields, so the corresponding CRDs must be installed to use the feature.
The standard release channel already contains all experimental resources and fields, so no additional CRDs are needed.
Experimental features are enabled purely by a Helm value, with no CRD installation required.
Only the GatewayClass and Gateway CRDs are needed, because HTTPRoute Retry is part of the core Gateway resource.

explanation: The excerpt states that the experimental release channel includes everything in the standard channel plus some experimental resources and fields, and that if you need a feature currently marked as experimental (for example, HTTPRoute Retry in the HTTPRoute resource), you must install the corresponding CRDs.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the experimental channel adds resources and fields on top of the standard channel, not that the standard channel already contains them.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt ties experimental features to installing the corresponding CRDs, and mentions Helm or the Cilium CLI only for enabling the Gateway API controller once CRDs are installed.
optionRationale.d: HTTPRoute Retry is given as an example of an experimental feature in the HTTPRoute resource, and the excerpt lists GatewayClass, Gateway and HTTPRoute as separate required CRDs.

citations.title: Installation
citations.quote:
Note that the **experimental** release channel includes everything in the **standard**
release channel plus some experimental resources and fields.

stem: An engineer creates a Cilium Gateway with `spec.addresses` set to `type: IPAddress` and `value: 172.18.0.140`, and no LB-IPAM annotation on the infrastructure. What does `kubectl get gateway my-gateway` show in the ADDRESS column?

options.text: The node IP of the Cilium agent
`<pending>` until an LB-IPAM pool is created
The value of `io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips`

explanation: The excerpt states that `spec.addresses` is used to specify the IP address of the gateway, and the sample output for a Gateway with `value: 172.18.0.140` shows `172.18.0.140` in the ADDRESS column with PROGRAMMED set to True.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt never mentions node IPs; the address comes from `spec.addresses`.
optionRationale.c: The sample output shows the address populated and PROGRAMMED True, with no pending state described.
optionRationale.d: The annotation is only relevant when it is present; here it is absent, so `spec.addresses` is used.

citations.title: Gateway API Addresses Support
citations.quote: The ``spec.addresses`` field is used to specify the IP address of the gateway.

stem: A Gateway manifest sets `io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips: "172.18.0.141"` under `spec.infrastructure.annotations` and also sets `spec.addresses` to `172.18.0.140`. Which address does the Gateway end up with?

options.text: 172.18.0.141, because the annotation takes precedence and `spec.addresses` is ignored
172.18.0.140, because `spec.addresses` always overrides annotations
Both addresses are assigned to the Gateway
Neither; the configuration is rejected as conflicting

explanation: The excerpt says that if the `io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips` annotation is already used in `spec.infrastructure.annotations` to specify the IP, the `spec.addresses` field will be ignored, and the sample output confirms the ADDRESS is 172.18.0.141.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the documented precedence: the annotation wins and `spec.addresses` is ignored.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt shows a single ADDRESS value, not two.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the field being ignored, not the configuration being rejected.

citations.title: Gateway API Addresses Support
citations.quote:
If you are already using the ``io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips`` in the ``spec.infrastructure.annotations`` to 
specify the IP, the ``spec.addresses`` field will be ignored.

stem: Which types of address does Cilium Gateway support in the `spec.addresses` field?

options.text: Only the IPAddress type
IPAddress and Hostname types
IPAddress, Hostname and NamedAddress types
Any type defined by the Gateway API specification

explanation: The excerpt states that the feature only supports IPAddress type of addresses, and that it works with the LB-IPAM.

optionRationale.b: Hostname is not listed as supported; the excerpt restricts support to IPAddress only.
optionRationale.c: NamedAddress is not mentioned at all in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Although the addresses field comes from the Gateway API specification, the excerpt explicitly limits Cilium's support to the IPAddress type.

citations.title: Gateway API Addresses Support
citations.quote: The feature only supports IPAddress type of addresses, and works with the LB-IPAM.

stem: Which field is used to specify the IP address of a Cilium Gateway?

options.text: `spec.addresses`
`spec.infrastructure.annotations`
`spec.listeners`
`spec.gatewayClassName`

explanation: The excerpt states that the `spec.addresses` field is used to specify the IP address of the gateway.

optionRationale.b: This is where the `io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips` annotation may be placed, but it is not the field the excerpt names for specifying the address.
optionRationale.c: Listeners define allowed routes, name, port and protocol in the sample, not the gateway IP.
optionRationale.d: This selects the GatewayClass (cilium) and does not carry an IP address.

citations.title: Gateway API Addresses Support
citations.quote: The ``spec.addresses`` field is used to specify the IP address of the gateway.

stem: How does the excerpt contrast the current behaviour of the `io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips` annotation with its planned future behaviour?

options.text: Today the annotation takes precedence over `spec.addresses`; in future it will be deprecated and then ignored if no `spec.addresses` are set
Today `spec.addresses` takes precedence; in future the annotation will take precedence
Today the annotation is ignored; in future it will take precedence over `spec.addresses`
The annotation is already ignored and will be removed without any warning

explanation: The excerpt says the annotation currently causes `spec.addresses` to be ignored, and that at a future date its use will be deprecated, after which it will be ignored if no `spec.addresses` are set.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the documented precedence both now and in future.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the opposite: the annotation currently wins and `spec.addresses` is ignored.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says warning logs and a warning Condition will be added, not that removal is silent.

citations.title: Gateway API Addresses Support
citations.quote:
At a future date the use of the ``io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips`` will be deprecated, and then after that, this annotation will be 
ignored if no ``spec.addresses`` are set.

stem: An engineer sets neither `spec.addresses` nor the `io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips` annotation on a Cilium Gateway. According to the excerpt, what will Cilium do?

options.text: Add warning logs to the Cilium agent logs and place a warning Condition on the Gateway
Reject the Gateway and leave it unprogrammed
Silently allocate an address from the default LB-IPAM pool
Fall back to the node IP without any warning

explanation: The excerpt states that in both cases — the annotation being used, and the annotation being ignored when no `spec.addresses` are set — warning logs will be added to the Cilium agent logs and a warning Condition will be placed on the Gateway.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes warnings, not rejection or an unprogrammed Gateway.
optionRationale.c: No default pool behaviour is described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt mentions warnings, and says nothing about falling back to a node IP.

citations.title: Gateway API Addresses Support
citations.quote:
In both cases, warning logs will be added to the Cilium agent logs, and a 
warning Condition will be placed on the Gateway.

stem: An engineer is writing a Cilium BGP advertisement and wants to attach the well-known community that signals a route should be blackholed. Which value should be placed in the Communities list?

options.text: `blackhole`
`no-export`
`0xffff029a:0`

explanation: The excerpt lists `blackhole` as an allowed well-known string alias, mapping to the hexadecimal value `0xffff029a` and the 16-bit pair value `65535:666`. The alias itself is what may be used as a `WellKnown` community value.

optionRationale.b: ``no-export`` is a valid well-known alias, but it maps to ``0xffffff01`` / ``65535:65281``, not to the blackhole community.
optionRationale.c: A three-part colon-separated value is the ``Large`` community form, and the excerpt gives no such value for blackhole; the 16-bit pair is ``65535:666``.
optionRationale.d: The hexadecimal form is ``0xffff029a``; appending a colon and a further number is not a form described in the excerpt.

stem: A network engineer needs to advertise a BGP Large Communities value in a Cilium BGP advertisement. Which format does the excerpt say a `Large` community takes?

options.text: Two 2-byte decimal numbers separated by a colon, such as `64512:100`
Three 4-byte decimal numbers separated by colons, such as `64512:100:50`
A well-known string alias mapped to a 32-bit numeric value
A single 4-byte decimal number

explanation: The excerpt states that `Large` represents a value of the BGP Large Communities Attribute as three 4-byte decimal numbers separated by colons, giving `64512:100:50` as the example.

optionRationale.a: Two 2-byte decimal numbers separated by a colon is the ``Standard`` form, not the ``Large`` form.
optionRationale.c: A well-known string alias is the ``WellKnown`` type, which maps to the standard 32-bit attribute.
optionRationale.d: A single 4-byte decimal number is one of the accepted ``Standard`` representations, not the ``Large`` format.

citations.title: Community
citations.quote: as three 4-byte decimal numbers separated by colons (for example: ``64512:100:50``).

stem: An engineer configuring a Cilium BGP advertisement wants to express a standard 32-bit community as a single 4-byte decimal number rather than as a colon-separated pair. According to the excerpt, is this permitted for the `Standard` type?

options.text: No, only the two 2-byte decimal numbers separated by a colon form is accepted.
No, standard communities must be given as a well-known string alias.
Yes, a `Standard` value may be a 4-byte decimal number or two 2-byte decimal numbers separated by a colon.
Yes, but only when the value is also accompanied by a `Large` community.

explanation: The excerpt describes `Standard` as a value of the standard 32-bit BGP Communities Attribute expressed as a 4-byte decimal number or two 2-byte decimal numbers separated by a colon, with `64512:100` as the example.

optionRationale.a: The colon-separated pair is only one of the two accepted representations, not the sole one.
optionRationale.b: A well-known string alias belongs to the separate ``WellKnown`` type.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt places no such condition on the ``Standard`` type.

citations.title: Community
citations.quote: as a 4-byte decimal number or two 2-byte decimal numbers separated by a colon (for example: ``64512:100``).

stem: During a maintenance window an operator wants to attach the well-known community whose 16-bit pair value is `65535:0`. Which well-known string alias should be used in the Communities list?

options.text: `internet`
`planned-shut`
`accept-own`
`llgr-stale`

explanation: The excerpt's mapping shows `planned-shut` with hexadecimal value `0xffff0000` and 16-bit pair value `65535:0`.

optionRationale.a: ``internet`` maps to ``0x00000000`` and the pair value ``0:0``.
optionRationale.c: ``accept-own`` maps to ``0xffff0001`` and the pair value ``65535:1``.
optionRationale.d: ``llgr-stale`` maps to ``0xffff0006`` and the pair value ``65535:6``.

stem: A team is reviewing a Cilium BGP configuration that lists community values. One entry is the string `no-peer`. Which type of community value is this, and what numeric pair does the excerpt associate with it?

options.text: A `Standard` value equivalent to `65535:65284`
A `Large` value equivalent to `65535:65284`
A `WellKnown` value equivalent to `65535:65284`
A `WellKnown` value equivalent to `65535:65283`

explanation: The excerpt lists `no-peer` among the `WellKnown` string aliases, with hexadecimal value `0xffffff04` and 16-bit pair value `65535:65284`.

optionRationale.a: ``Standard`` values are given as decimal numbers, not as well-known string aliases.
optionRationale.b: ``Large`` values are three 4-byte decimal numbers separated by colons, which does not match this alias.
optionRationale.d: ``65535:65283`` is the pair value for ``no-export-subconfed``, not ``no-peer``.

stem: An engineer must advertise the well-known community that maps to the hexadecimal value `0xffffff02`. Which alias should be configured, and what is its 16-bit pair value?

options.text: `no-export`, pair value `65535:65281`
`no-advertise`, pair value `65535:65282`
`no-export-subconfed`, pair value `65535:65283`
`route-filter-v4`, pair value `65535:3`

explanation: The excerpt's mapping shows `no-advertise` with hexadecimal value `0xffffff02` and 16-bit pair value `65535:65282`.

optionRationale.a: ``no-export`` maps to ``0xffffff01`` and the pair value ``65535:65281``.
optionRationale.c: ``no-export-subconfed`` maps to ``0xffffff03`` and the pair value ``65535:65283``.
optionRationale.d: ``route-filter-v4`` maps to ``0xffff0003`` and the pair value ``65535:3``.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with WireGuard-based encryption in its default configuration. An engineer asks which traffic is encrypted. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Only traffic between Cilium-managed pods is encrypted.
Pod-to-pod, pod-to-node and node-to-pod traffic are all encrypted.
Only node-to-node traffic is encrypted, with pod traffic left in plaintext.
All traffic on the host network is encrypted, including traffic to the kube-apiserver.

explanation: The excerpt states that by default WireGuard-based encryption only encrypts traffic between Cilium-managed pods. Node-to-node, pod-to-node and node-to-pod traffic are only added when node-to-node encryption is explicitly enabled.

optionRationale.b: This is the effect of enabling node-to-node encryption, not the default behaviour.
optionRationale.c: The default covers pod-to-pod traffic; node-to-node is the additional mode that must be enabled.
optionRationale.d: Host-network traffic to the kube-apiserver is deliberately excluded from node-to-node encryption, and is certainly not encrypted by default.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
By default, WireGuard-based encryption only encrypts traffic between Cilium-managed
pods.

stem: An engineer enables WireGuard node-to-node encryption and expects every node in the cluster to participate. Which nodes will automatically opt out of node-to-node encryption?

options.text: Nodes carrying the node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane label.
Nodes carrying the node-role.kubernetes.io/worker label.
Every node that has a CiliumNode CRD registered.
No nodes opt out; node-to-node encryption always applies cluster-wide.

explanation: Cilium automatically disables node-to-node encryption from and to Kubernetes control-plane nodes, identified by the node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane label, which is the default value of the node-encryption-opt-out-labels option.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the control-plane label, not a worker label, as the opt-out selector.
optionRationale.c: A CiliumNode CRD exists for nodes generally and is not the opt-out criterion.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly describes an automatic opt-out, so participation is not cluster-wide by default.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
Cilium automatically disables node-to-node encryption from and to
  Kubernetes control-plane nodes, i.e. any node with the
  ``node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane`` label will opt-out of node-to-node
  encryption.

stem: A worker node reboots and generates a new WireGuard private key, so its public key must be updated. Why does Cilium exclude control-plane nodes from node-to-node encryption by default?

options.text: To avoid a bootstrapping problem where the connection used to update the WireGuard public key would itself be encrypted with the key about to be replaced.
Because control-plane nodes never run Cilium-managed pods and therefore need no encryption.
Because the kube-apiserver cannot process WireGuard-encrypted packets at all.
To reduce CPU overhead on control-plane nodes during key rotation.

explanation: The excerpt explains that encrypting the kube-apiserver connection with WireGuard creates a bootstrapping problem: the connection used to update the public key would be encrypted with the very key being replaced, which is problematic when a node changes its key after a reboot or re-provisioning.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt notes that pod-to-pod traffic for Cilium-managed pods on control-plane nodes is still encrypted, so such pods are contemplated.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not claim the kube-apiserver cannot process such packets; it describes a key-update bootstrapping problem.
optionRationale.d: The stated reason is avoiding lockout from the control plane, not CPU savings.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
This creates a bootstrapping problem where the
  connection used to update the WireGuard public key is itself encrypted with
  the public key about to be replaced.

stem: An engineer wants to force node-to-node encryption from and to control-plane nodes. Which configuration achieves this, and what is the consequence?

options.text: Set node-encryption-opt-out-labels to an empty label selector; the engineer must then always manually update a node's public key in its CiliumNode CRD when a worker node's public key changes.
