citations.quote: There are as many entries as there are identities. Verify that these match by running the command:

stem: A platform team runs Cilium 1.16 in a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available, and they want the Cilium ingress controller's Envoy listener reachable directly on the host network. After enabling host network mode via Helm, what happens to the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode?

options.text: It is automatically disabled, because the two modes are mutually exclusive.
It remains active and both modes serve traffic simultaneously on different ports.
It is converted into a shared Ingress listener on port 8080.
It is left untouched but must be disabled manually before host network mode takes effect.

explanation: The excerpt states that enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode, and that the two are mutually exclusive. No manual step is required, and the modes cannot run together.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the modes are mutually exclusive, so they cannot both serve traffic at once.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes converting the Service mode into a shared listener; the Service mode is simply disabled.
optionRationale.d: The disabling is automatic, not a manual prerequisite.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium ingress controller host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

stem: A cluster runs the Cilium ingress controller in dedicated mode, and several Ingress resources are deployed. An engineer creates a new Ingress resource for host network exposure but omits the per-Ingress host listener port annotation. What is the consequence according to the excerpt?

options.text: The annotation is mandatory in this situation, so the Ingress resource must set ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port.
The Ingress resource silently falls back to the shared listener on port 8080.
The Ingress resource inherits the port from ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort.
The Ingress resource is rejected only if the global mode is shared rather than dedicated.

explanation: The excerpt says the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation is mandatory if the global mode is configured to dedicated, or if the Ingress resource sets the loadbalancer-mode annotation to dedicated and multiple Ingress resources are deployed.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the annotation as mandatory in this case, not as having a silent fallback.
optionRationale.c: The sharedListenerPort Helm flag belongs to the shared Ingress method, not to the dedicated per-Ingress annotation.
optionRationale.d: The mandatory condition applies when the global mode is dedicated, which is the opposite of what this option claims.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: This annotation is mandatory if the global Cilium ingress controller mode is configured to ``dedicated`` (``ingressController.loadbalancerMode``) or the ingress resource sets the ``ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode`` annotation to ``dedicated`` and multiple ``Ingress`` resources are deployed.

stem: How does the excerpt distinguish the shared Ingress and dedicated Ingress methods for specifying host network ports?

options.text: Shared Ingress ports are set globally via Helm flags, while dedicated Ingress ports are set per Ingress resource via annotations.
Shared Ingress ports are set per Ingress resource via annotations, while dedicated Ingress ports are set globally via Helm flags.
Both methods use only the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation, differing solely in the port range.
Both methods use only Helm flags, differing solely in whether TLS passthrough is enabled.

explanation: The excerpt lists two methods: Shared Ingress, configured globally via Helm flags such as sharedListenerPort, httpPort, httpsPort and tlsPassthroughPort; and Dedicated Ingress, configured per Ingress resource via annotations such as ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the two methods as described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: The annotation belongs to the dedicated method only; the shared method uses Helm flags.
optionRationale.d: The shared method uses Helm flags, but the dedicated method uses annotations, not flags.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: * Shared Ingress: Globally via Helm flags

stem: An engineer changes ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort from its default to a custom value. What guidance does the excerpt give about the port number to choose?

options.text: Choose a port number higher than 1023, because of binding to a privileged port.
Choose a port number lower than 1023 so that it is reserved for the ingress controller.
Choose exactly 8080, since any other value is unsupported.
Choose any port, as the excerpt gives no constraint on the value.

explanation: The excerpt advises that if you change sharedListenerPort, you should choose a port number higher than 1023, referring to binding to a privileged port.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt advises a port higher than 1023, not lower.
optionRationale.c: 8080 is only the default; the excerpt explicitly contemplates changing it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does give a constraint: a port higher than 1023.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: If you change it, you should choose a port number higher than ``1023`` (see `Bind to privileged port`_).

stem: An engineer exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service in a cluster that uses kube-proxy, and the backend application must see the original client IP. Which Service setting does the excerpt say is the only way to ensure source IP visibility in this situation?

options.text: Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on the Service.
Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` on the Service.
Leave `externalTrafficPolicy` unset so that Kubernetes defaults it to `Local`.
Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` and disable the `healthCheckNodePort`.

explanation: The excerpt states that with `Local`, nodes route only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP, and that in clusters using `kube-proxy` this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

optionRationale.b: ``Cluster`` is described as allowing the node to masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say that leaving the field unset defaults it to ``Local``; it only describes the two relevant settings.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the ``healthCheckNodePort`` is automatically set by Kubernetes when ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` is set, and does not suggest disabling it.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
Because of this, in clusters that use
  ``kube-proxy``, this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium ingress configuration (Ingress and Gateway API) and wants the backend pod to keep the client IP visible. What does the excerpt say about the need to set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` for this purpose?

options.text: It is required, because Cilium forwards ingress traffic to Envoy using masquerading.
It is not necessary, because Cilium always forwards ingress traffic to the local node and to Envoy via TPROXY, and the source IP remains visible via `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address`.
It is required only for Gateway API, while Ingress works with `Cluster`.
It is not necessary, but only if the `healthCheckNodePort` is manually configured.

explanation: The excerpt says that for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, it is not necessary to configure `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod via the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` fields.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says ingress traffic is forwarded to Envoy using TPROXY, which transparently forwards packets, not masquerading.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt treats Ingress and Gateway API together and does not distinguish them on this point.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not make source IP visibility conditional on manually configuring the ``healthCheckNodePort``.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
However, for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, **it is not
necessary** to configure ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` to keep the source IP
visible to the backend pod

stem: An engineer writes an Egress Gateway policy whose egressGateway stanza specifies both egressIP: 192.0.2.10 and interface: eth0, together with a nodeSelector. What does Cilium do with this policy?

options.text: It ignores the policy because egressIP and interface cannot both be specified.
It uses egressIP and silently ignores the interface field.
It uses interface and silently ignores the egressIP field.
It accepts the policy but falls back to the interface with the default route.

explanation: The excerpt states that the egressIP and interface properties cannot both be specified in the egressGateway spec, and that Egress Gateway Policies containing both properties are ignored by Cilium. Cilium therefore does not choose one property over the other; the policy is not applied.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not give egressIP precedence; it says policies containing both properties are ignored by Cilium.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not give interface precedence; it says policies containing both properties are ignored by Cilium.
optionRationale.d: The default-route fallback applies when both egressIP and interface are omitted, not when both are specified.

citations.title: Selecting and configuring the gateway node
citations.quote: The ``egressIP`` and ``interface`` properties cannot both be specified in the ``egressGateway`` spec. Egress Gateway Policies that contain both of these properties will be ignored by Cilium.

stem: A cluster uses the `multi-pool` IPAM mode. Its `default` `CiliumPodIPPool` currently contains `10.10.0.0/16`, and running pods still hold addresses from that range. The platform team must change the pool to use `10.20.0.0/16`. According to the excerpt, what approach should they use?

options.text: Split the cluster into two node groups and migrate workloads from nodes using the old CIDR to nodes using the new CIDR.
Delete the `CiliumPodIPPool` and immediately recreate it with `10.20.0.0/16`; existing pods will keep working without further action.
Add `10.20.0.0/16` as an additional CIDR and leave `10.10.0.0/16` in place; no workload migration is needed.
Update the in-use CIDR in place and restart only the Cilium operator; pods will receive new addresses on their next restart.

explanation: The excerpt states that changing the CIDR of a pool requires re-assigning the IPs of existing workloads. It recommends achieving this by splitting the cluster into two node groups so that workloads can be migrated from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR. The restriction described prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes, so simply recreating or updating the pool in place is not the described approach.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that deleting and recreating the pool lets existing pods keep working without further action; it describes a migration process because existing workloads must be re-assigned IPs.
optionRationale.c: Extending a pool with new CIDRs is possible, but the objective here is to change the existing default pool CIDR, and the excerpt says the restriction prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe updating an in-use CIDR in place as sufficient; it says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use and gives a node-group migration procedure instead.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote:
To change the CIDR of a pool, you need to re-assign the IPs of existing workloads. To achieve this, you can split the cluster
into two node groups, which allows you to migrate the workloads from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR.

stem: An engineer maintains an existing `CiliumPodIPPools` resource that is already in use by pods. They want to add a new IPv6 CIDR to the pool. Which statement reflects the limitation described in the excerpt?

options.text: They may extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but they cannot delete or update CIDRs already in use.
They may delete an in-use CIDR once the pods using it have been cordoned, because cordoning releases the CIDR from the pool.
They may update an in-use CIDR in place, provided the Cilium operator is restarted first.
They cannot add any new CIDRs to an existing pool; a new `CiliumPodIPPools` resource must always be created.

explanation: The excerpt says it is possible to extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use. It also explains that this restriction prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that cordoning releases an in-use CIDR from the pool; it says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not permit updating an in-use CIDR in place after restarting the Cilium operator; it says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says it is possible to extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, so it is not true that no new CIDRs can be added to an existing pool.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote:
It is possible to extend the pool adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to
delete or update the CIDRs already in use.

stem: In cluster 1, the global Service rebel-base has service.cilium.io/global: "true" and service.cilium.io/affinity: "local". A client pod in cluster 1 repeatedly curls rebel-base while healthy local backends exist. What should you observe?

options.text: Replies come from pods in cluster 1 only while healthy local backends exist; remote endpoints are used only if all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy.
Traffic is split evenly between local and remote backends because the Global Service always load-balances across all clusters.
Replies come only from remote-cluster pods, because local affinity means the local cluster is avoided.
Replies come from local backends only, and remote backends are never used even if every local backend is unavailable or unhealthy.

explanation: The annotation value local makes the Global Service prefer healthy local backends. Remote endpoints are used only when all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy. The excerpt also notes that none is the default and means no preference, while remote prefers remote endpoints.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says load-balancing across multiple clusters might not be ideal and that local affinity restricts traffic to healthy local backends; it does not describe even splitting while local backends are healthy.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt defines local as preferring endpoints from the local cluster if available, not as avoiding the local cluster.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly allows remote endpoints if and only if all local backends are not available or unhealthy.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote:
For example, if the value of annotation ``service.cilium.io/affinity`` is local,
the Global Service will load-balance across healthy ``local`` backends, and only user
remote endpoints if and only if all of local backends are not available or unhealthy.

stem: An engineer enables IPsec transparent encryption on a cluster and immediately finds that the `cilium` Pods will not start. Following the troubleshooting guidance for this section, what should be double-checked first?

options.text: That the IPsec `Secret` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.
That the IPsec `Secret` is deployed in the same namespace as the application Pods whose traffic is being encrypted.
That the encryption interface has been pinned with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`.
That the number of keys in use equals 2 per remote node per enabled IP family.

explanation: The excerpt's first troubleshooting step covers exactly this symptom: if the `cilium` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, the thing to double-check is whether the IPsec `Secret` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together. The other checks in the excerpt address different symptoms — a missing device warning in the logs, the expected key count, and key rotation timing — and none of them is presented as the cause of Pods failing to start.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt pairs the IPsec ``Secret`` with Cilium's own namespace, not with the namespace of the workloads being encrypted.
optionRationale.c: Setting the encryption interface is the remedy for a ``Device eth0 does not exist`` warning in the logs, not for Pods that fail to start.
optionRationale.d: The key count is a health check performed with ``cilium-dbg encrypt status`` on a running Pod; it cannot be inspected while the Pods are not starting.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, double-check if
   the IPsec ``Secret`` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

stem: Cilium is running with IPsec encryption enabled. While reviewing the Cilium log files, an engineer finds a `level=warning` message reading `Device eth0 does not exist`. What does the excerpt say to do?

options.text: Set the encryption interface with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`.
Increase the delay before old key cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.
Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented.
Confirm that the IPsec `Secret` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

explanation: The excerpt instructs you to check for `level=warning` and `level=error` messages in the Cilium log files, and states that if there is a warning message similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`, you should use `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX` to set the encryption interface. The other options are remedies drawn from unrelated parts of the excerpt: key rotation timing, SPI handling for `XfrmInStateProtoError`, and the namespace check for Pods that fail to start.

optionRationale.b: The ``ipsec-key-rotation-duration`` flag is suggested for lengthening the delay before cleanup when key rotation is expected to take longer, not for a missing device warning.
optionRationale.c: A proper new key rotation is the fix given for ``XfrmInStateProtoError`` caused by a key update without an incremented SPI, a different symptom entirely.
optionRationale.d: The namespace check applies when the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption; here the Pods are running and logging a warning.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If there is a warning message similar to ``Device eth0 does not exist``,
     use ``--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`` to set the encryption
     interface.

stem: A Cluster Mesh deployment spanning several clusters is rotating its IPsec keys. Because every cluster must be updated, the rotation takes considerably longer than usual, and `XfrmInNoStates` errors start appearing. Which action does the excerpt recommend?

options.text: Increase the delay before cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.
Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented.
Take no action, because `XfrmInNoStates` counters are only expected to rise while a rebooted node's new key is being deployed.
Set the encryption interface with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`.

explanation: The excerpt explains that if the old key is cleaned up before the new key's configuration is installed on all nodes, `XfrmInNoStates` errors result, and that the old key is removed after a default interval of 5 minutes while agents normally update their configuration within 1 minute. Where the rotation is expected to take longer — the excerpt's own example being Cluster Mesh with several clusters to update — it recommends increasing the delay before cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.

optionRationale.b: A proper new key rotation is the stated fix for ``XfrmInStateProtoError`` arising from a key update without an incremented SPI, not for slow Cluster Mesh rotation.
optionRationale.c: Rising ``XfrmInNoStates`` counters during a node reboot are indeed expected, but the excerpt separately attributes ``XfrmInNoStates`` to premature cleanup of the old key after a rotation, which is the situation described here.
optionRationale.d: The encryption interface setting addresses a ``Device eth0 does not exist`` warning and has no bearing on key rotation timing.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If you expect
   the key rotation to take longer for some reason (for example, in the case of
   Cluster Mesh where several clusters need to be updated), you can increase the
   delay before cleanup with agent flag ``ipsec-key-rotation-duration``.

stem: In cluster 1, the rebel-base Service has been annotated with service.cilium.io/shared="false". An engineer in cluster 2 then runs kubectl exec -ti deployment/x-wing -- curl rebel-base. What should they observe?

options.text: Replies only from pods in cluster 2.
Replies from pods in both clusters.
Replies only from pods in cluster 1.
No replies from any pods.

explanation: The excerpt states that, after the annotation is added in cluster 1, accessing the global service from cluster 2 shows replies from pods only in cluster 2, because the global service in cluster 1 is no longer shared.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says that from cluster 2 the replies come only from cluster 2, not from both clusters.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says that the global service in cluster 1 is no longer shared, so cluster 1 pods do not reply to this request from cluster 2.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that replies are seen from pods in cluster 2, not that no pods reply.

citations.title: Deploying a Simple Example Service
citations.quote: You will see replies from pods only from cluster 2, as the global service in cluster 1 is no longer shared.

stem: An engineer has just added service.cilium.io/shared="false" to the rebel-base Service in cluster 1. Before removing the annotation, they run kubectl exec -ti deployment/x-wing -- curl rebel-base from cluster 1. What should they observe?

options.text: Replies from pods in both clusters.
Replies only from pods in cluster 1.
Replies only from pods in cluster 2.
No replies from any pods.

explanation: The excerpt states that, after the annotation is added in cluster 1, accessing the global service from cluster 1 still shows replies from pods in both clusters.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says that from cluster 1 the replies still come from both clusters, not only from cluster 1.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says that from cluster 1 the replies still come from both clusters, not only from cluster 2.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that replies are still seen from pods in both clusters, not that no pods reply.

citations.title: Deploying a Simple Example Service
citations.quote: You will still see replies from pods in both clusters.

stem: A platform engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy under the behaviour described in the excerpt. The egress rule uses toEndpoints with matchLabels name: rebel-base and does not include any cluster label or cluster match expression. Which endpoints will the policy select?

options.text: Endpoints named rebel-base in the local cluster only.
Endpoints named rebel-base in every cluster in the Cluster Mesh.
Endpoints named rebel-base in cluster2 only.
No endpoints, because a cluster label is mandatory for toEndpoints.

explanation: The excerpt states that policies automatically select endpoints from the local cluster only unless one or more clusters are specifically targeted. Therefore, a toEndpoints selector with only name: rebel-base selects local endpoints. The excerpt also notes that in Cilium v1.18 or lower, policies used to select endpoints from all clusters by default, but that is not the behaviour described for the current policy default.

optionRationale.b: Selecting endpoints from all clusters was the default in Cilium v1.18 or lower, not the behaviour described for the current policy default.
optionRationale.c: Targeting cluster2 only requires an explicit cluster label such as io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster: cluster2.
optionRationale.d: A cluster label is not mandatory; without one, the policy selects endpoints from the local cluster only.

citations.title: Allowing Specific Communication Between Clusters
citations.quote:
Policies automatically select endpoints from the local cluster only, unless one
or multiple cluster are specifically targeted.

stem: An engineer wants x-wing in the local cluster to contact rebel-base in any cluster, not only the local cluster. Which matchExpressions entry in the toEndpoints selector achieves this?

options.text: key: io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster, operator: Exists
key: io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster, operator: DoesNotExist
key: cluster-name, operator: Exists
matchLabels: io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster: cluster2

explanation: The excerpt shows that explicitly allowing communication to all clusters uses a matchExpressions entry with key io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster and operator Exists. This targets endpoints regardless of which cluster they belong to.

optionRationale.b: DoesNotExist would not match endpoints that carry the cluster label, so it does not express the all-clusters selector shown in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt uses io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster in the matchExpressions entry, not cluster-name.
optionRationale.d: Setting io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster: cluster2 targets cluster2 specifically, not all clusters.

citations.title: Allowing Specific Communication Between Clusters
citations.quote:
matchExpressions:
         - key: io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster
           operator: Exists

stem: A policy contains two `toPorts` entries. Both entries use the same `PortProtocol` and select an overlapping list of endpoints. The first entry defines HTTP layer 7 rules, while the second defines DNS layer 7 rules. What happens?

options.text: The policy is rejected because the layer 7 rule types differ.
The HTTP and DNS rules are combined and both are enforced.
The HTTP rules are kept and the DNS rules are silently ignored.
The DNS rules are kept and the HTTP rules are silently ignored.

explanation: The excerpt states that layer 7 rules from multiple `toPorts` entries with the same `PortProtocol` and overlapping endpoints are combined only when they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

optionRationale.b: Combining is permitted only when the layer 7 rules are of the same type; here the types differ.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe silently ignoring one type; a type difference causes rejection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe silently ignoring one type; a type difference causes rejection.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote: If multiple ``toPorts`` rules with identical ``PortProtocol`` select an overlapping list of endpoints, then the layer 7 rules are combined together if they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

stem: A policy contains a layer 4 rule for a set of endpoints and also a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules for the same endpoints. What is the effect of the layer 7 portion of the second rule?

options.text: It has no effect.
It is enforced in addition to the first layer 4 rule.
It overrides the first layer 4 rule and permits only matching layer 7 requests.
It causes the policy to be rejected because layer 4 and layer 7 rules cannot coexist.

explanation: The excerpt states that when a layer 4 rule is specified and a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules is also specified, the layer 7 portions of the latter rule have no effect.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the layer 7 portions have no effect, not that they are enforced in addition.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe the layer 7 portion overriding the first layer 4 rule.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say the policy is rejected; it says the layer 7 portions have no effect.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote: If a layer 4 rule is specified in the policy, and a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules is also specified, then the layer 7 portions of the latter rule will have no effect.

stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy has been applied that whitelists traffic sent from any pods with label org=empire to deathstar pods with label org=empire, class=deathstar on TCP port 80. A tiefighter pod carrying the label org=empire sends a POST request to deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/request-landing. What is the expected result?

options.text: The request succeeds and returns Ship landed.
The request is blocked because the policy matches endpoint IP addresses rather than pod labels.
The request hangs because Cilium connection tracking permits only reply packets, not the initial request.
The request succeeds only if the xwing pod is also labelled org=empire.

explanation: The excerpt states that the policy whitelists traffic from pods with label org=empire to deathstar pods with label org=empire, class=deathstar on TCP port 80. It then says that only the tiefighter pods with the label org=empire will succeed, while the xwing pods will be blocked. Therefore the tiefighter request succeeds and returns Ship landed.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies; matching is by pod labels.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes stateful connection tracking as automatically allowing required reply packets; it does not say the initial request is blocked.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says xwing pods will be blocked; the tiefighter request succeeds because the source pod has org=empire, not because xwing is labelled.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: Now if we run the landing requests again, only the *tiefighter* pods with the label ``org=empire`` will succeed. The *xwing* pods will be blocked!

stem: An engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy for pods that may be rescheduled to different nodes. They are deciding whether to select the pods by endpoint IP address or by pod label. What does the excerpt say they should do?

options.text: Use endpoint IP addresses, because they remain stable when pods are rescheduled.
Use the labels assigned to the pods, because endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant and policies are applied based on labels irrespective of where or when the pod is running.
Use the deathstar service DNS name, because Cilium policies match on service names rather than pod identity.
Use both endpoint IP addresses and pod labels, because Cilium requires an IP address in every policy rule.

explanation: The excerpt says that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies and that labels assigned to pods should be used instead. It adds that policies are applied to the right pods based on labels irrespective of where or when the pod is running within the cluster.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies, not stable selection keys.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt discusses pod labels and endpoint IP addresses; it does not say policies match on service DNS names.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says to use labels instead of endpoint IP addresses; it does not require both.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: When using Cilium, endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies. Instead, you can use the labels assigned to the pods to define security policies.

stem: A platform team has installed Cilium with the host firewall enabled and applied a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses a NodeSelector to select a group of worker nodes. On one of those selected nodes, two workloads send traffic to destinations outside the cluster: pod A runs with hostNetwork: true, while pod B runs in its own pod network namespace. How does the host policy treat these two flows?

options.text: Both flows are covered, because the policy selects the node on which both pods are running.
Pod A's traffic is covered, because host policies apply to the host namespace including host-networking pods; pod B's traffic to a location outside the cluster is not covered.
Neither flow is covered, because host policies apply only to the node's own host namespace and never to any pod.
Only pod B's traffic is covered, because host policies explicitly exclude host-networking pods from the host namespace.

explanation: A host policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses a NodeSelector, and it applies to all the nodes that selector picks. Within each selected node, however, its scope is the host namespace, which expressly includes host-networking pods. Communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside the cluster fall outside that scope, so pod B's flow is not governed by the host policy even though its node is selected.

optionRationale.a: Selecting the node is necessary but not sufficient: the policy's scope inside the node is the host namespace, so a pod in its own network namespace sending traffic outside the cluster is not covered.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that host policies apply to the host namespace 'including host-networking pods', so host-networking pod traffic is covered rather than excluded.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the opposite: host-networking pods are included in the host namespace, and it is non-host-networking pods talking to locations outside the cluster that are excluded.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote: Host policies apply to all the nodes selected by their NodeSelector. In each selected node, they apply only to the host namespace, including host-networking pods. They don't apply to communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside of the cluster.

stem: An engineer has a LoadBalancer Service with spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges populated. By default the CIDR restrictions apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the NodePort and ClusterIP services created alongside it. The engineer wants those CIDRs to filter traffic for all externally exposed service types as well. Which action does the excerpt describe for this?

options.text: Enable bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true in Helm.
Add the annotation service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer to the Service.
Set service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy to deny.
Remove spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges so that no restrictions are applied.

explanation: The excerpt says that by default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP service. It then states that propagating the white-listed CIDRs to all externally exposed service types can be enabled in Helm via bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.

optionRationale.b: The service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer annotation is described as a way to avoid the creation of corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services, not as a way to propagate the CIDRs to them.
optionRationale.c: Setting service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy to deny turns the CIDR list into a deny-list; it does not propagate the list to the other service types.
optionRationale.d: Removing spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges would leave the field empty, and the excerpt says that if the field is empty, no restrictions for the access will be applied.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote: This option can be enabled in Helm via ``bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true``.

stem: An engineer enables IPsec encryption in a Cilium cluster, and immediately afterwards the Cilium Pods fail to start. What should be checked first?

options.text: Whether the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together
Whether the agent flag ipsec-key-rotation-duration has been increased above its default
Whether the number of keys in use equals 2 per remote node per enabled IP family
Whether the decryption interface list includes all native devices that may receive pod traffic

explanation: The excerpt's first troubleshooting step for Cilium Pods that fail to start after enabling encryption is to double-check that the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together. The other checks concern key counts, decryption interfaces and key rotation timing, which are diagnostics for a running agent rather than for Pods that will not start.

optionRationale.b: The ipsec-key-rotation-duration flag is mentioned only as a way to increase the delay before old key cleanup, for example in Cluster Mesh; it is not a startup check.
optionRationale.c: The 2-keys-per-remote-node-per-IP-family figure is the expected value reported by cilium-dbg encrypt status on a running agent, not a reason for Pods failing to start.
optionRationale.d: The decryption interface list is verified with cilium-dbg encrypt status once the agent is running, so it cannot be the first check when the Pods do not start.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, double-check if
   the IPsec ``Secret`` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

stem: After enabling encryption, a Cilium Pod starts but its logs contain a warning similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`. How should this be addressed?

options.text: Set the encryption interface with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`
Increase the delay before old key cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`
Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented
Move the IPsec Secret into the same namespace as Cilium

explanation: The excerpt states that if there is a warning message similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`, the remedy is to use `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX` to set the encryption interface. The other options address different problems: key rotation timing, SPI mismatches and Secret placement.

optionRationale.b: The ipsec-key-rotation-duration flag controls how long before old keys are cleaned up after a rotation; it has nothing to do with a missing device warning.
optionRationale.c: A proper new key rotation is the fix given for XfrmInStateProtoError caused by a key update without incrementing the SPI, not for a missing interface warning.
optionRationale.d: Namespace co-location of the Secret and Cilium is the check for Pods that fail to start, not for a device warning in a running Pod's logs.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If there is a warning message similar to ``Device eth0 does not exist``,
     use ``--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`` to set the encryption
     interface.

stem: An operator inspects `cilium-dbg encrypt status` and sees a non-zero error counter. What does the command provide in that case?

options.text: Additional information is displayed with the specific errors the kernel encountered
The agent automatically performs a new key rotation to clear the errors
The command reports only the total count, with details available solely in the Cilium logs
The command lists the CiliumNode objects that have not yet been propagated

explanation: The excerpt states that if the error counter is non-zero, additional information will be displayed with the specific errors the kernel encountered. It does not describe any automatic remediation or CiliumNode listing by this command.

optionRationale.b: Nothing in the excerpt says the command triggers a key rotation; a proper new key rotation is a manual fix for certain XfrmInStateProtoError causes.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the opposite: additional information with the specific kernel errors is displayed when the counter is non-zero.
optionRationale.d: CiliumNode propagation is discussed in relation to `No node ID found` drops, not as output of cilium-dbg encrypt status.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If the error counter is non-zero, additional information will be displayed
with the specific errors the kernel encountered.

stem: A platform team is rolling out Cilium on a new cluster and wants Pod-level rate limiting in place from the start. What is the default state of the bandwidth manager on a fresh installation, and what must they do?

options.text: It is enabled by default, so no action is needed beyond annotating Pods.
It is disabled by default on new installations, so Cilium must be installed with the bandwidth manager enabled.
It is enabled by default only when BPF Host Routing is also enabled.
It is disabled by default and can only be turned on by chaining the bandwidth CNI plugin.

explanation: The excerpt states that the bandwidth manager is disabled by default on new installations, and that to install Cilium with it enabled you must install Cilium with the bandwidth manager enabled. Nothing in the excerpt makes it conditional on BPF Host Routing, and the bandwidth manager explicitly does not use CNI chaining.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the opposite: it is disabled by default on new installations.
optionRationale.c: BPF Host Routing is strongly recommended as a companion, but the excerpt does not make the default enablement conditional on it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining and does not use the bandwidth CNI plugin.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote: Cilium's bandwidth manager is disabled by default on new installations.

stem: An engineer is asked why Cilium's bandwidth manager does not simply use the Kubernetes bandwidth CNI plugin. Which explanation matches the excerpt?

options.text: The bandwidth CNI plugin is based on EDT, which is less scalable than the TBF approach Cilium uses.
The bandwidth CNI plugin cannot be used with Kubernetes Pod annotations at all.
The bandwidth CNI plugin is based on TBF rather than EDT, and there are scalability concerns in particular for multi-queue network interfaces.
The bandwidth CNI plugin only works in tunneling mode, whereas Cilium needs direct routing.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the bandwidth manager is natively integrated into Cilium and does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin, because of scalability concerns in particular for multi-queue network interfaces; that plugin is based on TBF (Token Bucket Filter) instead of EDT.

optionRationale.a: The comparison is inverted: the CNI plugin uses TBF, while Cilium uses EDT.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say the CNI plugin is incompatible with annotations; its stated reason is scalability and its TBF basis.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says bandwidth enforcement is supported for direct routing as well as tunneling mode, and gives no such limitation for the CNI plugin.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
Due to scalability concerns in particular for multi-queue network
interfaces, it is not recommended to use the bandwidth CNI plugin which is
based on TBF (Token Bucket Filter) instead of EDT.

stem: After enabling encryption, the Cilium Pods fail to start. Which two things should you first double-check according to the troubleshooting guidance?

options.text: That the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together
That the IPsec Secret is deployed in the kube-system namespace while Cilium runs in its own namespace
That the encryption interface has been set with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`
That `cilium-dbg encrypt status` reports a non-zero error counter

explanation: The excerpt's first troubleshooting step for Cilium Pods that fail to start after enabling encryption is to double-check whether the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt requires the Secret and Cilium to be in the same namespace; it does not name kube-system or describe separate namespaces.
optionRationale.c: Setting the encryption interface is the remedy for a `Device eth0 does not exist` warning in the logs, not the first check for Pods failing to start.
optionRationale.d: Running `cilium-dbg encrypt status` is a later diagnostic step, and a non-zero error counter relates to kernel XFRM errors, not to Pods failing to start.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, double-check if
   the IPsec ``Secret`` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

stem: A colleague reports that after a key rotation, `XfrmInStateProtoError` errors are appearing. According to the excerpt, which of the following can cause this error?

options.text: The kernel decrypted a packet and then failed to look up the route for it
The key was updated without incrementing the SPI, also called `KEYID`
A received packet matched an XFRM state that is being deleted
Cilium dropped packets that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text

explanation: The excerpt lists two causes for `XfrmInStateProtoError`: updating the key without incrementing the SPI (also called `KEYID`), and a mismatch between the anti-replay seq on the source node and the anti-reply oseq on the destination node. Both are fixed by properly performing a new key rotation.

optionRationale.a: This describes `XfrmFwdHdrError` and `XfrmInError`, which occur when the kernel fails to look up the route for a decrypted packet.
optionRationale.c: This describes `XfrmInStateInvalid`, which can happen when packets are received while an XFRM state is being deleted.
optionRationale.d: This describes `XfrmOutPolBlock`, where Cilium dropped packets that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
``XfrmInStateProtoError`` errors can happen for the following reasons:
   1. If the key is updated without incrementing the SPI (also called ``KEYID``
   in ipsec_key_rotation instructions above).

stem: A platform team has a global service in cluster 1 with `service.cilium.io/affinity` set to `local`. All local backends in cluster 1 are healthy. A client in cluster 1 curls the global service. What does it observe?

options.text: Replies come only from pods in cluster 1.
Replies come from pods in both clusters, evenly balanced.
Replies come only from pods in cluster 2.
The request fails because affinity is set to `local`.

explanation: With the annotation value `local`, the Global Service load-balances across healthy local backends and uses remote endpoints only if all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy. Since the local backends are healthy, the client in cluster 1 sees replies from cluster 1 pods only.

optionRationale.b: Balanced replies from both clusters are what you see when no affinity preference applies, not when `local` is set and local backends are healthy.
optionRationale.c: Replies from cluster 2 only would correspond to the `remote` preference, not `local`.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the request succeeding with replies from cluster 1; affinity is a preference, not a failure condition.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity

stem: After setting `service.cilium.io/affinity=local` in cluster 1, an engineer inspects endpoints with `cilium-dbg service list --clustermesh-affinity`. How are the local endpoints shown?

options.text: Marked as `(preferred)`.
Marked as `(active)` only, with no preference marker.
Removed from the list entirely.
Marked as `(unhealthy)`.

explanation: Step 4 of the excerpt says that from cluster 1 the local endpoints are marked as preferred, and the sample output shows `(active) (preferred)` entries.

optionRationale.b: The `(active)` marker appears on all backends; the distinguishing marker for this case is `(preferred)`.
optionRationale.c: The endpoints remain listed; they are annotated with a preference marker.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not use an `(unhealthy)` marker in this output.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote:
From cluster 1, check the service endpoints, the local endpoints are marked
   as preferred.

stem: How does the `local` affinity value differ from the `remote` affinity value?

options.text: `local` prefers endpoints from the local cluster if available; `remote` prefers endpoints from a remote cluster if available.
`local` disables cross-cluster load-balancing entirely; `remote` enables it.
`local` applies only to ClusterIP services; `remote` applies only to NodePort services.
`local` is the default; `remote` must be set through ServiceExport.

explanation: The commented example defines `local` as preferring endpoints from the local cluster if available and `remote` as preferring endpoints from a remote cluster if available.

optionRationale.b: Both values express a preference among endpoints; neither is described as disabling cross-cluster load-balancing.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt makes no such service-type distinction.
optionRationale.d: The default is `none`, not `local`.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote:
# - local
     #    preferred endpoints from local cluster if available
     # - remote
     #    preferred endpoints from remote cluster if available

stem: After the L7 policy is in place, an engineer runs `kubectl exec xwing -- curl -s -XPOST deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/request-landing` and receives no response. Why?

options.text: The L7 rule permits only POST /v1/request-landing, so xwing's request is rejected with `Access denied`.
Because the rule builds on the identity-aware rule, traffic from pods without the label org=empire continues to be dropped, causing the connection to time out.
The path matches the exact URL, so xwing must use the regular expression /v1/.* instead.
xwing is calling port 80 over TCP, which the policy does not list in its toPorts section.

explanation: The excerpt states that the L7 rule builds on the identity-aware rule, so traffic from pods without the label org=empire continues to be dropped, which causes the connection to time out.

optionRationale.a: `Access denied` is the L7 response given to tiefighter for a disallowed call; xwing never reaches the L7 stage because it lacks the required identity label.
optionRationale.c: The note about exact path matching and the /v1/.* regular expression concerns which URLs are allowed, not the identity-based drop applied to xwing.
optionRationale.d: Port 80 with protocol TCP is the port listed in the policy's toPorts section, so this is not the reason.

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote:
As this rule builds on the identity-aware rule, traffic from pods without the label
``org=empire`` will continue to be dropped causing the connection to time out

stem: An engineer wants tiefighter to be allowed to reach any URL under /v1/ on deathstar, not just one exact endpoint. According to the excerpt, how should the path be written in the policy?

options.text: path: "/v1/*"
path: "/v1/"

explanation: The excerpt explains that `path` matches the exact URL, and that to allow anything under /v1/ a regular expression must be used, given as `path: "/v1/.*"`.

optionRationale.a: A single asterisk form is not the regular expression shown in the excerpt for matching anything under /v1/.
optionRationale.b: A bare /v1/ path would match only that exact URL, which is the limitation the regular expression is meant to overcome.
optionRationale.d: A double-asterisk form does not appear in the excerpt; the documented regular expression is /v1/.*.

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote:
Note that ``path`` matches the exact url, if for example you want
to allow anything under /v1/, you need to use a regular expression

stem: Which statement best captures the security rationale the excerpt gives for applying HTTP-layer policy between microservices?

options.text: Each service that calls deathstar's API should be limited to making only the set of HTTP requests it requires for legitimate operation, enforcing least-privilege isolation.
Each service should be given full access to deathstar's API so that legitimate maintenance operations are never blocked.
Each service should be given no access at all to deathstar's API, since any HTTP call carries risk.
Each service should be allowed to call any URL on port 80 over TCP, provided it carries the org=empire label.

explanation: The excerpt states that to provide the strongest security, each service calling deathstar's API should be limited to only the HTTP requests it requires for legitimate operation, implementing a least-privilege approach.

optionRationale.b: Full access is described as the simple scenario that the L7 policy improves upon, not the recommended approach.
optionRationale.c: No access at all is the other extreme of the simple scenario, not the least-privilege recommendation.
optionRationale.d: Allowing any URL on port 80 would not limit the service to the requests it requires, so it does not implement least privilege.

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote:
each service that calls *deathstar's* API should be
limited to making only the set of HTTP requests it requires for legitimate
operation

stem: An engineer wants to inspect the applied L7 policy from the command line. Which command does the excerpt show for observing the L7 policy?

options.text: `kubectl describe ciliumnetworkpolicies`
`cilium-dbg monitor -v --type l7`
`cilium-dbg policy get`
`kubectl exec tiefighter -- curl -s -XPOST deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/request-landing`

explanation: The excerpt introduces the policy inspection with the words 'You can observe the L7 policy via `kubectl`' followed by the command `kubectl describe ciliumnetworkpolicies`, whose output shows the rule named rule1.

optionRationale.b: `cilium-dbg monitor -v --type l7` is presented separately as a way to monitor HTTP requests live, not to observe the policy itself.
optionRationale.c: `cilium-dbg policy get` is shown as the cilium-dbg CLI way of listing policy, introduced after the kubectl describe output rather than as the command the excerpt uses to observe the L7 policy.
optionRationale.d: This curl command tests whether a request is permitted; it does not display the policy.

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote: You can observe the L7 policy via ``kubectl``:

stem: In the policy output shown by `kubectl describe ciliumnetworkpolicies`, which HTTP method and path are permitted for tiefighter?

options.text: Method PUT with path /v1/exhaust-port
Method POST with path /v1/request-landing
Method POST with path /v1/.*
Method GET with path /v1/request-landing

explanation: The described policy shows, under Rules and Http, `Method: POST` and `Path: /v1/request-landing`, matching the excerpt's statement that tiefighter is limited to a POST /v1/request-landing call.

optionRationale.a: PUT /v1/exhaust-port is the maintenance call the policy explicitly disallows.
optionRationale.c: The /v1/.* regular expression is only mentioned as an example of how to allow anything under /v1/, not as the path in this policy.
optionRationale.d: The method in the policy output is POST, not GET.

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote:
Method:  POST
           Path:    /v1/request-landing

stem: An engineer wants to watch HTTP requests being made through the policy in real time. Which approach does the excerpt present for this?

options.text: Running `kubectl describe ciliumnetworkpolicies` and reading the Events section.
Running `cilium-dbg policy get` and reading the Revision number.
Running `cilium-dbg monitor` with the `-v --type l7` flags.
Running `kubectl exec tiefighter -- curl -s -XPUT deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/exhaust-port`.

explanation: The excerpt states that it is also possible to monitor the HTTP requests live by using `cilium-dbg monitor`, and shows the invocation with `-v --type l7`.

optionRationale.a: `kubectl describe ciliumnetworkpolicies` displays the policy definition, and its Events section shows `<none>`; it is not the live monitoring tool.
optionRationale.b: `cilium-dbg policy get` lists the policy and its revision, not a live stream of HTTP requests.
optionRationale.d: The curl command generates a single request; it does not monitor requests live.

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote: It is also possible to monitor the HTTP requests live by using ``cilium-dbg monitor``:

stem: You maintain a CiliumPodIPPool named `default` in a cluster running in `multi-pool` IPAM mode. You want to add a second IPv4 CIDR to the pool so that new pods can draw addresses from a wider range. What does the excerpt say is permitted?

options.text: You can extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but you cannot delete or update CIDRs already in use.
You can freely add, delete and update any CIDRs in the pool, provided you restart the Cilium operator afterwards.
You cannot add new CIDRs at all; the only supported change is to delete CIDRs that are no longer in use.
You can add new CIDRs only after deleting the existing CiliumPodIPPool and letting `autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools` recreate it.

explanation: The excerpt states that extending the pool with new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs is possible, but deleting or updating CIDRs already in use is not. The restriction exists to prevent pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use, so unrestricted editing is wrong.
optionRationale.c: This inverts the rule: adding CIDRs is the permitted operation, not the forbidden one.
optionRationale.d: Deleting and recreating via `autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools` is mentioned only as an alternative route for updating an existing pool, not as a precondition for adding CIDRs.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote:
It is possible to extend the pool adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to

stem: An engineer writes a CiliumNetworkPolicy rule that contains neither an ingress section nor an egress section, but does set an endpointSelector. What is the effect of this rule?

options.text: It has no effect, because both ingress and egress are omitted.
It denies all traffic to and from the selected endpoints.
It allows all traffic to and from the selected endpoints.
It is rejected because at least one of ingress or egress is mandatory.

explanation: The excerpt states that either ingress, egress, or both can be provided, and that if both are omitted the rule has no effect. A rule with only a selector therefore does nothing.

optionRationale.b: The whitelist model means non-matching traffic is dropped pursuant to the enforcement modes, but an empty rule does not itself impose a deny; the excerpt says it has no effect.
optionRationale.c: An empty rule does not allow traffic; the excerpt explicitly says it has no effect.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say a rule is rejected for lacking ingress and egress; it says the rule has no effect.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote:
Either ingress, egress, or both can be
provided. If both ingress and egress are omitted, the rule has no effect.

stem: A policy contains two rules: one matches a narrow set of traffic and another matches a broader set that includes the narrow one. What does Cilium allow?

options.text: Only the traffic matching the narrow rule, since the broader rule is redundant.
All traffic matching the broader rule.
Only traffic matching the intersection of the two rules.
Nothing, because overlapping rules conflict and are dropped.

explanation: Under the whitelist model, if one rule matches a broader set of traffic than another, all traffic matching the broader rule is allowed. Overlap does not create a conflict.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the broader rule's traffic is allowed, not that the narrow rule takes precedence.
optionRationale.c: The intersection is not the deciding factor here; the excerpt says traffic matching the broader rule is allowed.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes no conflict or drop for overlapping rules; it describes the union being allowed.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote:
If two rules exist, and one
would match a broader set of traffic, then all traffic matching the broader
rule will be allowed.

stem: Two policy rules partially overlap, so some traffic matches rule one, some matches rule two, and some matches both. Which traffic is allowed?

options.text: Only traffic matching both rules simultaneously.
Only traffic matching exactly one of the two rules.
Traffic matching the union of the two rules.
No traffic, until the overlap is resolved.

explanation: The excerpt states that if there is an intersection between two or more rules, traffic matching the union of those rules will be allowed.

optionRationale.a: That describes the intersection, but the excerpt says the union is allowed.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not restrict allowance to traffic matching exactly one rule.
optionRationale.d: There is no requirement to resolve overlap; the union is simply allowed.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote:
If there is an intersection between two or more rules,
then traffic matching the union of those rules will be allowed.

stem: Traffic arrives at an endpoint and matches none of the rules in the applicable policy. What happens to it?

options.text: It is allowed, because the whitelist model only restricts matched traffic.
It is dropped pursuant to the `policy_enforcement_modes`.
It is logged and then allowed by default.
It is queued until a matching rule is added.

explanation: The excerpt says that if traffic does not match any of the rules, it will be dropped pursuant to the `policy_enforcement_modes`.

optionRationale.a: The whitelist model means only matching traffic is allowed; non-matching traffic is dropped.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt mentions no log-then-allow behaviour; it says the traffic is dropped.
optionRationale.d: There is no queuing behaviour described in the excerpt.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote:
Finally, if
traffic does not match any of the rules, it will be dropped pursuant to the
`policy_enforcement_modes`.

stem: An engineer wants to apply a rule to nodes rather than endpoints. Which selector must be used, and where can it be used?

options.text: `EndpointSelector`, in any CiliumNetworkPolicy.
`NodeSelector`, only in CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicies.
`NodeSelector`, in any CiliumNetworkPolicy.
`EndpointSelector`, only in CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicies.

explanation: The excerpt states that `NodeSelector` selects all nodes subject to the rule and can only be used in CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicies.

optionRationale.a: `EndpointSelector` selects endpoints, not nodes.
optionRationale.c: `NodeSelector` is restricted to CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicies, not any policy.
optionRationale.d: `EndpointSelector` selects endpoints, and the restriction to clusterwide policies applies to `NodeSelector`.

stem: A rule specifies both an `EndpointSelector` and a `NodeSelector`. What does the excerpt say about this?

options.text: It is valid, and the rule applies to both endpoints and nodes.

They are mutually exclusive and cannot both be empty.
It is valid only in CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicies.

optionRationale.a: The two selectors are mutually exclusive, so a rule cannot apply to both.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe silently ignoring one selector; it says they are mutually exclusive.

EndpointSelector and NodeSelector cannot be both empty and

stem: An engineer wants to be able to list and delete policy rules later by a chosen identifier. Which field of the rule should be used?

options.text: `Description`
`Labels`
`Ingress`
`EndpointSelector`

optionRationale.a: `Description` is a free form string not interpreted by Cilium, and rules cannot be identified by comment.
optionRationale.c: `Ingress` holds the ingress rules, not an identifier for listing or deleting.
optionRationale.d: `EndpointSelector` selects the endpoints the rule applies to, not an identifier for the rule.

stem: A NetworkPolicy is imported into Cilium via Kubernetes. What label is automatically assigned to the resulting policy rule?

`io.cilium.k8s.policy.namespace=NAME`, where `NAME` is the resource name.
`io.cilium.k8s.policy.description=NAME`, where `NAME` is the resource name.
No label is assigned automatically; the user must add one.

explanation: The excerpt states that policy rules imported via Kubernetes automatically get the label `io.cilium.k8s.policy.name=NAME` assigned, where `NAME` corresponds to the name specified in the resource.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives the label key as `io.cilium.k8s.policy.name`, not a namespace key.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt gives the label key as `io.cilium.k8s.policy.name`, not a description key.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the label is assigned automatically on import.

stem: An engineer adds a `Description` to a policy rule and later tries to identify the rule by that comment. What does the excerpt say?

The description is a free form string not interpreted by Cilium, and rules cannot be identified by comment.
The description is converted into a label automatically.
The description must be unique across all rules.

explanation: The excerpt says the description is a string which is not interpreted by Cilium, can be used to describe intent and scope in human readable form, and that rules cannot be identified by comment.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly says the description is not interpreted by Cilium and rules cannot be identified by comment.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes no conversion of description into a label; labels are a separate field.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt imposes no uniqueness requirement on the description.

stem: Which statement best describes the model on which all policy rules are based?

options.text: A blacklist model, where each rule blocks traffic that matches it.
A whitelist model, where each rule allows traffic that matches it.
A priority model, where the first matching rule wins.
A quota model, where each rule limits traffic volume.

explanation: The excerpt opens by stating that all policy rules are based upon a whitelist model, in which each rule allows traffic that matches the rule.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes a whitelist, not a blacklist, model.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes union of matching rules, not first-match priority.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about traffic volume limits.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote:
All policy rules are based upon a whitelist model, that is, each rule in the
policy allows traffic that matches the rule.

`kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg service list | grep KubeProxyReplacement`

optionRationale.b: `cilium-dbg service list` is used later to validate that the eBPF kube-proxy replacement created the NodePort service; it is not the command given for checking the replacement mode.
optionRationale.c: `--verbose` is offered for full details, but the excerpt does not pair it with grepping for `KUBE-SVC`; that string appears in the `iptables-save` check.
optionRationale.d: `iptables-save` is run in the host namespace to confirm that no `iptables` rule for the service is present, not to check the replacement mode.

`iptables-save | grep KUBE-SVC`

stem: A layer 7 rule set contains several application protocol rules. Under what condition is a layer 7 request permitted?

options.text: Only if every rule in the list matches the request.
If at least one of the rules matches the request.
Only if the request matches the first rule in the list.
Only if the request matches none of the rules, since the rules are deny lists.

explanation: Each member of `L7Rules` consists of a list of application protocol rules, and a layer 7 request is permitted if at least one of the rules matches.

optionRationale.a: The requirement is at least one match, not a match of every rule.
optionRationale.c: There is no first-match-only semantics described.
optionRationale.d: The rules are not described as deny lists; a match permits the request.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote:
Each member consists of a list of application protocol rules. A layer 7
request is permitted if at least one of the rules matches.

stem: A `toPorts` entry selects a port but specifies no layer 7 rules at all. How is traffic on that port treated?

options.text: All traffic is permitted.
All traffic is denied.
Only HTTP traffic is permitted.
The policy is rejected for having an empty rule set.

explanation: The excerpt states that if no rules are specified, then all traffic is permitted. The Go comment likewise notes that if none of the port level rule types are set, no additional port level rules are applied.

optionRationale.b: An empty rule set does not deny traffic; it permits all of it.
optionRationale.c: No protocol-specific restriction is applied when no rules are specified.
optionRationale.d: An empty rule set is allowed and simply applies no additional port level rules.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote:
If no rules are
specified, then all traffic is permitted.

stem: A request violates an enforced layer 7 policy. What does Cilium do, where possible?

options.text: It always drops the packet silently with no response.
It crafts an application protocol specific access denied message, such as an HTTP 403 or a DNS REFUSED response.
It resets the TCP connection and returns an HTTP 500 error.
It redirects the request to the Cilium agent pod for logging.

explanation: The excerpt states that a violation does not result in packet drops; instead, if possible, an application protocol specific access denied message is crafted and returned, giving an HTTP 403 for HTTP requests or a DNS REFUSED response for DNS requests.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly says the result is not packet drops.
optionRationale.c: No TCP reset or HTTP 500 is described; the example given is HTTP 403.
optionRationale.d: No redirection to the agent pod for logging is described.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote:
not result in packet drops. Instead, if possible, an application
          protocol specific access denied message is crafted and returned, e.g.
          an *HTTP 403 access denied* is sent back for HTTP requests which
          violate the policy, or a *DNS REFUSED* response for DNS requests.

stem: An engineer wants to add layer 7 rules to a `HostPolicies` entry. Which layer 7 rule type is currently functional there?

optionRationale.c: Only DNS is functional; HTTP cannot be specified in `HostPolicies`.

stem: An engineer wants to write a policy that restricts traffic in the host namespace of a set of nodes, selecting those nodes by label. Which resource form does the excerpt say host policies take?

A CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy with a NodeSelector instead of an EndpointSelector
A CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy with an EndpointSelector instead of a NodeSelector
A CiliumNetworkPolicy with a nodeName field in place of a selector

explanation: The excerpt states that host policies take the form of a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy with a NodeSelector instead of an EndpointSelector. The cluster-wide scope and the substitution of NodeSelector for EndpointSelector are both required.

optionRationale.a: The resource kind is wrong: the excerpt specifies CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy, not the namespaced CiliumNetworkPolicy.
optionRationale.c: This inverts the substitution: the NodeSelector replaces the EndpointSelector, not the other way round.
optionRationale.d: No nodeName field is mentioned; the excerpt describes a NodeSelector.

stem: A cluster administrator has written a host policy that selects a group of worker nodes. Which traffic does that policy govern on each selected node?

options.text: All traffic on the node, including communications between non-host-networking pods and destinations outside the cluster
Only traffic in the host namespace, including host-networking pods, and not communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside the cluster
Only traffic between non-host-networking pods and locations outside the cluster
Only traffic originating from the Cilium agent itself on the node

explanation: The excerpt says host policies apply to all nodes selected by their NodeSelector, and in each selected node they apply only to the host namespace, including host-networking pods. It explicitly excludes communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside the cluster.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly excludes communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside the cluster, so the policy is not all-encompassing.
optionRationale.c: This is precisely the traffic the excerpt says host policies do not apply to.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt scopes the policy to the host namespace including host-networking pods, not to the Cilium agent alone.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote:
In
each selected node, they apply only to the host namespace, including
host-networking pods. They don't apply to communications between
non-host-networking pods and locations outside of the cluster.

stem: You are validating WireGuard encryption on a three-node cluster. You open a bash shell in a Cilium pod and run `cilium-dbg status | grep Encryption`. Which output indicates that WireGuard has been enabled correctly?

options.text: `Encryption: Wireguard [cilium_wg0 (Pubkey: <..>, Port: 51871, Peers: 2)]`
`Encryption: Wireguard [cilium_wg0 (Pubkey: <..>, Port: 51871, Peers: 3)]`
`Encryption: Wireguard [cilium_wg0 (Pubkey: <..>, Port: 51871, Peers: 0)]`
`Encryption: Disabled`

explanation: The excerpt states that the number of peers should correspond to the number of nodes subtracted by one. On a three-node cluster that is two peers, which matches the sample output showing `Peers: 2`.

optionRationale.b: This equals the full node count rather than the node count minus one, so it does not match the stated expectation.
optionRationale.c: Zero peers would not correspond to a number of nodes subtracted by one on a three-node cluster.
optionRationale.d: This reports encryption as disabled, which contradicts the goal of confirming WireGuard is enabled.

citations.title: Validate the Setup

Check that WireGuard has been enabled (number of peers should correspond to

stem: A platform team creates a LoadBalancer service with spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges set to 192.168.1.0/24. A pod in the same cluster then connects to the service's ClusterIP. What does Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement do with the source-range field for that connection?

options.text: It ignores the field, so the pod can access the service internally.
It drops the connection because the pod's IP is not in 192.168.1.0/24.
It applies the field only if the pod's IP falls outside the cluster CIDR.
It rewrites the source ranges to the pod CIDR before evaluating the connection.

explanation: The excerpt states that when the service is accessed from inside the cluster, the kube-proxy replacement ignores the field whether or not it is set, so any pod or host process in the cluster can reach the LoadBalancer service internally.

optionRationale.b: The field is ignored for in-cluster access, so it cannot cause a drop for a pod connection.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt makes no distinction based on whether the pod IP is inside or outside the cluster CIDR; the field is simply ignored for internal access.
optionRationale.d: No rewriting of source ranges is described; the field is ignored for internal access.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote:
When accessing the service from inside a cluster, the kube-proxy replacement will
ignore the field regardless whether it is set.

stem: A team wants the CIDR list in loadBalancerSourceRanges to block traffic from certain CIDRs while allowing everything else. Which annotation and value achieve this?

options.text: service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny
service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: allow
service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer
bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true

explanation: Cilium supports turning the list into a deny-list through the service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy annotation, which accepts allow or deny; setting it to deny blocks traffic from the listed CIDRs while allowing the rest.

optionRationale.b: The allow value is the default behaviour, which treats the list as an allow-list rather than a deny-list.
optionRationale.c: The service.cilium.io/type annotation is used to avoid creating corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services, not to invert the CIDR policy.
optionRationale.d: bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes is a Helm option that propagates the CIDRs to all externally exposed service types; it does not turn the list into a deny-list.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote:
This
behavior can be achieved through the ``service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy``
annotation which accepts the values of ``allow`` or ``deny``.

stem: A cluster operator wants the white-listed CIDRs to be enforced not only on the LoadBalancer service but also on the NodePort and ClusterIP service types that are externally exposed. Which Helm setting enables this?

options.text: bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true
service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny
service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer
spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges with an empty list

optionRationale.b: The src-ranges-policy annotation switches between allow and deny semantics; it does not propagate the CIDRs to other service types.
optionRationale.c: The service.cilium.io/type annotation is used to avoid creating the corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services, the opposite of propagating ranges to them.
optionRationale.d: An empty loadBalancerSourceRanges means no restrictions are applied, not that ranges are propagated to other types.

citations.quote: This option can be enabled in Helm via ``bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true``.
