stem: Which statement best describes the default interpretation of loadBalancerSourceRanges in Cilium?

options.text: It specifies an allow-list of CIDRs, so traffic not originating from those CIDRs is automatically dropped.
It specifies a deny-list of CIDRs, so traffic from those CIDRs is dropped and everything else is allowed.
It specifies a list of CIDRs that are exempt from all Cilium policy enforcement.
It specifies a list of CIDRs that are only used for NodePort services.

explanation: The excerpt states that loadBalancerSourceRanges by default specifies an allow-list of CIDRs, meaning traffic originating not from those CIDRs is automatically dropped.

optionRationale.b: Deny-list behaviour is opt-in via the service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny annotation, not the default.
optionRationale.c: The field filters traffic by source IP; it does not exempt CIDRs from policy enforcement.

stem: An operator has set both `spec.eni.subnet-ids` and `spec.eni.subnet-tags` on the CiliumNode resource. How does the operator treat these two fields when narrowing the candidate subnets?

options.text: It uses `subnet-ids` and ignores `subnet-tags` entirely.
It uses `subnet-tags` and ignores `subnet-ids` entirely.
It requires a subnet to appear in `subnet-ids` and also match all `subnet-tags`.
It rejects the configuration and allocates no ENI until one field is removed.

explanation: The excerpt states that when `subnet-ids` is set, `subnet-tags` are ignored, so only the ID list governs candidacy.

optionRationale.b: The precedence runs the other way: it is `subnet-tags` that are ignored when `subnet-ids` is set.
optionRationale.c: That describes an intersection of both filters, but the excerpt says `subnet-tags` are ignored once `subnet-ids` is set.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes no rejection behaviour; it simply gives `subnet-ids` precedence.

stem: A CiliumNode has `spec.eni.security-groups` populated with a list of Security Group IDs, and `spec.eni.security-group-tags` is also populated. Which Security Groups are attached to the newly created ENI?

options.text: The IDs listed in `spec.eni.security-groups`.
The Security Groups in the account matching `spec.eni.security-group-tags`.
The Security Group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.
The union of the IDs in `spec.eni.security-groups` and the tag-matched Security Groups.

explanation: The excerpt gives a strict order: `spec.eni.security-groups` is consulted first, and if set those are the IDs attached, so the tag field is never reached.

optionRationale.b: Tag matching is only consulted when `spec.eni.security-groups` is not set.
optionRationale.c: Inheriting from `eth0` is the last resort, used only when neither of the other fields is set.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes a precedence order, not a union of the two sources.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
The field ``spec.eni.security-groups`` is consulted first. If this is set
    then these will be the Security Group IDs attached to the newly created ENI.

stem: Neither `spec.eni.security-groups` nor `spec.eni.security-group-tags` is set on the CiliumNode. What Security Groups does the newly created ENI receive?

options.text: It inherits the security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.
It is created with the account's default Security Group.
It is created with no Security Groups attached.
It inherits the security group IDs of the primary ENI of another node in the same subnet.

explanation: The third step of the computation states that when none of the fields are set, the ENI inherits the security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names `eth0` inheritance, not the account default Security Group.
optionRationale.c: An ENI with no Security Groups is not described; inheritance from `eth0` is the stated outcome.
optionRationale.d: Inheritance is from `eth0` of the same instance, not from another node.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
Finally if none of the above fields are set then the newly created ENI will
    inherit the security group IDs of ``eth0`` of the instance.

stem: An operator wants the operator to attach Security Groups to new ENIs by matching tags rather than by listing IDs. Which field should be set, and what does the operator do with it?

options.text: Set `spec.eni.security-group-tags`; the operator lists all Security Groups in the account and attaches the ones matching the tags.
Set `spec.eni.security-group-tags`; the operator attaches only the single Security Group whose tags match most closely.
Set `spec.eni.security-groups`; the operator interprets the entries as tag filters.
Set `spec.eni.subnet-tags`; the operator derives Security Groups from the matching subnets.

explanation: The excerpt says that if `spec.eni.security-group-tags` is set, the operator lists all Security Groups in the account and attaches the ones matching the list of tags.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes attaching all matching Security Groups, not a single best match.
optionRationale.c: `spec.eni.security-groups` holds Security Group IDs, not tag filters.
optionRationale.d: `spec.eni.subnet-tags` narrows subnets and has nothing to do with Security Group selection.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
The field ``spec.eni.security-group-tags`` is consulted. If this is set then
    the operator will list all Security Groups in the account and will attach to
    the ENI the ones that match the list of tags passed.

stem: Which AWS API calls does the operator use to create and attach the ENI to the EC2 instance?

options.text: `CreateNetworkInterface` and `AttachNetworkInterface`.
`CreateNetworkInterface` and `AssociateAddress`.
`RunInstances` and `AttachNetworkInterface`.
`CreateSubnet` and `CreateNetworkInterface`.

explanation: The excerpt states that the ENI is created and attached using the `CreateNetworkInterface` and `AttachNetworkInterface` API calls.

optionRationale.b: `AssociateAddress` is not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: `RunInstances` is not mentioned; the instance already exists.
optionRationale.d: `CreateSubnet` is not mentioned; subnets are selected, not created.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
The ENI is then created and attached to the EC2 instance using the
``CreateNetworkInterface`` and ``AttachNetworkInterface`` API calls.

stem: A platform team runs a selectorless Service backed by two manually managed EndpointSlice objects. They annotate the first slice with `service.cilium.io/weight: "70"` and the second with `service.cilium.io/weight: "30"`, but the Service uses the default load-balancing algorithm rather than Maglev. What happens to the weights?

options.text: The weights are honoured regardless of algorithm, so traffic splits roughly 70/30.
The weights are only honoured when the Service uses Maglev, so they are not applied.
The weights are rejected and the EndpointSlices are deleted.
The weights are converted into Maglev hash seeds automatically.

explanation: The excerpt states that weights are only honoured for the Service referenced by the EndpointSlice when it uses the Maglev load-balancing algorithm, whether configured globally or selected per service. Without Maglev, the weights are not applied.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly conditions weight honouring on Maglev, so an algorithm-independent split is wrong.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt says EndpointSlices are deleted for using weights.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt never mentions converting weights into hash seeds.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
Weights are only honored for the Service referenced by that ``EndpointSlice``
when it uses the Maglev load-balancing algorithm, whether Maglev is configured
globally or selected per service through ``service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm``.

stem: An engineer wants to select Maglev for a single Service using the `service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm` annotation rather than configuring Maglev globally. Which prerequisite does the excerpt identify?

options.text: `bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true` must be set.
The Service must be of type NodePort.
The EndpointSlices must all carry weight `100`.
The Service must have a selector.

explanation: The excerpt says per-service algorithm selection requires `bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true`.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not tie per-service algorithm selection to the NodePort type.
optionRationale.c: Weights are relative and need not add up to 100, and no such prerequisite is stated.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the feature as primarily intended for selectorless Services, so a selector is not a prerequisite.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote: Per-service algorithm selection requires ``bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true``.

stem: A Service is backed by two EndpointSlices with weights `70` and `30`. Later, the second EndpointSlice is changed from weight `30` to weight `0`. What is the effect on traffic?

options.text: The second slice's backends are removed immediately and existing connections are reset.
The second slice's backends enter maintenance: existing connections continue, but new traffic goes entirely to the first slice.
The weight `0` is treated as invalid and ignored, so the split stays 70/30.
New traffic is split evenly between both slices.

explanation: A weight of `0` marks those backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue while new traffic is steered to other backends. The excerpt confirms the first slice then receives 100% of the new traffic share.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says existing connections can continue, not that they are reset.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says invalid values are ignored, but `0` is a valid value with a defined maintenance meaning.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states new traffic is steered entirely to the remaining non-maintenance backends.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
A weight of ``0`` marks those
backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue
while new traffic is steered to other backends.

stem: Which annotation assigns a backend weight on a per-EndpointSlice basis?

options.text: `service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm`
`service.cilium.io/weight`
`kubernetes.io/service-name`
`discovery.k8s.io/weight`

explanation: The excerpt states that backend weights can be assigned on a per-EndpointSlice basis through the `service.cilium.io/weight` annotation.

optionRationale.a: That annotation selects the load-balancing algorithm per service, not the weight.
optionRationale.c: That is a label used to associate the EndpointSlice with a Service in the example.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt never mentions this annotation.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
Backend weights can be assigned on a per-``EndpointSlice`` basis through the
``service.cilium.io/weight`` annotation.

stem: What is the valid range for the `service.cilium.io/weight` annotation value?
explanation: The excerpt states that valid values range from `0` to `65535`.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says weights are relative and do not need to add up to 100, and gives a wider range.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt includes `0` as valid, with a maintenance meaning.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt gives `65535` as the upper bound, not `255`.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote: Valid values range from ``0`` to ``65535``.

stem: Two EndpointSlices for a Service carry weights `70` and `30`. An engineer assumes the weights must total `100` and plans to rescale them. What does the excerpt say about this?

options.text: Weights are relative and do not need to add up to `100`.
Weights must always total exactly `100`.
Weights must total `65535`.
Weights are absolute connection counts.

explanation: The excerpt states that weights are relative and do not need to add up to `100`.

optionRationale.b: This contradicts the excerpt's statement that weights are relative.
optionRationale.c: `65535` is the upper bound of a single weight value, not a required total.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes weights as relative, not as absolute connection counts.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote: Weights are relative and do not need to add up to ``100``.

stem: A single EndpointSlice contains two endpoints, `10.0.0.11` and `10.0.0.12`, and is annotated with `service.cilium.io/weight: "70"`. How does the weight apply?

options.text: It applies only to the first endpoint in the slice.
It applies to all backends in that EndpointSlice.
It is divided evenly between the two endpoints.
It applies only to endpoints that also carry the annotation.

explanation: The excerpt states that the configured weight applies to all backends in a given EndpointSlice.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the weight applies to all backends, not just the first.
optionRationale.c: No division between endpoints is described.
optionRationale.d: The annotation is on the EndpointSlice, not on individual endpoints.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote: The configured weight applies to all backends in a given ``EndpointSlice``.

stem: For which kind of Service does the excerpt say the annotation-based weighting is primarily intended?

options.text: Selectorless Services backed by multiple manually managed EndpointSlice objects.
Services of type LoadBalancer with automatic endpoint management.
Headless Services with a single EndpointSlice.
Services using the random load-balancing algorithm.

explanation: The excerpt says the feature is primarily intended for selectorless Services backed by multiple manually managed EndpointSlice objects, where each EndpointSlice can assign a different weight.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not mention LoadBalancer Services or automatic endpoint management.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes multiple EndpointSlice objects, not a single one.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt ties weight honouring to Maglev, not the random algorithm.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
This is primarily intended for selectorless Services backed by multiple
manually managed ``EndpointSlice`` objects, where each ``EndpointSlice`` can
assign a different weight to the backends it contributes to the Service.

stem: You are configuring a Cluster Mesh with Helm and want to avoid repeating the same remote-cluster information in every cluster's values file. You therefore place all remote clusters in a single `clusters.yaml` file that every cluster's values file references. What does the excerpt say makes this possible?

options.text: Cilium ignores the local cluster from the list of remote clusters.
Cilium automatically rewrites the cluster list at install time to remove duplicates.
The Helm chart merges all values files into one and applies it only to the first cluster.
Cilium requires the local cluster to be listed first, so the remaining entries can be shared.

explanation: The excerpt states that a shared `clusters.yaml` holding all remote clusters works because Cilium ignores the local cluster from the list of remote clusters, so the same list can be reused in each cluster's values file.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe any rewriting or de-duplication of the cluster list; it attributes the behaviour to Cilium ignoring the local cluster.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt says values files are merged and applied to only the first cluster; the point is that the same information need not be repeated.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not require the local cluster to be listed first; it says the local cluster is ignored from the list of remote clusters.

citations.title: Configure Cluster Mesh with Helm
citations.quote:
The ``clusters.yaml`` file contains all the remote clusters so that you don't
have to repeat the same information in every cluster's values file. Note that
this is possible since Cilium ignores the local cluster from the list of remote
clusters.

stem: An engineer must expose the Cluster Mesh control plane and wants a stable LoadBalancer IP, which the excerpt describes as typically the best option. Which value of `clustermesh.apiserver.service.type` should be used?

options.text: NodePort
ClusterIP
LoadBalancer
ExternalName

explanation: Among the listed values, LoadBalancer uses a stable LoadBalancer IP and is described as typically the best option, which matches the engineer's requirement.

optionRationale.a: NodePort requires stable Node IPs and may force the Cluster Mesh to reconnect to a different node if a node disappears.
optionRationale.b: ClusterIP requires the ClusterIPs to be routable between clusters, which the excerpt says is typically only available via the helm chart installation method.
optionRationale.d: ExternalName is not among the values listed for ``clustermesh.apiserver.service.type`` in the excerpt.

citations.title: Configure Cluster Mesh with Helm
citations.quote:
LoadBalancer:
        A Kubernetes service of type LoadBalancer is used to expose the control
        plane. This uses a stable LoadBalancer IP and is typically the best option.

stem: A team exposes the Cluster Mesh control plane with a NodePort service. According to the excerpt, what risk arises if a node disappears?

options.text: The ClusterIPs stop being routable between clusters and the mesh must be reinstalled.
The Cluster Mesh may have to reconnect to a different node, and if all nodes become unavailable you may have to re-connect the clusters to extract new node IPs.
The shared CA is invalidated and certificates must be regenerated with certgen.
Cilium ignores the local cluster from the list of remote clusters and drops it from the mesh.

explanation: The excerpt notes that NodePort requires stable Node IPs; if a node disappears the Cluster Mesh may have to reconnect to a different node, and if all nodes become unavailable you may have to re-connect the clusters to extract new node IPs.

optionRationale.a: Routable ClusterIPs are a requirement of the ClusterIP option, not a consequence of a node disappearing under NodePort.
optionRationale.c: The shared CA and certgen relate to the certificate method, not to the NodePort exposure described here.
optionRationale.d: Ignoring the local cluster from the list of remote clusters explains why a shared ``clusters.yaml`` works; it is unrelated to node loss.

citations.title: Configure Cluster Mesh with Helm
citations.quote:
This requires stable Node IPs. If a node disappears, the Cluster Mesh may
        have to reconnect to a different node. If all nodes have become
        unavailable, you may have to re-connect the clusters to extract new node
        IPs.

stem: You are troubleshooting a Cilium mutual authentication setup and want to confirm that the Cilium agent and operator themselves have registered delegate Identities with the SPIRE Server. Which command do you run?

options.text: kubectl exec -n cilium-spire spire-server-0 -c spire-server -- /opt/spire/bin/spire-server entry show -parentID spiffe://spiffe.cilium/ns/cilium-spire/sa/spire-agent
kubectl exec -n cilium-spire spire-server-0 -c spire-server -- /opt/spire/bin/spire-server entry show -selector cilium:mutual-auth
kubectl get ciliumidentities
kubectl get cep -l app=echo -o=jsonpath='{.items[0].status.identity.id}'

explanation: The excerpt states that the Cilium agent and operator should have a registered delegate Identity with the SPIRE Server, and then shows the verification command using the `-parentID` flag with the SPIRE agent's SPIFFE ID. That command returns two entries, for `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-agent` and `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-operator`.

optionRationale.b: This command lists all entries carrying the `cilium:mutual-auth` selector, which the excerpt presents as the way to get all registered workload entries, not to check the agent and operator delegate Identities.
optionRationale.c: This lists Cilium Identities in Kubernetes; the excerpt uses it only to cross-check that the number of entries matches the number of identities.
optionRationale.d: This retrieves the Cilium Identity ID for the echo Pod, which is a step towards constructing that workload's SPIFFE ID, not towards verifying the agent and operator.

citations.title: Verify SPIFFE Identities
citations.quote: Verify that the Cilium agent and operator have Identities on the SPIRE server:

stem: A colleague has retrieved the Cilium Identity for the echo Pod and now wants to check that this workload is registered on the SPIRE server. Which SPIFFE ID should be passed to `spire-server entry show -spiffeID`?

options.text: spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-operator
spiffe://spiffe.cilium/ns/cilium-spire/sa/spire-agent
spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/$IDENTITY_ID
spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-agent

explanation: The excerpt explains that the SPIFFE ID for a workload is based on the `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/$IDENTITY_ID` format, where `$IDENTITY_ID` is a workload's Cilium Identity. In the worked example the echo Pod's identity is 17947, giving `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/17947`.

optionRationale.a: This is the Parent ID of the workload entry, not the workload's own SPIFFE ID; the excerpt notes the cilium-operator appears in the Parent ID because it creates SPIRE entries for Cilium Identities.
optionRationale.b: This is the SPIFFE ID of the SPIRE agent, used as the parent when checking the agent and operator delegate Identities.
optionRationale.d: This is the SPIFFE ID of the Cilium agent's own entry, not a workload identity derived from a Cilium Identity.

citations.title: Verify SPIFFE Identities
citations.quote:
The SPIFFE ID for a workload is 
based on the ``spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/$IDENTITY_ID`` format, where ``$IDENTITY_ID`` is a workload's Cilium Identity.

stem: An engineer inspects an HTTPRoute and finds a condition of type `ResolvedRefs` with Status `True`. What does this tell them?

options.text: The referenced services were found and are valid references.
The HTTPRoute configuration was correct and accepted.
All referenced secrets were found and have permission for use.
The route has been programmed into Envoy by the Cilium Gateway controller.

explanation: For HTTPRoute status, the excerpt lists `ResolvedRefs` as meaning the referenced services were found and are valid references. `Accepted` is the condition covering whether the HTTPRoute configuration was correct and accepted.

optionRationale.b: That is the meaning of the `Accepted` condition type for an HTTPRoute, not `ResolvedRefs`.
optionRationale.c: That description belongs to `ResolvedRefs` on the Gateway's status conditions, which concerns referenced secrets, not the HTTPRoute's service references.
optionRationale.d: Programming into Envoy is described by the `Programmed` condition on the Gateway, not by `ResolvedRefs` on an HTTPRoute.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: ``ResolvedRefs``: The referenced services were found and are valid references.

stem: An engineer is running a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available, and wants the Cilium ingress controller's Envoy listener reachable directly on the host network. After enabling host network mode via Helm, which statement describes the resulting Service configuration?

options.text: The LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode is automatically disabled, because the two modes are mutually exclusive.
A LoadBalancer Service is still created, but it is bound only to the loopback interface.
A NodePort Service is retained alongside the host listener so that both paths remain available.
The Service type is switched to ExternalName so that the host listener can be reached by DNS name.

explanation: Host network mode and the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode cannot coexist: enabling host network mode automatically disables the Service-based mode. The listener is then exposed on all interfaces rather than on a Service.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 and/or ::), not restricted to loopback, and says nothing about retaining a LoadBalancer Service.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the two modes are mutually exclusive, so a NodePort Service is not retained alongside the host listener.
optionRationale.d: No ExternalName Service type is mentioned anywhere in the excerpt; the Service mode is disabled, not converted.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium ingress controller host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

stem: An engineer enables host network mode and wants the shared HTTP listener to be reachable on a host port different from the shared listener port, while leaving the other shared listeners on the default. Which Helm value should be set?

options.text: ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort
ingressController.hostNetwork.httpPort
ingressController.hostNetwork.tlsPassthroughPort
ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port

explanation: The httpPort value sets the host network port for the shared HTTP listener specifically. If it is unset or 0, the sharedListenerPort value is used instead, which is why the other listeners stay on the default.

optionRationale.a: sharedListenerPort sets the port for the Envoy listener generally and is the fallback for the individual listeners; changing it would move all shared listeners, not just HTTP.
optionRationale.c: tlsPassthroughPort applies to the shared TLS passthrough listener, not the HTTP listener.
optionRationale.d: This is an annotation applied per Ingress resource for dedicated ingress, not a Helm value for the shared HTTP listener.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: ``ingressController.hostNetwork.httpPort``: Host network port to expose the shared HTTP listener. If unset or ``0``, ``sharedListenerPort`` is used.

stem: A cluster runs the Cilium ingress controller in dedicated mode, and several Ingress resources are deployed. An engineer creates a new Ingress resource for host network exposure but omits the per-Ingress port annotation. What is the consequence?

options.text: The Ingress falls back to the shared listener port 8080, which is shared across all Ingress resources.
The Ingress is rejected because the host-listener-port annotation is mandatory in this situation.
The Ingress is accepted, but the port clashes are resolved automatically by Cilium.
The Ingress uses the tlsPassthroughPort value as its host listener port.

explanation: The ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation is mandatory when the global mode is dedicated, or when the Ingress sets the loadbalancer-mode annotation to dedicated and multiple Ingress resources are deployed. The port must be unique per Ingress resource, so it cannot simply be shared.

optionRationale.a: Although the default port is 8080, the excerpt states it can only be used for a single Ingress resource as it needs to be unique per Ingress resource, so it cannot be shared across all of them.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt warns that misconfiguration might result in port clashes and instructs the operator to configure unique ports; it does not describe automatic resolution.
optionRationale.d: tlsPassthroughPort is a Helm value for the shared TLS passthrough listener, not a fallback for a dedicated Ingress host listener port.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: This annotation is mandatory if the global Cilium ingress controller mode is configured to ``dedicated`` (``ingressController.loadbalancerMode``) or the ingress resource sets the ``ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode`` annotation to ``dedicated`` and multiple ``Ingress`` resources are deployed.

stem: A Cilium Egress Gateway policy uses an egressGateway nodeSelector with matchLabels testLabel: testVal. Three nodes in the cluster carry that label and are named node-c, node-a and node-b. Which node acts as the gateway node for the policy?

options.text: node-a, because the first node in lexical ordering based on node name is selected when several nodes match.
node-c, because the most recently created matching node is selected.
All three nodes act as gateway nodes and share the SNAT traffic.
No node is selected, because a nodeSelector matching more than one node is ambiguous and the policy is ignored.

explanation: When several nodes match the label set given in nodeSelector, Cilium picks the first node in lexical ordering based on node name. Among node-a, node-b and node-c, that is node-a.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says nothing about creation time; the tie-break is lexical ordering by node name.
optionRationale.c: A single gateway node is selected per policy; the excerpt describes selecting one node, not sharing traffic across all matches.
optionRationale.d: An ambiguous match is resolved by lexical ordering, not by ignoring the policy. The excerpt only says policies specifying both egressIP and interface are ignored.

citations.title: Selecting and configuring the gateway node
citations.quote:
In case multiple nodes are a match for the given set of labels, the
    first node in lexical ordering based on their name will be selected.

stem: A Cluster Mesh deployment needs longer than usual to complete a key rotation across several clusters. Which agent flag can be used to increase the delay before the old key is cleaned up?

options.text: `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`
`encryption.ipsec.interface`
`XfrmInStateProtoError`
`cilium-dbg encrypt status`

explanation: If the key rotation is expected to take longer, for example in Cluster Mesh where several clusters need to be updated, the delay before cleanup can be increased with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.

optionRationale.b: This is a Helm value for selecting the encryption interface, not a flag for the cleanup delay.
optionRationale.c: This is an XFRM error counter name, not a configurable flag.
optionRationale.d: This is a diagnostic command, not a flag that changes rotation timing.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
you can increase the
   delay before cleanup with agent flag ``ipsec-key-rotation-duration``.

stem: An engineer sees `XfrmInStateProtoError` errors on a node. Which two situations are documented as causes?

options.text: The key was updated without incrementing the SPI, or the source node encrypts using a different anti-replay seq from the anti-reply oseq on the destination node
A packet was received while an XFRM state was being deleted, or the kernel failed to route a packet for a deleted pod
The kernel failed to allocate memory, or the sequence number of an encryption XFRM configuration reached its maximum value
Cilium dropped packets that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text, or the destination node's IP address changed

explanation: `XfrmInStateProtoError` errors can happen if the key is updated without incrementing the SPI (also called `KEYID`), or if the source node encrypts the packets using a different anti-replay seq from the anti-reply oseq on the destination node. Both can be fixed by properly performing a new key rotation.

optionRationale.b: These describe `XfrmInStateInvalid` and `XfrmFwdHdrError`/`XfrmInError` respectively.
optionRationale.c: These describe `XfrmFwdHdrError`/`XfrmInError` and `XfrmOutStateSeqError` respectively.
optionRationale.d: These describe `XfrmOutPolBlock` and the `No node ID found` drops respectively.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
``XfrmInStateProtoError`` errors can happen for the following reasons:
   1. If the key is updated without incrementing the SPI (also called ``KEYID``
   in ipsec_key_rotation instructions above).

stem: Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations program to the root cgroup. Which TCP event is this program specifically used to monitor?

options.text: Transitions into the ESTABLISHED state
Every send operation performed by a TCP socket
Packet reception in the networking driver
Ingress decryption of IPsec packets

explanation: The socket operations program attached to the root cgroup is used to monitor for TCP state transitions, specifically for ESTABLISHED state transitions, and when a socket transitions into ESTABLISHED with a node local peer a socket send/recv program is attached.

optionRationale.b: Send operations are the domain of the socket send/recv hook, not the socket operations hook.
optionRationale.c: Packet reception in the driver is the XDP hook.
optionRationale.d: IPsec ingress decryption is handled by the L3 Encryption object and the xfrm layer.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations
  program to the root cgroup and uses this to monitor for TCP state transitions,
  specifically for ESTABLISHED state transitions.

stem: A TCP socket managed by Cilium transitions into the ESTABLISHED state and has a node local peer, possibly a local proxy. What does Cilium do at this point?

options.text: It attaches a socket send/recv program to the socket
It attaches an XDP program to the networking driver
It inserts a prefilter CIDR map entry for the peer
It marks the packet for encryption and passes it to the xfrm layer

explanation: The socket operations hook monitors ESTABLISHED transitions, and when a socket transitions into ESTABLISHED state with a node local peer a socket send/recv program is attached.

optionRationale.b: XDP attachment is not described as a response to socket state transitions.
optionRationale.c: Prefilter CIDR maps are supplied by the Cilium agent for XDP filtering, not for socket state transitions.
optionRationale.d: Marking for encryption belongs to the L3 Encryption object on egress, not to the socket operations hook.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
When
  a socket transitions into ESTABLISHED state if the TCP socket has a node
  local peer (possibly a local proxy) a socket send/recv program is attached.

stem: Which statement describes what the socket send/recv hook can do when it runs on a send operation performed by a TCP socket?

options.text: It can inspect the message and either drop the message, send the message to the TCP layer, or redirect the message to another socket
It can perform a map lookup on the destination IP and forward the packet to a configured L3/L4 endpoint
It can mark the packet for decryption and pass it to the Linux xfrm layer
It can look up a packet's associated identity and policy in a map to enforce L3 and L4 policy

explanation: At the socket send/recv hook the program can inspect the message and either drop it, send it to the TCP layer, or redirect it to another socket, which Cilium uses to accelerate datapath redirects.

optionRationale.b: Destination IP map lookup and forwarding to L3/L4 endpoints is the Service object's behaviour.
optionRationale.c: Marking for decryption and passing to xfrm is the L3 Encryption object's ingress behaviour.
optionRationale.d: Identity and policy map lookup for L3/L4 enforcement is the Endpoint Policy object.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
At this point the hook can inspect the message
  and either drop the message, send the message to the TCP layer, or redirect
  the message to another socket.

stem: A Cilium prefilter object runs an XDP program with a set of prefilter rules. How does it decide whether to drop a packet or allow it to be processed by the stack?

options.text: It performs a lookup in a set of CIDR maps supplied by the Cilium agent
It performs a map lookup on the destination IP and optionally destination port
It looks up the packet's associated identity and policy in a map
It reads the decryption key encoded in the IPsec header

explanation: The prefilter object uses a set of CIDR maps supplied by the Cilium agent to do a lookup, after which the packet is either dropped, for example when the destination is not a valid endpoint, or allowed to be processed by the stack.

optionRationale.b: Destination IP and optional port lookup describes the Service object.
optionRationale.c: Identity and policy lookup describes the Endpoint Policy object.
optionRationale.d: Reading the key from the IPsec header is how ingress decryption avoids a map lookup in the L3 Encryption object.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
Specifically,
  a set of CIDR maps supplied by the Cilium agent are used to do a lookup and the packet
  is either dropped, for example when the destination is not a valid endpoint, or allowed to be processed by the stack.

stem: Which Cilium datapath object is described as the primary object responsible for mapping packets to identities and enforcing L3 and L4 policies?

options.text: The Endpoint Policy object
The Prefilter object
The Service object
The L3 Encryption object

explanation: The Endpoint Policy object uses a map to look up a packet's associated identity and policy, and is described as the primary object in the Cilium datapath responsible for mapping packets to identities and enforcing L3 and L4 policies.

optionRationale.b: The Prefilter object runs an XDP program with CIDR map lookups for early filtering.
optionRationale.c: The Service object performs destination IP and port lookups to forward to L3/L4 endpoints.
optionRationale.d: The L3 Encryption object handles marking for encryption and decryption via the xfrm layer.

  datapath responsible for mapping packets to identities and enforcing L3 and L4 policies.

stem: On ingress, how does the L3 Encryption object obtain the key needed to decrypt a packet?

options.text: The key is encoded in the IPsec header, so no map lookup is needed on ingress
It performs a map lookup using the destination IP to find available keys
It looks up the packet's identity in the endpoint policy map
It queries the CIDR maps supplied by the Cilium agent

explanation: On ingress the L3 Encryption object marks packets for decryption and passes them to the xfrm layer; the key required for decryption is encoded in the IPsec header, so no map lookup is needed on ingress.

optionRationale.b: A destination IP map lookup to determine keys is the egress behaviour, not ingress.
optionRationale.c: The endpoint policy map maps packets to identities and policy, not to decryption keys.
optionRationale.d: CIDR maps belong to the prefilter object for XDP filtering.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
The key required
  for decryption is encoded in the IPsec header so on ingress we do not need to
  do a map lookup to find the decryption key.

stem: A Cilium agent is running on a node and a container's traffic must be monitored and policy enforced on everything the container sends out. The container is connected to the host through a veth pair. Which attachment point does Cilium use to achieve this?

options.text: The XDP hook in the networking driver, which runs on packet reception before any other processing.
The TC ingress hook of the host side of the veth pair.
The socket operations hook attached to the root cgroup, which runs on TCP events.
The socket send/recv hook, which runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket.

explanation: Cilium attaches to the TC ingress hook on the host side of the veth pair, which lets it monitor and enforce policy on all traffic exiting a container. XDP runs at the earliest point in the driver on packet reception and is suited to filtering and DDoS protection, while the socket hooks operate on TCP socket events and send operations rather than on the veth device.

optionRationale.a: XDP is the earliest hook in the networking driver and is described as ideal for filtering and DDoS protection, not as the veth attachment point for container egress policy.
optionRationale.c: The socket operations hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events such as ESTABLISHED transitions; it is not the veth attachment point described for container traffic.
optionRationale.d: The socket send/recv hook runs on every send operation of a TCP socket and is used to accelerate datapath redirects, not to attach to the host side of a veth pair.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote: By attaching to the TC ingress hook of the host side of this veth pair Cilium can monitor and enforce policy on all traffic exiting a container.

stem: A three-node cluster has both IPv4 and IPv6 enabled and IPsec encryption is active. No key rotation is in progress. An engineer runs `cilium-dbg encrypt status` in a Cilium Pod and sees `Keys in use: 8`. What does this indicate?

options.text: The key count is as expected for this cluster configuration.
The key count is too high; it should be 4 because there are three nodes.
The key count is too low; it should be 12 because there are three nodes and two IP families.
The key count indicates that a key rotation is currently ongoing.

explanation: The number of keys in use should be 2 per remote node per enabled IP family. In a three-node cluster with both IPv4 and IPv6 enabled and no key rotation, there should be 8 keys in use on each node, so 8 is correct.

optionRationale.b: The expected count is 2 per remote node per IP family, not 2 per node overall; with three nodes and two families the expected count is 8, not 4.
optionRationale.c: The expected count is 2 per remote node per IP family, giving 8 for three nodes and two families, not 12.
optionRationale.d: During a key rotation the count can double to 4 per remote node per IP family, which would give 16 here, not 8; 8 is the normal value.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote: The number of keys in use should be 2 per remote node per enabled IP family. During a key rotation, it can double to 4 per remote node per IP family.

stem: After enabling encryption, the Cilium Pods fail to start. What should be checked first?

options.text: Whether the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.
Whether the `ipsec-key-rotation-duration` agent flag has been increased.
Whether the decryption interface list includes all native devices.
Whether the `XfrmOutPolBlock` counter is non-zero.

explanation: If the Cilium Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, the guidance is to double-check whether the IPsec Secret and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

optionRationale.b: The `ipsec-key-rotation-duration` flag is used to increase the delay before old key cleanup when key rotation is expected to take longer, not to fix Pods that fail to start.
optionRationale.c: The decryption interface list is checked with `cilium-dbg encrypt status` once encryption is running, not as a first step when Pods fail to start.
optionRationale.d: `XfrmOutPolBlock` is an XFRM error counter for packets Cilium dropped that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text; it is not the first thing to check when Pods fail to start.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote: If the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, double-check if the IPsec ``Secret`` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

stem: A Cilium log contains a warning similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`. Which Helm setting should be used to set the encryption interface?

options.text: `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`
`--set ipsec-key-rotation-duration=ethX`
`--set encryption.interface=ethX`
`--set ipsec.interface=ethX`

explanation: If there is a warning message similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`, the guidance is to use `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX` to set the encryption interface.

optionRationale.b: `ipsec-key-rotation-duration` is an agent flag for the delay before old key cleanup, not a Helm setting for the encryption interface.
optionRationale.c: The setting is `encryption.ipsec.interface`, not `encryption.interface`.
optionRationale.d: The setting is `encryption.ipsec.interface`, not `ipsec.interface`.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote: If there is a warning message similar to ``Device eth0 does not exist``, use ``--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`` to set the encryption interface.

stem: A Cilium operator is creating a new ENI for an EC2 instance. The operator's configuration sets both `spec.eni.subnet-ids` and `spec.eni.subnet-tags`. Which subnets are considered candidates for the new ENI?

options.text: Only subnets whose IDs appear in `subnet-ids`; `subnet-tags` is ignored.
Only subnets that match every tag in `subnet-tags`; `subnet-ids` is ignored.
Subnets that either have an ID in `subnet-ids` or match all tags in `subnet-tags`.
Subnets that have an ID in `subnet-ids` and also match all tags in `subnet-tags`.

explanation: When `subnet-ids` is set, `subnet-tags` is ignored, so only the subnets whose IDs are listed in `subnet-ids` are candidates.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the precedence: the excerpt states that `subnet-tags` is ignored when `subnet-ids` is set, not the other way round.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe a union of the two filters; it states that `subnet-tags` is ignored when `subnet-ids` is set.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not require both filters to match; it states that `subnet-tags` is ignored when `subnet-ids` is set.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
Note that when ``subnet-ids`` is set, ``subnet-tags`` are
ignored.

stem: A Cilium operator is creating an ENI. `spec.eni.security-groups` is not set, but `spec.eni.security-group-tags` is set. How are the Security Group IDs for the new ENI determined?

options.text: The operator lists all Security Groups in the account and attaches the ones that match the list of tags.
The new ENI inherits the security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.
The operator attaches every Security Group in the account.
The operator attaches the Security Groups whose IDs are listed in `spec.eni.security-groups`.

explanation: With `spec.eni.security-groups` unset and `spec.eni.security-group-tags` set, the operator lists all Security Groups in the account and attaches those matching the tags.

optionRationale.b: Inheriting from `eth0` is the final fallback, used only when neither `security-groups` nor `security-group-tags` is set.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the operator attaches the ones that match the tags, not all Security Groups.
optionRationale.d: `spec.eni.security-groups` is not set in this scenario, so its IDs cannot be used.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
the operator will list all Security Groups in the account and will attach to
the ENI the ones that match the list of tags passed.

stem: A Cilium operator is creating an ENI. Which two API calls does it use to create and attach the ENI to the EC2 instance?

options.text: `CreateNetworkInterface` and `AttachNetworkInterface`.
`CreateNetworkInterface` and `AssociateNetworkInterface`.
`AllocateAddress` and `AttachNetworkInterface`.
`RunInstances` and `AttachNetworkInterface`.

optionRationale.c: `AllocateAddress` is not mentioned; the create call is `CreateNetworkInterface`.
optionRationale.d: `RunInstances` is not mentioned; the create call is `CreateNetworkInterface`.

citations.title: ENI Creation

The ENI is then created and attached to the EC2 instance using the
``CreateNetworkInterface`` and ``AttachNetworkInterface`` API calls.

stem: A Cilium operator is creating an ENI. Neither `spec.eni.security-groups` nor `spec.eni.security-group-tags` is set. Which Security Group IDs are attached to the new ENI?

options.text: The security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.
The security group IDs of the primary ENI of the instance.
No Security Group IDs are attached.
The security group IDs of every ENI on the instance.

the newly created ENI will
inherit the security group IDs of ``eth0`` of the instance.

stem: A LoadBalancer service has spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges set to 192.168.1.0/24. By default, which services does this CIDR restriction apply to?

options.text: Only the LoadBalancer service, not the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP services.
The LoadBalancer service and its corresponding NodePort service, but not ClusterIP.
All service types created for the service, including NodePort and ClusterIP.
Only the ClusterIP service, because NodePort and LoadBalancer are externally exposed.

explanation: By default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the NodePort or ClusterIP services that are installed alongside it.

optionRationale.b: The restriction does not extend to NodePort by default.
optionRationale.c: Propagating to all externally exposed types requires the Helm option bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.
optionRationale.d: The restriction applies to the LoadBalancer service, not the ClusterIP service.

stem: An engineer wants to prevent Cilium from creating the NodePort and ClusterIP services that normally accompany a LoadBalancer service. Which annotation achieves this?

options.text: service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer
service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny

optionRationale.c: src-ranges-policy: allow is the default allow-list behaviour; it does not affect service creation.
optionRationale.d: bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes is a Helm value that propagates CIDRs to other service types; it does not prevent their creation.

stem: What is the effect of leaving spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges empty on a LoadBalancer service?

options.text: No restrictions on access are applied.
All external traffic is dropped.
Only in-cluster traffic is allowed.
The service is not programmed by the kube-proxy replacement.

explanation: If the field is empty, no restrictions for access will be applied.

optionRationale.b: An empty list does not drop traffic; it applies no restrictions.
optionRationale.c: In-cluster traffic is always allowed regardless of the field.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not state that an empty field prevents programming.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote: If the field is empty, no restrictions for the access will be applied.

stem: A platform team wants to rate limit individual Pods using Cilium's bandwidth manager. A colleague suggests deploying the Kubernetes bandwidth CNI plugin alongside Cilium, arguing that Cilium will chain to it. Which statement best describes how Cilium's bandwidth manager relates to that plugin?

options.text: Cilium's bandwidth manager is natively integrated into Cilium, does not rely on CNI chaining, and does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin.
Cilium's bandwidth manager requires the bandwidth CNI plugin to be installed first, because it delegates all shaping to that plugin.
Cilium's bandwidth manager chains to the bandwidth CNI plugin only when tunnelling mode is enabled.
Cilium's bandwidth manager replaces the bandwidth CNI plugin's TBF implementation with a second CNI plugin that Cilium invokes at Pod creation.

explanation: The bandwidth manager is described as natively integrated into Cilium and explicitly does not rely on CNI chaining, so it does not use the bandwidth CNI plugin at all. The plugin is in fact discouraged because of scalability concerns, particularly for multi-queue network interfaces, since it is based on TBF rather than EDT.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states the opposite: the bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining and does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin.
optionRationale.c: No such conditional chaining is described; the bandwidth manager is natively integrated and does not use the plugin in any mode.
optionRationale.d: Cilium does not invoke a second CNI plugin; the bandwidth manager is natively integrated into Cilium itself.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
The bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining and is natively integrated
into Cilium instead. Hence, it does not make use of the `bandwidth CNI

stem: An engineer enables Cilium's bandwidth manager on a cluster but leaves legacy routing through the upper stack in place, without BPF Host Routing. What does the guidance warn may result?

options.text: Potentially undesired high latency, so Bandwidth Manager is strongly recommended to be used in combination with BPF Host Routing.
The bandwidth annotations are silently ignored and no rate limiting is applied to any Pod.
Cilium falls back to the bandwidth CNI plugin based on TBF automatically.
Ingress bandwidth enforcement stops working while egress enforcement continues normally.

explanation: The guidance strongly recommends using Bandwidth Manager together with BPF Host Routing, because legacy routing through the upper stack could potentially result in undesired high latency.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt warns of high latency, not of the annotations being ignored.
optionRationale.c: The bandwidth manager does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin at all, so no such fallback is described.
optionRationale.d: The warning concerns latency from legacy routing, not a split between ingress and egress enforcement.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
It is strongly recommended to use Bandwidth Manager in combination with
   BPF Host Routing as otherwise legacy routing
   through the upper stack could potentially result in undesired high latency

stem: A Pod carries the annotations kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth: "10M" and kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth: "20M". How does Cilium's bandwidth manager enforce each of these two limits?

options.text: Egress is enforced on egress at the native host networking devices using EDT, while ingress is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.
Both egress and ingress are enforced using EDT at the native host networking devices.
Egress is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation, while ingress is enforced using EDT.
Both egress and ingress are enforced by the bandwidth CNI plugin using TBF.

explanation: The excerpt states that the egress-bandwidth is enforced on egress at the native host networking devices using EDT (Earliest Departure Time), while the ingress-bandwidth is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.

optionRationale.b: Only egress uses EDT; ingress uses an eBPF-based token bucket.
optionRationale.c: The mechanisms are the other way round: egress uses EDT and ingress uses the token bucket.
optionRationale.d: The bandwidth manager does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin, and TBF is the plugin's mechanism, not Cilium's.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
The ``egress-bandwidth`` is enforced on egress at
the native host networking devices using EDT (Earliest Departure Time), while the ``ingress-bandwidth``
is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.

stem: An operator needs to know which host devices Cilium will treat as native devices for bandwidth enforcement, and wants to override the selection manually. Which description matches the documented behaviour?

options.text: Native devices are auto detected as those with the default route on the host or with Kubernetes InternalIP or ExternalIP assigned, with InternalIP preferred; names can be set manually in the devices helm option, and each listed device must be named the same on all Cilium-managed nodes.
Native devices are auto detected as those carrying the kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth annotation, and the devices helm option accepts only a single device name.
Native devices are auto detected as those with the default route only; ExternalIP is always preferred over InternalIP when both exist.
Native devices must always be listed manually in the devices helm option, because no auto detection is performed.

explanation: The excerpt says native devices are auto detected as those having the default route on the host or having Kubernetes InternalIP or ExternalIP assigned, with InternalIP preferred over ExternalIP if both exist. Devices can be specified manually in the devices helm option, and each listed device has to be named the same on all Cilium-managed nodes.

optionRationale.b: Annotations are applied to Pods, not used to detect host devices, and the example devices='eth0,eth1,eth2' shows multiple devices are accepted.
optionRationale.c: Auto detection also covers InternalIP or ExternalIP, and InternalIP is preferred over ExternalIP, not the reverse.
optionRationale.d: Auto detection is performed; manual specification is offered as a way to change the detected devices.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
The native host networking devices are auto detected as native devices which have
the default route on the host or have Kubernetes ``InternalIP`` or ``ExternalIP`` assigned.
``InternalIP`` is preferred over ``ExternalIP`` if both exist.

stem: A Cilium-managed pod on a node is the source of a TCP connection. The connection completes its handshake and moves into the ESTABLISHED state, and the peer is a node-local process. Which behaviour does Cilium exhibit at that moment?

options.text: The socket operations program, attached to the root cgroup, detects the ESTABLISHED transition and, because the socket has a node local peer, attaches a socket send/recv program to the socket.
The XDP program attached to the container's veth pair drops the packet so that the connection must be re-established through the proxy.
The L3 Encryption object performs a map lookup on the destination IP and marks the socket for encryption before any further processing.
The Service object performs a map lookup on the destination IP and port and forwards the packet to one of the configured L3/L4 endpoints.

explanation: Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations program to the root cgroup and uses it to monitor TCP state transitions, specifically ESTABLISHED. When a socket transitions into ESTABLISHED and the TCP socket has a node local peer (possibly a local proxy), a socket send/recv program is attached.

optionRationale.b: XDP runs at the earliest point in the networking driver on packet reception and is used for filtering such as dropping malicious traffic; it is not what reacts to a TCP state transition on an established socket.
optionRationale.c: The L3 Encryption object's map lookup on the destination IP happens on egress to decide whether a packet should be encrypted; it is not triggered by a socket entering ESTABLISHED.
optionRationale.d: The Service object does a map lookup on destination IP and optionally port for packets received by that object and forwards to L3/L4 endpoints; it is not the component that attaches a program on an ESTABLISHED transition.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations
  program to the root cgroup and uses this to monitor for TCP state transitions,
  specifically for ESTABLISHED state transitions.

stem: A Cilium Egress Gateway policy contains an egressGateway block with nodeSelector matchLabels testLabel: testVal, and three nodes in the cluster carry that label with the names node-c, node-a and node-b. Which node acts as the gateway node for the policy?

options.text: node-a, because the first node in lexical ordering based on node name is selected when several nodes match.
node-c, because the most recently created matching node is selected.
All three nodes act as gateway nodes and share the SNAT work.
No node is selected, because more than one node matches the label set.

explanation: When several nodes match the nodeSelector labels, Cilium picks the first node in lexical ordering based on node name, so node-a is chosen.

optionRationale.b: Selection is by lexical ordering of node names, not by creation time.
optionRationale.c: A single gateway node is selected for the policy; the matching set is narrowed to one node.
optionRationale.d: Multiple matches are resolved by lexical ordering rather than causing the policy to fail.

citations.title: Selecting and configuring the gateway node
citations.quote:
In case multiple nodes are a match for the given set of labels, the
    first node in lexical ordering based on their name will be selected.

stem: An Egress Gateway policy selects gateway nodes with nodeSelector matchLabels testLabel: testVal. Three nodes carry that label, named node-c, node-a and node-b. Which node acts as the gateway node?

options.text: node-a, because it is first in lexical ordering by name.
node-b, because it is the median name.
node-c, because it is last in lexical ordering by name.
All three nodes act as gateway nodes and share the SNAT load.

explanation: When multiple nodes match the labels, the first node in lexical ordering based on their name is selected.

optionRationale.b: Lexical ordering selects the first name, not the median.
optionRationale.c: Lexical ordering selects the first name, not the last.
optionRationale.d: Only one node is selected; the excerpt does not describe load sharing across all matching nodes.

citations.title: Selecting and configuring the gateway node
citations.quote: In case multiple nodes are a match for the given set of labels, the first node in lexical ordering based on their name will be selected.

stem: An egress gateway policy selects gateway nodes with nodeSelector matchLabels testLabel: testVal, and three nodes in the cluster carry that label. How does Cilium choose which of the matching nodes acts as the gateway node?

options.text: It selects the first node in lexical ordering based on node name.
It selects the node with the lowest IP address on the egress interface.
It selects all matching nodes and load-balances egress traffic across them.
It drops the traffic, because more than one node matches the selector.

explanation: When several nodes match the label set, the first node in lexical ordering by name is chosen as the gateway node.

optionRationale.b: Selection is based on node name ordering, not on interface IP addresses.
optionRationale.c: Only one node is selected; the policy does not spread traffic over all matching nodes.
optionRationale.d: Traffic is dropped only when no node matches the label set, not when several do.

citations.title: Selecting and configuring the gateway node
citations.quote:
In case multiple nodes are a match for the given set of labels, the
    first node in lexical ordering based on their name will be selected.

stem: A kind cluster runs in cluster-pool IPAM mode with a cluster-wide pool of 10.0.0.0/8 and /24 per-node PodCIDRs. An engineer upgrades the Cilium Helm release with `ipam.mode=multi-pool`, sets `ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools.default.ipv4.cidrs='{10.0.0.0/8}'` and `ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools.default.ipv4.maskSize=24`, and sets `extraConfig.enable-cluster-pool-to-multi-pool-migration=true`. The upgrade also sets `operator.rollOutPods=true` and `rollOutCiliumPods=false`. What is the immediate effect of this upgrade?

options.text: The Cilium ConfigMap is updated and only the Cilium operator is restarted; the operator creates a `default` CiliumPodIPPool with CIDR 10.0.0.0/8 and mask size 24.
All Cilium agents are restarted and immediately begin allocating from the new multi-pool IPAM mode.
The operator creates a CiliumPodIPPool named `cluster-pool` with CIDR 10.0.0.0/8 and mask size 24.
The Cilium ConfigMap is updated and the Cilium operator is restarted, but no CiliumPodIPPool is created until an agent is restarted.

explanation: The Helm upgrade updates the Cilium ConfigMap and restarts only the Cilium operator. Because `ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools` is configured, the operator creates the `default` CiliumPodIPPool with the same CIDR and per-node mask size used by cluster-pool IPAM. The agents are not restarted because `rollOutCiliumPods=false`.

optionRationale.b: The upgrade sets `rollOutCiliumPods=false`, so agents are not restarted by the upgrade; they must be restarted separately.
optionRationale.c: The pool name is `default`, not `cluster-pool`; the example uses `autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools.default`.
optionRationale.d: The operator creates the pool during the upgrade, as shown by the subsequent `kubectl get ciliumpodippool default` output.

citations.title: Practical Example
citations.quote:

stem: An engineer wants to stop pods in a Cilium cluster from sending unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside the cluster, so that the window in which packets to not-yet-discovered remote endpoints leave unencrypted is closed. Which approach does Cilium describe as a workaround?

optionRationale.d: allowRemoteNodeIdentities is a fallback that permits unencrypted traffic associated with a node identity; it does not prevent unencrypted egress.

The TCP connection succeeds because the password is correct, but the session is read-only.
The TCP connection succeeds and the agent logs a warning about address translation.
The CiliumBGPPeerConfig is rejected because TCP MD5 passwords cannot be used with address translation.

explanation: TCP MD5 passwords sign the packet header, so they cannot be used when the session is address-translated by Cilium; the Cilium Agent's pod IP address must be the address the BGP peer sees. If the header is changed, the TCP connection will not succeed and appears as a dial timeout.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states the connection will not succeed, not that it becomes read-only.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the connection will not succeed, not that it succeeds with a warning.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes a connection failure, not rejection of the CiliumBGPPeerConfig.

citations.title: MD5 Password
citations.quote: Because TCP MD5 passwords sign the header of the packet they cannot be used if the session is address-translated by Cilium (in other words, the Cilium Agent's pod IP address must be the address that the BGP peer sees).

options.text: password
md5-password
auth
secret

explanation: The secret referenced by authSecretRef should contain a key with the name password.

optionRationale.b: md5-password is not the key name given in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: auth is not the key name given in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: secret is not the key name given in the excerpt.

citations.quote: ``AuthSecretRef`` should reference the name of a secret in the BGP secrets namespace (if using the Helm chart this is ``kube-system`` by default). The secret should contain a key with a name of ``password``.

stem: An engineer is preparing to shut down a node that runs Cilium and participates in BGP sessions. The node is selected for BGP by the label enable-bgp=true. The engineer first runs `kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets`, then runs `kubectl label node <node-name> --overwrite enable-bgp=false`. What is the immediate effect of the label change on the node's BGP sessions?

options.text: All BGP sessions on the node are shut down.
The BGP sessions remain up but routes are withdrawn after the Stale Timer expires.
The BGP sessions are reset and re-established with a new router ID.
Only BGP sessions for Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster are shut down.

explanation: Changing the CiliumBGPClusterConfig node selector label so that the node is no longer selected shuts down all BGP sessions on that node. The excerpt states that reconfiguring the BGP sessions by modifying or removing the node selector label will shut down all BGP sessions on the node.

optionRationale.b: The Stale Timer applies only when Graceful Restart with Notification is supported by the peer; the label change itself shuts down the sessions immediately.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention resetting sessions or changing router IDs; it says the sessions are shut down.
optionRationale.d: The label change affects all BGP sessions on the node, not only those related to a particular service traffic policy.

stem: A node is being shut down for maintenance. The node is selected for BGP by the label enable-bgp=true, and BGP Graceful Restart is disabled. After the engineer runs `kubectl label node <node-name> --overwrite enable-bgp=false`, how quickly should the BGP peer withdraw routes towards the node?

options.text: Immediately after the label change.
After the Stale Timer expires.
After the BGP peer sends a Notification message.
After the node is fully shut down.

explanation: With BGP Graceful Restart disabled, the BGP peer should withdraw routes immediately after the node is unselected by the label change. The excerpt states that if you disable the BGP Graceful Restart feature, the BGP peer should withdraw routes immediately after step 2.

optionRationale.b: The Stale Timer is relevant only when Graceful Restart with Notification is supported by the peer.
optionRationale.c: A Notification is sent by the BGP Control Plane when the node is unselected only if the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification; with Graceful Restart disabled, withdrawal is immediate.
optionRationale.d: The withdrawal happens before the node is shut down; waiting until after shutdown would risk breaking traffic.

citations.title: Shutting Down a Node

If you disable the BGP Graceful Restart feature, the BGP peer should withdraw

stem: During node shutdown preparation, an engineer drains the node with `kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets`. What is the effect of this drain on Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster?

options.text: It removes all Pods on the node from the Service endpoints and prevents those Services from redirecting traffic to the node.
It shuts down all BGP sessions on the node.
It causes the BGP peer to withdraw routes immediately.
It resets ongoing Service traffic destined for the node.

explanation: Draining the node evicts all workloads, which removes all Pods on the node from the Service endpoints and prevents Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster from redirecting traffic to the node. The excerpt describes this as the first step to avoid packet loss.

optionRationale.b: BGP sessions are shut down by reconfiguring the BGP sessions via the node selector label, not by draining.
optionRationale.c: Route withdrawal is triggered by the label change, not by draining.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt warns that some ongoing traffic may be reset after route withdrawal and ECMP rehashing, not by the drain itself.

stem: A node is being shut down for maintenance. The node is selected for BGP by the label enable-bgp=true. The engineer drains the node and then runs `kubectl label node <node-name> --overwrite enable-bgp=false`. The BGP Graceful Restart feature is disabled. How long should the engineer wait before shutting down the node, according to the guidance?

options.text: The BGP peer should withdraw routes immediately after the label change, so no waiting is required.
The engineer must wait for the Stale Timer to expire.
The engineer must wait for the BGP Notification to be sent and acknowledged.
The engineer must wait for the ECMP rehashing to complete.

explanation: When BGP Graceful Restart is disabled, the BGP peer should withdraw routes immediately after the node is unselected (step 2). Therefore, no additional waiting for route withdrawal is needed beyond that immediate action.

optionRationale.b: The Stale Timer is relevant only when Graceful Restart with Notification is supported by the peer.
optionRationale.c: A BGP Notification is sent when the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification, but that is a different case; here Graceful Restart is disabled entirely.
optionRationale.d: ECMP rehashing occurs after route withdrawal and may affect ongoing traffic, but it is not a waiting period defined in the steps.

stem: An engineer is shutting down a node that participates in BGP sessions. The node is selected by the label enable-bgp=true. The engineer drains the node and then changes the label to enable-bgp=false. BGP Graceful Restart is enabled, and the BGP peer supports Graceful Restart with Notification (RFC 8538). When will the peer withdraw routes towards the node?

options.text: After the Stale Timer defined in RFC 8538 expires.
Immediately after the label change.
After the BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification to the peer.
After the node is fully shut down.

explanation: When Graceful Restart is enabled and the peer supports Graceful Restart with Notification, the peer will withdraw routes after the Stale Timer (defined in RFC 8538) expires.

optionRationale.b: Immediate withdrawal occurs when Graceful Restart is disabled or when the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification.
optionRationale.c: A BGP Notification is sent when the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification, leading to immediate withdrawal, not delayed withdrawal.
optionRationale.d: The withdrawal happens before the node is shut down; the node shutdown is the final step after waiting.

citations.title: Shutting Down a Node

stem: A node is being prepared for shutdown. The node is selected for BGP by the label enable-bgp=true. The engineer drains the node and then runs `kubectl label node <node-name> --overwrite enable-bgp=false`. BGP Graceful Restart is enabled, but the BGP peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification. What happens to the routes towards the node?

options.text: The BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification to the peer, and the peer withdraws routes immediately after the label change.
The peer withdraws routes after the Stale Timer expires.
The peer keeps the routes until the node is shut down.
The BGP Control Plane withdraws routes locally without notifying the peer.

explanation: If the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification, the BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification to the peer when the node is unselected, and the peer withdraws routes immediately after step 2.

optionRationale.b: The Stale Timer applies only when the peer supports Graceful Restart with Notification.
optionRationale.c: Routes are withdrawn before node shutdown; waiting is required to allow the peer to remove routes.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that the BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification to the peer, not that it withdraws routes locally without notification.

citations.quote:
If the BGP peer does not support the Graceful Restart with Notification, it
    will withdraw routes immediately after step 2 because the BGP Control Plane

stem: An engineer is following the recommended steps to shut down a node that runs Cilium and participates in BGP sessions. The node is selected for BGP by the label enable-bgp=true. After draining the node and changing the label to enable-bgp=false, the engineer waits for the BGP peer to remove routes. What is the purpose of waiting before shutting down the node?

options.text: To allow the BGP peer to remove routes towards the node, because during this period the peer may still send traffic to the node.
To allow the node to re-establish BGP sessions with a new label.
To allow the Cilium agent to restart and apply the new label.
To allow ECMP rehashing to complete before the node is shut down.

explanation: The wait is to give the BGP peer time to remove routes towards the node. During this period, the peer may still send traffic to the node, and shutting down prematurely could break ongoing traffic for Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster.

optionRationale.b: The label change shuts down BGP sessions; the goal is not to re-establish them.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention restarting the Cilium agent as part of the procedure.
optionRationale.d: ECMP rehashing occurs after route withdrawal and may cause traffic redirection, but the waiting period is specifically for route removal by the peer.

Wait for a while until the BGP peer removes routes towards the node. During

stem: In the procedure for shutting down a node that participates in BGP sessions, what is the first step recommended to avoid packet loss as much as possible?

options.text: Drain the node to evict all workloads.
Reconfigure the BGP sessions by modifying the node selector label.
Wait for the BGP peer to remove routes.
Shut down the node.

explanation: The first step is to drain the node to evict all workloads, which removes Pods from Service endpoints and prevents Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster from redirecting traffic to the node.

optionRationale.b: Reconfiguring BGP sessions is the second step, after draining.
optionRationale.c: Waiting for route removal is the third step.
optionRationale.d: Shutting down the node is the final step.
