stem: An engineer is preparing to shut down a node that runs Cilium and participates in BGP sessions. The node is selected for BGP by the label enable-bgp=true. The engineer first runs `kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets`, then runs `kubectl label node <node-name> --overwrite enable-bgp=false`. The BGP peer supports Graceful Restart with Notification (RFC 8538) and Graceful Restart is enabled. What is the expected behaviour of the BGP peer after the label change?

options.text: The BGP peer will withdraw routes after the Stale Timer defined in RFC 8538 expires.
The BGP peer will withdraw routes immediately after the label change because the BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification.
The BGP peer will never withdraw routes until the node is shut down.
The BGP peer will withdraw routes only after the node is shut down and the BGP session times out.

explanation: When Graceful Restart is enabled and the peer supports Graceful Restart with Notification (RFC 8538), the peer withdraws routes after the Stale Timer defined in RFC 8538 expires. The immediate withdrawal occurs only if the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification, in which case the BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification upon unselecting the node.

optionRationale.b: This describes the behaviour when the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification, not when it does.
optionRationale.c: The peer does eventually withdraw routes; it does not wait indefinitely.
optionRationale.d: Route withdrawal is triggered by the BGP session shutdown from unselecting the node, not by the node shutdown itself.

citations.title: Shutting Down a Node
citations.quote: If the BGP peer supports the Graceful Restart with Notification (:rfc:`8538`), it will withdraw routes after the Stale Timer (defined in the :rfc:`8538#section-4.1`) expires.

stem: In the procedure for shutting down a node that participates in BGP, what is the purpose of draining the node first?

options.text: To remove all Pods on the node from the Service endpoints and prevent Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster from redirecting traffic to the node.
To shut down all BGP sessions on the node by removing the CiliumBGPClusterConfig node selector label.
To force the BGP peer to withdraw routes immediately by sending a BGP Notification.
To enable BGP Graceful Restart so that the peer withdraws routes after the Stale Timer expires.

explanation: Draining the node evicts all workloads, which removes all Pods on the node from the Service endpoints and prevents Services with externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster from redirecting traffic to the node. The other options describe actions or effects associated with later steps or different configurations.

optionRationale.b: Shutting down BGP sessions is done by reconfiguring the BGP sessions via the node selector label, not by draining.
optionRationale.c: Sending a BGP Notification occurs when unselecting the node if the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification; draining does not send BGP Notifications.
optionRationale.d: Graceful Restart is a BGP feature that must be enabled separately; draining does not enable it.

citations.title: Shutting Down a Node
citations.quote: Drain the node to evict all workloads. This will remove all Pods on the node from the Service endpoints and prevent Services with ``externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster`` from redirecting traffic to the node.

stem: An engineer creates a LoadBalancer service with the annotation service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr and sets port: 8080 and targetPort: 80. The service is using DSR with IPIP. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: The service will work because IPIP encapsulates the original packet including the port information.
The service will work because the annotation service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr overrides the port mismatch.
The service will fail because with IPIP the service frontend port must equal the backend target port.
The service will work but only if the backend pods are on nodes labeled service.cilium.io/node=beefy.

explanation: When using the IPIP dispatch, the service frontend port must be equal to the backend (target) port because IPIP does not carry port information. Therefore port 8080 and targetPort 80 will not work. The other options are incorrect: IPIP does not carry port information, the annotation does not override the port requirement, and node labeling is a separate concern for selective exposure.

optionRationale.a: IPIP does not carry port information; the inner packet retains the original destination port, so the backend must listen on the same port.
optionRationale.b: The annotation selects DSR mode but does not change the port matching requirement.
optionRationale.d: Node labeling is relevant for selective service exposure, not for resolving a port mismatch.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
When using the IPIP dispatch, the service frontend port must be equal to the
    backend (target) port given IPIP does not carry port information unlike Geneve.

stem: A Cilium cluster uses DSR with IPIP and also selective service node exposure via the service.cilium.io/node annotation. The service is exposed only on nodes labeled service.cilium.io/node=beefy. Where must the backend Pods run?

options.text: On any node in the cluster, because the load balancing node fully translates the traffic.
On nodes that are part of the exposure set (nodes labeled service.cilium.io/node=beefy).
On nodes that are not part of the exposure set, to avoid conflicts.
On the same node as the load balancer frontend, regardless of labels.

explanation: With DSR IPIP combined with selective service node exposure, the backend Pods must run on nodes that are part of the exposure set because the backend node terminates the inbound IPIP traffic and rewrites the reply, requiring the service to be present on the backend node. Only nodes that host neither the frontend nor any backend may be left out. The other options are incorrect: SNAT forwarding allows backends anywhere, but DSR IPIP does not; nodes outside the exposure set cannot host backends; and co-location with the frontend is not required.

optionRationale.a: This describes SNAT forwarding, not DSR IPIP.
optionRationale.c: Backends must be on nodes in the exposure set, not outside it.
optionRationale.d: There is no requirement for backends to be on the same node as the frontend; they must be on nodes in the exposure set.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
Therefore, when DSR
    IPIP is combined with `Selective Service Node Exposure`_, the backend Pods
    must run on nodes that are part of the exposure set

stem: Which Helm values are required to enable per-service DSR with IPIP dispatch using the service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr annotation?

options.text: bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true and loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip
loadBalancer.mode=dsr and bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true
bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true and loadBalancer.mode=snat
loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=geneve and bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true

explanation: The excerpt states that annotation-based DSR requires bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true together with an explicit loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip to define how per-service DSR packets are dispatched. The other options are incorrect: loadBalancer.mode=dsr is not mentioned as required (the example keeps the global default as SNAT), loadBalancer.mode=snat alone is not sufficient, and geneve is a different dispatch mode.

optionRationale.b: loadBalancer.mode=dsr is not required; the example keeps loadBalancer.mode=snat.
optionRationale.c: loadBalancer.mode=snat is the global default but does not enable DSR IPIP by itself.
optionRationale.d: geneve is a different dispatch mode, not IPIP.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
this requires
``bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true`` together with an explicit
``loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip`` to define how the per-service DSR packets are
dispatched to backends.

stem: What does selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enable on backend nodes?

options.text: It enables Geneve encapsulation for service traffic.
It enables inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes, stripping the outer header and delivering the inner packet to the local backend Pod.
It enables SNAT forwarding mode globally.
It enables the service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm annotation.

explanation: The excerpt states that selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enables the inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes (stripping the outer header and delivering the inner packet to the local backend Pod), so no additional setting is required. The other options are incorrect: Geneve is a different dispatch mode, SNAT is a different forwarding mode, and the lb-algorithm annotation is enabled by a different setting (bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true).

optionRationale.a: Geneve is a different dispatch mode, not enabled by dsrDispatch=ipip.
optionRationale.c: SNAT is a different forwarding mode; dsrDispatch=ipip does not enable it globally.
optionRationale.d: The lb-algorithm annotation is enabled by bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true, not by dsrDispatch=ipip.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
Selecting ``loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip`` automatically enables the inbound IPIP
termination on the backend nodes (stripping the outer header and delivering the
inner packet to the local backend Pod), so no additional setting is required:

stem: Which Helm values are required to opt into DSR IPIP on a per-service basis through the service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr annotation while keeping the global default forwarding mode as SNAT?

options.text: bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true and loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip
loadBalancer.mode=dsr and loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=geneve
bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true only
loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip only, without bpf.lbModeAnnotation

explanation: The excerpt states that annotation-based DSR and SNAT mode requires bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true together with an explicit loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip to define how the per-service DSR packets are dispatched to backends.

optionRationale.b: The example keeps loadBalancer.mode=snat and uses dsrDispatch=ipip, not geneve.
optionRationale.c: bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true is for annotation-based load balancing algorithm selection, not for enabling DSR mode.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true is required together with loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip.

citations.quote:
this requires
``bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true`` together with an explicit
``loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip`` to define how the per-service DSR packets are

stem: What happens on the node hosting the selected backend Pod when a packet arrives encapsulated by DSR with IPIP?

options.text: Cilium forwards the encapsulated packet back to the load balancing node for DNAT.
Cilium terminates the tunnel, strips the outer header, DNATs and delivers the inner packet to the backend Pod identified by the outer destination address.
Cilium drops the packet because IPIP termination must be enabled separately with an additional setting.
Cilium replaces the inner packet's destination with the load balancing node address before delivery.

explanation: The excerpt states that the encapsulated packet is routed to the node hosting the Pod, where Cilium terminates the tunnel, strips the outer header, DNATs and delivers the inner packet to the backend Pod identified by the outer destination address. It also notes that selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enables inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes, so no additional setting is required.

optionRationale.a: The packet is delivered locally after DNAT; it is not sent back to the load balancing node.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enables the inbound IPIP termination, so no additional setting is required.
optionRationale.d: The inner packet is delivered to the backend Pod identified by the outer destination address; the destination is not replaced with the load balancing node address.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
The encapsulated packet is routed to the node hosting that Pod, where Cilium
terminates the tunnel, strips the outer header, DNATs and delivers the inner
packet to the backend Pod identified by the outer destination address.

stem: Which Helm setting automatically enables inbound IPIP termination on backend nodes when using DSR with IPIP?

options.text: loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip
bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true
loadBalancer.mode=snat
bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true

explanation: The excerpt states that selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enables the inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes, so no additional setting is required.

optionRationale.b: bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true is required for annotation-based DSR/SNAT mode selection, but it does not itself enable IPIP termination.
optionRationale.c: loadBalancer.mode=snat sets the global default forwarding mode to SNAT, not IPIP termination.
optionRationale.d: bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true enables annotation-based load balancing algorithm selection, not IPIP termination.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
Selecting ``loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip`` automatically enables the inbound IPIP
termination on the backend nodes

stem: An engineer sets `monitor-aggregation` to `maximum` in the Cilium ConfigMap and expects the most aggressive coalescing available. What tracing behaviour results?

options.text: It is equivalent to `medium`, so events are generated for send packets on every new connection, on unseen TCP flags, and on average once per interval.
It generates a tracing event on every receive and send packet.
It generates a tracing event on every send packet only.
It suppresses all tracing events except packets dropped by Cilium.

explanation: `maximum` is described as an alias for the most aggressive aggregation level, and currently it is equivalent to setting `monitor-aggregation` to `medium`. The `medium` behaviour is the one described for new connections, unseen TCP flags and the reporting interval.

optionRationale.b: That is the behaviour of `none`, which generates an event on every receive and send packet.
optionRationale.c: That is the behaviour of `low`, which generates an event on every send packet.
optionRationale.d: Dropped packets do produce one event per packet at `medium`, but `maximum` is not a drop-only mode; it is equivalent to `medium`.

citations.title: ConfigMap Options
citations.quote:
``maximum`` - An alias for the most aggressive aggregation level. Currently
    this is equivalent to setting ``monitor-aggregation`` to ``medium``.

stem: An engineer sets `monitor-aggregation` to `low` and enables socket load-balancing. Which description matches the resulting tracing behaviour?

options.text: A tracing event is generated on every send packet, and reverse-direction (recv) socket trace events are suppressed.
A tracing event is generated on every receive and send packet, and all socket trace events are emitted.
A tracing event is generated only for connect system calls, and no packet events are produced.
A tracing event is generated on every new connection and on average once per interval, and all socket trace events are emitted.

explanation: At the `low` level a tracing event is generated on every send packet. When socket load-balancing is enabled, the `lowest`/`low` level suppresses reverse-direction (recv) socket trace events.

optionRationale.b: That combines the `none` packet behaviour with the `none` socket behaviour, not `low`.
optionRationale.c: Emitting socket trace events only for connect system calls corresponds to `medium`/`maximum`, not `low`.
optionRationale.d: The new-connection and interval behaviour belongs to `medium`, and emitting all socket trace events belongs to `none`.

citations.title: ConfigMap Options
citations.quote: ``low`` - Generate a tracing event on every send packet.

stem: After listing all SPIRE entries with the cilium:mutual-auth selector, an engineer runs kubectl get ciliumidentities to cross-check them. What should match?

options.text: The identity ID listed under NAME should match the digits at the end of the SPIFFE ID.
The identity ID listed under NAME should match the Entry ID of the corresponding SPIRE entry.
The identity ID listed under NAME should match the Revision number of the corresponding SPIRE entry.
The identity ID listed under NAME should match the Parent ID of the corresponding SPIRE entry.

explanation: The cross-check is between the Cilium identity name and the trailing digits of the SPIFFE ID, since the SPIFFE ID is built as spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/$IDENTITY_ID.

optionRationale.b: The Entry ID is a UUID assigned by the SPIRE server and is unrelated to the Cilium identity number.
optionRationale.c: The Revision field is a version counter on the entry, not the identity number.
optionRationale.d: The Parent ID is a SPIFFE ID of the registering component, such as the operator, not the workload identity number.

stem: An engineer runs `kubectl get cep -l app=echo -o=jsonpath='{.items[0].status.identity.id}'` and obtains the value 17947. Which SPIFFE ID should be used to look up the echo Pod's registration on the SPIRE server?

explanation: The SPIFFE ID for a workload is constructed using the format `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/$IDENTITY_ID`, where `$IDENTITY_ID` is the workload's Cilium Identity. With the Cilium Identity 17947, the correct SPIFFE ID is `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/identity/17947`.

optionRationale.b: This is the SPIFFE ID of the Cilium agent, not a workload identity derived from a Cilium Identity.

stem: An existing cluster is running kube-proxy as a DaemonSet. An engineer wants to remove kube-proxy to prepare for Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement. Which sequence of commands should they use?

options.text: kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; iptables-save | grep -v KUBE | iptables-restore
kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; iptables-save | grep KUBE | iptables-restore
kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; iptables -F
kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; systemctl restart kubelet

explanation: The excerpt provides the exact commands: delete the kube-proxy DaemonSet, delete the kube-proxy ConfigMap to avoid reinstallation during a kubeadm upgrade, and run on each node with root permissions: iptables-save | grep -v KUBE | iptables-restore. This removes KUBE-related iptables rules.

optionRationale.b: The grep pattern is inverted; it would keep only KUBE rules instead of removing them.
optionRationale.c: iptables -F flushes all rules, which is not what the excerpt recommends.
optionRationale.d: Restarting kubelet is not mentioned in the excerpt for this purpose.

$ # Delete the configmap as well to avoid kube-proxy being reinstalled during a Kubeadm upgrade
$ kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy
$ # Run on each node with root permissions:
$ iptables-save | grep -v KUBE | iptables-restore

optionRationale.b: Setting autoMount.enabled=true would not disable the auto-mount.
optionRationale.c: /run/cilium/cgroupv2 is the default auto-mount path, not necessarily the host mount point.
optionRationale.d: /sys/fs/cgroup is given as an example only if cgroup v2 is mounted there; it is not a universal value.

stem: When deploying Cilium with the eBPF kube-proxy replacement, what does the kubeProxyReplacement setting control if set to true?

It disables all service handling and requires kube-proxy to be running.

optionRationale.c: Setting it to true enables the replacement, not disables service handling.

stem: How does the Cilium ingress controller expose its Envoy listener on the host when host network mode is enabled?

options.text: On all interfaces, using 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.
Only on the loopback interface, using 127.0.0.1.
Only on the node's primary IP address, selected at startup.
On a ClusterIP address allocated by the LoadBalancer Service.

explanation: In host network mode the listener is exposed on all interfaces, with 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.

optionRationale.b: The listener is not restricted to loopback.
optionRationale.c: No selection of a single primary node IP is described; all interfaces are used.
optionRationale.d: Host network mode disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode, so no such Service address is used.

citations.quote: The listener is exposed on all interfaces (``0.0.0.0`` for IPv4 and/or ``::`` for IPv6).

stem: A team wants to change the host network port used by the shared Cilium ingress controller Envoy listener away from its default. What guidance applies to the port number they choose?

options.text: They should choose a port number higher than 1023.
They must choose a port number lower than 1024.
They must choose port 8080, since it cannot be changed.
They must choose a port that is unique per Ingress resource.

explanation: The sharedListenerPort flag sets the host network port for the Envoy listener, with a default of 8080. If it is changed, a port number higher than 1023 should be chosen, referring to binding to a privileged port.

optionRationale.b: The guidance is the opposite: choose a port higher than 1023.
optionRationale.c: The default is 8080, but the value can be changed.
optionRationale.d: Uniqueness per Ingress resource applies to the dedicated per-Ingress annotation, not to the shared listener port.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: The default port is ``8080``. If you change it, you should choose a port number higher than ``1023``

stem: A platform team runs a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available. They enable the Cilium ingress controller in host network mode via Helm. What happens to the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode for the ingress controller?

options.text: It is automatically disabled, because host network mode and the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode are mutually exclusive.
It remains enabled and both modes expose the Envoy listener simultaneously.
It is converted into a ClusterIP Service that forwards to the host network listener.
It is left unchanged but must be disabled manually before host network mode can take effect.

explanation: Enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode; the two are mutually exclusive, so no manual step is required.

optionRationale.b: The two modes are mutually exclusive, so they cannot both expose the listener at once.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says nothing about converting the Service to ClusterIP; it says the Service mode is disabled.
optionRationale.d: The disabling is automatic, not a manual prerequisite.

citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium ingress controller host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

stem: An engineer enables the Cilium ingress controller host network mode with Helm and leaves the shared listener port at its default. On which interfaces is the Envoy listener exposed?

options.text: Only on the loopback interface of each node.
Only on the node IP address used by the Cilium agent.
On all interfaces, using 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.
Only on the interfaces selected by the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation.

explanation: In host network mode the listener is exposed on all interfaces, bound to 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.

optionRationale.a: The listener is not restricted to loopback; it is exposed on all interfaces.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not limit exposure to a single node IP address.
optionRationale.d: The annotation sets a port, not a set of interfaces.

stem: A team enables host network mode for the Cilium ingress controller and wants to change the global host network port used by the shared Envoy listener. They set ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort. What is the default value of this setting, and what constraint applies if it is changed?

options.text: The default is 80, and any value may be chosen because the listener runs as root.
The default is 8080, and a changed value should be a port number higher than 1023.
The default is 443, and a changed value must be lower than 1024.
The default is 0, which means a random port is chosen on every restart.

explanation: The sharedListenerPort defaults to 8080, and if changed the engineer should choose a port number higher than 1023 to avoid binding to a privileged port.

optionRationale.a: The default is 8080, not 80, and the guidance is to pick a port above 1023.
optionRationale.c: The default is 8080, not 443, and the guidance is for ports above 1023, not below 1024.
optionRationale.d: The default is 8080; 0 is the unset value for the httpPort, httpsPort and tlsPassthroughPort settings, not for sharedListenerPort.

citations.quote: ``ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort``: Host network port to expose the Cilium ingress controller Envoy listener. The default port is ``8080``. If you change it, you should choose a port number higher than ``1023``

stem: Host network mode is enabled for the Cilium ingress controller. The engineer sets ingressController.hostNetwork.httpsPort to 0 and does not set ingressController.hostNetwork.httpPort. Which port is used for the shared HTTPS listener?

options.text: Port 443, because that is the conventional HTTPS port.
A port allocated dynamically by the Cilium agent.
The value of sharedListenerPort, because an unset or 0 httpsPort falls back to it.
No HTTPS listener is created when httpsPort is 0.

explanation: For the shared HTTPS listener, if httpsPort is unset or 0, sharedListenerPort is used. The same fallback applies to httpPort and tlsPassthroughPort.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt gives no special treatment for 443; the fallback is sharedListenerPort.
optionRationale.b: No dynamic allocation is described; the fallback is a specific configured value.
optionRationale.d: A value of 0 means the fallback is used, not that the listener is omitted.

options.text: ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port
ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode
ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort
ingress.cilium.io/host-network-port

explanation: The per-Ingress annotation for the host network port is ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port. Its default is 8080, but it must be unique per Ingress resource.

optionRationale.b: ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode selects shared or dedicated mode; it does not set the port.
optionRationale.c: This is a Helm value for the global shared listener, not a per-Ingress annotation.
optionRationale.d: This annotation name does not appear; the correct name is host-listener-port.

stem: The global Cilium ingress controller mode is configured to dedicated via ingressController.loadbalancerMode, and several Ingress resources are deployed. What must each Ingress resource provide, and why?

options.text: Nothing extra; the controller assigns a unique port automatically to each Ingress resource.

The ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation, because the port must be unique per Ingress resource and the annotation is mandatory in dedicated mode when multiple Ingress resources are deployed.
The ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode annotation set to shared, so that all Ingress resources reuse one port.
A NodePort Service per Ingress resource, because host network mode is disabled in dedicated mode.

explanation: In dedicated mode, or when an Ingress sets ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode to dedicated and multiple Ingress resources are deployed, the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation is mandatory because the port must be unique per Ingress resource.

optionRationale.a: No automatic assignment is described; the annotation is mandatory in this situation.
optionRationale.c: Setting the mode to shared contradicts the dedicated configuration and does not satisfy the requirement.
optionRationale.d: Host network mode is not disabled in dedicated mode, and no NodePort Service per Ingress is described.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: This annotation is mandatory if the global Cilium ingress controller mode is configured to ``dedicated`` (``ingressController.loadbalancerMode``) or the ingress resource sets the ``ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode`` annotation to ``dedicated`` and multiple ``Ingress`` resources are deployed.

stem: A toFQDNs rule uses the matchPattern value *.cilium.io. Which domain name does this pattern match?

options.text: sub.cilium.io
cilium.io
sub.sub.cilium.io
app.cilium.io.example.com

explanation: A single asterisk within a domain allows zero or more valid DNS characters except the dot separator. Therefore *.cilium.io matches sub.cilium.io but not cilium.io or sub.sub.cilium.io.

optionRationale.b: The pattern *.cilium.io does not match cilium.io because the asterisk does not cover the absence of a subdomain label before the dot.
optionRationale.c: The pattern *.cilium.io does not match sub.sub.cilium.io because the asterisk does not cross the dot separator.
optionRationale.d: The pattern *.cilium.io matches names ending in .cilium.io, not names that merely contain cilium.io followed by further labels.

citations.title: DNS based
citations.quote:
``*.cilium.io`` will match ``sub.cilium.io`` but not
    ``cilium.io`` or ``sub.sub.cilium.io``.

options.text: test.app.cilium.io

cilium.io.test
app.cilium.com

explanation: The **. prefix is a special wildcard that matches all cascaded subdomains in the prefix. Therefore **.cilium.io matches both app.cilium.io and test.app.cilium.io, but not cilium.io itself.

optionRationale.b: The **.cilium.io pattern does not match cilium.io, because the wildcard covers subdomains only.
optionRationale.c: The pattern is anchored to the cilium.io suffix, so a name with cilium.io as a leading label does not match.
optionRationale.d: The pattern requires the cilium.io suffix, so a name ending in cilium.com does not match.

citations.title: DNS based
citations.quote:
``**.cilium.io`` pattern will match both
    ``app.cilium.io`` and ``test.app.cilium.io`` but not ``cilium.io``.

They have already built the standalone DNS proxy image locally and created the kind cluster with Cilium installed from source. They now need to make the locally built image available inside the kind cluster. Which command should they run?

options.text: kind load docker-image quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest
make docker-standalone-dns-proxy-image
kubectl rollout restart ds -n kube-system cilium

The image must first be built with `make docker-standalone-dns-proxy-image`, but that command builds the image rather than loading it into the kind cluster.

optionRationale.b: This command builds the standalone DNS proxy container image from source; it does not load the image into the kind cluster.
optionRationale.c: This command restarts the Cilium agent DaemonSet to apply configuration changes; it does not load an image into kind.

stem: An engineer wants to prevent a pod from sending unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside the cluster, without enabling encryption strict mode. Which approach is described as a workaround?

options.text: Define an egress policy that either completely disallows traffic to reserved:world identities, or only allows egress to a subset of trusted IP addresses using toCIDR, toCIDRSet and toFQDN rules.
Set encryption.strictMode.ingress.enabled to true so that all cluster-internal ingress traffic must arrive through the WireGuard tunnel.
Set encryption.strictMode.egress.allowRemoteNodeIdentities to true to permit unencrypted traffic to node identities.
Switch to direct routing mode so that the node CIDR and pod CIDR do not overlap.

explanation: The excerpt states that one workaround is to ensure the endpoint is not allowed to send unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside the cluster. This can be achieved by defining an egress policy which either completely disallows traffic to reserved:world identities, or only allows egress traffic to addresses outside the cluster to a certain subset of trusted IP addresses using toCIDR, toCIDRSet and toFQDN rules.

optionRationale.b: Strict mode ingress concerns cluster-internal ingress traffic arriving at local endpoints, not egress to arbitrary external targets.
optionRationale.c: Setting allowRemoteNodeIdentities to true allows unencrypted traffic to node identities; it does not restrict egress to arbitrary external targets.
optionRationale.d: Direct routing mode with non-overlapping node and pod CIDRs is a requirement for disabling dynamic lookups in strict mode egress, not a workaround for unencrypted egress to arbitrary targets.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
One workaround for this issue is to ensure that the endpoint is not allowed to
send unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside of the cluster.

stem: A cluster uses encryption strict mode ingress. Which limitation applies to this mode?

options.text: Node-to-node encryption for WireGuard is not protected by strict mode ingress; enforcement only applies to cluster-internal pod traffic destined for local endpoints.
Strict mode ingress protects node-to-node WireGuard encryption but not cluster-internal pod traffic.
Strict mode ingress is supported only with IPsec and not with WireGuard.
Strict mode ingress requires the pod CIDR to be IPv4 and leaks IPv6 traffic.

explanation: The excerpt states that node-to-node encryption for WireGuard is not protected by strict mode ingress, and that enforcement only applies to cluster-internal pod traffic destined for local endpoints.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the limitation: node-to-node WireGuard encryption is the unprotected case, while cluster-internal pod traffic to local endpoints is enforced.
optionRationale.c: Strict mode ingress requires WireGuard encryption and is not supported with IPsec, the opposite of this option.
optionRationale.d: The IPv4 requirement and IPv6 leak are limitations of strict mode egress, not strict mode ingress.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
Node-to-node encryption for wireguard is not protected by strict mode 
  ingress. Enforcement only applies to cluster-internal pod traffic destined
  for local endpoints.

stem: An engineer applies a manifest that creates a Deployment for each of three microservices and a Service named deathstar. The Service is intended to load-balance traffic to the deathstar pods across two replicas. Which label selector must the deathstar Service use for this to work?

options.text: org=empire, class=deathstar
org=empire, class=tiefighter
org=alliance, class=xwing
k8s-app=kube-dns

explanation: The deathstar Deployment is identified with the labels (org=empire, class=deathstar), and the deathstar-service load-balances traffic to all pods carrying that label pair. The other label pairs belong to the tiefighter and xwing deployments, and k8s-app=kube-dns is the label shown on the DNS endpoints, not on the deathstar pods.

optionRationale.b: org=empire, class=tiefighter identifies the tiefighter landing-request client, not the deathstar webservice pods.
optionRationale.c: org=alliance, class=xwing identifies the alliance ship's client service, not the deathstar pods.
optionRationale.d: k8s-app=kube-dns appears on the coredns endpoints in the endpoint list, not on the deathstar pods.

citations.title: Deploy the Demo Application
citations.quote: It also includes a deathstar-service, which load-balances traffic to all pods with label (``org=empire, class=deathstar``).

stem: A single-node cluster has Cilium installed and kube-dns working. An engineer deploys the demo application and then runs `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg endpoint list`. What will the output show?

options.text: All endpoints in the cluster, because the command targets the Cilium DaemonSet and this is a single-node installation.
Only the endpoints running on the same node as the selected Cilium pod, because endpoint listing is always node-local.
Only the deathstar endpoints, because the demo application is the most recently deployed workload.
No endpoints, because endpoint listing requires a multi-node installation.

explanation: The excerpt states that in a single-node installation the command `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg endpoint list` lists them all, whereas in a multi-node installation only the endpoints on the same node are listed. Since the scenario is a single-node cluster, every endpoint is shown.

optionRationale.b: Node-local listing is the behaviour described for a multi-node installation, not a single-node one.
optionRationale.c: The command lists endpoints generally; nothing in the excerpt restricts output to the most recently deployed workload.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the command as listing all endpoints in a single-node installation, so it does not require multiple nodes.

citations.title: Deploy the Demo Application

in a single-node installation
``kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg endpoint list`` lists them all, but in a

stem: In the Star Wars-inspired demo application, which component runs an HTTP webservice on port 80 that is exposed through a Kubernetes Service to load-balance requests across two pod replicas?

options.text: deathstar
tiefighter
xwing
kube-dns

explanation: The excerpt says the deathstar runs an HTTP webservice on port 80, exposed as a Kubernetes Service that load-balances requests to deathstar across two pod replicas. The tiefighter and xwing are landing-request client services, and kube-dns is the DNS component that must be operating correctly before deployment.

optionRationale.b: tiefighter represents a landing-request client service on a typical empire ship, not the port 80 webservice.
optionRationale.c: xwing represents a similar client service on an alliance ship, not the port 80 webservice.
optionRationale.d: kube-dns is the DNS service that must be operating correctly; it is not the demo webservice on port 80.

citations.title: Deploy the Demo Application

stem: A cluster is handling a large number of fragmented datagrams. Which statement describes the default capacity limit for fragmentation maps in Cilium?

options.text: The IPv4 and IPv6 fragmentation maps each default to 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node.
The IPv4 and IPv6 fragmentation maps each default to 16k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node.
The IPv4 fragmentation map defaults to 8k and the IPv6 fragmentation map defaults to 16k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node.
The IPv4 and IPv6 fragmentation maps share a single default limit of 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node.

explanation: The table lists both IPv4 Fragmentation and IPv6 Fragmentation with a default limit of 8k, and the scale implication is a maximum of 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node for each map. The 16k figure belongs to other maps such as the masquerade and egress policy maps.

optionRationale.b: 16k is the default limit for the IPv4 Masq, IPv6 Masq, Egress Policy and Node maps, not the fragmentation maps.
optionRationale.c: Both fragmentation maps have the same default limit of 8k; the excerpt does not give IPv6 a larger default.
optionRationale.d: The table lists the two fragmentation maps separately, each with its own 8k limit, rather than a single shared limit.

citations.title: eBPF Maps
citations.quote:
IPv4 Fragmentation       node             8k                Max 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node
IPv6 Fragmentation       node             8k                Max 8k fragmented datagrams in flight simultaneously on the node

stem: A Cilium datapath designer wants a BPF program that inspects packet data at the earliest possible moment after reception, before any other networking-stack processing, so that malicious traffic can be dropped with the best possible performance. Which BPF hook should the program be attached to?

options.text: The XDP hook
The traffic control ingress hook
The socket operations hook
The socket send/recv hook

explanation: XDP sits at the earliest point in the networking driver and runs the program upon packet reception, directly on the packet data before any other processing, which the excerpt describes as the best possible packet processing performance and ideal for filtering programs that drop malicious or unexpected traffic.

optionRationale.b: The tc ingress hook is also attached to a networking interface but runs after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet, so it is not the earliest point.
optionRationale.c: The socket operations hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events, not on packet reception in the driver.
optionRationale.d: The socket send/recv hook runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket, which is far removed from packet reception.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
The XDP BPF hook is at the earliest point possible in the networking driver
  and triggers a run of the BPF program upon packet reception.

stem: An engineer is choosing between the XDP hook and the traffic control ingress hook for a program that must apply L3/L4 endpoint policy and redirect traffic to endpoints. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two hooks?

options.text: The tc ingress hook runs after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet and has access to most of the metadata associated with a packet, making it ideal for local node processing such as L3/L4 endpoint policy.
The tc ingress hook runs before the networking stack has done any processing of the packet, which is why it is preferred for dropping malicious traffic at the driver.
The XDP hook runs after the L3 layer of the stack and therefore has access to more packet metadata than the tc ingress hook.
The XDP hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events, whereas the tc ingress hook is attached to a networking interface.

explanation: The excerpt states that tc ingress programs are attached to a networking interface, same as XDP, but run after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet, before the L3 layer, with access to most of the packet metadata, which makes the hook ideal for local node processing such as applying L3/L4 endpoint policy and redirecting traffic to endpoints.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the ordering: tc ingress runs after initial processing, not before any processing; running at the driver is the XDP position.
optionRationale.c: XDP is the earliest hook in the driver, not a hook that runs after the L3 layer.
optionRationale.d: The cgroup-attached hook that runs on TCP events is the socket operations hook, not XDP.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
BPF programs attached to the traffic
  control (tc) ingress hook are attached to a networking interface, same as
  XDP, but will run after the networking stack has done initial processing
  of the packet.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with eBPF-based masquerading enabled. An engineer inspects the node and finds that the eBPF masquerading program is attached to eth0 and eth1. A pod on that node sends a packet to an address outside the cluster, and the packet leaves through a device that does not run the masquerading program. What happens to the packet?

options.text: It is masqueraded to the IPv4 address of the output device, because the program is attached to at least one device on the node.
It is not masqueraded, because masquerading can take place only on devices which run the eBPF masquerading program.
It is masqueraded by falling back to iptables-based masquerading for that device.
It is dropped, because eBPF masquerading requires every output device to run the program.

explanation: The eBPF masquerading program only acts on the devices it is attached to. A packet sent from a pod to an outside address is masqueraded only if the output device runs the program, so a packet leaving through a device without the program is not masqueraded.

optionRationale.a: Attachment to eth0 and eth1 says nothing about a different output device; the program must run on the device the packet actually leaves through.
optionRationale.c: No iptables fallback per device is described; the eBPF implementation is a distinct mode.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says such packets are not masqueraded, not that they are dropped.

citations.title: eBPF-based
citations.quote:
Masquerading can take place only on those devices which run the eBPF
masquerading program.

stem: An engineer enables eBPF-based masquerading with the bpf.masquerade=true helm option and does not set the devices option. Which devices will the eBPF masquerading program be attached to?

options.text: All devices on the node, regardless of any other feature.
Only the device carrying the default route.
The devices selected by the BPF NodePort device detection mechanism.
No devices until the devices option is set explicitly.

explanation: When the devices option is not specified, the program is automatically attached to the devices selected by the BPF NodePort device detection mechanism. The devices helm option exists to change this manually.

optionRationale.a: Attachment is not to every device; it follows the NodePort device detection mechanism unless overridden.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the BPF NodePort device detection mechanism, not the default-route device.
optionRationale.d: Attachment happens automatically; an explicit devices setting is only needed to change it manually.

citations.title: eBPF-based
citations.quote:
If not specified, the program will be automatically
attached to the devices selected by :ref:`the BPF NodePort device detection
mechanism <Nodeport Devices>`.

stem: What is the purpose of applying an L7 policy that limits each service calling deathstar's API to only the HTTP requests it requires?

options.text: To provide the strongest security by enforcing least-privilege isolation between microservices.
To allow all empire ships full access to deathstar's API.
To deny all access to deathstar's API from any pod.
To enable monitoring of HTTP requests with cilium-dbg monitor.

explanation: The excerpt states that to provide the strongest security (i.e., enforce least-privilege isolation) between microservices, each service should be limited to only the HTTP requests it requires.

optionRationale.b: Full access is the opposite of least-privilege isolation.
optionRationale.c: Denying all access is not least-privilege isolation; it is no access at all.
optionRationale.d: Monitoring is a separate capability, not the purpose of the L7 policy.

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote:
to
provide the strongest security (i.e., enforce least-privilege isolation)
between microservices, each service that calls *deathstar's* API should be
limited to making only the set of HTTP requests it requires for legitimate
operation.

stem: A user reports that `kubectl get gateway -A` returns no resources, with an error indicating the resource type is not found. What should the engineer check?

options.text: Whether the Gateway API CRDs are installed.
Whether the Gateway class is set to `cilium`.
Whether a LoadBalancer implementation is present.
Whether the Cilium Operator logs show reconciliation errors.

explanation: The excerpt states that if the Gateway API resource type (Gateway, HTTPRoute, etc.) is not found, you should make sure that the Gateway API CRDs are installed. The other checks apply when the resource exists but has issues such as missing address or incorrect class.

optionRationale.b: The class check is relevant when the Gateway exists but is not programmed, not when the resource type is missing.
optionRationale.c: A missing LoadBalancer implementation would result in no address, not a missing resource type.
optionRationale.d: Operator logs may contain debugging information, but the specific advice for a missing resource type is to check CRD installation.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: If the Gateway API resource type (``Gateway``, ``HTTPRoute``, etc.) is not found, make sure that the Gateway API CRDs are installed.

stem: Which condition type indicates that all referenced secrets were found and have permission for use?

options.text: Accepted
Programmed
ResolvedRefs
AttachedRoutes

explanation: The excerpt defines `ResolvedRefs` as the condition where all referenced secrets were found and have permission for use. `Accepted` means the configuration was accepted, and `Programmed` means it was programmed into Envoy.

optionRationale.a: `Accepted` indicates the Gateway configuration was accepted, not secret resolution.
optionRationale.b: `Programmed` indicates the configuration was programmed into Envoy.
optionRationale.d: `AttachedRoutes` is a field in listener status, not a condition type for secret resolution.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: ``ResolvedRefs``: all referenced secrets were found and have permission for use.

stem: An engineer runs `kubectl get gateway -A` and receives an error that the resource type `Gateway` is not found. What should the engineer check?

options.text: Whether the Gateway API CRDs are installed.
Whether the Gateway class is set to `cilium`.
Whether a LoadBalancer service is assigned to the Gateway.
Whether the Gateway is programmed.

explanation: If the Gateway API resource type (such as `Gateway` or `HTTPRoute`) is not found, the engineer should make sure that the Gateway API CRDs are installed. The other checks apply only once the resource type exists and can be listed.

optionRationale.b: The class check is relevant only after the Gateway resource is found.
optionRationale.c: The LoadBalancer check is relevant only after the Gateway resource is found.
optionRationale.d: The programmed status is relevant only after the Gateway resource is found.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: If the Gateway API resource type (``Gateway``, ``HTTPRoute``, etc.) is not found, make sure that the Gateway API CRDs are installed.

stem: An engineer enables the Cilium ingress controller in host network mode and does not set ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort. On which port does the Cilium ingress controller Envoy listener listen by default?

options.text: 0, meaning a port is chosen at random

explanation: The sharedListenerPort flag sets the host network port for the Envoy listener, and its default is 8080. If you change it, you should choose a port number higher than 1023.

optionRationale.b: 1023 is the threshold below which you should not choose a port; it is not the default.
optionRationale.c: 443 is not given as the default for the shared listener port.
optionRationale.d: A value of 0 is described for the httpPort, httpsPort and tlsPassthroughPort flags, which then fall back to sharedListenerPort; it is not the default of sharedListenerPort itself.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: ``ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort``: Host network port to expose the Cilium ingress controller Envoy listener. The default port is ``8080``.

stem: A cluster uses the dedicated ingress mode, and several Ingress resources are deployed. An engineer wants to expose the Cilium ingress controller Envoy listener on the host network for one of those Ingress resources. Which annotation must be set on that Ingress resource, and what constraint applies to its value?

options.text: ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port, with a value that is unique per Ingress resource and preferably higher than 1023.
ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode, with the value dedicated, which also sets the port.
ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort, set as an annotation on the Ingress resource.
ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port, which may be shared by all Ingress resources as long as it is above 1023.

explanation: The host-listener-port annotation sets the host network port for the Envoy listener. It is mandatory when the global mode is dedicated or when the Ingress resource sets the loadbalancer-mode annotation to dedicated and multiple Ingress resources are deployed, and it must be unique per Ingress resource.

optionRationale.b: The loadbalancer-mode annotation selects shared or dedicated mode; it does not set the host network port.
optionRationale.c: sharedListenerPort is a Helm flag for the shared listener, not a per-Ingress annotation.
optionRationale.d: The port can only be used for a single Ingress resource because it needs to be unique per Ingress resource.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: ``ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port``:  Host network port to expose the Cilium ingress controller Envoy listener. The default port is ``8080`` but it can only be used for a single ``Ingress`` resource as it needs to be unique per ``Ingress`` resource.

stem: An engineer inspects a SPIRE entry for a workload and sees that its Parent ID is `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-operator`. What does this indicate about how the entry was created?

options.text: The Cilium operator created the SPIRE entry for the Cilium Identity.
The Cilium agent created the SPIRE entry on behalf of the workload.
The SPIRE server created the entry automatically when the Pod started.
The workload created its own entry by registering with the SPIRE server.

explanation: The Cilium operator is listed as the Parent ID because the Cilium operator creates SPIRE entries for Cilium Identities as they are created.

optionRationale.b: The Cilium agent has its own registered delegate Identity, but the excerpt states that the operator registers Identities on behalf of the workloads.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe the SPIRE server creating entries automatically; it describes the operator creating them.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe workloads self-registering; registration is performed by the operator.

citations.title: Verify SPIFFE Identities
citations.quote: That is because the Cilium operator creates SPIRE entries for Cilium Identities as they are created.

stem: An engineer lists all SPIRE entries with `-selector cilium:mutual-auth` and then runs `kubectl get ciliumidentities`. How should the engineer confirm that the two sets match?

options.text: The identity ID listed under NAME in the ciliumidentities output should match the digits at the end of each SPIFFE ID.
The Entry ID of each SPIRE entry should match the identity ID under NAME.
The Parent ID of each SPIRE entry should match the identity ID under NAME.
The Selector of each SPIRE entry should match the identity ID under NAME.

explanation: The excerpt states that the identity ID listed under NAME should match with the digits at the end of the SPIFFE ID.

optionRationale.b: The Entry ID is a UUID for the SPIRE entry, not the Cilium Identity ID.
optionRationale.c: The Parent ID identifies the parent agent or operator, not the Cilium Identity ID.
optionRationale.d: The Selector is a label such as `cilium:mutual-auth`, not the Cilium Identity ID.

citations.title: Verify SPIFFE Identities
citations.quote: The identify ID listed under ``NAME`` should match with the digits at the end of the SPIFFE ID executed in the previous command.

stem: A Cilium Gateway API HTTPRoute includes a RequestHeaderModifier filter with the configuration `remove: ["x-request-id"]` and a prefix match for `/remove-a-request-header`. A client sends a GET request to `http://$GATEWAY/remove-a-request-header` that originally carries an `X-Request-Id` header. What does the echo server receive?

options.text: The request arrives without the `X-Request-Id` header, because the filter removes it.
The request arrives with `X-Request-Id` set to an empty string, because removal blanks the value.
The request arrives with the original `X-Request-Id` value unchanged, because `remove` only applies to response headers.
The request is rejected with an error, because `remove` cannot be used with a prefix match.

explanation: The `remove` keyword takes a list of header names and strips them from the incoming request. The example shows that after adding the `remove-a-request-header` prefix match, the `x-request-id` header no longer appears in the echo server's response body.

optionRationale.b: Removal deletes the header rather than setting it to an empty value; the example response omits `X-Request-Id` entirely.
optionRationale.c: The `remove` action applies to incoming requests, not responses, and the example confirms the header is gone.
optionRationale.d: The example pairs `remove` with a prefix match successfully; no error is shown.

citations.title: Modify incoming HTTP Requests
citations.quote: You can also remove headers with the ``remove`` keyword and a list of header names.

stem: An engineer configures a RequestHeaderModifier filter with `set: - name: x-request-id, value: set-cilium-header-value` and attaches it to the `/edit-a-request-header` prefix match. A client sends a GET request to that path with an existing `X-Request-Id` header. What header value does the echo server observe?

options.text: `set-cilium-header-value`
The original client-supplied value, because `set` only adds headers that are absent.
Both the original value and `set-cilium-header-value`, as duplicate entries.
No `X-Request-Id` header at all, because `set` replaces the header with an empty value.

explanation: The `set` action edits an existing header by specifying the header name and the new value. The example response for `/edit-a-request-header` shows `X-Request-Id` with the value `set-cilium-header-value`.

optionRationale.b: `set` is described as the action to edit an existing header, so it overwrites rather than only adding when absent.
optionRationale.c: The example shows a single value, not duplicates.
optionRationale.d: The header is present with the new value, not removed.

citations.title: Modify incoming HTTP Requests
citations.quote: To edit an existing header, use the ``set`` action to specify the value of the header to modify as well as the new header value to set.

stem: A request passes through a Cilium Gateway whose HTTPRoute has a RequestHeaderModifier filter configured to add a header. After the request reaches the echo server, where can an engineer confirm that the Gateway added the header?

options.text: In the body of the response sent back from the echo server, which lists the incoming request headers.
Only in the Gateway's own access logs, because the echo server strips added headers.
In the HTTP status code returned by the Gateway.
In the `X-Forwarded-For` header, which is repurposed to carry added headers.

explanation: The echo server returns the incoming request headers in the response body, so an added header such as `My-Header-Name` appears there alongside the other request headers.

optionRationale.b: The example shows the added header in the echo server's response body, not only in Gateway logs.
optionRationale.c: The status code does not enumerate headers; the body does.
optionRationale.d: `X-Forwarded-For` carries the client address, not arbitrary added headers.

citations.title: Modify incoming HTTP Requests
citations.quote: If the curl succeeds, you can see the HTTP Header from the incoming request in the body of the response sent back from the echo server. You can also see that the Gateway added the header.

stem: Which keyword is used in a RequestHeaderModifier filter to delete one or more headers from an incoming HTTP request?

options.text: `remove`
`set`
`add`
`delete`

explanation: The excerpt states that headers can be removed with the `remove` keyword followed by a list of header names.

optionRationale.b: `set` is used to edit an existing header's value, not to delete it.
optionRationale.c: `add` is not mentioned as a removal keyword in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: `delete` is not the keyword used; the excerpt uses `remove`.

stem: A team exposes Cilium ingress (Ingress API) through a Service and wants the backend pod to receive the client IP via the X-Forwarded-For and X-Envoy-External-Address fields. Do they need to set externalTrafficPolicy: Local on the Service?

options.text: No, it is not necessary; Cilium ingress preserves source IP visibility without requiring externalTrafficPolicy: Local.
Yes, it is required; without Local the backend pod will never see the source IP.
Yes, but only if kube-proxy is installed.
No, but only if the Service is of type NodePort rather than LoadBalancer.

explanation: For Cilium's ingress config (both Ingress and Gateway API), it is not necessary to configure externalTrafficPolicy: Local to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod via X-Forwarded-For and X-Envoy-External-Address. This is because Cilium always forwards ingress traffic to Envoy using TPROXY on the local node.

optionRationale.b: This contradicts the explicit statement that Local is not necessary for Cilium ingress config.
optionRationale.c: kube-proxy presence does not change the Cilium ingress behaviour described.
optionRationale.d: The statement applies to Cilium ingress config generally, not only to NodePort Services.

stem: A platform team exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service and sets externalTrafficPolicy to Local. They want to confirm that only nodes with local backend pods are considered healthy by an upstream load balancer. Which behaviour should they expect from the health check endpoint?

options.text: Requests to http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz return 200 on nodes that have local pods running and non-200 on nodes that do not.
Requests to http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz return 200 on every node regardless of whether local pods are running.
Requests to http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz return non-200 on nodes that have local pods running and 200 on nodes that do not.
The healthCheckNodePort is only opened when externalTrafficPolicy is set to Cluster, so no health check endpoint is available.

explanation: With externalTrafficPolicy: Local, Kubernetes automatically sets the healthCheckNodePort, and the node opens that port. Requests to http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz return 200 on nodes that have local pods running and non-200 on nodes that do not. Cilium implements this for general Loadbalancer Services, although the behaviour differs for Cilium ingress config.

optionRationale.b: This describes the Cluster setting, where nodes route to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, not the Local health check contract.
optionRationale.c: The status codes are inverted: 200 is returned on nodes with local pods, non-200 on nodes without.
optionRationale.d: The healthCheckNodePort is automatically set by Kubernetes when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set, not when it is Cluster.

Cluster
External

stem: A team exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a Loadbalancer Service with externalTrafficPolicy set to Cluster. What effect does this setting have on routing and source IP?

options.text: The node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, and the node may masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see the source IP.
The node routes only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP, guaranteeing source IP visibility.
The node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly and never masquerades the source IP, so the backend pod always sees the source IP.
The node routes only to Pods on the local node and always masquerades the source IP.

explanation: With externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster, the node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly. Upstream load balancers expect to be able to send traffic to any node and have it reach a backend Pod, and the node may masquerade the source IP. Consequently, the backend pod may not see the source IP.

optionRationale.b: This describes the Local setting, not Cluster.
optionRationale.c: Cluster does not guarantee source IP visibility; the node may masquerade the source IP.
optionRationale.d: This combines the routing behaviour of Local with masquerading, which is not what Cluster does.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
``Cluster``: Node will route to all endpoints across the cluster evenly. This
  has a couple of other effects: Firstly, upstream loadbalancers will expect to
  be able to send traffic to any node and have it end up at a backend Pod, and
  the node *may* masquerade the source IP.

stem: An engineer is exposing Cilium ingress (using the Ingress resource) through a LoadBalancer Service and wants the backend pod to see the client's source IP. They are deciding whether to set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`. What does Cilium require for source IP visibility in this case?

options.text: `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` must be set, because it is the only way to ensure source IP visibility in all clusters.
`externalTrafficPolicy: Local` is not necessary; the source IP remains visible to the backend pod via the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` fields.
`externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` must be set, because Cilium always masquerades the source IP when using TPROXY.
Source IP visibility is impossible for Cilium ingress because all ingress traffic is forwarded using TPROXY, which hides the client IP.

explanation: For Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, it is not necessary to configure `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod, because the source IP is preserved via the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` fields.

optionRationale.a: This is true for clusters using `kube-proxy` in general, but the excerpt explicitly states that for Cilium ingress config it is not necessary.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say Cilium always masquerades the source IP with TPROXY; it says TPROXY transparently forwards packets.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the opposite: source IP remains visible via the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` fields.

citations.quote:
for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, **it is not
necessary** to configure ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` to keep the source IP

stem: A Cilium cluster uses transparent encryption. An endpoint is permitted to initiate traffic to targets outside the cluster. A new pod is created on a remote node, but the local node has not yet learned that the pod's IP address belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint. During this time, the endpoint sends packets to that IP address. What does Cilium do with those initial packets?

options.text: It sends them unencrypted, because it must assume the destination IP address is outside the cluster.
It drops them until the endpoint information has propagated.
It encrypts them using the local node's encryption key.
It encrypts them using the encryption key of the remote node.

explanation: Transparent encryption uses the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to decide whether a destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that a particular IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or newly joined remote Cilium host, it has to assume the destination is outside the cluster, so the initial packets are sent unencrypted. Only once the information has propagated and Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node does it start encrypting packets using the encryption key of the remote node.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the initial packets are sent out unencrypted, not dropped; dropping would be a policy action, not the described encryption behaviour.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that once the endpoint is known, encryption uses the encryption key of the remote node, not the local node's key.
optionRationale.d: Encryption with the remote node's key begins only after Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node; before that, packets are unencrypted.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
In such a case there is a time window during which Cilium will send out the
initial packets unencrypted, as it has to assume the destination IP address is
outside of the cluster.

stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy selects pods with app=client and contains an egress rule with toFQDNs.matchPattern set to `*.cilium.io`. The DNS proxy observes a response for `cilium.io` and another for `sub.sub.cilium.io`. Which of these names will have its IPs inserted into the generated L3 rule?

options.text: Neither `cilium.io` nor `sub.sub.cilium.io`.
Both `cilium.io` and `sub.sub.cilium.io`.
`cilium.io` only.
`sub.sub.cilium.io` only.

explanation: The pattern `*.cilium.io` uses a single `*` that matches zero or more valid DNS characters except the `.` separator. It therefore matches `sub.cilium.io` but not `cilium.io` (no leading label) and not `sub.sub.cilium.io` (two labels before the dot). To cover cascaded subdomains the `**.` prefix would be needed.

optionRationale.b: A single `*` does not span the `.` separator, so neither name is covered.
optionRationale.c: `*.cilium.io` requires at least the wildcard label to be present; the bare apex `cilium.io` is explicitly excluded.
optionRationale.d: `sub.sub.cilium.io` has two labels before `cilium.io`, which a single `*` cannot match.

citations.title: DNS based
citations.quote:
``*`` within a domain allows 0 or more valid DNS characters, except for the
    ``.`` separator. ``*.cilium.io`` will match ``sub.cilium.io`` but not
    ``cilium.io`` or ``sub.sub.cilium.io``.

stem: How does Cilium handle the start of additional pods labelled role=frontend once the first such pod has already been given an identity that is permitted to initiate connections to the identity of the role=backend pod?

options.text: It resolves the identity via a key-value store, with no action performed on any cluster node hosting role=backend pods.
It installs a new IP address filter on every node hosting a role=backend pod before the pod is allowed to start.
It assigns a fresh, unique identity to each new pod, which must then be separately allowed to reach the role=backend identity.
It delays the new pod until every cluster node has been updated with the security rules for that pod.

explanation: Because Cilium bases security on a label-derived identity that can be shared between pods, starting further role=frontend pods only requires resolving that identity via a key-value store; nothing has to be done on the nodes hosting role=backend pods, and the start is delayed only until the identity is resolved.

optionRationale.b: Installing IP address filters on backend nodes is the traditional approach that Cilium replaces, not what Cilium does.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the identity can be shared between pods, so subsequent frontend pods reuse the existing identity rather than each needing a new one.
optionRationale.d: Updating security rules on all other cluster nodes is the costly step Cilium avoids; only identity resolution is required.

citations.title: Identity-Based
citations.quote:
The subsequent start of additional ``role=frontend`` pods
only requires to resolve this identity via a key-value store, no action has to
be performed on any of the cluster nodes hosting ``role=backend`` pods.

stem: A global service named rebel-base exists in a Cluster Mesh. In cluster 1, an engineer runs `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=remote --overwrite` and then, from cluster 1, runs `kubectl exec -ti deployment/x-wing -- curl rebel-base`. Which pods reply?

options.text: Only pods in cluster 2, because the remote endpoints are now preferred.
Only pods in cluster 1, because the local endpoints remain preferred until the annotation is removed.
Pods in both clusters, because the annotation only takes effect on the cluster where the Service object is defined.
No pods reply, because setting the value to remote disables local backends entirely and the remote ones are not yet healthy.

explanation: Setting the affinity annotation to remote makes the remote endpoints the preferred destination, so traffic from cluster 1 is served by cluster 2's pods. The excerpt records that after changing the value to remote, accessing the global service from cluster 1 gives replies from pods in cluster 2 only, and the endpoint listing shows the remote backends marked as preferred.

optionRationale.c: The annotation is applied to the global service and changes which endpoints are preferred for access from cluster 1; the excerpt shows the replies changing immediately after the annotate command.
optionRationale.d: The remote value expresses a preference rather than disabling local backends, and the excerpt shows replies still arriving, from cluster 2.

stem: A cluster runs in `multi-pool` IPAM mode with a single `CiliumPodIPPool` named `default` whose IPv4 CIDR is `10.10.0.0/16`. An engineer applies a change that replaces that CIDR with `10.20.0.0/16` while pods on two nodes still hold addresses from the old range. What does the Cilium operator do in response?

options.text: It logs a warning for each CIDR block still in use by a node but removed from the pool.
It refuses the update and reverts the pool to the previous CIDR.
It silently reassigns the affected pods to addresses from the new CIDR.
It deletes the `CiliumNodes` of the affected nodes automatically.

explanation: The excerpt states that the operator reports a warning for each CIDR block still in use by a node but removed from the pool, and shows the corresponding log lines with `msg="CIDR from pool still in use by node"`. The update itself is accepted; the operator does not revert it, reassign pod IPs, or delete `CiliumNodes` on its own — those are manual steps in the migration procedure.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the update being applied and the operator merely warning; nothing reverts the pool.
optionRationale.c: Reassigning IPs is done by evicting and rescheduling workloads, not by the operator silently.
optionRationale.d: Deleting `CiliumNodes` is a manual step performed with `kubectl delete cn` for each node group.

docker push quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest
kubectl apply -f quay.io/cilium/standalone-dns-proxy:latest

stem: A platform team wants `cilium monitor` to show DNS query names and HTTP request URLs for traffic leaving pods in the `default` namespace, rather than only packet-level events. Which change achieves this?

options.text: Create a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` with L7 rules for the relevant ports, which causes matching flows to be redirected to the proxy.
Restart the Cilium agent with L3/L4 event reporting disabled so that only application-layer events remain.
Add a `matchPattern` entry to the `endpointSelector` of an existing L3/L4 policy.
Run `hubble observe` with the `-t l7` filter, which upgrades captured L3/L4 events into L7 flow details.

explanation: By default the monitor gives visibility only into L3/L4 packet events. To obtain L7 visibility you create a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` that specifies L7 rules; flows matching an L7 rule become visible to Cilium and are redirected to the proxy, so `cilium monitor` or `hubble observe` shows the L7 flow details. Note that such a policy also restricts traffic, so it is not a pure observation tool.

optionRationale.b: Nothing in the excerpt describes disabling L3/L4 reporting; the documented route to L7 visibility is an L7 policy.
optionRationale.c: `matchPattern` belongs under the `dns` rules of a `toPorts` entry, not inside `endpointSelector`, and the selector does not create L7 visibility.
optionRationale.d: The `-t l7` filter selects L7 flows for display; it does not itself produce L7 details, which require the traffic to be proxied by an L7 policy.

stem: An engineer applies the policy below to pods in the `default` namespace. A pod then attempts an HTTP request to an endpoint in the `default` namespace on TCP port 9090. What is the result?

options.text: The request is dropped, because the policy restricts egress and nothing matches the L4 section of either rule.
The request is allowed and appears in `hubble observe` output as an L7 HTTP flow.
The request is allowed but only L3/L4 details are shown, since port 9090 has no L7 rule.
The request is proxied and allowed, because `http: [{}]` matches all ports for endpoints in the `default` namespace.

explanation: The policy restricts egress communication and drops anything that is not matched. The HTTP rule covers only ports TCP/80 and TCP/8080, so traffic to port 9090 matches neither the DNS rule nor the HTTP rule and is dropped.

optionRationale.b: Only traffic on the ports named in the `toPorts` sections is picked up and proxied; port 9090 is not among them.
optionRationale.c: Unmatched egress is dropped rather than allowed, so there is no flow to observe at all.
optionRationale.d: The `http: [{}]` rules apply only to the ports listed in the same `toPorts` entry, namely 80 and 8080.
