stem: A cluster-wide policy named default-deny is applied. It selects every endpoint whose io.kubernetes.pod.namespace is not kube-system, and its only egress rule permits UDP port 53 to the kube-dns endpoints in kube-system with a DNS matchPattern of '*'. A client outside the cluster then requests the /details endpoint of an application exposed through Cilium Ingress. What is the result?

options.text: The request is denied, and the response returned to the client is HTTP 403.
The request is allowed, because the policy contains no ingress section and therefore only restricts egress.
The request is allowed, because the reserved:ingress identity is excluded from the endpointSelector.
The request is dropped at the TCP layer, so the client receives no HTTP response at all.

explanation: The policy denies all traffic by default, and the excerpt states that with it applied the request to /details is denied for external and in-cluster traffic. The captured session shows the client receiving an HTTP 403 Forbidden with server: envoy, so the denial is surfaced as an HTTP response rather than a silent connection failure.

optionRationale.b: The policy is described as blocking all traffic by default; the absence of an ingress section does not leave ingress unrestricted, and the observed result is a denial.
optionRationale.c: The endpointSelector excludes only the kube-system namespace; nothing in the policy exempts the reserved:ingress identity, which is handled by a separate policy later in the flow.
optionRationale.d: The captured output shows a complete HTTP exchange ending in 403 Forbidden, not a dropped connection.

attachments.title: The default-deny policy
attachments.body:
---
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "default-deny"
spec:
  description: "Block all the traffic (except DNS) by default"
  egress:
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
        k8s-app: kube-dns
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: '53'
        protocol: UDP
      rules:
        dns:
        - matchPattern: '*'
  endpointSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace
      operator: NotIn
      values:
      - kube-system

stem: After a default-deny policy has blocked traffic to an application behind Cilium Ingress, a second CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy named allow-ingress-egress is applied. It selects endpoints for which reserved:ingress exists and allows egress to the cluster entity. What effect does this have?

options.text: It allows the ingress proxy to reach endpoints in the cluster, so requests to /details succeed from both an external client and an in-cluster client.
It allows only external traffic, because the cluster entity covers endpoints outside the cluster rather than inside it.
It has no effect until the default-deny policy is deleted, because cluster-wide policies are evaluated in creation order.
It allows the ingress proxy to reach the cluster, but in-cluster clients remain blocked because they do not carry the reserved:ingress identity.

explanation: The policy grants egress from the reserved:ingress identity to all cluster identities, and the captured session shows both the external curl and the in-cluster client from deployment/client receiving the /details payload. The excerpt notes that allowing all traffic from reserved:ingress to all cluster identities is generally the more reliable option, since Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure.

optionRationale.b: The policy targets the cluster entity, and the excerpt's own output shows the in-cluster client succeeding, so the rule is not limited to external traffic.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes creation-order evaluation or a requirement to delete the default-deny policy first; the allow policy takes effect alongside it.
optionRationale.d: The captured output shows the in-cluster client from deployment/client receiving the same JSON payload, so in-cluster traffic is no longer blocked.

attachments.title: The allow policy
attachments.body:
---
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-egress
spec:
  description: "Allow all the egress traffic from reserved ingress identity to any endpoints in the cluster"
  endpointSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: reserved:ingress
      operator: Exists
  egress:
  - toEntities:
    - cluster

``cluster`` identities, given that Cilium Ingress is part of the networking

stem: You are writing a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that must select the Cilium Ingress proxy itself, so that you can grant it egress to the rest of the cluster. Which endpointSelector expression identifies that proxy?

options.text: A matchExpressions entry with key reserved:ingress and operator Exists.
A matchExpressions entry with key io.kubernetes.pod.namespace and operator NotIn, with the value kube-system.
A matchLabels entry setting k8s-app to kube-dns.
A matchExpressions entry with key reserved:ingress and operator NotIn, with the value cluster.

explanation: The allow policy in the excerpt selects the ingress proxy by matching on the reserved:ingress identity with the Exists operator, then permits egress to the cluster entity.

optionRationale.b: That expression is the endpointSelector of the default-deny policy, which selects everything outside kube-system rather than the ingress proxy.
optionRationale.c: The k8s-app: kube-dns label appears in the default-deny policy's toEndpoints match for DNS egress, not as a way to select the ingress proxy.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt uses the Exists operator for reserved:ingress; NotIn with the value cluster is not a selector it shows.

stem: A default-deny CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy is in place and you are now adding a policy to let the Cilium Ingress proxy reach application endpoints. Which approach does the guidance favour, and why?

options.text: Allow all traffic from the reserved:ingress identity to all cluster identities, because Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure.
Allow egress from reserved:ingress to specific identities only, because broad cluster access would bypass the default-deny policy.
Allow ingress to the application endpoints from the world entity, because the ingress proxy appears as world to those endpoints.
Allow egress from reserved:ingress to kube-dns on UDP port 53, because name resolution is the only requirement of the proxy.

explanation: The excerpt acknowledges that a NetworkPolicy selecting reserved:ingress and allowing egress to specific identities could also be used, but concludes that allowing all traffic from reserved:ingress to all cluster identities is probably more reliable, given that Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt presents the specific-identity approach as possible but less reliable than the broad cluster allowance, not as the favoured option.
optionRationale.c: The policy shown grants egress from reserved:ingress to the cluster entity; nothing in the excerpt describes the proxy as the world entity for this purpose.
optionRationale.d: DNS egress to kube-dns is the exception carved out in the default-deny policy, not the recommended way to let the ingress proxy reach application endpoints.

stem: A cluster runs the Cilium BGP Control Plane with no aggregation fields configured on its CiliumBGPAdvertisement resources. A Service of type ClusterIP is assigned the address 10.96.14.37. What prefix does the BGP Control Plane advertise for that service VIP?

options.text: 10.96.14.0/24, the subnet containing the VIP
10.96.14.37/32, the exact route for the VIP
10.96.0.0/16, the cluster's service CIDR
Nothing is advertised until an aggregation length is set

explanation: Without any aggregation configuration, the BGP Control Plane advertises exact routes for service VIPs, which for an IPv4 address means a /32 prefix. The aggregation length fields exist precisely to change this default, so 10.96.14.37/32 is what is advertised here.

optionRationale.a: A /24 is what you would get by setting aggregationLengthIPv4 to 24, but no aggregation is configured in this scenario.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt never mentions advertising the whole service CIDR; the default is the exact VIP route.
optionRationale.d: Aggregation is optional; the default behaviour is to advertise exact routes, not to withhold them.

citations.title: Prefix Aggregation
citations.quote:
By default, the Cilium BGP Control Plane advertises exact routes for service
VIPs (/32 or /128 prefixes).

stem: An engineer applies the CiliumBGPAdvertisement below. A Service matching the selector has ClusterIP 10.96.14.37 and ExternalIP 192.0.2.10. Which prefixes are advertised for these two addresses?
explanation: The aggregation length applies to the ClusterIP, so 10.96.14.37 is advertised as 10.96.14.0/24. The aggregation fields are ignored when advertising ExternalIP of services with externalTrafficPolicy: Local, and in any case the excerpt only describes aggregation lengths for the service VIP prefixes; the ExternalIP is advertised as its exact /32 route.

optionRationale.a: This assumes aggregation also applies to the ExternalIP, which the excerpt does not support.
optionRationale.c: This ignores aggregationLengthIPv4 entirely, which does apply to the ClusterIP.
optionRationale.d: This inverts the behaviour, aggregating the ExternalIP and leaving the ClusterIP exact.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with its eBPF kube-proxy replacement enabled. An engineer deploys a Pod that declares a hostPort but no hostIP. On which addresses on the node will that Pod be reachable?

options.text: Only on the loopback address, such as 127.0.0.1:hostPort.
On the node's detected local addresses used for NodePort services, and additionally through the loopback address on the node.
Only on the node's ExternalIP, because hostPort always prefers the public address.
On every address of every node in the cluster, because hostPort is cluster-wide.

explanation: When a hostPort is given without a hostIP, the Pod is exposed to the outside world using the same local addresses from the node that were detected and used for exposing NodePort services, and it is also reachable through the loopback address on the node.

optionRationale.a: Loopback access is additional, not the only exposure; the node's detected local addresses are also used.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the detected addresses used for NodePort services are used, such as the InternalIP or ExternalIP if set — not the ExternalIP alone.
optionRationale.d: The exposure described is on the node's own local addresses, not on every node in the cluster.

stem: An engineer wants Cilium's native hostPort mapping without adopting the Helm CNI chaining option cni.chainingMode=portmap. What is required?

Create a Kubernetes Service of type NodePort for each hostPort, because hostPort is configured through a service object.

stem: A Pod manifest specifies both hostPort and a hostIP of 0.0.0.0. How is the Pod exposed?

options.text: Only on 0.0.0.0 as a literal address, and nowhere else.
Only through the loopback address on the node.
The same as if no hostIP had been specified.
The Pod is not exposed at all, because 0.0.0.0 is rejected for hostIP.

explanation: A hostIP of 0.0.0.0 behaves the same as if a hostIP was not specified, so the Pod is exposed on the node's detected local addresses and through loopback.

optionRationale.b: Loopback is included in the no-hostIP behaviour, but it is not the only exposure.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt gives 0.0.0.0 the same behaviour as no hostIP; it does not say the Pod is left unexposed.

options.text: It must be below 1024 so that it can be bound by the node.
It must not reside in the configured NodePort port range, to avoid collisions.
It must match the containerPort value exactly.
It must be chosen from the range reserved for the loopback address.

explanation: The hostPort must not fall inside the configured NodePort port range, so that collisions are avoided.

options.text: A Kubernetes Service of type NodePort was created for the workload.
Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement exposed the container as a HostPort under port 8080.
An iptables rule was installed in the host namespace to forward the port.
The hostPort feature is disabled and the entry is a leftover from kube-proxy.

explanation: The service list shows a HostPort service type with frontend 192.168.178.29:8080 and backend 10.29.207.199:80, which validates that the eBPF kube-proxy replacement exposed the container as HostPort under the specified port 8080.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt separately shows that no iptables rule for the HostPort service is present.
optionRationale.d: A HostPort entry in the service list is the evidence that the feature is working, not that it is disabled.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with its eBPF kube-proxy replacement enabled. A Deployment is created with the container port 80 and `hostPort: 8080`, and no `hostIP` is set. On which addresses can the nginx container be reached from outside the Pod?

options.text: Only on the node's loopback address, at `127.0.0.1:8080`.
On the node's detected local addresses used for NodePort services (such as the InternalIP or ExternalIP), and also through the loopback address on the node at `127.0.0.1:8080`.
Only on the Pod's own IP address, because host port mapping requires an explicit `hostIP` to be reachable from the node.
On every address of every node in the cluster, because the host port is plumbed as a Kubernetes Service of type NodePort.

explanation: When a `hostPort` is given without a `hostIP`, the Pod is exposed to the outside world using the same local addresses from the node that were detected and used for exposing NodePort services, and it is additionally reachable through the node's loopback address at `127.0.0.1:hostPort`.

optionRationale.a: The loopback address is one of the ways the Pod is reachable, but it is not the only one; the node's detected local addresses are also used.
optionRationale.c: No `hostIP` is needed for reachability; without one, the node's detected local addresses are used, and the Pod's own IP is not the address described for host port exposure.
optionRationale.d: Host port is not configured through a Kubernetes service object; it piggy-backs on the service handling behaviour, so it is not a cluster-wide NodePort service.

Creating a Kubernetes Service of type NodePort for each host port, because host port is configured through a service object.
Nothing at all: host port support is part of kube-proxy and is inherited automatically by Cilium.

stem: A cluster runs the CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy shown in the attachment. A pod with labels org=empire and class=mediabot in the default namespace is scheduled on node1 and sends traffic to an external address. What happens to that traffic?

options.text: It is routed through node2 and SNATed with the egress IP 10.168.60.100.
It is SNATed on node1 using the first IPv4 address of the interface enp0s8.
It leaves the cluster without SNAT because the destination 0.0.0.0/0 is not matched by the policy.
It is dropped because the pod is not on the gateway node.

explanation: The policy selects pods with org=empire and class=mediabot in the default namespace, and its nodeSelector restricts it to node1. Traffic from those pods on node1 to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 is routed through the gateway node labelled node.kubernetes.io/name: node2, which SNATs it with the egress IP 10.168.60.100.

optionRationale.b: The interface field is only an alternative to egressIP; here egressIP is set, so the interface is not used.
optionRationale.c: The policy explicitly lists 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 as destinationCIDRs, so all traffic leaving the cluster is matched.
optionRationale.d: The policy routes traffic through the gateway node; it does not drop traffic from pods on other nodes.

attachments.title: The egress gateway policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-sample
spec:
  # Specify which pods should be subject to the current policy.
  # Multiple pod selectors can be specified.
  selectors:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        org: empire
        class: mediabot
        # The following label selects default namespace
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: default
    nodeSelector: # optional, if not specified the policy applies to all nodes
      matchLabels:
        node.kubernetes.io/name: node1 # only traffic from this node will be SNATed
  # Specify which destination CIDR(s) this policy applies to.
  # Multiple CIDRs can be specified.
  destinationCIDRs:
  - "0.0.0.0/0"
  - "::/0"

  # Configure the gateway node.
  egressGateway:
    # Specify which node should act as gateway for this policy.
    nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        node.kubernetes.io/name: node2

    # Specify the IP address used to SNAT traffic matched by the policy.
    # It must exist as an IP associated with a network interface on the instance.
    egressIP: 10.168.60.100

    # Alternatively it's possible to specify the interface to be used for egress traffic.
    # In this case the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses assigned to that interface will be used
    # as egress IP.
    # interface: enp0s8

traffic originating from pods with the ``org: empire`` and ``class: mediabot``
labels in the ``default`` namespace on node ``node1`` and destined to ``0.0.0.0/0`` or ``::/0``
(i.e. all traffic leaving the cluster) to be routed through the gateway node with the
``node.kubernetes.io/name: node2`` label, which will then SNAT said
traffic with the ``10.168.60.100`` egress IP.

stem: In the CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy shown in the attachment, the egressGateway block specifies egressIP: 10.168.60.100. What requirement must this address satisfy?

It must be the first IPv4 address assigned to the interface named in the interface field.
It must be a public address allocated by the cloud provider.
It must be the address of the node selected by the pod selector's nodeSelector.

stem: A cluster runs the Star Wars demo. You apply the CiliumNetworkPolicy below. A pod labelled org=empire, class=deathstar is running on a node in zone A, and a pod labelled org=empire, class=tiefighter is running on a node in zone B. The tiefighter pod sends a request to the deathstar pod on TCP port 80. What is the result?

options.text: The request is allowed, because the policy selects pods by their labels rather than by endpoint IP addresses.
The request is blocked, because the two pods are on different nodes and the policy only covers same-node traffic.
The request is blocked, because the tiefighter pod does not carry the class=deathstar label required by the endpointSelector.
The request is allowed only if the deathstar pod's IP address is also listed in the fromEndpoints section.

explanation: The policy selects the destination with endpointSelector matchLabels org=empire and class=deathstar, and admits traffic from any endpoint labelled org=empire on TCP port 80. Because Cilium matches on pod labels, the location of either pod within the cluster does not matter, so the tiefighter pod (org=empire) reaches the deathstar pod on port 80.

optionRationale.b: Cilium applies policies to the right pods based on labels irrespective of where they run in the cluster, so node placement is not a factor.
optionRationale.c: The class=deathstar label is required on the destination, which the deathstar pod has; the source only needs org=empire, which tiefighter has.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies, and the policy contains no IP addresses at all.

kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy

  name: "rule1"
spec:
  description: "L3-L4 policy to restrict deathstar access to empire ships only"

    matchLabels:
      org: empire
      class: deathstar
  ingress:

stem: An engineer is writing a Layer 7 DNS policy and wants queries for `sub.cilium.io` to be allowed, but queries for `cilium.io` itself must not be allowed by that same entry. Which `matchPattern` value achieves this?

options.text: `*.cilium.io`
`*cilium.io`
`cilium.io`
`*.*.cilium.io`

explanation: A `*` within a domain allows zero or more valid DNS characters except the `.` separator, so `*.cilium.io` matches `sub.cilium.io` but not `cilium.io`.

optionRationale.b: Without the dot separator before `cilium.io`, the pattern would also match the bare name `cilium.io`, which the engineer wants to exclude.
optionRationale.c: This is an exact name, not a pattern, and would allow only `cilium.io` itself.
optionRationale.d: This requires an extra label before `cilium.io` and would not match `sub.cilium.io`.

options.text: `*` on its own
`matchName: "*"`

explanation: The excerpt states that `*` alone matches all names and inserts all IPs in DNS responses into the cilium-agent DNS cache.

optionRationale.b: `*.*` is a pattern with a literal dot separator and does not match all names.
optionRationale.c: `*.*.*` likewise requires separators and does not match all names.
optionRationale.d: `matchName` allows queries for domains that match exactly, so a wildcard is not the mechanism it provides.

stem: A pod selected by a CiliumNetworkPolicy performs a query for the short name `servicename`, which succeeds because the DNS search list completes it to `servicename.namespace.svc.cluster.local.`. The policy's DNS rules allow only `matchName: "cilium.io"`. What happens to the query?

options.text: It is refused, because the completed FQDN must itself be allowed with `matchName` or `matchPattern`.
It is allowed, because the DNS proxy evaluates only the name as typed, before the search list is applied.
It is allowed, because queries completed by the search list bypass Layer 7 DNS policy.
It is refused, because `matchName` cannot be used for cluster-internal names and only `matchPattern` is evaluated.

explanation: Queries that rely on the DNS search list to complete the FQDN must be allowed in their entirety; a query for `servicename` that succeeds with `servicename.namespace.svc.cluster.local.` must have the latter allowed with `matchName` or `matchPattern`.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the completed FQDN must be allowed, so evaluation is not limited to the name as typed.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt exempts search-list-completed queries from policy.
optionRationale.d: `matchName` is explicitly named as one of the two ways to allow the completed FQDN.

citations.title: DNS Policy and IP Discovery

Similarly, queries that rely on the DNS search list to complete the
       FQDN must be allowed in their entirety.

stem: A cluster runs its own DNS resolver outside the cluster DNS service, and a policy author is considering intercepting DNS traffic to that resolver in order to populate `toFQDNs` rules. What guidance applies?

options.text: Strongly prefer intercepting DNS traffic only to the cluster DNS service, such as `kube-dns`, because other resolvers broaden the trust boundary for DNS-based policy decisions.
Intercepting any resolver is equivalent, because the DNS proxy validates every response before caching the IPs.
Intercepting other resolvers is preferred, because the cluster DNS service cannot populate `toFQDNs` rules.
Intercepting other resolvers is required whenever `matchPattern` is used instead of `matchName`.

explanation: The excerpt strongly prefers intercepting DNS traffic only to the cluster DNS service, such as `kube-dns`, since intercepting traffic to other resolvers broadens the trust boundary and may allow less-trusted DNS servers to influence the IPs learned for `toFQDNs` rules.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt warns that less-trusted DNS servers may influence the IPs learned, so the choice of resolver is not equivalent.
optionRationale.c: The DNS proxy is described as collecting IPs used to populate L3 `DNS based` `toFQDNs` rules, and the example intercepts `kube-dns`.
optionRationale.d: No such requirement linking `matchPattern` to non-cluster resolvers appears in the excerpt.

citations.title: DNS Policy and IP Discovery
citations.quote:
When using Layer 7 DNS policy, strongly prefer intercepting DNS traffic
   only to the cluster DNS service, such as ``kube-dns``.

A client Deployment using nginx and a server Deployment using nicolaka/netshoot
A client Deployment using nicolaka/netshoot and a server Deployment using nicolaka/netshoot
A client Deployment using nginx and a server Deployment using nginx

explanation: The procedure deploys an nginx server and a netshoot client containing nping. In the manifest the client Deployment uses the image nicolaka/netshoot and the server Deployment uses the image nginx.

optionRationale.b: The roles are the other way round: netshoot is the client because it contains nping, and nginx is the server.
optionRationale.c: Only the client uses netshoot; the server Deployment uses nginx.
optionRationale.d: Only the server uses nginx; the client Deployment uses nicolaka/netshoot so that nping is available.

stem: An engineer enables graceful restart on a CiliumBGPPeerConfig but does not set restartTimeSeconds. A Cilium Agent then restarts. How long does the peering router wait, by default, before removing the routes previously advertised by the Cilium BGP control plane?

options.text: 120 seconds
15 seconds
Until the Cilium Agent sends a new BGP OPEN message, with no timer involved
The routes are withdrawn immediately, because no RestartTime was configured

explanation: The excerpt gives the default explicitly: the default value of RestartTime is 120 seconds. The timer starts when the peer receives the TCP FIN and moves to Idle, and the routes are removed when it expires.

optionRationale.b: 15 seconds appears only in the example manifest as an explicitly configured restartTimeSeconds value, not as a default.
optionRationale.c: The peer starts its RestartTime timer on receiving the TCP FIN; the wait is bounded by that timer rather than by the next OPEN message.
optionRationale.d: Graceful restart is what prevents immediate withdrawal; the default timer still applies when restartTimeSeconds is omitted.

citations.title: Graceful Restart
citations.quote: Default value of ``RestartTime`` is 120 seconds.

stem: A Cilium Agent managing BGP peering is restarted. The peering router receives a TCP FIN on the BGP session. What does the router do, and what happens to traffic in the datapath while the Agent restarts?

options.text: It changes its BGP state to Idle and starts its RestartTime timer, while the datapath continues to forward traffic with no disruption.
It immediately withdraws all routes learned from Cilium, and forwarding stops until the Agent reconnects.
It keeps the session in Established state and ignores the FIN until a new BGP OPEN message arrives.
It changes its BGP state to Idle and starts its RestartTime timer, but the datapath drops traffic until the session is re-established.

explanation: On receiving the TCP FIN the peer changes its BGP state to Idle and starts its RestartTime timer. Because the peering router does not withdraw the routes immediately and the datapath continues to forward traffic during the Agent restart, there is no traffic disruption.

optionRationale.b: Immediate withdrawal is exactly what graceful restart avoids; the peer waits for the RestartTime timer instead.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the peer changes its BGP state to Idle on receiving the TCP FIN, so it does not stay in Established.
optionRationale.d: The state transition and timer are right, but the excerpt states the datapath continues to forward traffic during Agent restart, so there is no disruption.

citations.title: Graceful Restart
citations.quote:
On receiving this TCP FIN, the peer changes its BGP state to ``Idle`` and
starts its ``RestartTime`` timer.

stem: A cluster's Cilium Agent takes roughly 40 seconds to boot after a restart. You want the peering BGP router to keep the routes it learned from the Cilium BGP control plane for as long as possible during that restart, but you also want the peer to remove them if the Agent fails to come back. Which configuration should you apply?

options.text: A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and `restartTimeSeconds: 15`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and `restartTimeSeconds: 60`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: false` and `restartTimeSeconds: 60`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and no `restartTimeSeconds`, relying on the 120-second default

explanation: `RestartTime` is the time advertised to the peer within which the Cilium BGP control plane is expected to re-establish the BGP session after a restart, and on its expiration the peer removes the routes previously advertised. Because the Agent here needs about 40 seconds to boot, the value must be greater than that boot time, so 60 seconds is the suitable choice. A value of 15 seconds would expire before the Agent is back, and the default of 120 seconds is not the tightest fit for the stated requirement.

optionRationale.a: 15 seconds is shorter than the roughly 40-second boot time, so the peer's timer would expire and the routes would be removed before the session is re-established.
optionRationale.c: Graceful restart must be enabled for the capability to be advertised and for the peer to hold routes; disabling it defeats the purpose.
optionRationale.d: The 120-second default is valid, but the question asks for the setting that keeps routes only as long as needed while still covering the boot time, which 60 seconds does more precisely.

attachments.title: Peer configuration under consideration
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
 kind: CiliumBGPPeerConfig
 metadata:
   name: cilium-peer
 spec:
   gracefulRestart:
     enabled: true
     restartTimeSeconds: 15

stem: You enable graceful restart on a CiliumBGPPeerConfig. During a Cilium Agent restart, the Agent closes the BGP TCP socket and a TCP FIN reaches the peering BGP router. What does the peer do, and what happens to traffic in the datapath?

options.text: The peer changes its BGP state to `Idle` and starts its `RestartTime` timer, while the datapath continues to forward traffic with no disruption.
The peer immediately withdraws all routes received from the Cilium BGP control plane, and the datapath drops traffic until the session is re-established.
The peer keeps the session in `Established` state and continues receiving route updates from the restarting Agent throughout the restart.
The peer changes its BGP state to `Idle` and starts its `RestartTime` timer, but the datapath stops forwarding traffic until the Agent boots.

explanation: On receiving the TCP FIN, the peer changes its BGP state to `Idle` and starts its `RestartTime` timer. In the event of a Cilium Agent restart, the peering BGP router does not withdraw routes received from the Cilium BGP control plane immediately, and the datapath continues to forward traffic during the Agent restart, so there is no traffic disruption.

optionRationale.b: The peer does not withdraw the routes immediately; that is the point of graceful restart, and the datapath keeps forwarding.
optionRationale.c: The peer moves to `Idle` on receiving the TCP FIN rather than staying in `Established`.
optionRationale.d: The state transition and timer are right, but the datapath continues to forward traffic during the restart, so there is no disruption.

starts its ``RestartTime`` timer.

stem: A cluster runs in Multi-Pool IPAM mode. A pod is created in a namespace that carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=green-pool, while the pod itself carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=blue-pool. Both pools exist and both have selectors that would match the pod. Which pool is the pod's IP allocated from?

options.text: blue-pool, because the annotation on the pod takes precedence over the annotation on the namespace
green-pool, because the namespace annotation is evaluated first
The default pool, because conflicting annotations are ignored
Allocation fails, because the pod matches more than one pool

explanation: The explicit pool annotation is the first item in the precedence order, and it may be placed either on the pod or on the namespace of the pod. The pod's own annotation is the one that names the pool, so blue-pool is used; the namespace annotation does not override it.

optionRationale.b: The namespace annotation is an alternative place to put the explicit pool name, not a higher-priority source than the pod's own annotation.
optionRationale.c: The default pool is only used when neither the pod nor the namespace has an explicit pool annotation, or when no selectors match.
optionRationale.d: The exactly-one-pool rule applies to matching pools via selectors; here the pool is named explicitly by annotation.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
You can explicitly name the pool for a pod using the ``ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=<pool-name>`` annotation, 
     either on the pod or the namespace of the pod.

stem: An engineer wants pods in namespace `empire` to draw IPv4 addresses from one pool and IPv6 addresses from a different pool, without relying on label selectors. Which annotations should be set?

options.text: ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool for both families, applied twice
ipam.cilium.io/ipv4-pool=<pool-name> and ipam.cilium.io/ipv6-pool=<pool-name>
ipam.cilium.io/require-pool-match="true" together with ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool
spec.podSelector and spec.namespaceSelector on the CiliumPodIPPool

explanation: The excerpt states that different pools can be specified for IPv4 and IPv6 using the ipv4-pool and ipv6-pool annotations. These can be placed on the pod or on its namespace.

optionRationale.a: The plain ip-pool annotation names a single pool; the per-family variants exist precisely to name different pools for each family.
optionRationale.c: require-pool-match only blocks allocation until a non-default pool matches; it does not select per-family pools.
optionRationale.d: Selectors are the second precedence step, not the way to name different pools per IP family.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
You can specify different pools for IPv4 and IPv6 using the 
     ``ipam.cilium.io/ipv4-pool=<pool-name>`` and ``ipam.cilium.io/ipv6-pool=<pool-name>`` annotations.

stem: A CiliumPodIPPool defines both spec.podSelector and spec.namespaceSelector. A pod carries labels matching the podSelector, but its namespace does not match the namespaceSelector. What is the result when the pod requests an IP?

options.text: The pod gets an IP from the pool, because matching either selector is sufficient
The pod gets an IP from the pool only if it also carries the ip-pool annotation
The pod is not allocated an IP from that pool, because both the pod and its namespace must match their respective selectors
IP allocation fails with an error because the selectors conflict

explanation: When both selectors are defined, both the pod and its namespace must match their respective selectors for the pod to be allocated an IP from the pool. A namespace mismatch therefore disqualifies the pod from that pool.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt requires both to match, not either.
optionRationale.b: The annotation is a separate, higher-precedence mechanism; it is not a condition for selector matching.
optionRationale.d: Allocation failure with a logged error occurs when a pod matches more than one pool, not when a selector does not match.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
If both selectors are defined, both the pod and its namespace must match 
     their respective selectors in order for the pod to be allocated an IP from the pool.

stem: A pool's selectors are intended to match a newly created pod, but at the moment of IP allocation Cilium does not yet know about that pool. The pod has no explicit pool annotation. What happens, and how can the engineer prevent it?

options.text: Allocation fails; set ipam.cilium.io/require-pool-match="true" to allow the default pool as a fallback
The pod is allocated an IP from the default pool; set ipam.cilium.io/require-pool-match="true" on the pod or namespace to block allocation until a non-default pool matches
The pod is allocated an IP from the default pool; set spec.allowFirstIP to true on the pool to prevent this
The pod is allocated an IP from the default pool; nothing can change this behaviour

explanation: The excerpt states that when the pool is not known to Cilium at allocation time, whether from race conditions or misconfiguration, the pod receives an IP from the default pool. The require-pool-match annotation blocks allocation until the pod matches a non-default pool.

optionRationale.a: Allocation does not fail in this case; it falls back to the default pool, and require-pool-match blocks rather than permits the fallback.
optionRationale.c: allowFirstIP controls whether the first address of an allocated CIDR is allocatable; it has nothing to do with pool selection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly offers require-pool-match as a way to change this behaviour.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
In the case that your pool is not known to Cilium at the time of IP allocation, either due to race conditions or 
     misconfiguration, the pod will be allocated an IP from the default pool.

stem: Two CiliumPodIPPool resources have overlapping selectors, and a pod matches both of them for the same IP family. What is the outcome?

options.text: The pod receives an IP from the pool with the lowest name in alphabetical order
The pod receives an IP from the default pool
IP allocation fails and an error is logged
The pod receives one IP from each matching pool

explanation: A pod must match exactly one pool for a given IP family. If it matches more than one pool, IP allocation fails and an error is logged, which is why overlapping selectors must be avoided.

optionRationale.a: No tie-breaking by name is described; multiple matches are an error.
optionRationale.b: The default pool is the fallback when no selectors match or no annotation is present, not when several pools match.
optionRationale.d: A pod does not receive an address from each matching pool; the multiple match is rejected.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
A pod must match exactly one pool for a given IP family. If it matches more than one pool,
     IP allocation fails and an error is logged.

stem: An operator changes the value of the ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool annotation on a pod that is already running, hoping to move it to another pool. What is the effect?

options.text: The pod is immediately re-allocated an IP from the newly named pool
The pod keeps its IP until the next restart, at which point the new pool is used
The change has no effect, because the annotations are only considered when a pod is created
The change causes IP allocation to fail and an error to be logged

explanation: The excerpt states that the annotations are only considered when a pod is created, and that changing the ip-pool annotation on an already running pod has no effect.

optionRationale.a: No re-allocation occurs for a running pod.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives no such restart behaviour; the annotation simply has no effect on the running pod.
optionRationale.d: An error is logged when a pod matches more than one pool, not when an annotation is changed on a running pod.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
The annotations are only considered when a pod is created. Changing the ``ip-pool``
annotation on an already running pod has no effect.

stem: A cluster runs in Multi-Pool IPAM mode. A pod is created in a namespace that carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=blue-pool, but the pod itself carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=green-pool. Both pools exist and both have free addresses. Which pool is the pod's IP allocated from?

options.text: green-pool, because the annotation on the pod takes precedence over the annotation on its namespace
blue-pool, because the namespace annotation is evaluated before the pod annotation
The default pool, because conflicting annotations cause the explicit pool selection to be ignored
Neither pool: allocation fails because the pod matches two pools

explanation: The explicit pool annotation is the first item in the precedence order, and it may be placed either on the pod or on the namespace of the pod. The pod's own annotation is the one that names the pool for that pod, so green-pool is used. The failure case for matching more than one pool concerns label selectors, not annotations: a pod must match exactly one pool for a given IP family, and overlapping selectors are what cause allocation to fail.

optionRationale.b: The namespace annotation is an alternative place to put the explicit pool name, not an earlier step in the precedence order; the pod's own annotation names the pool.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the precedence order makes conflicting annotations fall back to the default pool; the default pool is used only when there is no explicit annotation and no selector match.
optionRationale.d: The 'exactly one pool' rule applies to matching pools via selectors; overlapping selectors are what make allocation fail, not an annotation on the pod.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
You can explicitly name the pool for a pod using the ``ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=<pool-name>`` annotation, 
     either on the pod or the namespace of the pod.

stem: An operator is creating a CiliumPodIPPool with a /24 IPv4 CIDR and wants the very first address of that CIDR to be handed out to pods rather than reserved. Which field must be set to true when the pool is created?

options.text: spec.allowFirstIP
spec.allowLastIP
spec.ipv4.maskSize
spec.ipam.pools.requested

explanation: By default the first and last address of each allocated CIDR from a CiliumPodIPPool are reserved. Setting spec.allowFirstIP to true when creating the pool makes the first address allocatable independently of the last. Note that this field, like spec.allowLastIP, is immutable, so it must be set at creation time.

optionRationale.b: spec.allowLastIP controls the last address of the CIDR, not the first.
optionRationale.c: maskSize sets the size of the per-node PodCIDRs carved from the pool; it does not control whether the first address is reserved.
optionRationale.d: spec.ipam.pools.requested is a field of the CiliumNode resource listing per-node pool requests, not a field of CiliumPodIPPool.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
By default, the first and last address of each allocated CIDR from a
``CiliumPodIPPool`` are reserved and cannot be allocated. Set
``spec.allowFirstIP`` or ``spec.allowLastIP`` to ``true`` when creating the pool
to make either address allocatable independently.

stem: A cluster's nodes each have a different default gateway address, and the network team does not want to enumerate every node's peer address in the Cilium BGP configuration. They add a peer named "tor-switch" with peerASN 65000 and set autoDiscovery mode to "DefaultGateway" with addressFamily ipv6. What must the ToR switches be configured with so that Cilium's nodes can establish sessions?

options.text: A static neighbor entry for every Cilium node address, listed individually under the peer group.
A "bgp listen range" covering the relevant IP prefix, so the switch accepts sessions from a range of addresses.
A separate peer group per Cilium node, each with its own local ASN.
An eBGP multihop configuration with a TTL greater than one on each Cilium node.

explanation: Default gateway auto-discovery removes the need to know each node's exact peer address, but the ToR switch must be told to accept dynamic neighbours. The excerpt states that ToR switches must be configured with "bgp listen range" to support dynamic BGP neighbours, which lets the switch accept sessions from a specific IP prefix range.

optionRationale.a: This is precisely what auto-discovery is designed to avoid; the switch listens on a prefix range instead of knowing each node address.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt requires each ToR switch to be configured with the same local ASN, not a per-node peer group with differing ASNs.
optionRationale.d: Multihop TTL is not mentioned anywhere in the requirements for default gateway auto-discovery.

attachments.title: Peer configuration using default gateway auto-discovery
attachments.body:
peers:
 - name: "tor-switch"
   peerASN: 65000
   autoDiscovery:
     mode: "DefaultGateway"
     defaultGateway:
       addressFamily: ipv6  # Can be "ipv4" or "ipv6"
   peerConfigRef:
     name: "cilium-peer"

citations.title: Default Gateway Auto-Discovery
citations.quote: ToR switches must be configured with "bgp listen range" to support dynamic BGP neighbors.

stem: An engineer applies the peer configuration below on every node in a cluster. On one node the default gateway for the IPv6 address family is a link-local address. What is the outcome for that node?

options.text: Cilium establishes the BGP session using the link-local address as the peer address.
Cilium falls back to the IPv4 default gateway and establishes the session there.
The link-local address is not supported as a default gateway, so no session is established on that basis.
Cilium establishes the session but ignores the peerConfigRef session parameters.

explanation: The excerpt closes with an explicit limitation: a link-local address as default gateway is not supported. A node whose discovered IPv6 default gateway is link-local therefore cannot use it for auto-discovered peering.

optionRationale.a: Directly contradicted by the stated limitation on link-local default gateways.
optionRationale.b: Nothing in the excerpt describes falling back to the other address family; the address family is fixed by the configuration.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the peer configuration referenced by peerConfigRef is used for session parameters, with no exception for link-local gateways.

stem: A platform team wants Cilium's BGP control plane to announce Service virtual IPs to an upstream router so that clients outside the cluster can reach those Services directly. Which combination of fields must appear in a CiliumBGPAdvertisement resource to achieve this?

options.text: Set `advertisementType` to `Service` and set `service.addresses` to one or more of `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` or `ExternalIP`.
Set `advertisementType` to `PodCIDR` and set `service.addresses` to `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` or `ExternalIP`.
Set `advertisementType` to `Service` and set `service.addresses` to `IngressIP`, `NodePort` or `ExternalIP`.
Set `advertisementType` to `Service` and set `service.addresses` to `ClusterIP` only, because the other address kinds are advertised automatically.

explanation: The excerpt states that to advertise the service virtual IPs you specify the `advertisementType` field as `Service` and the `service.addresses` field as `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` or `ExternalIP`. The selector then narrows which Services are covered.

optionRationale.b: `PodCIDR` is not the advertisement type used for Service virtual IPs; the excerpt names `Service` as the value of `advertisementType` for this purpose.
optionRationale.c: `IngressIP` and `NodePort` are not among the address kinds listed; the permitted values are `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` and `ExternalIP`.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt presents `LoadBalancerIP`, `ClusterIP` and `ExternalIP` as alternatives you choose from, not as something advertised automatically alongside `ClusterIP`.

attachments.title: The advertisement resource under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
 kind: CiliumBGPAdvertisement

   name: bgp-advertisements
   labels:
     advertise: bgp
 spec:
   advertisements:
     - advertisementType: "Service"
       service:
         addresses:
           - ClusterIP
           - ExternalIP
           - LoadBalancerIP
       selector:
         matchExpressions:
           - { key: bgp, operator: In, values: [ blue ] }

stem: A cluster runs a Service that has a `ClusterIP`, an `ExternalIP` and a load-balancer ingress IP. The BGP control plane advertises the Service's virtual IPs to peers. Which prefixes does Cilium announce for these VIPs?

options.text: Exact host routes: /32 for IPv4 VIPs and /128 for IPv6 VIPs.
The cluster's pod CIDR, from which the VIPs are reachable.
The node's primary interface subnet, so that the whole subnet is routed to the advertising node.
A /24 aggregate covering the Service CIDR, with the VIPs reachable through it.

explanation: The excerpt notes that the Cilium BGP Control Plane advertises exact routes for the VIPs, using /32 or /128 prefixes. Nothing broader is announced for a Service VIP.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt is about advertising Service virtual IPs, and states the routes are exact VIP routes rather than a pod CIDR.
optionRationale.c: Advertising the node's interface subnet is not described; the advertisement covers the VIP itself as an exact route.
optionRationale.d: A /24 aggregate of the Service CIDR is not mentioned; the excerpt specifies /32 or /128 prefixes for the VIPs.

stem: An engineer applies the CiliumBGPAdvertisement shown in the attachment. Which Services will have their virtual IPs advertised?

options.text: Services whose labels satisfy the `matchExpressions` entry requiring the label `bgp` to have the value `blue`.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium 1.18. An engineer applies a CiliumNetworkPolicy that uses the fromRequires field to establish base label requirements for endpoints labelled env=prod. What is the status of this field in that release?

options.text: It is deprecated, and it has been removed as of Cilium 1.19.
It is fully supported and is the recommended way to express base label requirements.
It was removed in Cilium 1.17 and replaced by fromEndpoints.
It is only honoured for egress policies, having been dropped for ingress.

explanation: The fromRequires and toRequires fields are deprecated as of Cilium 1.17.x and have been removed as of Cilium 1.19. On a 1.18 cluster the field is therefore deprecated but not yet removed, so a policy using it is on borrowed time.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states the fields are deprecated as of 1.17.x and removed as of 1.19, so they are not a recommended construct in 1.18.
optionRationale.c: The removal is stated as of Cilium 1.19, not 1.17; 1.17.x is when the deprecation began.

stem: An engineer wants any endpoint carrying env=prod to be reachable only from sources that also carry env=prod, and wants this requirement to hold regardless of what other ingress rules in the cluster allow. Which field establishes such a base requirement, and what does it do on its own?

options.text: fromRequires; it sets constraints that must be met for the selected endpoints to be reachable, but grants no access by itself.
fromEndpoints; it both sets the base requirement and grants access to matching sources in a single rule.
fromRequires; it grants access to every source that matches the requirement, without needing any further rule.
toRequires; it sets the ingress base requirement, while fromRequires is reserved for egress.

explanation: The fromRequires field establishes label requirements which serve as a foundation for any fromEndpoints relationship. It is a list of additional constraints which must be met in order for the selected endpoints to be reachable, and these constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves — traffic is only allowed when rules matching fromEndpoints are also present.

optionRationale.b: fromEndpoints is the rule that grants access; the base requirement is the job of fromRequires, and the excerpt explicitly says fromRequires needs to be combined with other rules.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that fromRequires does not grant access privileges by itself and that the rule allows nothing on its own.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt pairs fromRequires with fromEndpoints for ingress and toRequires with toEndpoints for egress, so the roles are the other way round.

be met in order for the selected endpoints to be reachable. These additional
constraints do not grant access privileges by themselves, so to allow traffic
there must also be rules which match ``fromEndpoints``.

Lower the MTU to 3498, which also upgrades the driver.
Set the combined channels to 2, which enables native XDP regardless of driver version.
Install the `kernel-ng` package again, since the driver version is tied to the kernel package.

A reported 2.2.6 is therefore too old and the driver must be brought up to at least 2.2.8. Lowering the MTU and adjusting channels are separate adapter settings and do not change the driver version.

optionRationale.c: Setting combined channels to 2 is required for XDP, but the excerpt gives a minimum driver version of 2.2.8 independently of the channel setting.

stem: A platform team is upgrading to a Cilium release where policies select endpoints from the local cluster only unless a remote cluster is explicitly targeted. They have an existing egress rule that selects pods labelled name=rebel-base with no cluster label at all, and they now want it to reach rebel-base pods in every cluster, including the local one. Which change to the rule achieves this?

options.text: Add a matchExpressions entry with key io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster and operator Exists to the toEndpoints selector.
Add a matchLabels entry setting io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster to the local cluster name.
Leave the selector unchanged and set the cluster-name ConfigMap option to a wildcard value.
Add a toEndpoints entry for each remote cluster, each with io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster set to that cluster's name.

explanation: The excerpt shows a policy that explicitly allows pods to communicate to all clusters by adding a matchExpressions clause with key io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster and operator Exists to the toEndpoints selector. Because policies otherwise select endpoints from the local cluster only unless one or multiple clusters are specifically targeted, the Exists expression is what widens the selection to every cluster.

optionRationale.b: Setting the label to the local cluster name targets only the local cluster, which is the opposite of reaching all clusters.
optionRationale.c: The cluster-name option supplies the name of the cluster; the excerpt gives no wildcard value for it.
optionRationale.d: Listing each remote cluster by name targets those clusters specifically, not all clusters, and would also omit the local one.

   endpointSelector:
     matchLabels:
       name: x-wing

stem: A platform team runs Cilium 1.16 in a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available. They enable host network mode for the Cilium Gateway API and configure a Gateway listener on port 8080. Which statement describes the resulting exposure of that listener?

options.text: The listener is exposed on all interfaces, using 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.
The listener is exposed only on the node IP addresses that are selected as Gateway status addresses.
The listener is exposed through a LoadBalancer Service, because host network mode and LoadBalancer Service mode are both active.
The listener is exposed on a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than on port 8080.

explanation: Host network mode exposes the Gateway directly on the host network, and the listener is exposed on all interfaces — 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6. The port configured on the Gateway listener (8080 here) is the port used, since the port for a Gateway is specified via spec.listeners.port.

optionRationale.b: The status address handling concerns the GatewayStatusAddress field and its 16-address limit, not the interfaces on which the listener is bound.
optionRationale.c: Enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode; the two are mutually exclusive.
optionRationale.d: The randomly assigned node port applies to the generated Service when TCPRoute or UDPRoute traffic is involved, not to the listener port configured on the Gateway.

stem: An engineer enables host network mode for the Cilium Gateway API and then routes traffic to a Gateway using a TCPRoute. What happens to that traffic and to the port it arrives on?

options.text: The traffic bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly, which is a NodePort Service using a randomly assigned port from the node port range.
The traffic is processed by Envoy and arrives on the port configured in spec.listeners.port of the Gateway.
The traffic bypasses Envoy and reaches a LoadBalancer Service that exposes the configured Gateway listener port.
The traffic is dropped, because host network mode disables the Gateway API entirely when a TCPRoute is present.

explanation: Host network mode is not compatible with TCPRoute and UDPRoute. Their traffic bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly; enabling host network mode turns that Service into a NodePort Service, which gets a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than the port configured on the Gateway listener.

optionRationale.b: Envoy is bypassed for TCPRoute and UDPRoute traffic, and the configured listener port is not the one used once host network mode is enabled.
optionRationale.c: The generated Service is normally a LoadBalancer Service, but enabling host network mode turns it into a NodePort Service.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the routes are incompatible with host network mode and describes how their traffic is handled; it does not say the Gateway API is disabled or the traffic dropped.

A Service advertisement with `addresses: [LoadBalancerIP]` and a selector using `matchExpressions: - {key: bgp, operator: In, values: [blue]}`
A Service advertisement with `addresses: [ClusterIP]` and a selector using `matchExpressions: - {key: bgp, operator: Exists}`
A Service advertisement with no `selector` field at all, relying on Cilium to select all Services by default

optionRationale.b: This is the selective example that advertises only Services labelled `bgp: blue`, not all Services.
optionRationale.c: `ClusterIP` is not one of the address types shown, and an `Exists` operator is never mentioned in the excerpt.

stem: A platform team wants a single egress policy to cover two separate sets of gateway nodes, one labelled testLabel=testVal1 and another labelled testLabel=testVal2. Which field should they use to declare both sets in the same policy?

options.text: The `egressGateways` list field, with one entry per node selector.
The `egressGateway` field, repeated once per node selector.
The `nodeSelector` field at the top level of the policy, with multiple `matchLabels` entries.
The `egressGatewayNodes` list field, with one entry per node selector.

explanation: The excerpt states that multiple gateway nodes can be selected in the same policy and that they are configured using the `egressGateways` list field. Each entry on that list takes the same configuration options as the singular `egressGateway` field, so two node selectors become two list entries.

optionRationale.b: The singular `egressGateway` field is the single-gateway form; the excerpt describes the list field `egressGateways` for selecting multiple gateway nodes in one policy.
optionRationale.c: `nodeSelector` is a per-entry field inside the gateway configuration, not a top-level field that accepts several `matchLabels` blocks.
optionRationale.d: No field named `egressGatewayNodes` appears in the excerpt; the list field is called `egressGateways`.

The assignment is based on the node's Kubernetes name, sorted alphabetically.

stem: A cluster has been running workloads for several months when an administrator changes its cluster ID and cluster name in place. What does the documentation say the administrator must do afterwards, and why?

options.text: Restart all workloads, because the cluster ID is used to generate the security identity and it will need to be re-created in order to establish access across clusters.
Nothing further is required, because the cluster name and ID are only read when the Cilium agent first starts.
Reinstall Cilium on the cluster, because the cluster name must be assigned at installation time and cannot be changed afterwards.
Restart only the Cilium agents, because the cluster ID is used solely to route traffic between the clustermesh-apiserver instances.

explanation: The documentation warns that if you change the cluster ID and/or cluster name in a cluster with running workloads, you will need to restart all workloads, since the cluster ID is used to generate the security identity and it will need to be re-created in order to establish access across clusters.

optionRationale.b: The documentation explicitly requires action after such a change; it does not say the values are only read at first start.
optionRationale.c: The documentation does not say the change is impossible or that Cilium must be reinstalled; it says the workloads must be restarted.
optionRationale.d: The stated reason concerns the security identity and access across clusters, and the instruction is to restart all workloads, not only the agents.

stem: A platform engineer applies the following Gateway manifest to a cluster running Cilium. What address does the Gateway report once it has been reconciled?

options.text: 172.18.0.140, because spec.addresses takes precedence over the infrastructure annotation
172.18.0.141, because the io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips annotation is used and spec.addresses is ignored
No address is reported, because the two conflicting IP specifications cause the Gateway to fail validation
Both addresses are reported, because Cilium allocates one address per listener

explanation: When the io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips annotation is present in spec.infrastructure.annotations, it is the annotation that determines the address and the spec.addresses field is ignored. The documented output for exactly this configuration shows ADDRESS 172.18.0.141, so the value in spec.addresses (172.18.0.140) never takes effect.

optionRationale.a: This inverts the documented precedence: the annotation wins and spec.addresses is ignored, not the other way round.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes no validation failure; the configuration is accepted and simply resolves to the annotation's address.
optionRationale.d: The Gateway reports a single ADDRESS column value, and the excerpt shows only 172.18.0.141 for this manifest.

attachments.title: The Gateway under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
 kind: Gateway
 metadata:
   name: my-gateway
 spec:
   infrastructure:
     annotations:
       io.cilium/lb-ipam-ips: "172.18.0.141"
   addresses: # This will be ignored
   - type: IPAddress
     value: 172.18.0.140 
   gatewayClassName: cilium
   listeners:
   - allowedRoutes:
       namespaces:
         from: Same
     name: web-gw
     port: 80
     protocol: HTTP

stem: An engineer wants to pin a Cilium Gateway to a specific IP address using the Gateway API's spec.addresses field. Which address type does Cilium support for this field?

options.text: IPAddress only
IPAddress and Hostname
IPAddress, Hostname and NamedAddress
Any type defined by the Gateway API specification

explanation: Cilium's support for spec.addresses is deliberately narrow: only the IPAddress type is supported, and the address is expected to come from LB-IPAM. Other address types permitted by the Gateway API specification are not handled.

optionRationale.b: Hostname is a Gateway API address type, but the excerpt states that only IPAddress is supported.
optionRationale.c: NamedAddress is not mentioned as supported; the excerpt restricts support to IPAddress alone.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly narrows the specification's set of address types to one, so not every type is supported.

stem: A client pod called mediabot sends traffic to the nginx-service ClusterIP. You run `hubble observe --all` and see a flow from `default/mediabot` to `default/nginx-service:80` marked `pre-xlate-fwd TRACED`, immediately followed by a flow to `default/nginx:80` marked `post-xlate-fwd TRANSLATED`. What do these two events represent?

options.text: The datapath events before and after socket load-balancing translation between the service and the selected service endpoint.
A DNS resolution of the service name followed by the resulting connection to the backend pod.
A policy verdict denying the first flow and allowing the second flow after the endpoint is selected.
The reverse direction of an established connection, first traced and then translated back to the client.

explanation: Hubble prints datapath events before and after socket LB translation between the service and the selected service endpoint, which is exactly what the `pre-xlate-fwd` and `post-xlate-fwd` pair shows: the flow to the service address is traced, then the translated flow to the backend pod is shown.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes socket LB translation between service and endpoint, not DNS resolution; no DNS event appears in the output.
optionRationale.c: The events are marked TRACED and TRANSLATED, not as policy verdicts; the excerpt does not describe a denial.
optionRationale.d: The reverse direction is shown by the `pre-xlate-rev` and `post-xlate-rev` events, not by the forward pair described here.

attachments.title: Hubble output for mediabot
attachments.body:
$ hubble observe --all | grep mediabot
 Jan 13 13:47:20.932: default/mediabot (ID:5618) <> default/nginx-service:80 (world) pre-xlate-fwd TRACED (TCP)
 Jan 13 13:47:20.932: default/mediabot (ID:5618) <> default/nginx:80 (ID:35772) post-xlate-fwd TRANSLATED (TCP)
 Jan 13 13:47:20.932: default/nginx:80 (ID:35772) <> default/mediabot (ID:5618) pre-xlate-rev TRACED (TCP)
 Jan 13 13:47:20.932: default/nginx-service:80 (world) <> default/mediabot (ID:5618) post-xlate-rev TRANSLATED (TCP)
 Jan 13 13:47:20.932: default/mediabot:38750 (ID:5618) <> default/nginx (ID:35772) pre-xlate-rev TRACED (TCP)

The Hubble
output prints datapath events before and after socket LB translation between service

stem: A client pod called mediabot is sending traffic to the nginx-service ClusterIP. You run `hubble observe --all` and see the flows, but the cilium agent logs contain the message `Failed to setup socket load-balancing tracing with Hubble.` You still want to see the pre- and post-translation datapath events for this socket. What should you do?

options.text: Trace the packets with `cilium-dbg monitor` instead, for example using `-v -t trace-sock`.
Re-run `hubble observe --all` with the `--all` flag removed so that only translated flows are shown.
Run `crictl inspectp -o=json $POD_ID | grep cgroup` on the node and re-enable Hubble socket LB tracing with the resulting path.
Use `kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=PodName:.metadata.name,PodUID:.metadata.uid` to map the socket cookie to the pod, then re-run Hubble.

explanation: The excerpt states that socket LB tracing with Hubble requires the cilium agent to detect pod cgroup paths, and that if the agent reports `Failed to setup socket load-balancing tracing with Hubble.` you can trace packets using `cilium-dbg monitor` instead. The example shows `cilium-dbg monitor -v -t trace-sock` producing the pre-xlate-fwd, post-xlate-fwd, pre-xlate-rev and post-xlate-rev events.

optionRationale.b: Dropping `--all` does not address the failure to set up socket load-balancing tracing; the excerpt offers `cilium-dbg monitor` as the alternative, not a different Hubble flag combination.
optionRationale.c: The `crictl inspectp` command is given only for gathering the cgroup path to include in a GitHub issue, not as a way to re-enable Hubble socket LB tracing.
optionRationale.d: The PodUID column is used to correlate a cgroup id with a pod's cgroup path; it does not restore Hubble socket LB tracing.

$ kubectl exec -n kube-system cilium-rt2jh -- cilium-dbg monitor -v -t trace-sock

 CPU 11: [post-xlate-fwd] cgroup_id: 479586 sock_cookie: 7123674, dst [10.244.1.246]:80 tcp
 CPU 11: [pre-xlate-rev] cgroup_id: 479586 sock_cookie: 7123674, dst [10.244.1.246]:80 tcp

citations.quote: If you see a message in cilium agent ``Failed to setup socket load-balancing tracing with Hubble.``, you can trace packets using ``cilium-dbg monitor`` instead.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium 1.9 with default settings. A pod is selected by a CiliumNetworkPolicy that allows ingress on port 80/TCP from a particular client pod, and it is also selected by a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that denies ingress on port 80/TCP from that same client pod. What is the result for a connection from that client to port 80 on the server pod?

options.text: The connection is denied, because deny policies take precedence over allow policies.
The connection is allowed, because the allow policy is more specific than the clusterwide deny policy.
The connection is allowed, because deny policies must be enabled explicitly and are not active by default in 1.9.
The connection is denied only if the client pod is also selected by a policy, because the server pod stays in default-allow mode.

explanation: Deny policies take precedence over allow policies, and this holds regardless of whether the policies involved are Cilium Network Policies, Clusterwide Cilium Network Policies or even Kubernetes Network Policies. The allow on 80/TCP therefore cannot override the deny on the same port. Deny policies have also been available and enabled by default since Cilium 1.9, so no extra enablement step is needed.

optionRationale.b: Precedence does not depend on the scope or specificity of the policy: deny wins over allow whether the policy is a Cilium Network Policy, a Clusterwide Cilium Network Policy or a Kubernetes Network Policy.
optionRationale.c: Deny policies are available and enabled by default since Cilium 1.9, so the deny is active without any opt-in.
optionRationale.d: Pods enter default-deny mode as soon as a single policy selects them, so the server pod does not remain in a default-allow state once it is selected.

citations.title: Deny Policies
citations.quote:
Deny policies take precedence over allow policies, regardless of whether they
are a Cilium Network Policy, a Clusterwide Cilium Network Policy or even a
Kubernetes Network Policy.

stem: An administrator applies the following policy. Which statement describes its effect?

options.text: Ingress from the world entity is denied on all pods managed by Cilium in all namespaces, while traffic from everywhere else, including existing inter-cluster policies, is still allowed.
All ingress to every pod is denied, because the endpointSelector is empty and therefore matches everything.
Ingress from the world entity is denied only in the namespace where the policy is created, because it is a namespaced CiliumNetworkPolicy.
Ingress from the world entity is denied, and all other ingress is also denied because no allow rule is present.

explanation: The policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy with an empty endpointSelector, so it applies to all pods managed by Cilium in all namespaces. Its ingressDeny blocks the world entity, while the ingress rule allows the all entity, so traffic from everywhere except world continues to be permitted and existing inter-cluster policies are still allowed.

optionRationale.b: The empty endpointSelector widens the set of selected pods, but the policy denies only the world entity rather than all ingress.
optionRationale.c: The resource is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy, not a namespaced CiliumNetworkPolicy, so its effect is cluster-wide.
optionRationale.d: The policy includes an ingress rule allowing the all entity, so other ingress is not denied.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "external-lockdown"
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}
  ingressDeny:
  - fromEntities:
    - "world"
  ingress:
  - fromEntities:
    - "all"

citations.title: Deny Policies
citations.quote:
The following policy will deny ingress from "world" on all namespaces on all
Pods managed by Cilium. Existing inter-cluster policies will still be allowed
as this policy is allowing traffic from everywhere except from "world".

stem: A team wants to write a deny policy that blocks requests to a specific URL path on an otherwise allowed service, and another that blocks traffic to a specific external domain name. What does Cilium support here?

options.text: Neither is supported: deny policies cannot enforce at Layer 7, so a URL cannot be specifically denied, and toFQDNs cannot be used to deny traffic to a specific domain name.
Both are supported, provided the deny policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy rather than a namespaced one.
Denying a URL is supported at Layer 7, but denying a specific domain name with toFQDNs is not.
Denying a specific domain name with toFQDNs is supported, but denying a URL at Layer 7 is not.

explanation: Deny policies do not support policy enforcement at Layer 7, which means specifically denying a URL is not possible, and they do not support toFQDNs, which means specifically denying traffic to a specific domain name is not possible either.

optionRationale.b: The limitation applies to deny policies generally; using a clusterwide policy does not add Layer 7 or toFQDNs deny support.
optionRationale.c: Layer 7 enforcement, including denying a URL, is explicitly not supported by deny policies.
optionRationale.d: toFQDNs, that is denying traffic to a specific domain name, is explicitly not supported by deny policies.

citations.title: Deny Policies
citations.quote:
Deny policies do not support: policy enforcement at L7, i.e., specifically
denying an URL and ``toFQDNs``, i.e., specifically denying traffic to a specific
domain name.

stem: An engineer sets `connectRetryTimeSeconds: 5` on a BGP peer configuration to speed up reconnection after losing connectivity. What range of values can the actual ConnectRetryTimer take?

options.text: Exactly 5 seconds, because the configured value is used as-is
Anywhere from 5 up to but not including 10 seconds, because random jitter is applied internally
Anywhere from 0 up to but not including 5 seconds, because jitter is subtracted from the configured value
Exactly 10 seconds, because the configured value is always doubled

explanation: Random jitter is applied to the configured value internally, so the actual value used for the ConnectRetryTimer falls within the interval `[ConnectRetryTimeSeconds, 2 * ConnectRetryTimeSeconds)`. With a configured value of 5, that is from 5 up to but not including 10.

optionRationale.a: Jitter is applied internally, so the configured value is not used verbatim.
optionRationale.c: The interval starts at the configured value, not below it; jitter is not subtracted.
optionRationale.d: The upper bound of the interval is exclusive, and the value is not fixed at double the configured value.

citations.title: Timers
citations.quote:
As random jitter is applied to the configured value internally, the actual value used for the
``ConnectRetryTimer`` is within the interval ``[ConnectRetryTimeSeconds, 2 * ConnectRetryTimeSeconds)``.

stem: A BGP peer configuration is created without specifying any timer values. What KeepaliveTimer does the BGP Control Plane use?

options.text: 3 seconds
9 seconds
30 seconds
120 seconds

explanation: The default for the KeepaliveTimer, set by `keepAliveTimeSeconds`, is 30. The values 3 and 9 are the minimum possible values recommended for datacenter deployments, and 120 is the default for the ConnectRetryTimer.

optionRationale.a: 3 is the minimum possible value recommended for datacenter networks, not the default.
optionRationale.b: 9 is the minimum possible value recommended for the hold timer, not the keepalive default.
optionRationale.d: 120 is the default for the ConnectRetryTimer, not the KeepaliveTimer.

citations.title: Timers
citations.quote: KeepaliveTimer    ``keepAliveTimeSeconds``     30

stem: An engineer applies the following CiliumBGPPeerConfig to a BGP peer in a datacenter Kubernetes cluster. The peer session drops, and the engineer measures how long Cilium waits before attempting to reconnect. Which statement describes the delay that can be observed?

options.text: The delay is always exactly 5 seconds, because the configured value is used verbatim.
The delay is somewhere in the interval from 5 seconds up to but not including 10 seconds, because random jitter is applied to the configured value.
The delay is somewhere in the interval from 5 seconds up to and including 10 seconds, because random jitter is applied to the configured value.
The delay is 120 seconds, because connectRetryTimeSeconds is ignored unless the HoldTimer is left at its default.

explanation: The documentation states that random jitter is applied internally to the configured ConnectRetryTimer value, so the actual value used lies within the interval [ConnectRetryTimeSeconds, 2 * ConnectRetryTimeSeconds). With connectRetryTimeSeconds set to 5, the observed delay falls between 5 seconds inclusive and 10 seconds exclusive.

optionRationale.a: Jitter is applied internally, so the configured value is not used verbatim.
optionRationale.c: The interval is half-open: the upper bound, twice the configured value, is excluded.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt gives no such dependency; connectRetryTimeSeconds is a configurable timer in its own right, and 120 is merely its default.
