apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
 kind: CiliumBGPPeerConfig
 metadata:
   name: cilium-peer
 spec:
   timers:
     connectRetryTimeSeconds: 5
     holdTimeSeconds: 9
     keepAliveTimeSeconds: 3

citations.title: Timers
citations.quote:
As random jitter is applied to the configured value internally, the actual value used for the
``ConnectRetryTimer`` is within the interval ``[ConnectRetryTimeSeconds, 2 * ConnectRetryTimeSeconds)``.

stem: A node has an interface named lo carrying several addresses, including a loopback address and an IPv6 link-local address. A CiliumBGPAdvertisement selects that interface with advertisementType "Interface". Which addresses are advertised to BGP peers?

options.text: All IP addresses on the interface, each as an exact /32 or /128 route.
Only the loopback and IPv6 link-local addresses, since those are the stable ones.
The interface's addresses excluding those from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 ranges, each as an exact /32 or /128 route.
The interface's addresses aggregated into the smallest covering prefix for the interface.

explanation: Interface IPs are advertised as exact routes, and addresses drawn from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 ranges are excluded from advertisement. So the remaining addresses go out as /32 or /128 prefixes, never as an aggregate.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly excludes several address ranges, so not every address on the interface is advertised.
optionRationale.b: It is the reverse: loopback and IPv6 link-local addresses are among those that are not advertised.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the addresses are advertised as exact routes (/32 or /128 prefixes), not aggregated.

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote:
The interface IPs are advertised as exact routes (``/32`` or ``/128`` prefixes).
IP addresses from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 address ranges are not advertised.

stem: Which advertisementType in a CiliumBGPAdvertisement is used to advertise IP addresses assigned on a local interface?

options.text: "Interface"
"PodCIDR"
"LoadBalancerIP"
"ClusterIP"

explanation: The advertisement type for advertising IP addresses assigned on a local interface is "Interface", with the interface selected by name under the interface field.

optionRationale.b: PodCIDR is not the type used for local interface addresses; the excerpt's example uses "Interface".
optionRationale.c: LoadBalancerIP is not the type used for local interface addresses; the excerpt's example uses "Interface".
optionRationale.d: ClusterIP is not the type used for local interface addresses; the excerpt's example uses "Interface".

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote:
- advertisementType: "Interface"
       interface:
         name: lo

stem: A cluster uses a multi-homing setup where a common node's loopback address must be reachable through several BGP sessions running over different network interfaces. Which Cilium capability supports this?

options.text: Advertising arbitrary IP addresses assigned on a local interface to BGP peers.
Advertising only the pod CIDR of the node to BGP peers.
Advertising only addresses that Cilium itself has assigned to interfaces.
Advertising the cluster's service VIPs to BGP peers.

explanation: Advertising arbitrary IP addresses assigned on a local interface is what makes multi-homing setups possible, where a common node's loopback address is advertised via multiple BGP sessions over different network interfaces.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes advertising interface IP addresses, not restricting advertisement to the pod CIDR.
optionRationale.c: Cilium does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned local interfaces; the administrator configures them, yet they can still be advertised.
optionRationale.d: Service VIP advertisement is not what the excerpt describes for this multi-homing use case.

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote:
This can be useful for example in multi-homing setups, where a common node's loopback address can be advertised
via multiple BGP sessions over different network interfaces.

stem: Who is responsible for configuring the IP addresses on an arbitrary local interface that is not owned by Cilium, before those addresses can be advertised?

options.text: Cilium assigns them automatically when the advertisement is created.
The BGP peer assigns them through the session.
The node administrator must configure them themselves.
The Kubernetes control plane assigns them from the pod CIDR.

explanation: Cilium does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned local interfaces, so the node administrator must configure those addresses themselves.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: Cilium does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned local interfaces.
optionRationale.b: Nothing in the excerpt gives the BGP peer a role in assigning local interface addresses.
optionRationale.d: The pod CIDR is not mentioned as a source of addresses for arbitrary local interfaces.

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote:
Cilium does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary (non-Cilium-owned) local interfaces,
 the node administrator must configure them themselves.

stem: In what form are interface IP addresses advertised to BGP peers?

options.text: As exact routes, using /32 or /128 prefixes.
As the natural prefix length of the interface's subnet.
As a summary route covering all interfaces on the node.
As a default route pointing at the node.

explanation: The excerpt states that interface IPs are advertised as exact routes, that is /32 or /128 prefixes.

optionRationale.b: The advertisement uses host prefixes (/32 or /128), not the subnet's natural prefix length.
optionRationale.c: No summary route across interfaces is described; each address is an exact route.
optionRationale.d: A default route is not mentioned; the advertisement consists of exact host routes.

citations.title: Interface IPs
citations.quote: The interface IPs are advertised as exact routes (``/32`` or ``/128`` prefixes).

stem: A node has a loopback interface named lo carrying the address 10.0.0.5/32, and the interface is administratively enabled and operationally up. A CiliumBGPAdvertisement with advertisementType "Interface" and interface name lo is applied. What does the BGP control plane advertise to peers for this interface?

options.text: The exact route 10.0.0.5/32.
The connected subnet route 10.0.0.0/24.
Nothing, because addresses on the loopback range are never advertised.
Nothing, because Cilium does not manage addresses on non-Cilium-owned interfaces.

explanation: Interface IPs are advertised as exact routes, so a /32 address on the interface becomes a /32 prefix. The exclusion list covers addresses from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 address ranges — 10.0.0.5 is not in any of those ranges, so it is advertised. The fact that Cilium does not manage addresses on arbitrary interfaces only means the administrator must configure them; it does not prevent advertisement.

optionRationale.b: Interface IPs are advertised as exact routes (/32 or /128 prefixes), not as the covering subnet prefix.
optionRationale.c: The loopback range is excluded, but 10.0.0.5 is a regular address, not a loopback-range address; the interface merely happens to be named lo.
optionRationale.d: Cilium not managing the addresses means the node administrator configures them; it does not stop the BGP control plane advertising them.

attachments.title: The advertisement under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
 kind: CiliumBGPAdvertisement
 metadata:
   name: bgp-advertisements
   labels:
     advertise: bgp
 spec:
   advertisements:
     - advertisementType: "Interface"
       interface:
         name: lo

stem: An engineer wants to advertise the IP addresses of a local interface to BGP peers using the Interface advertisement type. Which condition must the interface satisfy for its IP addresses to be advertised?

options.text: It must be administratively enabled and in operationally up or unknown state.
It must be administratively enabled and in operationally up state only.
It must be a Cilium-owned interface with addresses managed by Cilium.
It must carry at least one address outside the loopback and link-local ranges, regardless of its state.

explanation: The interface must be administratively enabled and in operationally up or unknown state in order to advertise its IP addresses. Cilium does not manage addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned interfaces, so the node administrator configures them, but Cilium ownership is not a precondition for advertisement.

optionRationale.b: The unknown operational state is also acceptable, not only up.
optionRationale.c: Cilium explicitly does not manage IP addresses on arbitrary non-Cilium-owned local interfaces; the administrator configures them.
optionRationale.d: The interface state is a hard requirement; address ranges only exclude certain addresses from being advertised, they do not replace the state condition.

stem: You are enabling TLS between a Cilium Gateway and the backend workload. You run a JSON patch against the backend deployment that adds a volume named secret-volume, mounting the example-cert secret at /etc/secret-volume, and adds two environment variables to the container. Which two environment variables does the patch add?

options.text: TLS_SERVER_CERT set to /etc/secret-volume/crt and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY set to /etc/secret-volume/key
TLS_SERVER_CERT set to /etc/secret-volume/tls.crt and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY set to /etc/secret-volume/tls.key
TLS_CERT set to /etc/secret-volume/crt and TLS_KEY set to /etc/secret-volume/key
TLS_SERVER_CERT set to /etc/secret-volume and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY set to /etc/secret-volume

explanation: The patch adds the secret's tls.crt key at path crt and its tls.key key at path key inside the mounted volume, then points TLS_SERVER_CERT at /etc/secret-volume/crt and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY at /etc/secret-volume/key.

optionRationale.b: The secret keys are tls.crt and tls.key, but the volume items map them to the paths crt and key, so the environment variables reference the mapped paths, not the original key names.
optionRationale.c: The environment variable names in the patch are TLS_SERVER_CERT and TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY, not TLS_CERT and TLS_KEY.
optionRationale.d: The variables point at the individual files crt and key inside the mount, not at the mount directory itself.

- op: add
    path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/volumeMounts
    value:
    - name: secret-volume
      mountPath: /etc/secret-volume
  - op: add
    path: /spec/template/spec/volumes
    value:
    - name: secret-volume
      secret:
        secretName: example-cert
        items:
        - key: tls.crt
          path: crt
        - key: tls.key
          path: key
  - op: add
    path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-
    value:
      name: TLS_SERVER_CERT
      value: /etc/secret-volume/crt
  - op: add
    path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-
    value:
      name: TLS_SERVER_PRIVKEY

The backend container reads its certificate and key from files mounted from the `example-cert` Secret, and the Service has been updated so that its `https` port 443 targets container port 8443. Which BackendTLSPolicy correctly attaches the TLS configuration to that Service port and validates the backend certificate for `www.example.com`?

options.text: A policy whose `targetRefs` entry has `kind: Service`, `name: backend` and `sectionName: https`, and whose `validation` sets `hostname: www.example.com` with `caCertificateRefs` pointing at the `example-ca` ConfigMap.

A policy whose `targetRefs` entry has `kind: Service`, `name: backend` and `sectionName: https`, and whose `validation` sets `hostname: www.example.com` with `caCertificateRefs` pointing at the `example-cert` Secret.

A policy whose `targetRefs` entry has `kind: Service`, `name: backend` and `sectionName: https`, and whose `validation` sets `hostname: backend` with `caCertificateRefs` pointing at the `example-ca` ConfigMap.

A policy whose `targetRefs` entry has `kind: Service`, `name: backend` and `sectionName: https`, and whose `validation` sets `hostname: www.example.com` with `caCertificateRefs` pointing at the `example-ca` ConfigMap, plus a `port: 8443` field under `validation`.

explanation: The BackendTLSPolicy targets the Service by name and by the named port `https`, and its `validation` block names the hostname the gateway should expect from the backend together with a reference to the CA certificate ConfigMap. The certificate Secret is mounted into the backend container; it is not the CA reference in the policy.

optionRationale.c: The hostname in `validation` is the name the gateway validates against the backend certificate, which the example sets to `www.example.com`, not the Service name.

Add a `tls` stanza to the `backend` Service manifest so that the Service itself terminates TLS on port 443.
Change the `backend` Service so that port 443 targets container port 443 instead of 8443.
Add the `example-cert` Secret to the HTTPRoute `backendRefs` so the route can present the certificate to the backend.

optionRationale.d: The HTTPRoute change in the excerpt is only to replace the backend reference port with 443; certificates are not added to `backendRefs`.

stem: An egress gateway policy omits both the `egressIP` and the `interface` properties. How does Cilium choose the egress interface and egress IPs?

options.text: It selects the network interface with the default route, and uses the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses on that interface as the egress IPs.
It selects the first interface in lexical order, and uses the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses on that interface as the egress IPs.
It performs a route lookup per packet in the datapath and uses the source address chosen by the lookup as the egress IP.
It refuses to select an egress IP, so matching traffic is dropped with the reason `No Egress IP configured`.

explanation: Omitting both properties is a supported configuration: Cilium selects the interface carrying the default route as the egress interface and takes the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses on it as the egress IPs.

optionRationale.b: Lexical ordering applies to selecting among matching gateway nodes, not to selecting a network interface.
optionRationale.c: Per-packet route lookup in the datapath is how the interface is determined when an explicit egressIP is given, not when both properties are omitted.
optionRationale.d: Omitting both properties is a valid third way of configuring the egress IP, so no drop occurs on that ground.

stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy contains the egressGateway block below. The cluster has three nodes carrying the label testLabel: testVal, named node-c, node-a and node-b. Which node acts as the gateway node for this policy?

optionRationale.c: A single gateway node is selected per policy; the excerpt describes selecting one node, not spreading traffic across all matches.
optionRationale.d: Multiple matches are not an error: the excerpt states that the first node in lexical ordering based on name will be selected.

Labels are matched regardless of their source, because the source defaults to `any:`.
The selector fails, because a source must always be provided.

explanation: If no source is provided, the label source defaults to `any:`, which matches all labels regardless of their source.

optionRationale.a: Restricting matching to `k8s:` would require the source to be given explicitly.
optionRationale.b: `reserved:` covers special reserved labels and is not the default.
optionRationale.d: A source is optional; omitting it simply defaults to `any:`.

The matching label must have the `unspec:` source.
The matching label must have the `reserved:` source.

explanation: Including a source limits matching to a particular type: if a source is provided, the source of the selecting and matching labels need to match.

optionRationale.b: Matching across any source is the behaviour when no source is given, not when one is provided.
optionRationale.c: `unspec:` is for labels with unspecified source, not a requirement for explicit selectors.
optionRationale.d: `reserved:` is one particular source, not a requirement for all explicit selectors.

stem: A platform team scales a Deployment from 3 pods to 300 pods, all carrying the same set of security-relevant labels. What happens to the number of distinct identities used to enforce policy for these pods?

options.text: It stays the same, because all endpoints sharing the same set of security-relevant labels share the same identity.
It grows in proportion to the replica count, because each endpoint is given its own identity.
It grows only until the cluster-wide identifier space is exhausted, after which identities are reused at random.
It stays the same only if the pods are scheduled on the same node, since identities are node-scoped.

explanation: An identity is identified by labels and is given a cluster-wide unique identifier. The endpoint is assigned the identity matching its security-relevant labels, so all endpoints sharing the same set of security-relevant labels share the same identity. Scaling replicas of the same application therefore does not multiply identities, which is what allows policy enforcement to scale to a massive number of endpoints.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the model: identities are derived from the label set, not allocated per endpoint, so replicas of the same application share one identity.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes identities as cluster-wide unique and shared by label set; it says nothing about exhaustion or random reuse.
optionRationale.d: Identities are described as cluster-wide unique, not scoped to a node, so scheduling placement does not change the identity count.

citations.title: Identity

all endpoints which share the same set of
`security relevant labels` will share the same identity

stem: An engineer asks which property of an endpoint determines the identity it is assigned. Which answer is correct?

options.text: The endpoint's security-relevant labels
The IP address allocated to the endpoint
The node on which the endpoint is scheduled
The namespace in which the endpoint was created

explanation: The endpoint is assigned the identity which matches the endpoint's security-relevant labels. An identity is identified by labels and given a cluster-wide unique identifier, so the label set — not addressing or placement — is what selects the identity.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt ties identity to labels, not to the endpoint's IP address.
optionRationale.c: Placement is not mentioned as a factor; identities are cluster-wide and label-derived.
optionRationale.d: Namespace is not the determining property described; the security-relevant label set is.

citations.title: Identity

The endpoint is assigned the identity which matches the endpoint's
`security relevant labels`

stem: Two pods in different namespaces carry exactly the same set of security-relevant labels. How does Cilium treat their identities?

options.text: They share the same identity, because the identity is determined by the shared set of security-relevant labels.
They receive different identities, because identities are unique per namespace.
They receive different identities, because each endpoint is assigned a unique identifier of its own.
They share an identity only if a policy explicitly selects both namespaces.

explanation: All endpoints which share the same set of security-relevant labels will share the same identity. The identity is identified by labels and given a cluster-wide unique identifier, so matching label sets across namespaces map to one identity.

optionRationale.b: Nothing in the model makes identities namespace-scoped; they are cluster-wide and label-derived.
optionRationale.c: The unique identifier belongs to the identity, which is shared by all endpoints with the same security-relevant labels, not allocated per endpoint.
optionRationale.d: Sharing an identity follows from the label set itself, not from a policy selecting namespaces.

Layer 4 enforcement
Layer 7 enforcement
Layer 2 enforcement

optionRationale.b: Layer 4 is not the comparison drawn for identity-based basic connectivity.
optionRationale.c: Layer 7 is not the comparison drawn; identity enforcement is described as basic connectivity.
optionRationale.d: Layer 2 is not mentioned; the stated equivalent is Layer 3.

stem: Which statement best describes what an identity is in Cilium?

options.text: A label-identified, cluster-wide unique identifier assigned to endpoints and used to enforce basic connectivity.
A per-node numeric tag used only for encrypting traffic between nodes.
A DNS name resolved at request time to decide whether traffic is allowed.
A policy object that must be created manually before any endpoint can communicate.

explanation: Every endpoint is assigned an identity, which is what is used to enforce basic connectivity between endpoints. An identity is identified by labels and given a cluster-wide unique identifier, and endpoints sharing the same security-relevant labels share it.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes identities as cluster-wide and label-based, not as per-node tags for encryption.
optionRationale.c: Identity is label-based, not a DNS name resolved at request time.
optionRationale.d: Identities are assigned to endpoints automatically based on their security-relevant labels; they are not manually created policy objects.

stem: A cluster runs a large number of pods that churn frequently. An engineer argues that filtering on pod IP addresses is the simplest way to allow role=frontend pods to reach role=backend pods. What does Cilium do instead?

options.text: It derives a security identity from pod labels and enforces policy on that identity rather than on IP addresses.
It keeps IP-based filters but compresses the allowed addresses into a single CIDR per node.
It assigns a fixed IP address to every pod with the same labels so that one filter covers them all.
It relies on network address translation to map all frontend pods onto one shared address.

explanation: Cilium separates security from network addressing: the identity of a pod is derived through labels, and that identity is what policy allows or denies. IP-based filtering is described as the traditional approach whose rule updates on every node make it hard to scale.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes IP-based filtering as the traditional architecture being avoided, not as something Cilium optimises by aggregating addresses into per-node CIDRs.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that each pod is assigned an individual IP address; it never says pods sharing labels share an address.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the per-pod IP model avoids unnecessary NAT, so NAT is not the mechanism used.

citations.title: Identity-Based
citations.quote:
Cilium entirely separates security from network addressing.
Instead, security is based on the identity of a pod, which is derived through
labels.

stem: In the traditional example given, a node allows a connection to destination 10.1.1.2 only from a listed set of source addresses. What must happen on that node when a role=frontend pod is stopped?

options.text: The corresponding IP address must be removed from the list of allowed IP addresses.
The identity of the role=frontend pod must be revoked from the key-value store.
The destination address 10.1.1.2 must be reassigned to another pod.
The node must re-resolve the identity of all local role=backend pods.

explanation: In the IP-filter model, every time a pod with the relevant label is started or stopped, the rules on every cluster node running such pods must be updated by adding or removing the corresponding IP address from the list of allowed IP addresses.

optionRationale.b: Revoking an identity from a key-value store is part of the identity-based model, not the IP-filter example described.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says nothing about reassigning the destination address when a frontend pod stops.
optionRationale.d: Re-resolving identities belongs to the identity-based model; the traditional example is about editing address lists.

citations.title: Identity-Based
citations.quote:
Every time a new pod with the label ``role=frontend`` or ``role=backend`` is
either started or stopped, the rules on every cluster node which run any such
pods must be updated by either adding or removing the corresponding IP address
from the list of allowed IP addresses.

stem: A Kubernetes Pod runs three application containers. How does Cilium represent this Pod on the network?

options.text: As a single endpoint, because all containers sharing a common IP address are grouped together
As three separate endpoints, one per container, each with its own IP address
As a single endpoint only if the containers bind to different ports
As an endpoint pair, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6

explanation: Cilium groups all application containers that share a common address into one endpoint, and a Kubernetes Pod is the typical example of that model. The containers in the Pod therefore appear as a single endpoint rather than one endpoint each.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the model: containers sharing an address are grouped together, not split into one endpoint per container.
optionRationale.c: Port binding plays no part in how endpoints are formed; the grouping is based on the shared IP address.
optionRationale.d: Dual-stack addressing is a property of a single endpoint, not a reason to create two endpoints.

citations.title: Endpoint
citations.quote: All application containers which share a common address are grouped together in what Cilium refers to as an endpoint.

stem: Two application containers on the same cluster node both need to listen on port 80. Why does Cilium's addressing model allow this without a conflict?

options.text: Cilium assigns each endpoint its own IP address, so the full Layer 4 port range is available to each endpoint
Cilium rewrites the port numbers in transit so that each container sees a different port
Cilium places the two containers in the same endpoint, so only one of them binds to port 80
Cilium reserves well known ports below 1024 for the agent and remaps container ports above that range

explanation: Because every endpoint receives an individual IP address, each endpoint can use the entire Layer 4 port range. Containers on the same node can therefore all bind to well known ports such as 80 without conflicting.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt attributes the lack of conflict to per-endpoint IP addresses, not to port rewriting.
optionRationale.c: Containers sharing an address form one endpoint, but that is not what removes the port conflict between two separate containers.
optionRationale.d: No port reservation or remapping scheme is described; the mechanism is individual IP allocation.

citations.title: Endpoint
citations.quote: Allocating individual IP addresses enables the use of the entire Layer 4 port range by each endpoint.

stem: A cluster is running with the default Cilium configuration. Which addresses does each endpoint receive?

options.text: Both an IPv6 and an IPv4 address
An IPv4 address only
An IPv6 address only
Whichever address family the Pod requests in its specification

explanation: The default behaviour of Cilium is to assign both an IPv6 and an IPv4 address to every endpoint. Either address can then be used to reach the endpoint.

optionRationale.b: IPv4-only is not the default; the default assigns both families.
optionRationale.c: IPv6-only results from disabling IPv4 with --enable-ipv4=false, which is a configuration change from the default.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the assignment as Cilium's default behaviour, not something requested per Pod.

citations.title: Endpoint
citations.quote: The default behavior of Cilium is to assign both an IPv6 and IPv4 address to every endpoint.

stem: An engineer wants endpoints to receive only an IPv6 address. Which option achieves this?

options.text: Set --enable-ipv4=false
Set --enable-ipv6=true
Set --enable-ipv4=true
Remove the IPv4 address from each endpoint after it is created

explanation: The excerpt states that the dual-stack default can be configured to allocate only an IPv6 address with the --enable-ipv4=false option.

optionRationale.b: No such option appears in the excerpt; enabling IPv6 is not what suppresses IPv4 allocation.
optionRationale.c: This is the opposite of what is needed and would keep IPv4 allocation on.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes a configuration option, not manual removal of addresses from endpoints.

citations.title: Endpoint
citations.quote: However, this behavior can be configured to only allocate an IPv6 address with the ``--enable-ipv4=false`` option.

stem: An endpoint has been assigned both an IPv6 and an IPv4 address. A client connects to the endpoint using its IPv6 address. How does Cilium treat this compared with a connection over the IPv4 address?

options.text: Either address can be used to reach the endpoint, and policy rules and load-balancing behave the same for both
Only the IPv4 address is subject to policy rules; the IPv6 address bypasses them
Only the IPv6 address can be used for load-balancing
The endpoint must be recreated before the second address family can be used

explanation: When both an IPv6 and an IPv4 address are assigned, either address can be used to reach the endpoint, and the same behaviour applies to policy rules, load-balancing and so on.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the same behaviour applies to policy rules for either address, so IPv6 does not bypass them.
optionRationale.c: Load-balancing is given as an example of behaviour that is the same for both address families, not restricted to IPv6.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt requires recreating the endpoint to use either address.

citations.title: Endpoint
citations.quote: If both an IPv6 and IPv4 address are assigned, either address can be used to reach the endpoint. The same behavior will apply with regard to policy rules, load-balancing, etc.

stem: An organisation runs several Kubernetes clusters in different regions and wants pods in one cluster to reach pods in another without NAT or address translation between them. Which Cluster Mesh capability provides this?

options.text: Pod-to-pod connectivity between clusters within a flat IP address space
Cluster-aware network policy enforcement
Cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing
Service affinity controls to prefer local or remote backends

explanation: Cluster Mesh extends Cilium networking across clusters and gives pod-to-pod connectivity between clusters within a flat IP address space, which is what allows pods to reach each other directly without address translation.

optionRationale.b: Cluster-aware network policy enforcement governs which traffic is allowed across clusters; it does not itself provide the flat addressing that makes direct pod-to-pod reachability possible.
optionRationale.c: Cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing concerns reaching services, not direct pod addressing across clusters.
optionRationale.d: Service affinity controls influence whether local or remote backends are preferred; they do not create a flat IP address space.

citations.title: Multi-Cluster (Cluster Mesh)
citations.quote: Pod-to-pod connectivity between clusters within a flat IP address space

stem: A platform team wants traffic for a service to stay in the local cluster when healthy backends exist there, falling back to remote clusters only when needed. Which Cluster Mesh capability should they use?

options.text: Cluster-aware network policy enforcement
Service affinity controls to prefer local or remote backends
Pod-to-pod connectivity within a flat IP address space
Cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing

explanation: Cluster Mesh provides service affinity controls that let you prefer local or remote backends, which is exactly the behaviour of keeping traffic local when possible.

optionRationale.a: Cluster-aware network policy enforcement controls whether traffic is permitted, not which backend location is preferred.
optionRationale.c: Flat pod-to-pod connectivity makes cross-cluster reachability possible but says nothing about preferring local backends.
optionRationale.d: Cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing makes remote backends reachable, but the preference for local over remote is the separate affinity capability.

Automatic provisioning of cloud load balancers per cluster
Replacement of the Kubernetes API server with a shared control plane
A single etcd datastore shared by all clusters

explanation: Among the listed benefits of extending Cilium networking across clusters is cluster-aware network policy enforcement.

optionRationale.b: Cloud load-balancer provisioning is not among the capabilities listed for Cluster Mesh.
optionRationale.c: Cluster Mesh extends Cilium networking across clusters; it does not replace the Kubernetes API server.
optionRationale.d: A shared etcd datastore is not one of the stated capabilities.

stem: A team operating multiple Kubernetes clusters for fault isolation and geographical distribution finds that traditional networking models struggle with service discovery, segmentation, policy enforcement and load-balancing across those clusters. What does Cluster Mesh do to address this?

options.text: It merges the clusters into a single Kubernetes cluster with one API server.
It extends Cilium networking across multiple Kubernetes clusters.
It requires all clusters to be in the same region and availability zone.
It replaces Kubernetes Services with a separate external load balancer.

explanation: Cluster Mesh addresses the challenges of multi-cluster networking by extending Cilium networking across multiple Kubernetes clusters, adding cross-cluster connectivity, policy enforcement, service discovery and affinity.

optionRationale.a: Cluster Mesh extends networking across clusters; it does not merge them into a single cluster with one API server.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes geographical distribution as a common reason for multi-cluster setups, not a restriction to one region.
optionRationale.d: Cluster Mesh provides cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing; it does not replace Kubernetes Services with an external load balancer.

citations.title: Multi-Cluster (Cluster Mesh)
citations.quote:
Cluster Mesh addresses these challenges by
extending Cilium networking across multiple Kubernetes clusters

stem: Which statement best describes what Cluster Mesh provides for services spread across several Kubernetes clusters?

options.text: Cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing
A flat IP address space limited to a single cluster
Policy enforcement that is unaware of which cluster traffic originates from
Backend selection that always prefers remote clusters

explanation: Cluster Mesh provides cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing, alongside pod-to-pod connectivity, cluster-aware policy enforcement and service affinity.

optionRationale.b: The flat IP address space is described as spanning clusters, not limited to one.
optionRationale.c: The policy enforcement provided is cluster-aware, not cluster-unaware.
optionRationale.d: Service affinity controls allow preferring local or remote backends; they do not always prefer remote.

citations.title: Multi-Cluster (Cluster Mesh)
citations.quote: Cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing

stem: A platform team is planning a two-cluster Cluster Mesh. A colleague asks whether a proxy or gateway must sit between the clusters for pod-to-pod traffic. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Pod-to-pod traffic is forwarded directly between nodes, including across cluster boundaries, with no additional proxy or gateway required.
All cross-cluster pod traffic must pass through the clustermesh-apiserver pod, which acts as the data-path gateway.
A LoadBalancer service in each cluster proxies pod-to-pod traffic between clusters.
Cross-cluster traffic requires an ingress gateway in each cluster to terminate and re-originate connections.

explanation: The excerpt states that pod-to-pod traffic is forwarded directly between nodes, including across cluster boundaries, without requiring any additional proxy or gateway. The clustermesh-apiserver is part of the control plane for exchanging state, not a data-path component.

optionRationale.b: The clustermesh-apiserver exposes and synchronises cluster state; it is not described as carrying pod traffic.
optionRationale.c: A LoadBalancer or NodePort service is mentioned only as a way to expose the embedded etcd over mTLS, not to forward pod traffic.
optionRationale.d: No gateway is needed at all, since traffic is forwarded directly between nodes across cluster boundaries.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
Pod-to-pod traffic is
forwarded directly between nodes, including across cluster boundaries, without
requiring any additional proxy or gateway.

stem: An engineer inspects a clustermesh-apiserver pod and wants to know which container is responsible for pulling remote cluster state into the local cluster. Which container is it?

options.text: etcd
apiserver
kvstoremesh
cilium-agent

explanation: The excerpt lists three containers in a typical clustermesh-apiserver pod and assigns kvstoremesh the role of synchronising remote cluster state from other clusters into the local cluster.

optionRationale.a: The etcd container stores the local cluster state that is exposed to remote clusters; it does not pull remote state in.
optionRationale.b: The apiserver container synchronises local Cilium and Kubernetes state into the local etcd instance, which is the opposite direction.
optionRationale.d: cilium-agent is not one of the containers listed for the clustermesh-apiserver pod.

``kvstoremesh``: Synchronizes remote cluster state from other clusters into

stem: A team running Cilium in kvstore mode wants to add Cluster Mesh. What happens to the existing kvstore etcd instance?

options.text: Cluster Mesh extends the existing kvstore etcd instance instead of deploying an additional embedded etcd instance.
Cluster Mesh always deploys a second embedded etcd instance alongside the existing one.
The existing kvstore etcd instance must be migrated to a persistent-volume-backed deployment before Cluster Mesh can be enabled.
Cluster Mesh replaces the kvstore etcd instance with the Kubernetes API server as the sole state store.

explanation: The excerpt states that when Cilium is already running in kvstore mode, Cluster Mesh extends the existing kvstore etcd instance rather than deploying an additional embedded etcd instance.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite: no additional embedded etcd instance is deployed in this case.
optionRationale.c: Persistence is not a prerequisite described here; the embedded etcd is noted as not requiring persistent storage.
optionRationale.d: The Kubernetes API server is not substituted for the kvstore; Cluster Mesh reuses the kvstore concepts.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
When Cilium is already running in kvstore mode,
Cluster Mesh extends the existing kvstore etcd instance instead of
deploying an additional embedded etcd instance.

stem: An operator is told the embedded etcd in a clustermesh-apiserver pod needs no persistent storage. What reason does the architecture give for this?

options.text: The entire state is rebuilt from kube-apiserver on startup.
The state is stored in a ConfigMap in the local cluster.
The state is held only in memory by the kvstoremesh container.
The state is replicated to remote clusters, which act as the durable store.

explanation: The excerpt explains that the embedded etcd is simple to operate because it is a single instance and does not require persistent storage, as the entire state is rebuilt from kube-apiserver on startup.

optionRationale.b: No ConfigMap-backed storage is described; the state is rebuilt from kube-apiserver.
optionRationale.c: kvstoremesh synchronises remote cluster state; it is not given as the reason persistent storage is unnecessary.
optionRationale.d: Remote clusters receive exposed state; they are not described as the durable backing store for the local etcd.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
This embedded
  etcd is simple to operate because it is a single instance and does not require
  persistent storage as the entire state is rebuilt from kube-apiserver on startup.

stem: How do Cilium agents make use of local and remote Cluster Mesh state when programming the datapath?

options.text: They use local Kubernetes API server state and remote Cluster Mesh state in a similar way to program the local datapath.
They use only remote Cluster Mesh state, ignoring the local Kubernetes API server.
They forward all state to the clustermesh-apiserver, which programs the datapath on their behalf.
They query the remote cluster's kube-apiserver directly for every datapath update.

explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium agents use local Kubernetes API server state and remote Cluster Mesh state in a similar way to program the local datapath.

optionRationale.b: Local Kubernetes API server state is explicitly part of what agents use.
optionRationale.c: Agents program the local datapath themselves; the clustermesh-apiserver exchanges state rather than programming datapaths.
optionRationale.d: Remote state reaches the local cluster through the Cluster Mesh control plane, not by agents querying a remote kube-apiserver.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
Cilium agents use local Kubernetes API server state and remote Cluster Mesh
state in a similar way to program the local datapath.

stem: A pod's egress traffic is denied by network policy. By default, what does the application on that pod observe?

options.text: An immediate connection failure, because Cilium sends a rejection notification back to the pod.
A connection timeout, because Cilium silently drops the denied packets.
A TCP reset from the destination host, because the remote endpoint refuses the connection.
Successful connection establishment followed by a policy audit event in the application log.

explanation: With the default behaviour, Cilium silently drops packets denied by egress policy, so applications experience connection timeouts rather than immediate connection failures.

optionRationale.a: Immediate rejection feedback is what the opt-in icmp deny response provides, not the default.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes silent dropping by Cilium, not a reset generated by the destination.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about connections succeeding or audit events reaching the application; the packets are dropped.

citations.title: Policy Deny Response Handling
citations.quote: By default, when network policy denies egress traffic from a pod, Cilium silently drops the packets.

stem: An application team complains that requests to forbidden destinations hang for a long time before failing. You want the source pod to receive an explicit rejection instead of waiting for a timeout. Which setting achieves this?

options.text: --policy-deny-response=icmp
--policy-deny-response=none
--policy-deny-response=reject
--policy-deny-response=timeout

explanation: Setting the deny response to icmp makes Cilium send an ICMP Destination Unreachable response back to the source pod when egress traffic is denied by policy, giving immediate feedback instead of a timeout.

optionRationale.b: none is the default and silently drops denied packets, which is exactly the timeout behaviour being complained about.
optionRationale.c: reject is not one of the documented values for this option.
optionRationale.d: timeout is not one of the documented values for this option.

citations.title: Policy Deny Response Handling
citations.quote: Send an ICMP Destination Unreachable response back to the source pod when egress traffic is denied by policy.

stem: You enable ICMP deny responses for egress policy denials, but applications still experience connection timeouts. Ingress policy on the source pod blocks ICMP. What is the cause?

options.text: ICMP deny responses only work for ingress traffic denial, so egress denials are always silent.
The deny response feature requires the none setting to be active at the same time.
The rejection notifications are themselves ICMP traffic, so blocking ICMP ingress prevents the application from receiving them.
ICMP deny responses are only sent when the destination is outside the cluster.

explanation: When using the icmp deny response, ICMP ingress traffic must be allowed by your network policies; if ingress policies block ICMP, applications will not receive the rejection notifications and will still experience connection timeouts.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: the feature applies to egress pod traffic denied by policy, and ingress denial behaviour is not supported.
optionRationale.b: none and icmp are alternative values of the same option, not settings used together.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt places no such restriction on the destination.

attachments.title: Observed behaviour

If ICMP traffic is blocked by ingress policies, applications will not receive 
the rejection notifications and will still experience connection timeouts.

citations.title: Policy Deny Response Handling
citations.quote: When using ``--policy-deny-response=icmp``, ensure that ICMP ingress traffic is allowed by your network policies.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the scope of the experimental icmp deny response?

options.text: It applies to both ingress and egress pod traffic denied by network policy.
It applies only to ipv4 and ipv6 egress pod traffic denied by network policy; ingress denial behaviour is not supported currently.
It applies only to ipv4 ingress pod traffic denied by network policy.
It applies to all traffic denied by policy, including traffic to and from the host.

explanation: The icmp deny response is experimental and only applies to ipv4 and ipv6 egress pod traffic denied by network policy; ingress traffic denial behaviour is not supported currently.

optionRationale.a: Ingress denial behaviour is explicitly not supported currently.
optionRationale.c: The feature covers egress, not ingress, and covers both ipv4 and ipv6.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt limits the feature to egress pod traffic and says nothing about host traffic.

citations.title: Policy Deny Response Handling
citations.quote: This is an experimental feature and only applies to ipv4 and ipv6 egress pod traffic denied by network policy.

stem: How does the icmp deny response differ from the default deny behaviour?

options.text: The default silently drops denied packets, whereas icmp sends an ICMP Destination Unreachable response back to the source pod.
The default sends an ICMP Destination Unreachable response, whereas icmp silently drops denied packets.
Both silently drop packets, but icmp additionally logs the drop to the application.
The default rejects traffic with a TCP reset, whereas icmp delays the rejection to reduce load.

explanation: The default (none) silently drops denied packets so applications see timeouts, while icmp sends an ICMP Destination Unreachable response back to the source pod, providing immediate feedback that the connection was rejected.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the two behaviours.
optionRationale.c: icmp does not merely log; it sends a response to the source pod.
optionRationale.d: The default is a silent drop, not a TCP reset, and icmp speeds up feedback rather than delaying it.

citations.title: Policy Deny Response Handling
citations.quote: Silently drop denied packets. Applications will experience connection timeouts when policy denies traffic.

stem: A security review finds that Hubble flow records in your cluster contain the passwords used in HTTP basic authentication. Which option must be enabled to stop this?

options.text: `--hubble-redact-http-userinfo`
`--hubble-redact-http-urlquery`
`--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny`
`--hubble-redact-enabled` alone, with no further options

explanation: URL user info covers credentials such as the password used in basic auth, and the dedicated option for redacting it is `--hubble-redact-http-userinfo`. Note that the umbrella `--hubble-redact-enabled` option is what enables Hubble to handle sensitive information at all, but the specific category of data is selected by the per-protocol options.

optionRationale.b: `--hubble-redact-http-urlquery` targets URL query (GET) parameters, not user info such as basic-auth passwords.
optionRationale.c: `--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny` operates on HTTP headers, whereas basic-auth credentials in the URL are user info.
optionRationale.d: `--hubble-redact-enabled` is the option that enables Hubble to handle sensitive information, but the excerpt presents the individual redaction features as separate options, so it does not by itself select user info.

citations.title: Security Implications
citations.quote: For HTTP: redacting URL user info (for example, password used in basic auth) (``--hubble-redact-http-userinfo``)

stem: An engineer wants Hubble to redact HTTP headers, keeping only a small set of named headers visible. Which option defines that set of headers that are not redacted?

options.text: `--hubble-redact-http-headers-allow`
`--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny`
`--hubble-redact-http-urlquery`
`--hubble-redact-http-userinfo`

explanation: The excerpt describes redacting all headers except those defined in the `--hubble-redact-http-headers-allow` list, which is the allow-list form of header redaction. The deny-list form is the alternative, used when only specific headers should be redacted.

optionRationale.b: `--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny` is the opposite approach: it redacts only the headers named in the list rather than preserving a set.
optionRationale.c: `--hubble-redact-http-urlquery` concerns URL query (GET) parameters, not headers.
optionRationale.d: `--hubble-redact-http-userinfo` concerns URL user info such as basic-auth passwords, not headers.

citations.title: Security Implications
citations.quote: For HTTP headers: redacting all headers except those defined in the ``--hubble-redact-http-headers-allow`` list or redacting only the headers defined in the ``--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny`` list

stem: A team deploys Cilium with default settings and inspects Layer 7 Hubble flows. What do they observe about sensitive information such as API keys and query parameters?

options.text: It is present in the flows, because Hubble does not redact it by default.
It is redacted by default, and redaction must be disabled to see it.
It is redacted only for HTTP, and never for other Layer 7 protocols.
It is never captured, because Layer 7 flows exclude query parameters.

explanation: Redaction is opt-in: by default Hubble does not redact potentially sensitive information present in Layer 7 Hubble Flows. Hardening requires enabling the `--hubble-redact-enabled` option.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the default; the excerpt states that Hubble does not redact by default.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt gives no such protocol-specific default; redaction is off by default and is enabled through the `--hubble-redact-enabled` option.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt lists query parameters among the potentially sensitive information present in Layer 7 flows, so they are not excluded.

citations.title: Security Implications
citations.quote: By default, Hubble does not redact potentially sensitive information present in `Layer 7 Hubble Flows <https://github.com/cilium/cilium/tree/master/api/v1/flow#flow-Layer7>`_.

stem: Which option enables Hubble to handle sensitive information present in Layer 7 flows, acting as the switch for the redaction features?

options.text: `--hubble-redact-enabled`
`--hubble-redact-http-urlquery`
`--hubble-redact-http-headers-allow`
`--hubble-redact-http-userinfo`

explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium provides the `--hubble-redact-enabled` option, which enables Hubble to handle sensitive information present in Layer 7 flows. The other options select particular categories of data to redact for supported protocols.

optionRationale.b: This option redacts URL query (GET) parameters; it is one of the per-protocol features, not the enabling switch.
optionRationale.c: This option defines the headers exempt from header redaction; it does not enable redaction overall.
optionRationale.d: This option redacts URL user info such as basic-auth passwords; it is a per-protocol feature rather than the enabling switch.

To harden security, Cilium provides the ``--hubble-redact-enabled`` option which
enables Hubble to handle sensitive information present in Layer 7 flows.

stem: An engineer needs to redact only a specific, named set of HTTP headers while leaving all other headers visible in Layer 7 flows. Which option fits, and how does it differ from the alternative header option?

options.text: `--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny`, which redacts only the headers defined in its list, whereas the allow option redacts all headers except those listed.
`--hubble-redact-http-headers-allow`, which redacts only the headers defined in its list, whereas the deny option redacts all headers except those listed.
`--hubble-redact-http-urlquery`, which redacts named headers as well as query parameters.
`--hubble-redact-enabled`, which redacts a fixed set of headers chosen by Hubble.

explanation: The excerpt offers two header modes: redacting all headers except those in the `--hubble-redact-http-headers-allow` list, or redacting only the headers in the `--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny` list. To redact only a named set, the deny list is the correct choice.

optionRationale.b: This swaps the two modes; the allow list preserves the named headers and redacts the rest.
optionRationale.c: `--hubble-redact-http-urlquery` concerns URL query (GET) parameters, not headers.
optionRationale.d: `--hubble-redact-enabled` is the option that enables Hubble to handle sensitive information; the excerpt does not describe it as redacting a fixed set of headers.

citations.title: Security Implications
citations.quote: For HTTP headers: redacting all headers except those defined in the ``--hubble-redact-http-headers-allow`` list or redacting only the headers defined in the ``--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny`` list

stem: An engineer proposes joining a production cluster and a shared development cluster into one Cluster Mesh so that services can be reached across both. What does Cilium's security model say about this plan?

options.text: It is acceptable, because Cilium performs sanity checks on all information received from remote clusters and blocks malicious data.
It is acceptable, because each cluster keeps its own separate trust domain and policies are never shared.
It should be avoided, because all clusters in a Cluster Mesh form a single trust domain and should be mutually trusted with equivalent security postures.
It is acceptable, because the Cilium operator in each cluster re-validates every remote identity before use.

explanation: Clusters joined in a Cluster Mesh share one trust domain, so the security posture of the weakest cluster matters to all of them. Cilium's sanity checks are not a substitute for trust: they cannot fully prevent a compromised cluster's control plane from propagating malicious information. Only mutually trusted clusters with equivalent security postures should be connected.

optionRationale.a: The sanity checks are explicitly described as unable to fully prevent a compromised cluster's control plane from propagating malicious information, so they are not a guarantee.
optionRationale.b: The opposite is true: all clusters connected in a Cluster Mesh form a single trust domain.
optionRationale.d: No such re-validation by the operator is described; the checks that exist are performed by Cilium and are not claimed to be sufficient.

citations.title: Security
citations.quote: All clusters connected in a Cluster Mesh form a single trust domain.

stem: A team argues that because Cilium runs sanity checks on data arriving from remote clusters, a compromised cluster in the mesh cannot do harm to the others. How should this claim be assessed?

options.text: It is correct, because the sanity checks fully prevent a compromised control plane from propagating malicious information.
It is incorrect, because the sanity checks cannot fully prevent a compromised cluster's Cilium control plane from propagating malicious information to other clusters.
It is correct, because a compromised cluster is automatically ejected from the mesh once the checks fail.
It is incorrect, because Cilium performs no checks at all on information received from remote clusters.

explanation: Cilium does perform various sanity checks on information received from remote clusters, but these checks cannot fully prevent a compromised cluster's Cilium control plane from propagating malicious information to other clusters. Trust between clusters therefore has to be established by other means, namely connecting only mutually trusted clusters with equivalent security postures.

optionRationale.a: This overstates the checks; they cannot fully prevent propagation of malicious information.
optionRationale.c: No automatic ejection mechanism is described; the checks are only sanity checks.
optionRationale.d: This understates the checks; Cilium does perform various sanity checks, they are simply not sufficient on their own.

citations.title: Security
citations.quote:
these checks cannot fully prevent a compromised cluster's Cilium
control plane from propagating malicious information to other clusters.

stem: Which statement best describes the trust relationship between clusters that are connected in a Cluster Mesh?

options.text: Each cluster remains an isolated trust domain, with trust negotiated per remote service.
Trust is established only for clusters that share the same cloud provider region.
All connected clusters form a single trust domain.
Trust is limited to the clusters that pass Cilium's sanity checks at connection time.

explanation: The defining property is that all clusters connected in a Cluster Mesh form a single trust domain. Because of this, the guidance is to connect only clusters that are mutually trusted and have equivalent security postures.

optionRationale.a: Clusters in a mesh do not remain isolated trust domains; they form a single trust domain.
optionRationale.b: No regional or cloud-provider condition on trust is stated.
optionRationale.d: Passing sanity checks is not what defines the trust boundary; the checks cannot fully prevent propagation of malicious information.

citations.title: Security
citations.quote: All clusters connected in a Cluster Mesh form a single trust domain.

stem: What guidance is given for deciding which clusters may be connected together in a Cluster Mesh?

options.text: Connect any clusters, provided Cilium's sanity checks are enabled on every cluster.
Connect only clusters that are mutually trusted and have equivalent security postures.
Connect only clusters that run the same Cilium version and the same CNI configuration.
Connect only clusters that are administered by the same team.

explanation: The stated guidance is to connect only clusters that are mutually trusted and have equivalent security postures. This follows from the fact that all connected clusters form a single trust domain and that sanity checks cannot fully prevent a compromised cluster from propagating malicious information.

optionRationale.a: Sanity checks are not sufficient protection, so enabling them is not the criterion given.
optionRationale.c: Version and CNI parity are not mentioned as the criterion; the criterion is mutual trust and equivalent security posture.
optionRationale.d: Common administration is not the stated criterion, even if it often correlates with trust.

citations.title: Security
citations.quote:
Only connect clusters that are mutually trusted and have equivalent security
postures.

stem: How does Cilium's handling of information from remote clusters compare with the trust requirement for joining a Cluster Mesh?

options.text: Cilium performs no checks, so trust between clusters is irrelevant.
Cilium performs various sanity checks, and these checks make mutual trust between clusters unnecessary.

Cilium performs various sanity checks, but because these cannot fully prevent a compromised control plane from propagating malicious information, clusters must still be mutually trusted with equivalent security postures.
Cilium performs checks only on policy manifests and not on any other information from remote clusters.

explanation: The two ideas work together: Cilium does perform various sanity checks on information received from remote clusters, but those checks cannot fully prevent a compromised cluster's Cilium control plane from propagating malicious information to other clusters. The operational consequence is that only mutually trusted clusters with equivalent security postures should be connected.

optionRationale.a: Cilium does perform various sanity checks, and trust is central to the guidance.
optionRationale.b: The checks are explicitly not sufficient to remove the need for mutual trust.
optionRationale.d: The checks are described as applying to information received from remote clusters generally, not only to policy manifests.

citations.title: Security
citations.quote:
While Cilium performs various sanity checks on information received from remote
clusters, these checks cannot fully prevent a compromised cluster's Cilium
control plane from propagating malicious information to other clusters.

stem: A platform team needs to group a large, changing set of pods so that other Cilium objects can address them without naming each pod individually. What does Cilium use to achieve this arbitrary grouping and selection?

options.text: Labels, which allow for arbitrary grouping and creation of sets
Fixed IP address ranges assigned per namespace
A numbered list of pod UIDs held by the operator
Node names, since each pod is bound to one node

explanation: Cilium describes, addresses and selects resources using labels, which are a generic, flexible and highly scalable way of addressing a large set of resources because they allow arbitrary grouping and creation of sets.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says nothing about grouping by IP ranges; it states that addressing and selection are done based on labels.
optionRationale.c: No such list is described; selection is label-based, not UID-based.
optionRationale.d: Node names are not mentioned as a grouping mechanism in the excerpt.

citations.title: Labels
citations.quote:
Labels are a generic, flexible and highly scalable way of addressing a large
set of resources as they allow for arbitrary grouping and creation of sets.

stem: A security team writes a Cilium network policy that must permit traffic between two particular groups of pods. On what basis does the policy select the endpoints that are allowed to communicate?

options.text: On the basis of the node each endpoint runs on
On the basis of the endpoints' labels
On the basis of the order in which the endpoints started
On the basis of the endpoints' container image digests

explanation: Network policies select pairs of endpoints which are allowed to communicate based on labels, and the policies themselves are also identified by labels.

optionRationale.a: Node placement is not the selection criterion described; selection is by labels.
optionRationale.c: Start order is not mentioned as a selection mechanism.
optionRationale.d: Image digests are not mentioned; the excerpt says selection is label-based.

citations.title: Labels
citations.quote:
`Network policies` select pairs of `endpoints` which are allowed to
  communicate based on labels.

stem: A cluster has hundreds of endpoints spread across many namespaces, and the team wants a single policy to cover a chosen subset of them. Which property of labels makes this practical?

options.text: Labels are generic, flexible and highly scalable, allowing arbitrary grouping and creation of sets
Labels are immutable once set, so the subset can never drift
Labels are unique per endpoint, so each endpoint must be selected individually
Labels are stored only on the node, so selection is local to each host

explanation: Labels are described as a generic, flexible and highly scalable way of addressing a large set of resources, because they allow for arbitrary grouping and creation of sets — which is what lets one policy cover a chosen subset of many endpoints.

optionRationale.b: Immutability is not claimed in the excerpt; the emphasis is on flexibility and arbitrary grouping.
optionRationale.c: Uniqueness per endpoint would defeat set-based selection, and the excerpt says the opposite: labels allow creation of sets.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say labels are node-local; it presents them as a scalable way of addressing a large set of resources.

citations.title: Labels
citations.quote:
Labels are a generic, flexible and highly scalable way of addressing a large
set of resources as they allow for arbitrary grouping and creation of sets.

stem: A Cilium pod is not in the `Running` state and you want to inspect the Hubble-related agent logs. Which command is appropriate?

options.text: kubectl describe -n kube-system pod/cilium-5bjkq
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium
kubectl logs -n kube-system -c cilium-agent -l k8s-app=cilium --tail=-1 | grep subsys=hubble
cilium status

explanation: The guidance is that if one or more pods are not in `Running` state, you look at the pod logs with `kubectl logs -n kube-system -c cilium-agent -l k8s-app=cilium --tail=-1 | grep subsys=hubble`. Describing the pod is the step for pods in `Pending` state, and the other commands only list pods or summarise status.

optionRationale.a: Describing the pod is recommended for pods in `Pending` state, not for reading logs of pods that are not `Running`.
optionRationale.b: This command only lists the pods and their status; it does not show agent logs.
optionRationale.d: `cilium status` gives a summary of component health, not the agent log lines.

stem: A cluster administrator is planning capacity for a new Cilium deployment and asks how much state synchronisation happens between the Cilium agents on different nodes. What does Cilium say about this?

options.text: Synchronisation is kept to a minimum for simplicity and scale, and occurs exclusively via the Key-Value store or with packet metadata.
Agents synchronise continuously through a dedicated gossip protocol between every pair of nodes.
Agents do not synchronise at all; each node is fully isolated and shares nothing with its peers.
Agents synchronise only through the Kubernetes API server, which acts as the single channel for all state exchange.

explanation: Cilium states that each node operates in a mostly autonomous manner and that synchronisation of state between agents on different nodes is kept to a minimum for simplicity and scale, occurring exclusively via the Key-Value store or with packet metadata.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names only the Key-Value store and packet metadata as channels, not a dedicated gossip protocol between every pair of nodes.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says synchronisation is kept to a minimum, not eliminated; it still occurs via the Key-Value store or packet metadata.
optionRationale.d: The Kubernetes API server is not mentioned; the excerpt names the Key-Value store and packet metadata.

citations.title: Node
citations.quote:
Synchronization of state between Cilium agents running on different nodes is
kept to a minimum for simplicity and scale.

stem: An engineer is told that a particular machine is a node in a Cilium cluster. Which statement best describes what that means?

options.text: It is an individual member of the cluster that must be running the cilium-agent.
It is any machine that has the Cilium CLI installed, whether or not it is part of the cluster.
It is the machine elected to run the Cilium Operator for the whole cluster.
It is a machine that only forwards traffic and runs no Cilium component of its own.

explanation: Cilium refers to a node as an individual member of a cluster, and each node must be running the cilium-agent.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt ties node membership to running the cilium-agent, not to having the CLI installed.
optionRationale.c: The Cilium Operator is not mentioned; the requirement given is that the cilium-agent runs on each node.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says each node must be running the cilium-agent, so a node does run a Cilium component.

citations.title: Node

Cilium refers to a node as an individual member of a cluster. Each node must be
running the ``cilium-agent``

stem: A new worker machine is joined to a Cilium cluster but the cilium-agent is not started on it. What does Cilium's description of a node require of this machine?

options.text: It must be running the cilium-agent, since each node must run it.
It needs only the Key-Value store client, because state exchange happens there.
It needs only packet metadata support, because that is the sole synchronisation channel.
It needs nothing extra, because nodes operate fully autonomously without any Cilium component.

explanation: The excerpt states that each node must be running the cilium-agent. A machine joined as a node without that agent does not meet the stated requirement.

optionRationale.b: The Key-Value store is named as a synchronisation channel, not as a replacement for running the cilium-agent.
optionRationale.c: Packet metadata is named as a synchronisation channel, not as a replacement for running the cilium-agent.
optionRationale.d: Nodes operate in a mostly autonomous manner, but the excerpt still requires the cilium-agent on each node.

stem: An engineer installs Cilium in two clusters using Helm and wants Cluster Mesh to work over a native-routed datapath. Both clusters allocate PodCIDRs from 10.0.0.0/8. Which Helm value satisfies the native routing CIDR requirement?

options.text: --set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8
--set nativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8
--set clusterPoolIPv4CIDR=10.0.0.0/8
--set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/16

explanation: For native-routed datapath modes, Cilium in each cluster must be configured with a native routing CIDR covering all PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters. With cluster CIDRs allocated from 10.0.0.0/8, the Helm option is --set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8.

optionRationale.b: The Helm value is named ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR, not nativeRoutingCIDR.
optionRationale.c: clusterPoolIPv4CIDR is not the option given for the native routing CIDR.
optionRationale.d: A /16 would not cover all PodCIDR ranges allocated from the 10.0.0.0/8 space.

citations.title: Additional Requirements for Native-routed Datapath Modes
citations.quote: Helm option ``--set ipv4NativeRoutingCIDR=10.0.0.0/8``

stem: A platform team runs Cluster Mesh across three clusters, each with PodCIDRs drawn from 10.0.0.0/8, and uses a native-routed datapath. They configure Cilium with a native routing CIDR of 10.0.0.0/8. What else must be true of the network between the clusters for pod-to-pod communication to work?

options.text: Firewall rules must allow pods in different clusters to reach each other on all ports the pods may use.
Only the nodes need connectivity; pod traffic is always encapsulated between clusters.
Firewall rules must allow pod traffic only on the Cilium health-check port.
Each cluster must use a distinct native routing CIDR that excludes the other clusters' PodCIDRs.

explanation: Beyond node connectivity, pods in all clusters must have IP connectivity between each other, and the network between clusters must allow pod-to-pod inter-cluster communication across any ports the pods may use, typically via firewall rules permitting pods in different clusters to reach each other on all ports.

optionRationale.b: The requirement is that pods in all clusters have IP connectivity between each other, not just the nodes.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt requires all ports the pods may use, not a single health-check port.
optionRationale.d: The native routing CIDR must cover all PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters, not exclude them.

citations.title: Additional Requirements for Native-routed Datapath Modes
citations.quote:
The network between clusters must allow pod-to-pod inter-cluster communication
  across any ports that the pods may use.

stem: In a native-routed Cluster Mesh deployment, what must the native routing CIDR configured in each cluster cover?

options.text: All the PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters
Only the PodCIDR range of the local cluster
Only the node IP addresses of the local cluster
The service CIDR ranges of all connected clusters

explanation: Cilium in each cluster must be configured with a native routing CIDR that covers all the PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters.

optionRationale.b: Covering only the local PodCIDR would not span the connected clusters.
optionRationale.c: The requirement concerns PodCIDR ranges, not node IP addresses.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt refers to PodCIDR ranges, not service CIDR ranges.

citations.title: Additional Requirements for Native-routed Datapath Modes
citations.quote:
Cilium in each cluster must be configured with a native routing CIDR that
  covers all the PodCIDR ranges across all connected clusters.

stem: You are preparing a multi-node cluster for Hubble observability and need to make sure the Hubble Relay can function. Which network requirement must be satisfied on every node running Cilium?

options.text: TCP port 4244 must be open on all nodes running Cilium.
UDP port 8472 must be open on all nodes running Cilium.
TCP port 6443 must be open on all nodes running Cilium.
TCP port 4245 must be open on all nodes running Cilium.

explanation: Hubble Relay needs TCP port 4244 to be open on every node that runs Cilium; without it Relay cannot operate correctly. The other ports are not the one named for this purpose.

optionRationale.b: UDP 8472 is not the port the excerpt ties to Relay operation.
optionRationale.c: TCP 6443 is not mentioned as a Hubble requirement.
optionRationale.d: 4245 is a plausible near-miss for the correct 4244, but it is not the stated port.

stem: After enabling Hubble, you run `cilium status` and see the line `Hubble Relay:       OK`. What does this tell you?

stem: Two pods with the same identity-relevant labels are started on different nodes in the same cluster. What identity do they receive?

options.text: Each pod gets a node-local identity, and the two identities are merged only when the pods communicate.
Both pods resolve to and share a single identity, because identities are valid across the entire cluster.
Each pod gets a distinct identity derived from its node name, so the two never match.
Both pods receive a new identity on every restart, so they share one only until the next restart.

explanation: Identities are cluster-wide. If pods on several nodes share the identity-relevant labels, they all resolve to and share a single identity, which is why coordination between cluster nodes is required.

optionRationale.a: Identities are not node-local; the excerpt states they are valid in the entire cluster and shared across nodes.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the identity is derived from the node name; sharing the identity-relevant labels is what makes the identity common.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes identity creation based on whether the label set has been queried before, not on pod restarts.

citations.title: Identity Management in the Cluster

Identities are valid in the entire cluster which means that if several pods or
containers are started on several cluster nodes, all of them will resolve and
share a single identity if they share the identity relevant labels.

stem: A Cilium agent on one node needs to derive the identity for a set of labels. How does it obtain the identity?

options.text: It queries the distributed key-value store, which either creates a new identity or returns the identity from the initial query for that label set.
It asks the Hubble Relay, which assigns identities based on observed network flows.
It computes the identity locally from a hash of the labels, with no coordination with other nodes.
It reads the identity from the pod's Kubernetes ServiceAccount token.

explanation: The endpoint identity is resolved with the help of the distributed key-value store, which supports the atomic operation of generating a new unique identifier only if the value has not been seen before. Depending on whether the label set was queried before, a new identity is created or the existing one is returned.

optionRationale.b: Hubble Relay is not involved in identity derivation; the excerpt attributes resolution to the distributed key-value store.
optionRationale.c: Local hashing would not require coordination between cluster nodes, which the excerpt says is required.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no mention of ServiceAccount tokens; identity is derived from the identity-relevant label subset.

citations.title: Identity Management in the Cluster
citations.quote:
The operation to resolve an endpoint identity is performed with the help of the
distributed key-value store which allows to perform atomic operations in the
form *generate a new unique identifier if the following value has not been seen
before*.

stem: Why does cluster-wide identity sharing require coordination between cluster nodes?

options.text: Because each node must broadcast its pod list to every other node on every scheduling event.
Because identities must be unique per node so that traffic can be routed back to the correct endpoint.
Because a single identity must be agreed across nodes, which the distributed key-value store provides through atomic create-if-not-seen operations.
Because the CNI plugin must be reinstalled on each node whenever a new identity is created.

explanation: Since identities are valid in the entire cluster, nodes must agree on them. The distributed key-value store allows the atomic operation of generating a new unique identifier if the value has not been seen before, so each node can derive the same identity for the same label subset.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes coordination through the key-value store, not broadcasting pod lists between nodes.
optionRationale.b: Identities are shared across nodes rather than unique per node, which is precisely why coordination is needed.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt links identity creation to CNI reinstallation.
