They must always be generated manually and imported as Secrets.
They are generated only by the Cilium agent at runtime and cannot be provided manually.
They are issued exclusively by the Kubernetes control plane's built-in CA.

explanation: The excerpt states that Cluster Mesh uses mTLS to secure control plane connections and that TLS certificates can be generated automatically or manually provided. It then lists the automatic options, but manual provisioning remains possible.

optionRationale.b: Manual provisioning is one option, but the excerpt explicitly allows automatic generation as well.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says certificates can be generated automatically or manually provided; it does not restrict generation to the agent at runtime.

stem: A platform team wants Cilium to derive identities from the labels `team.payments` and `team.search` on their pods, while ignoring labels such as `deploy-timestamp`. Which label prefix must they configure when starting the agent?

options.text: `team.`
`id.`
`deploy-timestamp`
`labels.`

explanation: Cilium derives identities only from labels whose names start with one of the configured meaningful prefixes. To make `team.payments` and `team.search` security relevant, the prefix `team.` must be in that list. The default prefix `id.` would not match them, and `deploy-timestamp` is exactly the kind of metadata label that should be excluded.

optionRationale.b: `id.` is the standard default prefix, so it would not capture labels beginning with `team.`.
optionRationale.c: `deploy-timestamp` is the metadata label the team wants ignored, not a prefix to make meaningful.
optionRationale.d: `labels.` is not a prefix used by these pods and would match nothing here.

stem: An engineer creates a pod carrying the labels `id.service1`, `id.groupA.service44` and `launched-at-2024`. The agent is running with its standard behaviour and no custom prefix list. Which labels are considered when deriving the pod's identity?

options.text: All three labels, because every pod label is security relevant.
Only `launched-at-2024`, because it is the most specific label.
`id.service1` and `id.groupA.service44`, because they start with the `id.` prefix.
None, because no prefix list was supplied at agent start.

explanation: With the standard behaviour, Cilium includes all labels beginning with `id.`, so `id.service1` and `id.groupA.service44` are meaningful. The `launched-at-2024` label is metadata and is not subject to identity derivation.

optionRationale.a: Not all labels are meaningful; labels may be used purely to store metadata.
optionRationale.b: A timestamp-style label is metadata, not a security relevant label.
optionRationale.d: The standard behaviour applies without any custom configuration, so the `id.` labels are still included.

stem: Why does Cilium require the user to specify a list of string prefixes of meaningful labels?

options.text: Because Cilium cannot read more than a fixed number of labels per pod.
Because Cilium must know which labels are meaningful and should be considered when deriving the identity.
Because prefixes are used to encrypt label values before they are stored.
Because prefixes determine which pods the CNI plugin will schedule.

explanation: Pods and workloads carry labels that may be pure metadata, so Cilium needs to be told which labels are meaningful and therefore subject to being considered when deriving the identity. The mechanism for that is the list of string prefixes.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt gives no limit on the number of labels per pod.
optionRationale.c: Prefixes select meaningful labels; nothing in the excerpt mentions encryption.
optionRationale.d: Pod scheduling is not what the prefix list controls; it controls identity derivation.

optionRationale.b: This label does not start with the `id.` prefix, so it is not included by the standard behaviour.
optionRationale.c: A timestamp label is metadata and does not start with `id.`.
optionRationale.d: This label does not start with the `id.` prefix, so it is not included by the standard behaviour.

stem: A cluster runs the Cilium agent with `enable-policy: always`. A pod has no CiliumNetworkPolicy selecting it in either direction. What happens to traffic to and from that pod?

options.text: All traffic is allowed, because no rule selects the pod.
Policy enforcement applies to the pod even though no rules select it, so only traffic permitted by policy is allowed.
Policy enforcement is disabled on the pod, so all traffic is allowed from any source or to any destination.
Ingress is enforced but egress is unrestricted until an egress rule selects the pod.

explanation: In `always` mode, policy enforcement is enabled on all endpoints even if no rules select specific endpoints. The absence of a selecting policy therefore does not leave the pod open.

optionRationale.a: This describes `default` mode, where endpoints have unrestricted network access until selected by policy.
optionRationale.c: This describes `never` mode, where enforcement is disabled on all endpoints even if rules select them.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe a mode that enforces one direction only by default; the per-direction behaviour belongs to `default` mode.

citations.title: Policy Enforcement Modes
citations.quote:
With always mode, policy enforcement is enabled on all endpoints even if no
  rules select specific endpoints.

stem: An engineer wants Cilium to permit all traffic from any source on ingress and to any destination on egress, regardless of which CiliumNetworkPolicies select the endpoints. Which policy enforcement mode achieves this?

options.text: default
always
never
audit

explanation: `never` mode disables policy enforcement on all endpoints, even if rules do select specific endpoints, so all traffic is allowed from any source on ingress or to any destination on egress.

optionRationale.a: In `default` mode, an endpoint that is selected by a policy permits only allowed traffic, so selecting policies would still restrict it.
optionRationale.b: `always` mode does the opposite: it enforces policy on all endpoints even when no rules select them.
optionRationale.d: `audit` is not one of the three policy enforcement modes described.

citations.title: Policy Enforcement Modes
citations.quote:
With never mode, policy enforcement is disabled on all endpoints, even if
  rules do select specific endpoints. In other words, all traffic is allowed
  from any source (on ingress) or destination (on egress).

stem: A team wants pods labelled app=myService to reach the external IP 20.1.1.1 and the whole 10.0.0.0/8 range, but never 10.96.0.0/12. Which egress rule set achieves this?

options.text: One egress rule with toCIDR: 20.1.1.1/32 and a second egress rule with toCIDRSet using cidr: 10.0.0.0/8 and except: 10.96.0.0/12
A single egress rule with toCIDRSet listing 20.1.1.1/32, 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.96.0.0/12
One egress rule with toCIDR: 10.0.0.0/8 and a second egress rule with toCIDRSet using cidr: 20.1.1.1/32 and except: 10.96.0.0/12
A single egress rule with toCIDR: 20.1.1.1/32 and toCIDRSet: 10.0.0.0/8, with 10.96.0.0/12 listed under except on the toCIDR entry

explanation: The policy separates the two intents: a plain toCIDR entry allows the single external IP 20.1.1.1/32, and a toCIDRSet entry allows 10.0.0.0/8 while carving out 10.96.0.0/12 with except. Each egress item is its own rule, so the IP and the CIDR set are expressed separately.

optionRationale.b: Listing 10.96.0.0/12 alongside the allowed ranges would permit it rather than exclude it; the exclusion must be expressed with except.
optionRationale.c: The CIDR set with the except clause is attached to the wrong range here, so the carve-out would apply to the single IP instead of 10.0.0.0/8.
optionRationale.d: toCIDR and toCIDRSet are separate fields on separate rules; except belongs to the toCIDRSet entry, not to a toCIDR entry.

kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "cidr-rule"
spec:

    matchLabels:
      app: myService
  egress:
  - toCIDR:
    - 20.1.1.1/32
  - toCIDRSet:
    - cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
      except:
      - 10.96.0.0/12

stem: After the policy shown is applied, a pod labelled app=myService tries to connect to 10.96.5.5. What is the result?

options.text: The connection is denied, because 10.96.0.0/12 is excluded from the allowed 10.0.0.0/8 range
The connection is allowed, because 10.96.5.5 falls inside 10.0.0.0/8
The connection is allowed, because the except list only applies to ingress traffic
The connection is denied, because only the single IP 20.1.1.1/32 is permitted for egress

explanation: The toCIDRSet entry allows 10.0.0.0/8 but lists 10.96.0.0/12 under except, so addresses inside that excluded prefix are not permitted even though they sit within the broader range. 10.96.5.5 is inside 10.96.0.0/12 and is therefore denied.

optionRationale.b: Being inside 10.0.0.0/8 is not sufficient, because the except clause removes 10.96.0.0/12 from the allowed set.
optionRationale.c: The except list is part of the egress toCIDRSet rule and has nothing to do with ingress.
optionRationale.d: The policy also allows 10.0.0.0/8 through the toCIDRSet rule, so egress is not limited to the single IP.

stem: You have just installed Cluster Mesh on two clusters and want to confirm that the components are up before moving on. Which command should you run against each cluster?

options.text: `cilium clustermesh status --context $CLUSTER1 --wait`
`cilium clustermesh connect --context $CLUSTER1`
`cilium status --wait --context $CLUSTER1`
`cilium clustermesh enable --context $CLUSTER1 --wait`

explanation: The validation step is to wait for the Cluster Mesh components to come up by invoking `cilium clustermesh status --wait` against each cluster context. The `--wait` flag makes the command block until the components are ready, and it also waits for a LoadBalancer service to be assigned an IP.

optionRationale.b: `connect` is not the validation command described; the excerpt only describes waiting on status for each cluster.
optionRationale.c: `cilium status` is the general agent health command, not the Cluster Mesh component check described here.
optionRationale.d: `enable` is not the command given for validating that the components have come up; the excerpt uses `status --wait`.

stem: You run `cilium clustermesh status --context $CLUSTER1 --wait` and the command keeps printing lines such as `⌛ Waiting (25s) for clusters to be connected: 2 nodes are not ready`. What is the command doing?

options.text: It is blocking until the clusters are connected, reporting how many nodes are not yet ready.
It has failed permanently because two nodes are unreachable and must be deleted.
It is waiting for the LoadBalancer service to be assigned an IP address.
It is waiting for the Cilium agents on the local cluster to be scheduled.

explanation: With `--wait`, the command keeps polling and prints progress lines showing how many nodes are not yet ready, until all nodes are connected to all clusters. The repeated `⌛ Waiting` lines are progress output, not a terminal failure.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the wait progressing from 2 nodes not ready to 1, then completing successfully, so it is not a permanent failure.
optionRationale.c: The LoadBalancer wait is reported separately, as `Service "clustermesh-apiserver" of type "LoadBalancer" found`; the `Waiting ... for clusters to be connected` line is about node connectivity.
optionRationale.d: The message concerns nodes not being connected to clusters, not local agent scheduling.

stem: The validation output ends with `✅ All 2 nodes are connected to all clusters [min:1 / avg:1.0 / max:1]` followed by a `🔌 Cluster Connections:` list showing `2/2 configured, 2/2 connected`. What does this tell you?

stem: A pod was launched on a node before Cilium was installed, so Cilium does not manage it. Which special identity is assigned to this endpoint?

options.text: reserved:unknown
reserved:unmanaged
reserved:init
reserved:world

explanation: An endpoint that is not managed by Cilium — for example a Kubernetes pod launched before Cilium was installed — is represented by the reserved:unmanaged identity.

optionRationale.a: reserved:unknown is used when the identity could not be derived at all, not for endpoints that Cilium simply does not manage.
optionRationale.c: reserved:init covers an endpoint whose identity has not yet been resolved during bootstrapping, not one that is permanently outside Cilium's management.
optionRationale.d: reserved:world covers any network endpoint outside the cluster, which is broader than an unmanaged in-cluster pod.

attachments.title: Special reserved identities
attachments.body:
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 Identity                     Numeric ID  Description                                       
+=============================+============+===================================================+
 ``reserved:unknown``         0           The identity could not be derived.                
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:host``            1           The local host. Any traffic that originates from  
                                          or is designated to one of the local host IPs.    
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:world``           2           Any network endpoint outside of the cluster       
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:unmanaged``       3           An endpoint that is not managed by Cilium, e.g.   
                                          a Kubernetes pod that was launched before Cilium  
                                          was installed.                                    
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:health``          4           This is health checking traffic generated by      
                                          Cilium agents.                                    
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:init``            5           An endpoint for which the identity has not yet    
                                          been resolved is assigned the init identity.      
                                          This represents the phase of an endpoint in which 
                                          some of the metadata required to derive the       
                                          security identity is still missing. This is       
                                          typically the case in the bootstrapping phase.    
                                                                                            
                                          The init identity is only allocated if the labels 
                                          of the endpoint are not known at creation time.   
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:remote-node``     6           The collection of all remote cluster hosts.       
                                          Any traffic that originates from or is designated 
                                          to one of the IPs of any host in any connected    
                                          cluster other than the local node.                
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:kube-apiserver``  7           Remote node(s) which have backend(s) serving the  
                                          kube-apiserver running.                           
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+
 ``reserved:ingress``         8           Given to the IPs used as the source address for   
                                          connections from Ingress proxies.                 
+-----------------------------+------------+---------------------------------------------------+

stem: A new endpoint is created but some of the metadata needed to derive its security identity is still missing, so its labels are not known at creation time. Which identity does it receive?

options.text: reserved:unknown
reserved:unmanaged

reserved:host

explanation: An endpoint whose identity has not yet been resolved is assigned the init identity, which represents the bootstrapping phase in which metadata required to derive the security identity is still missing. It is only allocated if the endpoint's labels are not known at creation time.

optionRationale.a: reserved:unknown means the identity could not be derived, rather than that derivation is still pending.
optionRationale.b: reserved:unmanaged is for endpoints Cilium does not manage, such as pods started before Cilium was installed.
optionRationale.d: reserved:host is for the local host and traffic to or from local host IPs.

reserved:world

reserved:ingress

explanation: reserved:world is the special identity for any network endpoint outside of the cluster.

optionRationale.a: reserved:remote-node covers remote cluster hosts, not arbitrary endpoints outside the cluster.

stem: How are special reserved identities distinguished from the identities assigned to endpoints managed by Cilium?

options.text: They are prefixed with the string reserved:
They are always assigned numeric ID 0
They are prefixed with the string special:
They are only used for endpoints in remote clusters

explanation: All endpoints managed by Cilium are assigned an identity, and the special identities that represent endpoints not managed by Cilium are prefixed with the string reserved:.

optionRationale.b: Only reserved:unknown has numeric ID 0; the other special identities have their own numeric IDs.
optionRationale.c: The documented prefix is reserved:, not special:.
optionRationale.d: Special identities cover many cases, including the local host, the world outside the cluster and unmanaged endpoints, not only remote clusters.

stem: An engineer wants to attach a label to a set of endpoints so that a policy can select them by key alone, without caring about any value. Which label format should be used?

options.text: `io.cilium.mykey=myvalue`
`io.cilium.mykey`
`mykey=io.cilium`
`io.cilium.mykey=`

explanation: The value portion of a label is optional and can be omitted entirely, leaving just the key, for example `io.cilium.mykey`. The key is the mandatory part; the value need not be supplied.

optionRationale.a: This is the full key=value form, which supplies a value rather than omitting it.
optionRationale.c: This reverses the intended order, putting the value-like portion first and the reverse-domain key second.
optionRationale.d: This still supplies a value, albeit an empty one, rather than omitting the value portion.

stem: An engineer is choosing a key for a new label and wants it to be unique across systems. Which convention does Cilium documentation recommend for achieving this?

options.text: Using the reverse domain name notion, e.g. `io.cilium.mykey=myvalue`.
Using an incrementing numeric suffix on a short key.
Using only uppercase characters in the key.
Omitting the key and relying on the value alone.

explanation: Uniqueness of the key is typically achieved by using the reverse domain name notion, for example `io.cilium.mykey=myvalue`.

optionRationale.b: No numeric-suffix convention is described; uniqueness comes from the reverse domain name notion.
optionRationale.c: Key names should typically consist of the character set ``[a-z0-9-.]``, which is lowercase.
optionRationale.d: The key portion is mandatory and must be unique, so it cannot be omitted.

citations.title: What is a Label?
citations.quote: This is typically achieved by using the reverse domain name notion, e.g. ``io.cilium.mykey=myvalue``.

stem: A label is described as a pair of strings. Which statement correctly describes the two portions?

options.text: Both the key and the value are mandatory.
The value is mandatory and the key is optional.
The key is mandatory and must be unique, while the value is optional.
Neither portion is mandatory, but both must be unique.

explanation: A label consists of a key and a value. The key portion is mandatory and must be unique, whereas the value portion is optional and can be omitted.

optionRationale.a: Only the key is mandatory; the value can be omitted.
optionRationale.b: This reverses the roles — the key is the mandatory portion, not the value.
optionRationale.d: The key is mandatory, and uniqueness is required of the key, not of both portions.

stem: A cluster runs CoreDNS in the kube-system namespace with the service account coredns. Cilium has just been installed and the kvstore is not yet reachable. What does Cilium do when it first sees these DNS pods?

options.text: It assigns identity 104 automatically, without contacting the kvstore.
It assigns identity 102 automatically, without contacting the kvstore.
It waits for the kvstore to become reachable before assigning any identity.
It assigns identity 106 automatically, without contacting the kvstore.

explanation: CoreDNS in kube-system with the coredns service account is a well-known identity with numeric ID 104, and well-known identities are handed out automatically without contacting external dependencies such as the kvstore. This is what allows policy enforcement for essential services during bootstrap.

optionRationale.b: 102 is the numeric ID of the kube-dns deployment, not of core-dns.
optionRationale.c: The whole point of well-known identities is that they are allocated without any external dependency, so no kvstore wait is needed.
optionRationale.d: 106 is the numeric ID for core-dns on EKS, which carries the additional eks.amazonaws.com/component=coredns label; the plain core-dns entry is 104.

automatically and will hand out a security identity without requiring to
contact any external dependencies such as the kvstore.

optionRationale.a: 102 is the plain kube-dns identity, which carries only the k8s-app=kube-dns label.
optionRationale.c: 104 is the core-dns identity, which uses the coredns service account.
optionRationale.d: 106 is the EKS variant of core-dns, labelled with eks.amazonaws.com/component=coredns.

stem: An operator is joining a new cluster to an existing Cluster Mesh. The existing clusters were installed with `maxConnectedClusters` set to 511. What must the new cluster's configuration be?

It must set the value to 65535 to match the identity limit.

explanation: All clusters across a Cluster Mesh must be configured with the same `maxConnectedClusters` value, so the new cluster must also use 511.

optionRationale.b: The value is not independent per cluster; all clusters in the mesh must share the same value.
optionRationale.c: 511 is the maximum supported value, so a higher value is not valid.
optionRationale.d: 65535 is the default cluster-local identity limit, not a `maxConnectedClusters` value.

stem: Which statement about changing `maxConnectedClusters` on a cluster that is already running Cilium is correct?

options.text: It can be changed at any time and takes effect after the Cilium agent restarts.
It can only be set once during Cilium installation and should not be changed for existing clusters.
It can be changed only while the cluster is disconnected from the mesh.
It can be changed freely as long as all clusters are updated together.

explanation: The option can only be set once during Cilium installation and should not be changed for existing clusters; changing it on a live cluster may cause connection disruption and incorrect policy enforcement.

optionRationale.a: A restart does not make the change safe; the option is fixed at installation time.
optionRationale.c: No such disconnected-cluster procedure is described; the option is simply not to be changed on existing clusters.
optionRationale.d: Updating all clusters together is not offered as a safe path; the option should not be changed for existing clusters at all.

stem: A team creates a Service annotated with service.cilium.io/global: "true" and does not set any other Cilium annotation. What is the resulting load-balancing behaviour across the clusters in the Cluster Mesh?

options.text: Backends are load-balanced across multiple clusters, because sharing is implicitly enabled.
Only local backends are used, because sharing must be opted into explicitly.
The Service is rejected by the agent until service.cilium.io/shared is set.
Backends are shared only with clusters that carry a matching service.cilium.io/shared annotation.

explanation: A Global Service load-balances across backends in multiple clusters by default, and this implicitly configures service.cilium.io/shared: "true". No further annotation is needed to enable sharing.

optionRationale.b: Sharing is the default for a Global Service, not something that must be opted into.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the behaviour described requires the shared annotation to be set explicitly; it is configured implicitly.
optionRationale.d: Sharing is not gated on a matching annotation in the other clusters.

stem: An engineer wants a Global Service to keep serving its own cluster's endpoints while also exposing remote endpoints, but must not share the local endpoints to other clusters. Which annotation achieves this?

options.text: service.cilium.io/shared: "false"
service.cilium.io/global: "false"
service.cilium.io/global: "true" on its own
service.cilium.io/shared: "true"

explanation: To prevent service backends from being shared to other clusters, the sharing option should be disabled with service.cilium.io/shared: "false". The example keeps service.cilium.io/global: "true" so the Service remains global and remote endpoints are still exposed.

optionRationale.b: Setting the global annotation to false would stop the Service being a Global Service at all, rather than controlling sharing.
optionRationale.c: The global annotation alone leaves sharing implicitly enabled, so local endpoints would be shared.
optionRationale.d: Setting shared to true is the default behaviour and does the opposite of what is required.

stem: After the policy below is applied, a client in another cluster can still reach the rebel-base Service, but clients in other clusters no longer see this cluster's rebel-base pods as backends. Which annotation in the manifest produces that effect?

options.text: service.cilium.io/shared: "false"
service.cilium.io/global: "true"
spec.type: ClusterIP
spec.selector: name: rebel-base

explanation: The shared annotation set to "false" prevents this cluster's service backends from being shared to other clusters, while the global annotation keeps the Service global so remote endpoints are still exposed.

optionRationale.b: The global annotation makes the Service a Global Service; on its own it would also share local endpoints.
optionRationale.c: The Service type controls how the Service is exposed locally, not whether backends are shared across clusters.
optionRationale.d: The selector determines which pods are backends; it does not control cross-cluster sharing.

stem: An engineer runs `hubble observe --pod deathstar --protocol http` and sees a flow from `default/tiefighter` to `default/deathstar-c74d84667-cx5kp:80` marked `http-request DROPPED` for `PUT http://deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/exhaust-port`. What does this output indicate?

options.text: The HTTP request was denied by policy at the application layer.
The HTTP request was allowed and forwarded to the backend.
The HTTP request was dropped because the source pod lacks the required label.
The HTTP request timed out because no policy matched it.

explanation: The output shows an `http-request DROPPED` verdict for a specific HTTP method and path, which corresponds to the request that was denied by policy. The excerpt states that the `PUT` request to `/v1/exhaust-port` is 'accessing an HTTP endpoint which is denied by policy', and the `hubble observe` output confirms it is `DROPPED`.

optionRationale.b: A forwarded request would appear as `FORWARDED`, as seen for the allowed `POST` request, not `DROPPED`.
optionRationale.c: The missing-label case applies to the `xwing` pod, which produces `Policy denied DROPPED (TCP Flags: SYN)` flows, not an HTTP-layer `DROPPED` for `tiefighter`.
optionRationale.d: A timeout would not produce an `http-request DROPPED` line; the excerpt shows the `xwing` request hanging and terminating with exit code 28, which is different.

stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy uses `toCIDR` to allow egress from selected pods to 10.0.0.0/24. A pod in that CIDR replies to a request from a selected endpoint. What does the policy allow?

options.text: The reply is automatically allowed, because endpoints selected by a `fromEndpoints` are automatically allowed to reply back to the respective destination endpoints.
The reply is dropped unless a separate ingress rule selects the replying pod.
The reply is allowed only if the destination CIDR is also listed in a `toCIDRSet`.
The reply is allowed only if the selected endpoint has a reserved identity.

explanation: The excerpt states that endpoints selected by a `fromEndpoints` are automatically allowed to reply back to the respective destination endpoints, so return traffic does not need a separate rule.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes automatic reply permission rather than requiring a separate ingress rule.
optionRationale.c: `toCIDRSet` is a separate field for destination prefixes with excluded subnets; it is not a prerequisite for replies.
optionRationale.d: Reserved identities are not mentioned in the excerpt and play no part in this behaviour.

stem: You need to allow egress from selected endpoints to a set of destination CIDRs, but must carve out certain subnets inside those CIDRs so that traffic to them is not allowed. Which field should you use?

options.text: `toCIDR`

`fromEndpoints`
`endpointSelector`

explanation: `toCIDRSet` lists destination prefixes/CIDRs along with an optional list of subnets of the destination prefix/CIDR to which communication is not allowed, which is exactly the carve-out requirement.

optionRationale.a: `toCIDR` only lists allowed destination prefixes/CIDRs and offers no way to exclude subnets.
optionRationale.c: `fromEndpoints` selects source endpoints, not destination prefixes.
optionRationale.d: `endpointSelector` selects the endpoints the policy applies to, not the destinations.

`toCIDRSet`
`endpointSelector`

stem: How do `toCIDR` and `toCIDRSet` differ in what they express about destination prefixes?

options.text: `toCIDR` allows an optional exclusion list of subnets; `toCIDRSet` does not.
`toCIDRSet` allows an optional exclusion list of subnets per destination prefix; `toCIDR` only lists allowed destination prefixes.
`toCIDR` applies to ingress while `toCIDRSet` applies to egress.
Both fields are identical apart from the name.

explanation: `toCIDR` is simply a list of allowed destination prefixes/CIDRs, whereas `toCIDRSet` adds an optional list of subnets of the destination prefix/CIDR to which communication is not allowed.

optionRationale.a: The exclusion list belongs to `toCIDRSet`, not `toCIDR`.
optionRationale.c: Both fields describe destinations that selected endpoints are allowed to talk to, so both are egress-oriented.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt distinguishes them by the optional exclusion list in `toCIDRSet`.

stem: A cluster is part of a Cluster Mesh and runs a global NodePort service. A client outside the cluster reaches the service through a node's NodePort and is only ever sent to backends in that same cluster. Cilium is not configured to replace kube-proxy. What explains this?

options.text: Global NodePort services load balance across local and remote backends only when Cilium replaces kube-proxy; otherwise only local backends are eligible through the NodePort.
Global services never include remote backends for NodePort access, regardless of how Cilium is configured.
Remote backends are excluded because the service lacks a service annotation marking it as global.
Remote backends are excluded because the client is outside the cluster and therefore has no Cilium identity.

explanation: The excerpt states that global NodePort services load balance across both local and remote backends only if Cilium is configured to replace kube-proxy (kubeProxyReplacement=true). Otherwise, only local backends are eligible for load balancing when accessed through the NodePort, which matches the observed behaviour.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes a configuration-dependent limitation, not an absolute one: with kube-proxy replacement, remote backends do become eligible.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt attributes the behaviour to the kube-proxy replacement setting, not to any service annotation.
optionRationale.d: Client identity is not mentioned; the limitation concerns how the NodePort path selects backends.

citations.title: Limitations

Global NodePort services load balance across both local and remote backends only

stem: An engineer wants a global service to load balance across local and remote backends when it is accessed from a Pod running in the host network, but the cluster does not replace kube-proxy. Which configuration overcomes the limitation?

options.text: Set socketLB.enabled=true and socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly=true.
Set kubeProxyReplacement=false and enable the NodePort on every node.
Set socketLB.enabled=true only, leaving host namespace socket load balancing off.
Nothing can be configured; host-network access to global services always uses local backends only.

explanation: The excerpt says the limitation for global services accessed by a Node or a Pod running in host network can be overcome by enabling SocketLB in the host namespace, with socketLB.enabled=true and socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly=true.

optionRationale.b: Setting kubeProxyReplacement=false is the condition that causes the limitation, not a remedy for it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt requires both settings, including socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly=true, to enable SocketLB in the host namespace.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly describes a way to overcome the limitation.

stem: How does the behaviour of a global service accessed through a NodePort differ between a cluster with kubeProxyReplacement=true and one without it?

options.text: With kubeProxyReplacement=true, both local and remote backends are load balanced; otherwise only local backends are eligible through the NodePort.
With kubeProxyReplacement=true, only local backends are used; otherwise both local and remote backends are eligible.
In both cases only local backends are eligible, but the remote backends remain visible in the service's endpoint list.
In both cases both local and remote backends are eligible, but the remote backends are reachable only over the tunnel.

explanation: The excerpt contrasts the two configurations: replacing kube-proxy allows load balancing across both local and remote backends, while without it only local backends are eligible when the service is accessed through the NodePort.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the two configurations described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says remote backends become eligible when kube-proxy is replaced, so the outcome is not the same in both cases.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that without kube-proxy replacement only local backends are eligible, so the outcome is not the same in both cases.

Otherwise, only local backends are eligible for

options.text: Only local backends.
Both local and remote backends.
Only remote backends.
Neither local nor remote backends, because host-network access is unsupported.

explanation: The excerpt states that for global services accessed by a Node or a Pod running in host network, both local and remote backends are used only with kube-proxy replacement or with SocketLB enabled in the host namespace; otherwise only local backends are eligible.

stem: A platform team runs a StatefulSet called `my-statefulset` in two clusters that are joined in a Cluster Mesh, and both are governed by the same Service. EndpointSlice synchronisation is enabled. What does Cilium do with the hostnames from the two clusters?

options.text: It synchronises them as is, without any form of conflict resolution.
It detects the duplicate hostnames and renames one set by appending the cluster name.

stem: A team wants pods labelled role=restricted to be unable to initiate any outbound connections, without naming any allowed destination. Which manifest achieves this?

optionRationale.c: Services based uses service endpoints containing backend IP addresses rather than DNS names.
optionRationale.d: Endpoints based requires both peers to be Cilium-managed and labelled, which an external API is not.

DNS information is acquired by routing DNS traffic via `DNS Proxy`
  with a separate policy rule.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium with `--enable-node-selector-labels=true`. An engineer notices that each remote node ends up with its own distinct security identity rather than sharing one. Which statement explains this?

options.text: By default all labels attached to the `Node` object are taken into account, which can result in a unique identity for each remote node.
Each remote node is always given the same identity as the local node, so the identities only appear distinct in the CLI output.
Node identities are allocated by the Cilium operator from the cluster-wide identity range, so each node necessarily gets a unique numeric ID.
The `--node-labels` flag must be set, otherwise no node identities are allocated at all.

explanation: With node selector labels enabled, every cilium-agent allocates a local security identity for all other nodes, but uses the remote-node scoped identity range. Because all labels on the `Node` object are considered by default, this can produce a unique identity per remote node. Filtering with `--node-labels` narrows this to security-relevant labels.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite: a different local security identity is allocated for all other nodes, and by default each remote node may get a unique identity.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the cilium-agent allocating the identity in the remote-node scoped range, not the operator allocating from a cluster-wide range.
optionRationale.d: `--node-labels` is an optional filter for security-relevant labels; it is not required for node identities to be allocated.

citations.title: Node based
citations.quote:
By default all labels that ``Node`` object has attached are taken into account,
which might result in allocation of **unique** identity for each remote-node.

stem: An engineer wants node identities to be based only on security-relevant node labels rather than every label on the `Node` object. Which flag achieves this?

options.text: `--node-labels`
`--enable-node-selector-labels`
`--policy-default-local-cluster`
`--node-selector-labels`

explanation: The excerpt states that it is possible to filter only security-relevant labels with the `--node-labels` flag, which avoids allocating a unique identity for each remote node when all node labels are considered.

optionRationale.b: This flag enables node selector labels in the first place; it does not filter which labels are used.
optionRationale.c: This option restricts node selection to the local cluster by default in a Cluster Mesh environment.
optionRationale.d: This is not a flag named in the excerpt; the Helm value is `nodeSelectorLabels`, but the filtering flag is `--node-labels`.

citations.title: Node based

For these cases it is also possible to filter only
security relevant labels  with ``--node-labels`` flag.

stem: A Cluster Mesh spans several clusters. An engineer applies a policy using `fromNodes` and finds that nodes from every cluster in the mesh are selected, although only local-cluster nodes were intended. Which option restricts node selection to the local cluster by default?

options.text: Enable `--policy-default-local-cluster` via the ConfigMap option `policy-default-local-cluster` or the Helm value `clustermesh.policyDefaultLocalCluster`.
Set `--enable-node-selector-labels=true` so that node identities become cluster-scoped.
Set `--node-labels` to the local cluster name so that only local nodes match.
Nothing can be done; `fromNodes` always selects nodes from all clusters in a Cluster Mesh.

explanation: By default, policies automatically select nodes from all clusters in a Cluster Mesh environment unless explicitly specified. To restrict node selection to the local cluster by default, the option `--policy-default-local-cluster` can be enabled via the ConfigMap option `policy-default-local-cluster` or the Helm value `clustermesh.policyDefaultLocalCluster`.

optionRationale.b: This flag controls whether node selector labels are used for identity allocation; it does not change the default cluster scope of node selection.
optionRationale.c: `--node-labels` filters which node labels are used for identity allocation, not which clusters are selected.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly gives an option for restricting node selection to the local cluster by default.

citations.title: Node based
citations.quote:
Note that by default policies automatically select nodes from all the clusters in
a Cluster Mesh environment unless it is explicitly specified. To restrict node
selection to the local cluster by default you can enable the option
``--policy-default-local-cluster`` via the ConfigMap option ``policy-default-local-cluster``
or the Helm value ``clustermesh.policyDefaultLocalCluster``.

stem: Consider the policy below. Which endpoints does it select, and what traffic does it permit?

options.text: Endpoints labelled `env=prod` may receive traffic only from nodes labelled `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane=""`.
Endpoints labelled `env=prod` may send traffic only to nodes labelled `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane=""`.
All endpoints in the cluster may receive traffic from any node, because `fromNodes` matches every node by default.
Endpoints labelled `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane=""` may receive traffic only from endpoints labelled `env=prod`.

explanation: The `endpointSelector` selects endpoints with `env: prod`, and the ingress `fromNodes` rule matches nodes labelled `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: ""`. The example therefore allows all endpoints with the label `env=prod` to receive traffic only from control plane nodes in the cluster (or Cluster Mesh).

optionRationale.b: The rule is an ingress rule using `fromNodes`, so it governs traffic received by the selected endpoints, not traffic they send.
optionRationale.c: `fromNodes` matches only nodes carrying the specified label; it does not match every node by default.
optionRationale.d: The selectors are the other way round: `env=prod` selects the endpoints and the control-plane label selects the source nodes.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "to-prod-from-control-plane-nodes"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      env: prod
  ingress:
    - fromNodes:
        - matchLabels:
            node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: ""

stem: An Ingress object defines two paths of type ImplementationSpecific: /impl and /impl.*. A client requests /impl. Which path handles the request, and why?

options.text: /impl.* handles it, because the longer regex is sorted ahead of /impl and matches the request first.
/impl handles it, because an exact string match always takes precedence over a regex match.
/impl handles it, because paths within a type are sorted in increasing order of string length.
Neither handles it, because ImplementationSpecific paths are treated as Prefix matches by Cilium.

explanation: Cilium treats ImplementationSpecific as a regular expression and orders matches by decreasing string length within each path type. The regex /impl.* is longer than /impl, so it is sorted ahead, and because the * operator lets it match /impl as well, the shorter /impl match is never reached.

optionRationale.b: Exact is a separate path type with its own precedence; both of these paths are ImplementationSpecific, so no exact match is involved.
optionRationale.c: The sort is in decreasing order of string length, not increasing, so the longer regex comes first.
optionRationale.d: Cilium defines ImplementationSpecific to be Regex, not Prefix; the excerpt notes that some other implementations use Prefix.

citations.title: Ingress Path Types and Precedence
citations.quote:
For example, if you have two ImplementationSpecific paths, ``/impl``, and ``/impl.*``,
the second will be sorted ahead of the first in the generated config.

stem: A cluster administrator is planning the Cilium deployment for a five-node cluster and asks how much state synchronisation between the Cilium agents on those nodes will be required. What should you tell them?

options.text: Each node must run the cilium-agent, and state synchronisation between agents is kept to a minimum, occurring exclusively via the Key-Value store or with packet metadata.
Each node must run the cilium-agent, and the agents continuously replicate their full endpoint and policy state to every other agent over a dedicated mesh.
Only one node needs to run the cilium-agent, and it distributes configuration to the remaining nodes over the Key-Value store.
Each node must run the cilium-agent, and state synchronisation between agents occurs exclusively through the Hubble Relay.

explanation: Cilium treats each node as an individual cluster member that must run the cilium-agent and operate in a mostly autonomous manner. Synchronisation of state between agents is deliberately kept to a minimum for simplicity and scale, and it occurs exclusively via the Key-Value store or with packet metadata.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says synchronisation is kept to a minimum, not that agents continuously replicate full state to every other agent.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that each node must be running the cilium-agent, not just one node.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt names the Key-Value store and packet metadata as the only synchronisation mechanisms, not Hubble Relay.

running the ``cilium-agent`` and will operate in a mostly autonomous manner.

stem: A platform team wants pod IPs and Services in their cluster to be reachable from routers outside the cluster, in an environment that supports BGP. Which Cilium capability is intended for this?

options.text: BGP Control Plane, which advertises routes to connected routers using BGP
BGP Control Plane, which programs the datapath so that pod traffic is routed between nodes
The Cilium CNI plugin, which advertises pod CIDRs to the underlying cloud provider's routing table
Hubble Relay, which exports flow information to external routers over BGP

explanation: BGP Control Plane exists to advertise routes to connected routers using BGP, making pod networks and/or Services reachable from outside the cluster where BGP is supported. It does not program the datapath, so it is not the mechanism for in-cluster reachability.

optionRationale.b: BGP Control Plane explicitly does not program the datapath; it only advertises routes to connected routers.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes route advertisement to connected routers via BGP, not a CNI plugin programming a cloud provider's routing table.
optionRationale.d: Hubble Relay is not mentioned in the excerpt, and BGP Control Plane is the feature described for advertising routes.

stem: An engineer proposes enabling the BGP Control Plane so that pods on different nodes in the same cluster can reach each other. What is wrong with this proposal?

BGP Control Plane only advertises Services, never pod networks
BGP Control Plane does not program the datapath, so it should not be used to establish reachability within the cluster
BGP Control Plane requires an external router inside every node before pod traffic can flow

explanation: The BGP Control Plane advertises routes to connected routers but does not program the datapath. It is therefore unsuitable for establishing reachability inside the cluster; its purpose is making pod networks and/or Services reachable from outside.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: because it does not program the datapath, it should not be used for in-cluster reachability.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt says BGP Control Plane makes pod networks and/or Services reachable from outside, so pod networks are in scope.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes advertising routes to connected routers; it does not require a router on every node.

Control Plane does not program the datapath , do not use it to establish

Only the cluster's DNS service, via BGP route advertisement

Only traffic that has already been observed by Hubble Relay

stem: An Ingress object carries the annotation `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: nlb`. Cilium's ingress controller creates the backing LoadBalancer Service for it. What happens to that annotation?

explanation: Cilium copies annotations whose values begin with a set of prefixes, and `service.beta.kubernetes.io` is one of the default prefixes. An annotation in that namespace is therefore carried over from the Ingress object to the LoadBalancer Service that Cilium generates.

optionRationale.b: Annotations on the Ingress are explicitly copied to the generated Service, so they are not dropped.
optionRationale.c: The copying behaviour is governed by annotation prefixes, not by the Ingress class name.

stem: A platform team wants the Cilium ingress controller's Envoy listener to run only on the nodes carrying the labels role=infra and component=ingress. Which Helm values achieve this?

stem: An engineer wants to confirm that traffic between two pods is actually being protected by WireGuard. Which command shows only the flows that are encrypted?

options.text: hubble observe --encrypted
hubble observe --unencrypted
hubble observe --reply
hubble observe --not-reply

explanation: Hubble can filter flows on whether they are encrypted via WireGuard or IPsec. The `--encrypted` flag restricts the output to encrypted flows only, which is exactly what is needed to confirm that traffic is being protected.

optionRationale.b: `--unencrypted` does the opposite: it shows only flows that are not encrypted, so it would not confirm protection.
optionRationale.c: `--reply` filters on direction (server-to-client), not on encryption.
optionRationale.d: `--not-reply` filters on direction, showing only non-reply flows, and says nothing about encryption.

optionRationale.c: Explicitly configuring datapath modes is what the getting_started guide is for; the quick installation handles configuration automatically.
optionRationale.d: The troubleshooting_k8s section is for resolving issues encountered during installation, not for performing it.

stem: What is the identity of an endpoint derived from?

options.text: The labels associated with the pod or workload represented by the endpoint.
The IP address assigned to the endpoint by the orchestration system.
The node on which the endpoint's pod is scheduled.
The security policy that selects the endpoint.

explanation: The identity is derived based on the labels associated with the pod or workload represented by the endpoint. Cilium creates the endpoint from the orchestration system event and then resolves its identity from those labels.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt ties identity to labels, not to the endpoint's IP address.
optionRationale.c: Node placement is not mentioned as a basis for identity.
optionRationale.d: Policies select endpoints; they are not the source from which identity is derived.

citations.title: What is an Identity?
citations.quote:
The identity of an endpoint is derived based on the `labels` associated with
the pod or workload represented by the `endpoint`_.

stem: A new pod is started in a Cilium-managed cluster. In what order does Cilium handle it?

options.text: It creates an endpoint from the orchestration system event, then resolves the endpoint's identity.
It resolves the identity first, then creates the endpoint from the orchestration system event.
It creates the endpoint and assigns an identity only once the pod receives traffic.
It resolves the identity from the orchestration system event without creating an endpoint.

explanation: When a pod or workload is started, Cilium first creates an endpoint based on the event received from the orchestration system to represent it on the network. As a next step, Cilium resolves the identity of the endpoint created.

optionRationale.b: The order is reversed: the endpoint is created first, and the identity is resolved as a next step.
optionRationale.c: Identity resolution follows endpoint creation directly; it does not wait for traffic.
optionRationale.d: An endpoint is always created to represent the workload on the network.

citations.title: What is an Identity?
citations.quote:
When a pod or workload is
started, Cilium will create an `endpoint`_ based on the event received from the
orchestration system to represent it on the network. As a next step, Cilium
will resolve the identity of the `endpoint`_ created.

stem: Which statement best describes what an endpoint represents in Cilium?

options.text: A representation on the network of a pod or workload, created from an orchestration system event.
A label set that is shared by every pod in the cluster.
A network interface created manually by the cluster administrator.
A record of the security policies applied to a node.

explanation: Cilium creates an endpoint based on the event received from the orchestration system to represent the pod or workload on the network, and then resolves that endpoint's identity from its labels.

optionRationale.b: Labels are what the identity is derived from; the endpoint itself represents the workload on the network.
optionRationale.c: Endpoints are created from orchestration system events, not manually by an administrator.
optionRationale.d: An endpoint represents a pod or workload, not a node's policy records.

citations.title: What is an Identity?
citations.quote:
Cilium will create an `endpoint`_ based on the event received from the
orchestration system to represent it on the network.

stem: You have deployed a Gateway named my-gateway and want to send a request to the details service through it. Which command retrieves the address to send the request to?

explanation: The address of a ready Gateway is read from the status, specifically the first entry of status.addresses, and stored in the GATEWAY shell variable so that curl can target it.

optionRationale.b: The address is published in the Gateway's status, not in its spec, so reading spec.addresses returns nothing.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt reads status.addresses[0].value; it does not read a listener hostname from the status.
optionRationale.d: The address is a status field, not an annotation on the Gateway's metadata.

The HTML page titled Simple Bookstore App
A JSON list of the three services details, reviews and ratings
An empty body, because the request path is not routed by the Gateway

optionRationale.c: The JSON returned describes one book; the list of services appears in the HTML page, not in this JSON response.

A redirect to /productpage?u=normal

stem: A client sends a GET request to the path /details on the gateway's external address. Which backend receives the request?

options.text: The details service on port 9080
The productpage service on port 9080
The my-gateway service on port 80
No backend, because the request lacks the magic header

explanation: The HTTPRoute defines a rule that matches the path prefix /details and sends traffic to the details service on port 9080. The second rule, which targets productpage, requires the magic header, the great query parameter, the / path prefix and the GET method, so a plain GET /details does not match it.

optionRationale.b: productpage is the backend of the second rule, which also requires the magic header and the great query parameter.
optionRationale.c: my-gateway is the Gateway resource that listens on port 80; it is not a backend service.
optionRationale.d: The magic header is required only by the second rule; the first rule matches /details without it.

attachments.title: The Gateway and HTTPRoute under test
attachments.body:
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: my-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: cilium
  listeners:
  - protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    name: web-gw
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: http-app-1
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: my-gateway
    namespace: default
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /details
    backendRefs:
    - name: details
      port: 9080
  - matches:
    - headers:
      - type: Exact
        name: magic
        value: foo
      queryParams:
      - type: Exact
        name: great
        value: example
      path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /
      method: GET
    backendRefs:
    - name: productpage
      port: 9080

stem: You have deployed the Cilium monitoring stack and want to open Grafana in a browser on your workstation. Which command makes Grafana reachable at http://localhost:3000?

options.text: kubectl -n cilium-monitoring port-forward service/grafana --address 0.0.0.0 --address :: 3000:3000

stem: You are deploying Cilium with Helm and want the Cilium Operator's Prometheus endpoint to serve TLS. You have created a secret named operator-tls containing tls.crt and tls.key. Which Helm flags enable TLS using that secret?

options.text: --set operator.prometheus.tls.enabled=true --set operator.prometheus.tls.server.existingSecret=operator-tls
--set operator.prometheus.tls.enabled=true --set operator.prometheus.tls.server.secretName=operator-tls
--set operator.prometheus.tls.server.enabled=true --set operator.prometheus.tls.existingSecret=operator-tls
--set operator.prometheus.tls.enabled=true --set operator.prometheus.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true

explanation: TLS on Operator Prometheus is switched on with operator.prometheus.tls.enabled=true, and the secret holding tls.crt and tls.key is named with operator.prometheus.tls.server.existingSecret. The mtls flag is a separate option that additionally uses ca.crt to verify client certificates.

optionRationale.b: The secret is referenced with existingSecret, not secretName.
optionRationale.c: The enabled flag sits at operator.prometheus.tls.enabled, not under server, and the secret key is server.existingSecret.
optionRationale.d: The mtls flag enables mutual TLS verification of client certificates; it does not name the secret holding the server key pair.

citations.title: Configure Operator Prometheus TLS

stem: You want the Cilium Operator's Prometheus endpoint to require clients to present a certificate, verified against a CA. You already have a secret with tls.crt and tls.key. What must you add to that secret, and which Helm flag enables the verification?

options.text: Add ca.crt to the secret and set operator.prometheus.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true
Add ca.crt to the secret and set operator.prometheus.tls.enabled=true
Add tls.ca to the secret and set operator.prometheus.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true
Add ca.crt to the secret and set operator.prometheus.tls.server.existingSecret=true

explanation: Mutual TLS on Operator Prometheus requires the ca.crt key in the same secret as tls.crt and tls.key, and the flag operator.prometheus.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true, which uses ca.crt to verify client certificates.

optionRationale.b: operator.prometheus.tls.enabled only turns on TLS; it does not enable verification of client certificates.
optionRationale.c: The required key is ca.crt, not tls.ca.
optionRationale.d: existingSecret takes the secret name; it is not a boolean that enables mTLS.

citations.title: Configure Operator Prometheus TLS
citations.quote: If you also want to enable mTLS, add key ``ca.crt`` to above secret.

stem: A colleague asks what the flag operator.prometheus.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true does when the referenced secret contains tls.crt, tls.key and ca.crt. What is its effect?

options.text: It uses ca.crt from the secret to verify client certificates.
It uses ca.crt from the secret to verify the operator's own serving certificate.
It generates a new CA and client certificates automatically.
It encrypts the secret at rest in the cluster.

explanation: The mtls flag makes the Operator Prometheus endpoint use the ca.crt key of the secret to verify certificates presented by clients, which is what mutual TLS adds on top of plain TLS.

optionRationale.b: The CA verifies client certificates, not the operator's serving certificate.
optionRationale.c: The flag consumes an existing ca.crt in the secret; it does not generate certificates.
optionRationale.d: The flag concerns TLS client verification, not secret storage.

citations.title: Configure Operator Prometheus TLS
citations.quote: --set operator.prometheus.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true # Use ca.crt of secret to verify client certificates

stem: A team applies the Gateway and HTTPRoute below. Requests arriving at the Gateway on port 80 with the path /echo are sent to which backends, and in what proportion?

options.text: All requests go to echo-1 on port 8080, because the first backendRef in the list takes precedence.
Requests are split evenly, 50/50, between echo-1 on port 8080 and echo-2 on port 8090.
Requests are split 50/50 between echo-1 and echo-2, but both are contacted on port 8080.
Requests are rejected until the Gateway reports an address in its ADDRESS column.

explanation: The HTTPRoute defines a single rule matching the path prefix /echo, with two backendRefs carrying weight 50 each. The weights are equal, so traffic is split evenly between the two Services, each on the port given in its own backendRef: echo-1 on 8080 and echo-2 on 8090.

optionRationale.a: Both backendRefs are listed with equal weights, so neither takes precedence; the split is even rather than first-match.
optionRationale.c: Each backendRef carries its own port, and the manifest gives echo-2 port 8090, not 8080.
optionRationale.d: The Gateway is created and listens on port 80; an empty ADDRESS column in the get output does not cause requests to be rejected.

attachments.title: The Gateway and HTTPRoute under test
attachments.body:
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: cilium-gw
spec:
  gatewayClassName: cilium
  listeners:
  - protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    name: web-gw-echo
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: example-route-1
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: cilium-gw
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /echo
    backendRefs:
    - kind: Service
      name: echo-1
      port: 8080
      weight: 50
    - kind: Service
      name: echo-2
      port: 8090
      weight: 50

Any path beginning with /echo, such as /echo/status.
Only paths under /echo-1 and /echo-2, the backend Service names.
Any path on the Gateway, because no other route is defined.

optionRationale.c: The backend Service names are not part of the path match; the match value is /echo.
optionRationale.d: The rule is scoped to the /echo path prefix, not to every path on the Gateway.

stem: An engineer wants the Hubble static exporter to write its events to a custom location instead of the default path. Which Helm value controls the target log file?

options.text: hubble.export.static.filePath
hubble.export.static.fileMaxSizeMb
hubble.export.static.fileMaxBackups
hubble.export.static.fileCompress

explanation: The option that sets the file path of the target log file is hubble.export.static.filePath, whose default is /var/run/cilium/hubble/events.log. The other options control rotation size, the number of rotated files kept, and compression, not the destination path.

optionRationale.b: fileMaxSizeMb sets the size in MB at which the export file is rotated, not where it is written.
optionRationale.c: fileMaxBackups sets how many rotated export files are kept, not the log file path.
optionRationale.d: fileCompress enables compression of rotated files; it does not choose the target file.

hubble.export.static.fileMaxBackups, set to 50
hubble.export.static.filePath, set to 50
hubble.export.static.fileCompress, set to 50

explanation: The size in MB at which the Hubble export file is rotated is controlled by hubble.export.static.fileMaxSizeMb, so setting it to 50 rotates at 50 MB. The default for this value is 10.

optionRationale.b: fileMaxBackups controls how many rotated files are kept, not the size at which rotation happens.
optionRationale.c: filePath is the path of the target log file and does not take a size in MB.
optionRationale.d: fileCompress is a boolean that enables compression of rotated files, not a size threshold.

hubble.export.static.filePath

stem: A pod starts up and needs a SPIFFE identity. It contacts the local SPIRE agent over the SPIFFE workload API and describes itself. What does the SPIRE agent do next?

options.text: It issues an SVID directly to the workload without contacting any other component.
It checks that the workload is who it claims to be, then connects to the SPIRE server and attests that the identity request is valid.
It forwards the request to the Cilium operator, which forms the root of trust for the trust domain.
It asks the workload to present an existing X.509 certificate before it will accept the request.

explanation: The agent validates the workload's claim and then attests the request to the SPIRE server, which is the root of trust. The agent does not mint identities on its own authority; it requests them from the server.

optionRationale.a: The agent does not issue the identity itself — it connects to the SPIRE server and attests the request first.
optionRationale.c: The SPIRE server, not the Cilium operator, forms the root of trust for the trust domain.
optionRationale.d: The X.509 keypair arrives in the SVID that is passed back to the workload, so the workload does not present one up front.

citations.title: Cilium and SPIFFE
citations.quote: The SPIRE agent then checks that the workload is really who it says it is, and then connects to the SPIRE server and attests that the workload is requesting an identity, and that the request is valid.

stem: How does Cilium's support for SPIFFE differ from the usual SPIRE flow?

options.text: Cilium agents obtain a common SPIFFE identity and can request identities on behalf of other workloads.
Cilium replaces the SPIRE server with the Cilium operator as the root of trust.
Cilium workloads must request their identity from the SPIRE server directly, bypassing the local agent.
Cilium drops the SVID format and returns identities as plain label sets instead.

explanation: In the usual SPIRE flow the workload requests its own information from the SPIRE server. With Cilium, the Cilium agents get a common SPIFFE identity and can ask for identities on behalf of other workloads.

optionRationale.b: The SPIRE server remains the root of trust; Cilium does not replace it with the operator.
optionRationale.c: That describes the usual SPIRE flow, not Cilium's support, where agents act on behalf of workloads.
optionRationale.d: The identity is still passed back in the SVID format, which includes an X.509 TLS keypair.

citations.title: Cilium and SPIFFE
citations.quote: In Cilium's support for SPIFFE, the Cilium agents get a common SPIFFE identity and can themselves ask for identities on behalf of other workloads.

stem: A workload receives its identity from the local SPIRE agent. In what format is the identity passed back, and what does it contain?

options.text: A URI of the form spiffe://trust.domain/path, containing only the trust domain and path.
A label set matching the Cilium Security Identity, containing no cryptographic material.
An SVID, which includes a TLS keypair in the X.509 version.
A signed JWT containing the node name and the pod's labels.

explanation: Once the agent has requested an identity from the SPIRE server, it passes it back to the workload in the SVID format, and that document includes a TLS keypair in the X.509 version.

optionRationale.a: The spiffe:// URI is what a SPIFFE identity looks like, not the document handed to the workload.
optionRationale.b: A label set describes a Cilium Security Identity, but the SVID carries cryptographic material.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the SVID with an X.509 TLS keypair, not a JWT.

citations.title: Cilium and SPIFFE
citations.quote: Once the SPIRE agent has requested an identity from the SPIRE server, it passes it back to the workload in the SVID (SPIFFE Verified Identity Document) format.

stem: A dynamic flow-log entry named `test001` specifies no `fileMaxSizeMb`, `fileMaxBackups` or `fileCompress` settings. What rotation behaviour applies to it?

options.text: Rotation is disabled and the file grows without limit
The defaults are used: 10 MB maximum size, 5 backups and compression off
The settings are inherited from the previous entry in the list
The entry is rejected until all three settings are provided

explanation: File rotation is configured per flow-log entry, and if an entry omits these settings the defaults are used: `fileMaxSizeMb: 10`, `fileMaxBackups: 5` and `fileCompress: false`.

optionRationale.a: Omitting the settings does not disable rotation; documented defaults apply instead.
optionRationale.c: Each entry accepts its own settings and falls back to the defaults, not to a neighbouring entry.
optionRationale.d: The entry is not rejected; the defaults fill in the missing values.

stem: A cluster runs the Star Wars demo with no CiliumNetworkPolicy applied. You run the two commands below. What is the result?

options.text: Both commands print `Ship landed`, because no rules are enforced yet.
Only the `tiefighter` command prints `Ship landed`, because it carries the `org=empire` label.
Only the `xwing` command prints `Ship landed`, because it is the first client to connect.
Both commands are dropped, because the `deathstar` service denies all traffic until a policy is created.

explanation: With no rules enforced, the deathstar service does not restrict who may request landing, so both the xwing and the tiefighter succeed and print `Ship landed`. The label-based restriction described for the deathstar service only takes effect once rules are enforced.

optionRationale.b: The `org=empire` label is the intended restriction from the deathstar's perspective, but it is not enforced in this state, so the tiefighter is not the only successful client.
optionRationale.c: There is no first-come behaviour; both clients succeed because no rules are enforced.
optionRationale.d: Nothing denies traffic in this state — the excerpt states that since no rules are enforced, both ships will be able to request landing.

The xwing has been given the `org=empire` label.

The tiefighter's request failed and the xwing's request was retried in its place.
