stem: A cluster's Kubernetes control plane cannot be configured to allocate PodCIDRs to nodes, so the platform team enables Cilium's cluster-pool IPAM mode instead. What does each Cilium agent do on startup in this mode?

options.text: It waits until the podCIDRs range is made available via the Cilium Node object for all enabled address families.
It allocates PodCIDRs itself from the cluster CIDR and writes them back to the Kubernetes Node object.
It starts immediately and requests individual pod IPs from the Hubble Relay on demand.
It falls back to the Kubernetes host-scope allocator until a PodCIDR is assigned.

explanation: In cluster-pool IPAM mode the agent does not begin allocating until the podCIDRs range has been published for every enabled address family through the Cilium Node object. This mode exists precisely for clusters where Kubernetes cannot hand out PodCIDRs or where finer control is required.

optionRationale.b: The agent waits for the range to be provided; it does not derive PodCIDRs from the cluster CIDR and write them to the Kubernetes Node object.
optionRationale.c: The agent waits for a PodCIDR range rather than starting immediately, and pod IP allocation is not performed by Hubble Relay.
optionRationale.d: No fallback to the Kubernetes host-scope allocator is described; the agent waits for the range instead.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
In this mode, the Cilium agent will wait on startup until the ``podCIDRs`` range
are made available via the Cilium Node ``v2.CiliumNode`` object for all enabled
address families

stem: An engineer inspects a CiliumNode object in a cluster using cluster-pool IPAM and wants to confirm the PodCIDR range assigned to that node. Which field holds it?

options.text: spec.ipam.podCIDRs
spec.podCIDR
status.ipam.podCIDRs
spec.nodeCIDR

explanation: The PodCIDR range for a node is carried in the CiliumNode resource under spec.ipam.podCIDRs, which may hold an IPv4 and/or IPv6 range.

optionRationale.b: spec.podCIDR is not the field named for the CiliumNode resource; the range lives under the ipam section.
optionRationale.c: The field is part of the spec, not the status subresource.
optionRationale.d: spec.nodeCIDR is not a field described for holding the PodCIDR range.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote: ``spec.ipam.podCIDRs`` IPv4 and/or IPv6 PodCIDR range

stem: Which statement best describes the cluster-pool IPAM mode?

options.text: The Cilium agent waits on startup until the podCIDRs range is made available via the Cilium Node object for all enabled address families.
The Cilium operator assigns each pod an IP directly from the Kubernetes API server's service CIDR.
The Cilium agent allocates pod IPs only after the kubelet reports them through the Node's status.
Pod IPs are handed out by the CNI plugin from a per-node range stored in a ConfigMap.

explanation: Cluster-pool IPAM is useful when Kubernetes cannot be configured to hand out PodCIDRs or when more control is needed; the agent waits until the podCIDRs range is available through the Cilium Node object for all enabled address families.

optionRationale.b: The range is published via the Cilium Node object, not taken from the service CIDR by the operator.
optionRationale.c: The agent waits for the range in the Cilium Node object, not for kubelet reporting through Node status.
optionRationale.d: No per-node range stored in a ConfigMap is described; the range is held in the Cilium Node object.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
This is useful if Kubernetes cannot be configured to hand out PodCIDRs or if
more control is needed.

stem: An engineer installs Cilium with Helm using `--set ipam.mode=kubernetes` and `--set k8s.requireIPv4PodCIDR=true`. What is the effect of the second setting?

options.text: The Cilium agent waits until an IPv4 PodCIDR is made available via the Kubernetes node resource.
The Cilium agent allocates IPv4 pod addresses from a cluster-wide pool held in the Cilium operator.
The Cilium agent refuses to start unless the Kubernetes node already has an IPv6 PodCIDR assigned.
The Cilium agent advertises the node's IPv4 PodCIDR to other nodes using BGP.

explanation: The `k8s-require-ipv4-pod-cidr` option instructs the Cilium agent to wait until an IPv4 PodCIDR is made available via the Kubernetes node resource. The Helm equivalent is `--set k8s.requireIPv4PodCIDR=true`, which only works together with `--set ipam.mode=kubernetes`.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes waiting for a PodCIDR on the node resource, not allocating from a cluster-wide pool in the operator.
optionRationale.c: The option concerns the IPv4 PodCIDR, not the IPv6 one, and it makes the agent wait rather than refuse to start.
optionRationale.d: BGP advertisement of PodCIDRs is not mentioned; the option only governs waiting for the PodCIDR to appear.

citations.title: Configuration
citations.quote:
instructs the Cilium agent to wait until
   an IPv4 PodCIDR is made available via the Kubernetes node resource.

stem: Which Helm value enables Kubernetes IPAM mode in Cilium?

options.text: `--set ipam.mode=kubernetes`
`--set k8s.requireIPv4PodCIDR=true`
`--set ipam.kubernetes=true`
`--set k8s.requireIPv6PodCIDR=true`

explanation: The excerpt states that the ConfigMap option `ipam: kubernetes` is defined with Helm as `--set ipam.mode=kubernetes`.

optionRationale.b: This value sets the requirement for an IPv4 PodCIDR and only works with `--set ipam.mode=kubernetes`; it does not itself enable Kubernetes IPAM.
optionRationale.c: The Helm value is `ipam.mode=kubernetes`; `ipam.kubernetes` is not the form given.
optionRationale.d: This value sets the requirement for an IPv6 PodCIDR and only works with `--set ipam.mode=kubernetes`; it does not enable Kubernetes IPAM.

citations.title: Configuration
citations.quote: ``ipam: kubernetes``: ``--set ipam.mode=kubernetes``.

stem: An engineer sets `ipam: kubernetes` in the Cilium ConfigMap with `enable-ipv4` set to `true`. Which option is enabled automatically as a result?

options.text: `k8s-require-ipv4-pod-cidr`
`k8s-require-ipv6-pod-cidr`
`enable-ipv6`
`ipam: cluster-pool`

explanation: Enabling `ipam: kubernetes` automatically enables `k8s-require-ipv4-pod-cidr` if `enable-ipv4` is `true`, and `k8s-require-ipv6-pod-cidr` if `enable-ipv6` is `true`.

optionRationale.b: The IPv6 PodCIDR requirement is enabled automatically only when `enable-ipv6` is `true`, not when `enable-ipv4` is.
optionRationale.c: `enable-ipv6` is a condition that triggers the IPv6 option; it is not itself enabled by Kubernetes IPAM mode.
optionRationale.d: `cluster-pool` is not mentioned in the excerpt, and Kubernetes IPAM mode does not switch to it.

citations.title: Configuration
citations.quote:
Enabling this option will
   automatically enable ``k8s-require-ipv4-pod-cidr`` if ``enable-ipv4`` is
   ``true``

stem: A cluster runs Cilium in CRD-backed IPAM mode. An operator removes an address from spec.ipam.available on a CiliumNode while that address is still allocated to a running pod. What is the result?

options.text: The pod keeps the address, and the address will not be available for re-allocation after it is released.
The pod is immediately restarted and receives a new address from the remaining pool.
The address is returned to the pool at once and can be handed to another pod.
The Cilium agent rejects the update and restores the address in spec.ipam.available.

explanation: Removing an address that is currently allocated does not disrupt the pod using it: the address continues to be used, but once released it is not offered for re-allocation.

optionRationale.b: Nothing in the mode triggers a restart of pods when the pool shrinks; the allocated address simply stays in use.
optionRationale.c: The address is explicitly not made available for re-allocation after release, so it cannot be handed out again.
optionRationale.d: The agent updates its pool from the field; it does not reject the change or write the address back.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote: When an IP is removed that is currently allocated, the IP will continue to be used but will not be available for re-allocation after release.

stem: You enable CRD-backed IPAM. Which Kubernetes object does each Cilium agent watch in order to learn its per-node allocation pool?

options.text: The ciliumnodes.cilium.io custom resource whose name matches the node the agent runs on
A CiliumNetworkPolicy in the agent's own namespace
The CiliumNodeConfig resource for the local node
The PodCIDR field of the Kubernetes Node object

explanation: In this mode the agent watches the ciliumnodes.cilium.io custom resource named after its own Kubernetes node, and takes the pool from spec.ipam.available.

optionRationale.b: CiliumNetworkPolicy governs traffic, not IP address management.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt names only ciliumnodes.cilium.io as the resource the agent watches.
optionRationale.d: The pool comes from the custom resource, not from the Node object's PodCIDR.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
each Cilium agent will start watching for a
Kubernetes custom resource ``ciliumnodes.cilium.io`` with a name matching the
Kubernetes node on which the agent is running.

stem: In CRD-backed IPAM mode, where does the Cilium agent record the addresses it has handed out on a node?

options.text: In the status.ipam.inuse field of the CiliumNode resource
In the spec.ipam.available field of the CiliumNode resource
In an annotation on each Pod that received an address
In the CiliumEndpoint resource for each pod

explanation: Allocation is reflected by adding the address to status.ipam.inuse; spec.ipam.available is the pool the agent reads from.

optionRationale.b: spec.ipam.available is the input pool of addresses, not the record of what is in use.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the record as living on the CiliumNode resource, not on pods.
optionRationale.d: CiliumEndpoint is not mentioned as the place where in-use addresses are recorded.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
Upon allocation of an IP in the allocation pool, the IP is added to the
``status.ipam.inuse`` field.

stem: A platform team defines a CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool whose block is given in CIDR notation. They want the first and last addresses of that CIDR to be withheld from allocation. Which field must they set, and to what value?

options.text: .spec.allowFirstLastIPs set to No
.spec.allowFirstLastIPs set to Yes
.spec.blocks[].start and .spec.blocks[].stop set to the second and second-to-last addresses
.spec.reservedIPs set to the first and last addresses

explanation: LB-IPAM allocates every address in a CIDR block by default. To withhold the first and last addresses of CIDR blocks, you set .spec.allowFirstLastIPs to No. The setting has no effect on blocks defined with start and stop, and it is ignored for /32 and /31 IPv4 CIDRs and /128 and /127 IPv6 CIDRs.

optionRationale.b: Setting the field to Yes keeps the default behaviour of using all IPs in the CIDR, so nothing is reserved.
optionRationale.c: Blocks defined with start and stop are explicitly excluded from this setting, so this does not reserve the first and last IPs of a CIDR.
optionRationale.d: No such field is described; reservation is controlled by .spec.allowFirstLastIPs.

citations.title: CIDRs, Ranges and reserved IPs
citations.quote:
If you wish to reserve the first and last IPs of CIDRs, you can set the 
``.spec.allowFirstLastIPs`` field to ``No``.

stem: An engineer sets .spec.allowFirstLastIPs to No on a pool, then defines one block as 10.0.0.0/24 in CIDR notation and a second block with .spec.blocks[].start and .spec.blocks[].stop. What is the effect of the setting on the two blocks?

options.text: The first and last IPs are reserved in the CIDR block only; the start/stop block is unaffected.
The first and last IPs are reserved in both blocks.
The first and last IPs are reserved in the start/stop block only; the CIDR block is unaffected.
The setting is rejected because a pool cannot mix CIDR and start/stop blocks.

explanation: The reservation setting applies only to blocks specified with .spec.blocks[].cidr. Blocks specified with .spec.blocks[].start and .spec.blocks[].stop are not affected, and a pool may contain multiple blocks of either form.

optionRationale.b: The setting is explicitly not applied to blocks defined with start and stop.
optionRationale.c: The position is reversed: the setting applies to CIDR blocks, not to start/stop blocks.
optionRationale.d: A pool can have multiple blocks, specified either with CIDR notation or with a start and stop IP, so mixing them is not rejected.

citations.title: CIDRs, Ranges and reserved IPs
citations.quote:
This setting only applies to blocks specified with ``.spec.blocks[].cidr`` and not to
blocks specified with ``.spec.blocks[].start`` and ``.spec.blocks[].stop``.

stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy named cidr-l4-rule is applied to the cluster. A pod labelled role=crawler attempts to open a TCP connection to 192.0.2.10 on port 443. What is the result?

options.text: The connection is allowed, because the destination falls inside 192.0.2.0/24.
The connection is dropped, because the policy only permits TCP on port 80 to that CIDR.
The connection is allowed, because egress rules without a matching toPorts entry are port-agnostic.
The connection is redirected to port 80 by the policy.

explanation: The policy allows role=crawler endpoints to reach 192.0.2.0/24 only over TCP port 80. Traffic to the same CIDR on any other port is not permitted, so the connection to port 443 is dropped.

optionRationale.a: Being inside the CIDR is necessary but not sufficient; the port restriction also applies.
optionRationale.c: The rule does contain a toPorts entry restricting traffic to TCP port 80, so it is not port-agnostic.
optionRationale.d: Cilium policies allow or deny traffic; they do not rewrite the destination port.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "cidr-l4-rule"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      role: crawler
  egress:
  - toCIDR:
    - 192.0.2.0/24
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "80"
        protocol: TCP

citations.title: CIDR-dependent Layer 4 Rule
citations.quote:
endpoints with the label ``role=crawler`` will
not be able to communicate with destinations in the CIDR ``192.0.2.0/24`` on
ports other than port 80.

stem: A pod labelled role=scraper, which does not carry the label role=crawler, tries to reach 192.0.2.20 on TCP port 80. The policy cidr-l4-rule is the only policy selecting these endpoints. What happens?

options.text: The connection is allowed, because port 80 to 192.0.2.0/24 is permitted by the policy.
The connection is allowed, because the pod is not selected by the endpointSelector.
The connection is denied, because the policy does not allow endpoints without the label role=crawler to reach that CIDR.
The connection is allowed only if the pod also has an ingress policy.

explanation: The policy explicitly does not permit endpoints lacking the role=crawler label to communicate with destinations in 192.0.2.0/24, so the scraper pod's connection is denied.

optionRationale.a: The port-80 allowance applies to endpoints selected by the policy, which this pod is not.
optionRationale.b: Not being selected does not grant access; the policy states such endpoints are not allowed to reach the CIDR.
optionRationale.d: Ingress policy on the pod has no bearing on this egress destination.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "cidr-l4-rule"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      role: crawler
  egress:
  - toCIDR:
    - 192.0.2.0/24
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "80"
        protocol: TCP

citations.title: CIDR-dependent Layer 4 Rule
citations.quote:
The policy does not allow Endpoints
without the label ``role=crawler`` to communicate with destinations in the CIDR
``192.0.2.0/24``.

stem: Which endpoints does the policy cidr-l4-rule select, and what egress does it grant them?

options.text: All endpoints in the cluster, granting egress to 192.0.2.0/24 on TCP port 80.
Endpoints labelled role=crawler, granting egress to 192.0.2.0/24 on TCP port 80.
Endpoints labelled role=crawler, granting egress to any CIDR on TCP port 80.
Endpoints labelled role=crawler, granting egress to 192.0.2.0/24 on all ports.

explanation: The endpointSelector matches role=crawler, and the egress rule combines toCIDR 192.0.2.0/24 with toPorts TCP port 80, so selected endpoints may reach that CIDR only on port 80.

optionRationale.a: The endpointSelector restricts the policy to endpoints labelled role=crawler, not the whole cluster.
optionRationale.c: The toCIDR field limits destinations to 192.0.2.0/24 rather than any CIDR.
optionRationale.d: The toPorts entry restricts traffic to TCP port 80 rather than all ports.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "cidr-l4-rule"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      role: crawler
  egress:
  - toCIDR:
    - 192.0.2.0/24
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "80"
        protocol: TCP

citations.title: CIDR-dependent Layer 4 Rule
citations.quote:
This example enables all endpoints with the label ``role=crawler`` to
communicate with all remote destinations inside the CIDR ``192.0.2.0/24``, but
they must communicate using TCP on port 80.

stem: A pod on node A sends traffic to a pod on node B, and no network security policies exist in the cluster. What is the result?

options.text: The traffic is dropped until a policy explicitly allows it.
The traffic is allowed, because in the absence of any network security policies all Pods can reach each other.
The traffic is allowed only if both pods share the same identity.
The traffic is masqueraded as it leaves node A, because the destination pod is outside the cluster.

explanation: Cilium does not block pod-to-pod traffic by default. Only once network security policies are in place does reachability become restricted, so with no policies at all every pod can reach every other pod.

optionRationale.a: This describes default-deny, which applies only once policies are in place; the excerpt states the opposite for the no-policy case.
optionRationale.c: Identity is not a precondition for connectivity here; the excerpt says all Pods can reach each other in the absence of policies.
optionRationale.d: Masquerading applies to traffic leaving the cluster as a client, not to pod-to-pod traffic between nodes.

citations.title: Pod-to-Pod Connectivity
citations.quote:
In the absence of any
network security policies, all Pods can reach each other.

stem: A pod running on a particular Linux node is created and receives its IP address. Where does that address come from?

options.text: From the prefix of the Linux node running the Pod.
From a cluster-wide pool shared by all nodes.
From the Kubernetes Service CIDR.
From the pod's own container runtime configuration, independent of the node.

explanation: With Cilium, each Pod gets an IP address from the node prefix of the Linux node running the Pod, so address allocation is tied to the node rather than to a cluster-wide pool.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt ties the address to the node prefix, not to a pool shared across the cluster.
optionRationale.c: The Service CIDR is not mentioned; the address comes from the node prefix.
optionRationale.d: Allocation is described as coming from the node prefix, not from the container runtime independently of the node.

citations.title: Pod-to-Pod Connectivity
citations.quote:
each Pod gets an IP address from the node prefix of the Linux node running the
Pod.

stem: A pod acts as a client and connects to a service that is outside the Kubernetes cluster. What happens to the traffic as it leaves the node?

options.text: It is dropped because the destination is not a known pod.
It is automatically masqueraded as it leaves the node.
It is routed without modification, since pod IPs are globally routable.
It is encapsulated to the destination service's node.

explanation: Pod IP addresses are typically local to the Kubernetes cluster, so when pods reach services outside the cluster as a client, the traffic is automatically masqueraded as it leaves the node.

optionRationale.a: Nothing in the excerpt drops such traffic; it is masqueraded instead.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states pod IPs are typically local to the cluster, and the traffic is masqueraded rather than left unmodified.
optionRationale.d: Encapsulation to a destination node is not described; the traffic is masqueraded as it leaves the node.

citations.title: Pod-to-Pod Connectivity
citations.quote:
If pods need to
reach services outside the cluster as a client, the network traffic is
automatically masqueraded as it leaves the node.

stem: A cluster runs Cilium on Azure. Which component derives the Azure instance ID for a node and records it in the node's CiliumNode resource?

options.text: The Cilium agent on that node, from the Kubernetes Node's .Spec.ProviderID field
The Cilium operator, from the Azure subscription's virtual machine scale set inventory
The Cilium CNI plugin, from the pod sandbox annotations written by the kubelet
Hubble Relay, from the flow metadata of the node's first pod

explanation: The agent on each node reads the Kubernetes v1.Node resource, extracts .Spec.ProviderID and uses it to derive the Azure instance ID. The operator's role begins afterwards, when it watches the CiliumNode resources and manages IPAM.

optionRationale.b: The operator watches ciliumnodes.cilium.io resources and manages allocation; it is the agent that derives the instance ID from the Node resource.
optionRationale.c: The CNI plugin is not described as deriving the Azure instance ID; the agent does so from .Spec.ProviderID.
optionRationale.d: Hubble Relay is an observability component and plays no part in deriving node identity for IPAM.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
The Cilium agent running on
each node will retrieve the Kubernetes ``v1.Node`` resource and extract the
``.Spec.ProviderID`` field in order to derive the `Azure instance ID

stem: On an Azure cluster, the Cilium operator has just discovered existing interfaces with associated IPs on an instance. Where does it publish those addresses so that the agent on the node can use them?

options.text: In the spec.ipam.available field of the node's CiliumNode resource
In the status.ipam.used field of the node's CiliumNode resource
In the .Spec.ProviderID field of the Kubernetes Node resource
In the agent configuration option for Azure allocation parameters

explanation: The operator scans Azure instances for existing interfaces with associated IPs and makes them available through spec.ipam.available. The status.ipam.used field is where it monitors addresses already in use, not where it publishes newly discovered ones.

optionRationale.b: status.ipam.used is monitored by the operator to track addresses in use; discovered addresses are published in spec.ipam.available.
optionRationale.c: .Spec.ProviderID is read by the agent to derive the Azure instance ID; it does not carry IP addresses.
optionRationale.d: Azure allocation parameters are agent configuration passed into the custom resource; they are not the field holding discovered IPs.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
It scans the Azure instances
for existing interfaces with associated IPs and makes them available via the
``spec.ipam.available`` field.

stem: An engineer notices that the Cilium operator keeps allocating additional IP addresses on an Azure node even though pods are not currently being created there. What explains this behaviour?

options.text: The operator allocates more IPs as needed to meet the IP pre-allocation watermark, so that IPs are always available
The operator allocates one IP per CiliumNode resource created on the node, regardless of demand
The agent requests a new IP each time it reads the .Spec.ProviderID field of the Node resource
The operator re-allocates every address listed in status.ipam.used on each reconciliation loop

explanation: The operator constantly monitors used addresses in status.ipam.used and allocates more IPs as needed to meet the IP pre-allocation watermark, which is what keeps a pool of addresses ready ahead of demand.

optionRationale.b: The number of CiliumNode resources is not what drives allocation; the pre-allocation watermark does.
optionRationale.c: Reading .Spec.ProviderID is how the agent derives the Azure instance ID at startup, not a trigger for IP allocation.
optionRationale.d: status.ipam.used is monitored to see which addresses are in use; the operator does not re-allocate them each loop.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
It will then constantly monitor the used IP
addresses in the ``status.ipam.used`` field and allocate more IPs as needed to
meet the IP pre-allocation watermark.

stem: A cluster administrator wants to change the kvstore endpoint and credentials that the cilium-agent on every node uses. Which Kubernetes resource in a standard Cilium deployment holds these common configuration values?

options.text: The ConfigMap
The DaemonSet
The Secret
The ClusterRole

explanation: The ConfigMap describes common configuration values passed to the cilium-agent, and the excerpt gives the kvstore endpoint and credentials as an example of such values. The DaemonSet describes the Cilium pod and the agent's command-line options, the Secret holds the credentials used to access the etcd kvstore, and the ClusterRole carries permissions for the Kubernetes API server.

optionRationale.b: The DaemonSet describes the Cilium pod deployed to each node, including the image tag and the command-line options passed to the cilium-agent, not the common configuration values.
optionRationale.c: The Secret describes the credentials used to access the etcd kvstore, but the common configuration values such as the kvstore endpoint are described by the ConfigMap.
optionRationale.d: The ClusterRole is part of the identity and permissions used by cilium-agent to access the Kubernetes API server when RBAC is enabled.

citations.title: Deployment
citations.quote:
A ``ConfigMap`` resource:  describes common configuration values that are
  passed to the cilium-agent, such as the kvstore endpoint and credentials,
  enabling/disabling debug mode, etc.

stem: An engineer needs to confirm which exact version of the Cilium docker container will run on each node, and which command-line options are passed to the cilium-agent. Which resource should they inspect?

options.text: The DaemonSet
The ConfigMap
The ServiceAccount
The Secret

explanation: The DaemonSet describes the Cilium pod deployed to each Kubernetes node, and its configuration includes the image tag indicating the exact version of the Cilium docker container and the command-line options passed to the cilium-agent. The other resources carry configuration values, identity and permissions, or kvstore credentials.

optionRationale.b: The ConfigMap carries common configuration values passed to the cilium-agent, not the image tag or the agent's command-line options.
optionRationale.c: The ServiceAccount is part of the identity used by cilium-agent to access the Kubernetes API server when RBAC is enabled.
optionRationale.d: The Secret describes the credentials used to access the etcd kvstore, if required.

citations.title: Deployment
citations.quote:
The
  configuration of this DaemonSet includes the image tag indicating the exact
  version of the Cilium docker container (e.g., v1.0.0) and command-line
  options passed to the cilium-agent.

stem: Kubernetes RBAC is enabled in a cluster running a standard Cilium deployment. The cilium-agent must authenticate to and be authorised by the Kubernetes API server. Which set of resources provides the identity and permissions for this?

options.text: ServiceAccount, ClusterRole, and ClusterRoleBindings
The DaemonSet and its ConfigMap
The Secret holding the etcd kvstore credentials
The ConfigMap holding the kvstore endpoint

explanation: The ServiceAccount, ClusterRole, and ClusterRoleBindings resources provide the identity and permissions used by cilium-agent to access the Kubernetes API server when Kubernetes RBAC is enabled. The Secret and ConfigMap relate to the etcd kvstore, and the DaemonSet describes the Cilium pod itself.

optionRationale.b: The DaemonSet describes the Cilium pod and the ConfigMap carries common configuration values; neither provides the RBAC identity and permissions for the API server.
optionRationale.c: The Secret describes the credentials used to access the etcd kvstore, if required, not the identity and permissions for the Kubernetes API server.
optionRationale.d: The ConfigMap describes common configuration values such as the kvstore endpoint, not the identity and permissions used to access the Kubernetes API server.

citations.title: Deployment
citations.quote:
``ServiceAccount``, ``ClusterRole``, and ``ClusterRoleBindings`` resources:
  the identity and permissions used by cilium-agent to access the Kubernetes
  API server when Kubernetes RBAC is enabled.

stem: A platform team wants every Cilium-managed endpoint in the cluster to be able to reach kube-dns on port 53/UDP, without listing each client workload. Which manifest achieves this?

options.text: A CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy whose endpointSelector matches the kube-dns pods and whose ingress rule uses an empty fromEndpoints entry with toPorts port "53" protocol UDP.
A CiliumNetworkPolicy in the kube-system namespace whose endpointSelector matches the kube-dns pods and whose egress rule uses an empty toEndpoints entry with toPorts port "53" protocol UDP.
A CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy whose endpointSelector matches all endpoints in the cluster and whose egress rule allows port "53" protocol UDP to any destination.
A CiliumNetworkPolicy in each application namespace whose endpointSelector matches the client pods and whose ingress rule allows port "53" protocol UDP.

explanation: The example is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that selects the kube-dns pods in kube-system and permits ingress to them from any endpoint, because the fromEndpoints list contains an empty selector. The port is restricted to 53/UDP.

optionRationale.b: The policy selects kube-dns and must describe traffic arriving at kube-dns, so the rule belongs under ingress, not egress; a namespaced policy also would not cover the whole cluster.
optionRationale.c: Selecting all endpoints and allowing egress to any destination is the opposite direction and does not restrict traffic to kube-dns on port 53/UDP.
optionRationale.d: A per-namespace policy selecting clients with an ingress rule does not match the kube-dns pods and does not scale to all Cilium-managed endpoints.

citations.title: Allow All Cilium Managed Endpoints To Communicate With Kube-dns
citations.quote:
The following example allows all Cilium managed endpoints in the cluster to communicate
with kube-dns on port 53/UDP in the ``kube-system`` namespace.

stem: After the policy below is applied, a pod in the default namespace resolves names through kube-dns successfully, but a pod in kube-system that is not labelled k8s-app=kube-dns cannot reach kube-dns on port 53/UDP. What explains this?

options.text: The endpointSelector selects only endpoints with both k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system and k8s-app: kube-dns, so the policy governs traffic to the kube-dns pods rather than to every pod in kube-system.
The empty fromEndpoints entry matches only endpoints in the same namespace as the selected pods, so pods outside kube-system are excluded.
The policy is cluster-wide, so it overrides any other policy and blocks all traffic that is not explicitly listed, including DNS from other kube-system pods.
The toPorts entry restricts traffic to UDP only, so any pod using TCP for DNS is denied.

explanation: The endpointSelector uses matchLabels with the kube-system namespace and the k8s-app: kube-dns label, so the policy applies to the kube-dns endpoints. The empty fromEndpoints entry allows all Cilium-managed endpoints to reach those selected pods on 53/UDP; it does not grant or govern traffic to unrelated pods in kube-system.

optionRationale.b: An empty fromEndpoints entry is not limited to the selected pods' namespace; it allows all Cilium-managed endpoints in the cluster.

stem: A team applies the Gateway and HTTPRoute below. Requests to /echo are sent to two Services, echo-1 on port 8080 and echo-2 on port 8090. How is traffic distributed between them?

options.text: Evenly, 50/50, because both backendRefs carry a weight of 50.
All traffic goes to echo-1, because it is listed first and weights are ignored for Services.
All traffic goes to echo-2, because port 8090 is not the listener port of 80.
Traffic is split by path prefix, with /echo going to echo-1 and any other path to echo-2.

explanation: The HTTPRoute lists two backendRefs, echo-1 on port 8080 and echo-2 on port 8090, each with weight 50. The weights are equal, so the split between the two Services is even at 50/50.

optionRationale.b: The order of backendRefs does not determine routing here; the weights of 50 and 50 produce an even split rather than sending everything to the first Service.
optionRationale.c: The backend Service ports (8080 and 8090) are independent of the Gateway listener port of 80, and echo-2 receives its weighted share of traffic.
optionRationale.d: The route has a single match on the /echo path prefix with both Services as backends; it does not route different paths to different Services.

---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: cilium-gw
spec:
  gatewayClassName: cilium
  listeners:
  - protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    name: web-gw-echo
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: example-route-1
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: cilium-gw
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /echo
    backendRefs:
    - kind: Service
      name: echo-1
      port: 8080
      weight: 50
    - kind: Service
      name: echo-2
      port: 8090
      weight: 50

stem: A team wants pods running under the service account "luke" to be able to issue HTTP GET /public requests on TCP port 80 to pods associated with the service account "leia". Which label does the policy use in its endpointSelector to select the destination pods?

options.text: io.cilium.k8s.policy.serviceaccount: leia
io.cilium.k8s.policy.serviceaccount: luke
app.kubernetes.io/name: leia
io.cilium.k8s.policy.serviceaccount: public

explanation: The endpointSelector determines which pods the policy applies to, and in this example it matches the service account label of the destination, "leia". The "luke" service account appears in fromEndpoints, which selects the sources allowed to reach those pods.

optionRationale.b: "luke" is the source service account, used in fromEndpoints, not in the endpointSelector.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt uses the io.cilium.k8s.policy.serviceaccount label, not an app.kubernetes.io/name label.
optionRationale.d: "public" is part of the HTTP path, not a service account label value.

stem: A platform team applies a CiliumNetworkPolicy directly with kubectl into the namespace `payments`. The policy's endpointSelector matches `app=ledger` and its rule contains no namespace selector. Which pods does the rule apply to?

options.text: Only pods labelled `app=ledger` in the `payments` namespace.
Pods labelled `app=ledger` in every namespace of the cluster.
All pods in the `payments` namespace, regardless of their labels.
No pods, because a namespace selector is mandatory for imported policies.

explanation: Policies imported directly with the API apply to all namespaces unless a namespace selector is specified. The absence of a namespace selector therefore widens the rule to matching pods cluster-wide, not just the namespace the object was created in.

optionRationale.a: This assumes the creating namespace confines the rule, but the policy applies to all namespaces unless a namespace selector is specified.
optionRationale.c: The endpointSelector still restricts the rule to pods labelled `app=ledger`; the namespace selector is what is missing, not the label selector.
optionRationale.d: A namespace selector is optional; without one the policy simply applies to all namespaces.

stem: A platform team applies the two policies below, one in ns1 and one in ns2. A pod in ns1 then sends traffic to a pod in ns2. What is the result?

options.text: The traffic is allowed, because the empty matchLabels selector matches every endpoint in the cluster.
The traffic is dropped, because the destination pod in ns2 only accepts traffic from endpoints in ns2.
The traffic is allowed, because the policy in ns1 has no egress section and therefore does not restrict egress.
The traffic is dropped, because the policy in ns1 has no egress section and therefore denies all egress by default.

explanation: Each policy selects all pods in its own namespace and allows ingress only from endpoints carrying the same (empty) label set, which in practice means endpoints in the same namespace. The destination pod in ns2 is therefore not permitted to receive traffic from a pod in ns1, so the connection is dropped. Note that the ns1 policy does not restrict egress at all, so the drop is enforced at the destination side.

optionRationale.a: The empty selector is evaluated within the policy's namespace context, not cluster-wide; the excerpt states that both source and destination have to be in the same namespace.
optionRationale.c: It is true that the ns1 policy does not restrict egress, but that does not make the connection succeed, because the ns2 policy still blocks ingress from ns1.
optionRationale.d: A policy with no egress section does not deny egress; the excerpt says pods can still communicate egress to anywhere unless the destination is in ns1 or ns2.
